Then he asked the younger son the same question. But the boy remained silent and stood with eyes cast down. No word escaped his lips. The father was pleased and said to him: âMy child, you have understood a little of Brahman. What It is cannot be expressed in words.â

âMen often think they have understood Brahman fully. Once an ant went to a hill of sugar. One grain filled its stomach. Taking another grain in its mouth it started homeward. On its way it thought, âNext time I shall carry home the whole hill.â That is the way shallow minds think. They donât know that Brahman is beyond oneâs words and thought. However great a man may be, how much can he know of Brahman? Åukadeva and sages like him may have been big ants; but even they could carry at the utmost eight or ten grains of sugar!

âAs for what has been said in the Vedas and the PurÄnas, do you know what it is like? Suppose a man has seen the ocean, and somebody asks him, âWell, what is the ocean like?â The first man opens his mouth as wide as he can and says: âWhat a sight! What tremendous waves and sounds!â The description of Brahman in the sacred books is like that. It is said in the Vedas that Brahman is of the nature of BlissâIt is SatchidÄnanda.

âÅuka and other sages stood on the shore of this Ocean of Brahman and saw and touched the water. According to one school of thought they never plunged into it. Those who do, cannot come back to the world again.

âIn samÄdhi one attains the Knowledge of Brahmanâone realizes Brahman. In that state reasoning stops altogether, and man becomes mute. He has no power to describe the nature of Brahman.

âOnce a salt doll went to measure the depth of the ocean. (All laugh.) It wanted to tell others how deep the water was. But this it could never do, for no sooner did it get into the water than it melted. Now who was there to report the oceanâs depth?â

A DEVOTEE: âSuppose a man has obtained the Knowledge of Brahman in samÄdhi. Doesnât he speak any more?â

MASTER: âÅankarÄchÄrya2 retained the âego of Knowledgeâ in order to teach others. After the vision of Brahman a man becomes silent. He reasons about It as long as he has not realized It. If you heat butter in a pan on the stove, it makes a sizzling sound as long as the water it contains has not dried up. But when no trace of water is left the clarified butter makes no sound. If you put an uncooked cake of flour in that butter it sizzles again. But after the cake is cooked all sound stops. Just so, a man established in samÄdhi comes down to the relative plane of consciousness in order to teach others, and then he talks about God.

âThe bee buzzes as long as it is not sitting on a flower. It becomes silent when it begins to sip the honey. But sometimes, intoxicated with the honey, it buzzes again.

âAn empty pitcher makes a gurgling sound when it is dipped in water. When it fills up it becomes silent. (All laugh.) But if the water is poured from it into another pitcher, then you will hear the sound again. (Laughter.)

âThe rishis of old attained the Knowledge of Brahman. One cannot have this so long as there is the slightest trace of worldliness. How hard the rishis laboured! Early in the morning they would go away from the hermitage, and would spend the whole day in solitude, meditating on Brahman. At night they would return to the hermitage and eat a little fruit or roots. They kept their minds aloof from the objects of sight, hearing, touch, and other things of a worldly nature. Only thus did they realize Brahman as their own inner consciousness.

âBut in the Kaliyuga, man, being totally dependent on food for life, cannot altogether shake off the idea that he is the body. In this state of mind it is not proper for him to say, âI am He.â When a man does all sorts of worldly things, he should not say, âI am Brahman.â Those who cannot give up attachment to worldly things, and who find no means to shake off the feeling of âIâ, should rather cherish the idea, âI am Godâs servant; I am His devotee.â One can also realize God by following the path of devotion.

âThe jnÄni gives up his identification with worldly things, discriminating, âNot this, not thisâ. Only then can he realize Brahman. It is like reaching the roof of a house by leaving the steps behind, one by one. But the vijnÄni, who is more intimately acquainted with Brahman, realizes something more. He realizes that the steps are made of the same materials as the roof: bricks, lime, and brick-dust. That which is realized intuitively as Brahman, through the eliminating process of âNot this, not thisâ, is then found to have become the universe and all its living beings. The vijnÄni sees that the Reality which is nirguna, without attributes, is also saguna, with attributes.

âA man cannot live on the roof a long time. He comes down again. Those who realize Brahman in samÄdhi come down also and find that it is Brahman that has become the universe and its living beings. In the musical scale there are the notes sÄ, re, gÄ, mÄ, pÄ, dhÄ, and ni; but one cannot keep oneâs voice on âniâ a long time. The ego does not vanish altogether. The man coming down from samÄdhi perceives that it is Brahman that has become the ego, the universe, and all living beings. This is known as vijnÄna.

âThe path of knowledge leads to Truth, as does the path that combines knowledge and love. The path of love, too, leads to this goal. The way of love is as true as the way of knowledge. All paths ultimately lead to the same Truth. But as long as God keeps the feeling of ego in us, it is easier to follow the path of love.

âThe vijnÄni sees that Brahman is immovable and actionless, like Mount Sumeru. This universe consists of the three gunasâsattva, rajas, and tamas. They are in Brahman. But Brahman is unattached.

âThe vijnÄni further sees that what is Brahman is the BhagavÄn, the Personal God. He who is beyond the three gunas is the BhagavÄn, with His six supernatural powers. Living beings, the universe, mind, intelligence, love, renunciation, knowledgeâall these are the manifestations of His power. (With a laugh) If an aristocrat has neither house nor property, or if he has been forced to sell them, one doesnât call him an aristocrat any more. (All laugh.) God is endowed with the six supernatural powers. If He were not, who would obey Him? (All laugh.)

âJust see how picturesque this universe is! How many things there are! The sun, moon, and stars; and how many varieties of living beings!âbig and small, good and bad, strong and weakâsome endowed with more power, some with less.â

VIDYÄSÄGAR: âHas He endowed some with more power and others with less?â

MASTER: âAs the All-pervading Spirit He exists in all beings, even in the ant. But the manifestations of His Power are different in different beings; otherwise, how can one person put ten to flight, while another canât face even one? And why do all people respect you? Have you grown a pair of horns? (Laughter.) You have more compassion and learning. Therefore people honour you and come to pay you their respects. Donât you agree with me?â

VidyÄsÄgar smiled.

The Master continued: âThere is nothing in mere scholarship. The object of study is to find means of knowing God and realizing Him. A holy man had a book. When asked what it contained, he opened it and showed that on all the pages were written the words âOm RÄmaâ, and nothing else.

âWhat is the significance of the GÄ«tÄ? It is what you find by repeating the word ten times. It is then reversed into âtÄgiâ, which means a person who has renounced everything for God. And the lesson of the GÄ«tÄ is: âO man, renounce everything and seek God alone.â Whether a man is a monk or a householder, he has to shake off all attachment from his mind.

âChaitanyadeva set out on a pilgrimage to southern India. One day he saw a man reading the GÄ«tÄ. Another man, seated at a distance, was listening and weeping. His eyes were swimming in tears. Chaitanyadeva asked him, âDo you understand all this?â The man said, âNo, revered sir, I donât understand a word of the text.â âThen why are you crying?â asked Chaitanya. The devotee said: âI see Arjunaâs chariot before me. I see Lord Krishna and Arjuna seated in front of it, talking. I see this and I weep.â

âWhy does a vijnÄni keep an attitude of love toward God? The answer is that âI-consciousnessâ persists. It disappears in the state of samÄdhi, no doubt, but it comes back. In the case of ordinary people the âIâ never disappears. You may cut down the aÅwattha tree, but the next day sprouts shoot up. (All laugh.)

âEven after the attainment of Knowledge this âI-consciousnessâ comes up, nobody knows from where. You dream of a tiger. Then you awake; but your heart keeps on palpitating! All our suffering is due to this âIâ. The cow cries, âHÄmbÄ!â, which means âIâ. That is why it suffers so much. It is yoked to the plough and made to work in rain and sun. Then it may be killed by the butcher. From its hide shoes are made, and also drums, which are mercilessly beaten. (Laughter.) Still it does not escape suffering. At last strings are made out of its entrails for the bows used in carding cotton. Then it no longer says, âHÄmbÄ! HÄmbÄ!â, âI! I!â, but âTuhu! Tuhu!â, âThou! Thou!â Only then are its troubles over. O Lord, I am the servant; Thou art the Master. I am the child; Thou art the Mother.

âOnce RÄma asked HanumÄn, âHow do you look on Me?â And HanumÄn replied: âO RÄma, as long as I have the feeling of âIâ, I see that Thou art the whole and I am a part; Thou art the Master and I am Thy servant. But when, O RÄma, I have the knowledge of Truth, then I realize that Thou art I, and I am Thou.â

âThe relationship of master and servant is the proper one. Since this âIâ must remain, let the rascal be Godâs servant.

âÂ âIâ and âmineââthese constitute ignorance. âMy houseâ, âmy wealthâ, âmy learningâ, âmy possessionsââthe attitude that prompts one to say such things comes of ignorance. On the contrary, the attitude born of Knowledge is: âO God, Thou art the Master, and all these things belong to Thee. House, family, children, attendants, friends, are Thine.â

âOne should constantly remember death. Nothing will survive death. We are born into this world to perform certain duties, like the people who come from the countryside to Calcutta on business. If a visitor goes to a rich manâs garden, the superintendent says to him, âThis is our gardenâ, âThis is our lakeâ, and so forth. But if the superintendent is dismissed for some misdeed, he canât carry away even his mango-wood chest. He sends it secretly by the gate-keeper. (Laughter.)

âGod laughs on two occasions. He laughs when the physician says to the patientâs mother, âDonât be afraid, mother; I shall certainly cure your boy.â God laughs, saying to Himself, âI am going to take his life, and this man says he will save it!â The physician thinks he is the master, forgetting that God is the Master. God laughs again when two brothers divide their land with a string, saying to each other, âThis side is mine and that side is yours.â He laughs and says to Himself, âThe whole universe belongs to Me, but they say they own this portion or that portion.â

âCan one know God through reasoning? Be His servant, surrender yourself to Him, and then pray to Him.

(To VidyÄsÄgar, with a smile) âWell, what is your attitude?â

VIDYÄSÄGAR (smiling): âSome day I shall confide it to you.â (All laugh.)

MASTER (laughing): âGod cannot be realized through mere scholarly reasoning.â

Intoxicated with divine love, the Master sang:

Who is there that can understand what Mother KÄli is?

Even the six darÅanas are powerless to reveal Her.

It is She, the scriptures say, that is the Inner Self

Of the yogi, who in Self discovers all his joy;

She that, of Her own sweet will, inhabits every living thing.

The macrocosm and microcosm rest in the Motherâs womb;

Now do you see how vast it is? In the MulÄdhÄra

The yogi meditates on Her, and in the SahasrÄra:

Who but Åiva has beheld Her as She really is?

Within the lotus wilderness She sports beside Her Mate, the Swan.3

When man aspires to understand Her, RÄmprasÄd must smile;

To think of knowing Her, he says, is quite as laughable

As to imagine one can swim across the boundless sea.

But while my mind has understood, alas! my heart has not;

Though but a dwarf, it still would strive to make a captive of the moon.

Continuing, the Master said: âDid you notice?

The macrocosm and microcosm rest in the Motherâs womb;

Now do you see how vast it is?

âAgain, the poet says:

Even the six darÅanas are powerless to reveal Her.

She cannot be realized by means of mere scholarship.

âOne must have faith and love. Let me tell you how powerful faith is. A man was about to cross the sea from Ceylon to India. Vibhishana said to him: âTie this thing in a corner of your wearing-cloth, and you will cross the sea safely. You will be able to walk on the water. But be sure not to examine it, or you will sink.â The man was walking easily on the water of the seaâsuch is the strength of faithâwhen, having gone part of the way, he thought, âWhat is this wonderful thing Vibhishana has given me, that I can walk even on the water?â He untied the knot and found only a leaf with the name of RÄma written on it. âOh, just this!â he thought, and instantly he sank.

âThere is a popular saying that HanumÄn jumped over the sea through his faith in RÄmaâs name, but RÄma Himself had to build a bridge

âIf a man has faith in God, then he need not be afraid though he may have committed sinânay, the vilest sin.â

Then Sri Ramakrishna sang a song glorifying the power of faith:

If only I can pass away repeating DurgÄâs name,

How canst Thou then, O Blessed One,

Withhold from me deliverance,

Wretched though I may be? aâ¦

The Master continued: âFaith and devotion. One realizes God easily through devotion. He is grasped through ecstasy of love.â

With these words the Master sang again:

How are you trying, O my mind, to know the nature of God?

You are groping like a madman locked in a dark room.

He is grasped through ecstatic love; how can you fathom Him without it?

Only through affirmation, never negation, can you know Him;

Neither through Veda nor through Tantra nor the six darÅanas.

It is in loveâs elixir only that He delights, O mind;

He dwells in the bodyâs inmost depths, in Everlasting Joy.

And, for that love, the mighty yogis practise yoga from age to age;

When love awakes, the Lord, like a magnet, draws to Him the soul.

He it is, says RÄmprasÄd, that I approach as Mother;

But must I give away the secret, here in the market-place?

From the hints I have given, O mind, guess what that Being is!

While singing, the Master went into samÄdhi. He was seated on the bench, facing west, the palms of his hands joined together, his body erect and motionless. Everyone watched him expectantly. VidyÄsÄgar, too, was speechless and could not take his eyes from the Master.

After a time Sri Ramakrishna showed signs of regaining the normal state. He drew a deep breath and said with a smile: âThe means of realizing God are ecstasy of love and devotionâthat is, one must love God. He who is Brahman is addressed as the Mother.

He it is, says RÄmprasÄd, that I approach as Mother;

But must I give away the secret, here in the market-place?

From the hints I have given, O mind, guess what that Being is!

âRÄmprasÄd asks the mind only to guess the nature of God. He wishes it to understand that what is called Brahman in the Vedas is addressed by him as the Mother. He who is attributeless also has attributes. He who is Brahman is also Åakti. When thought of as inactive, He is called Brahman, and when thought of as the Creator, Preserver, and Destroyer, He is called the Primordial Energy, KÄli.

âBrahman and Åakti are identical, like fire and its power to burn. When we talk of fire we automatically mean also its power to burn. Again, the fireâs power to burn implies the fire itself. If you accept the one you must accept the other.

âBrahman alone is addressed as the Mother. This is because a mother is an object of great love. One is able to realize God just through love. Ecstasy of feeling, devotion, love, and faithâthese are the means. Listen to a song:

As is a manâs meditation, so is his feeling of love;

As is a manâs feeling of love, so is his gain;

And faith is the root of all.

If in the Nectar Lake of Mother KÄliâs feet

My mind remains immersed,

Of little use are worship, oblations, or sacrifice.

âWhat is needed is absorption in Godâloving Him intensely. The âNectar Lakeâ is the Lake of Immortality. A man sinking in It does not die, but becomes immortal. Some people believe that by thinking of God too much the mind becomes deranged; but that is not true. God is the Lake of Nectar, the Ocean of Immortality. He is called the âImmortalâ in the Vedas. Sinking in It, one does not die, but verily transcends death.

Of little use are worship, oblations, or sacrifice.

If a man comes to love God, he need not trouble himself much about these activities. One needs a fan only as long as there is no breeze. The fan may be laid aside if the southern breeze blows. Then what need is there of a fan?

(To VidyÄsÄgar) âThe activities that you are engaged in are good. It is very good if you can perform them in a selfless spirit, renouncing egotism, giving up the idea that you are the doer. Through such action one develops love and devotion to God, and ultimately realizes Him.

âThe more you come to love God, the less you will be inclined to perform action. When the daughter-in-law is with child, her mother-in-law gives her less work to do. As time goes by she is given less and less work. When the time of delivery nears, she is not allowed to do any work at all, lest it should hurt the child or cause difficulty at the time of birth.

âBy these philanthropic activities you are really doing good to yourself. If you can do them disinterestedly, your mind will become pure and you will develop love of God. As soon as you have that love you will realize Him.

âMan cannot really help the world. God alone does thatâHe who has created the sun and the moon, who has put love for their children in parentsâ hearts, endowed noble souls with compassion, and holy men and devotees with divine love. The man who works for others, without any selfish motive, really does good to himself.

âThere is gold buried in your heart, but you are not yet aware of it. It is covered with a thin layer of clay. Once you are aware of it, all these activities of yours will lessen. After the birth of her child, the daughter-in-law in the family busies herself with it alone. Everything she does is only for the child. Her mother-in-law doesnât let her do any household duties.

âGo forward. A wood-cutter once entered a forest to gather wood. A brahmachÄri said to him, âGo forward.â He obeyed the injunction and discovered some sandal-wood trees. After a few days he reflected, âThe holy man asked me to go forward. He didnât tell me to stop here.â So he went forward and found a silver-mine. After a few days he went still farther and discovered a gold-mine, and next, mines of diamonds and precious stones. With these he became immensely rich.

âThrough selfless work, love of God grows in the heart. Then, through His grace, one realizes Him in course of time. God can be seen. One can talk to Him as I am talking to you.â

In silent wonder they all sat listening to the Masterâs words. It seemed to them that the Goddess of Wisdom Herself, seated on Sri Ramakrishnaâs tongue, was addressing these words not merely to VidyÄsÄgar, but to all humanity for its good.

It was nearly nine oâclock in the evening. The Master was about to leave.

MASTER (to VidyÄsÄgar, with a smile): âThe words I have spoken are really superfluous. You know all this; you simply arenât conscious of it. There are countless gems in the coffers of Varuna. But he himself isnât aware of them.â

VIDYÄSÄGAR (with a smile): âYou may say as you like.â

MASTER (smiling): âOh, yes. There are many wealthy people who donât know the names of all their servants, and are even unaware of many of the precious things in their houses.â (All laugh.)

Everybody was delighted with the Masterâs conversation. Again addressing VidyÄsÄgar, he said with a smile: âPlease visit the temple garden some timeâI mean the garden of Rasmani. Itâs a charming place.â

VIDYÄSÄGAR: âOh, of course I shall go. You have so kindly come here to see me, and shall I not return your visit?â

MASTER: âVisit me? Oh, never think of such a thing!â

VIDYÄSÄGAR: âWhy, sir? Why do you say that? May I ask you to explain?â

MASTER (smiling): âYou see, we are like small fishing-boats. (All smile.) We can ply in small canals and shallow waters and also in big rivers. But you are a ship. You may run aground on the way!â (All laugh.)

VidyÄsÄgar remained silent. Sri Ramakrishna said with a laugh, âBut even a ship can go there at this season.â

VIDYÄSÄGAR (smiling): âYes, this is the monsoon season.â (All laugh.)

M. said to himself: âThis is indeed the monsoon season of newly awakened love. At such times one doesnât care for prestige or formalities.â

Sri Ramakrishna then took leave of VidyÄsÄgar, who with his friends escorted the Master to the main gate, leading the way with a lighted candle in his hand. Before leaving the room, the Master prayed for the familyâs welfare, going into an ecstatic mood as he did so.

As soon as the Master and the devotees reached the gate, they saw an unexpected sight and stood still. In front of them was a bearded gentleman of fair complexion, aged about thirty-six. He wore his clothes like a Bengali, but on his head was a white turban tied after the fashion of the Åikhs. No sooner did he see the Master than he fell prostrate before him, turban and all.

When he stood up the Master said: âWho is this? Balaram? Why so late in the evening?â

BALARAM: âI have been waiting here a long time, sir.â

MASTER: âWhy didnât you come in?â

BALARAM: âAll were listening to you. I didnât like to disturb you.â

The Master got into the carriage with his companions.

VIDYÄSÄGAR (to M., softly): âShall I pay the carriage hire?â

M: âOh, donât bother, please. It is taken care of.â

VidyÄsÄgar and his friends bowed to Sri Ramakrishna, and the carriage started for Dakshineswar. But the little group, with the venerable VidyÄsÄgar at their head holding the lighted candle, stood at the gate and gazed after the Master until he was out of sight.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# ADVICE TO HOUSEHOLDERS

August 13, 1882

THE MASTER WAS CONVERSING with Kedar and some other devotees in his room in the temple garden. Kedar was a government official and had spent several years at Dacca, in East Bengal, where he had become a friend of Vijay Goswami. The two would spend a great part of their time together, talking about Sri Ramakrishna and his spiritual experiences. Kedar had once been a member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj. He followed the path of bhakti. Spiritual talk always brought tears to his eyes.

It was five oâclock in the afternoon. Kedar was very happy that day, having arranged a religious festival for Sri Ramakrishna. A singer had been hired by Ram, and the whole day passed in joy.

The Master explained to the devotees the secret of communion with God.

MASTER: âWith the realization of SatchidÄnanda one goes into samÄdhi. Then duties drop away. Suppose I have been talking about the ostÄd and he arrives. What need is there of talking about him then? How long does the bee buzz around? So long as it isnât sitting on a flower. But it will not do for the sÄdhaka to renounce duties. He should perform his duties, such as worship, japa, meditation, prayer, and pilgrimage.

âIf you see someone engaged in reasoning even after he has realized God, you may liken him to a bee, which also buzzes a little even while sipping honey from a flower.â

The Master was highly pleased with the ostÄdâs music. He said to the musician, âThere is a special manifestation of Godâs power in a man who has any outstanding gift, such as proficiency in music.â

MUSICIAN: âSir, what is the way to realize God?â

MASTER: âBhakti is the one essential thing. To be sure, God exists in all beings. Who, then, is a devotee? He whose mind dwells on God. But this is not possible as long as one has egotism and vanity. The water of Godâs grace cannot collect on the high mound of egotism. It runs down. I am a mere machine.

(To Kedar and the other devotees) âGod can be realized through all paths. All religions are true. The important thing is to reach the roof. You can reach it by stone stairs or by wooden stairs or by bamboo steps or by a rope. You can also climb up by a bamboo pole.

âYou may say that there are many errors and superstitions in another religion. I should reply: Suppose there are. Every religion has errors. Everyone thinks that his watch alone gives the correct time. It is enough to have yearning for God. It is enough to love Him and feel attracted to Him. Donât you know that God is the Inner Guide? He sees the longing of our heart and the yearning of our soul. Suppose a man has several sons. The older boys address him distinctly as âBÄbÄâ or âPÄpÄâ, but the babies can at best call him âBÄâ or âPÄâ. Now, will the father be angry with those who address him in this indistinct way? The father knows that they too are calling him, only they cannot pronounce his name well. All children are the same to the father. Likewise, the devotees call on God alone, though by different names. They call on one Person only. God is one, but His names are many.â

Thursday, August 24, 1882

Sri Ramakrishna was talking to Hazra on the long northeast verandah of his room, when M. arrived. He saluted the Master reverently.

MASTER: âI should like to visit Iswar Chandra VidyÄsÄgar a few times more. The painter first draws the general outlines and then puts in the details and colours at his leisure. The moulder first makes the image out of clay, then plasters it, then gives it a coat of whitewash, and last of all paints it with a brush. All these steps must be taken successively. VidyÄsÄgar is fully ready, but his inner stuff is covered with a thin layer. He is now engaged in doing good works; but he doesnât know what is within himself. Gold is hidden within him. God dwells within us. If one knows that, one feels like giving up all activities and praying to God with a yearning soul.â

So the Master talked with M.ânow standing, now pacing up and down the long verandah.

MASTER: âA little spiritual discipline is necessary in order to know what lies within.â

M: âIs it necessary to practise discipline all through life?â

MASTER: âNo. But one must be up and doing in the beginning. After that one need not work hard. The helmsman stands up and clutches the rudder firmly as long as the boat is passing through waves, storms, high wind, or around the curves of a river; but he relaxes after steering through them. As soon as the boat passes the curves and the helmsman feels a favourable wind, he sits comfortably and just touches the rudder. Next he prepares to unfurl the sail and gets ready for a smoke. Likewise, the aspirant enjoys peace and calm after passing the waves and storms of âwoman and goldâ.

âSome are born with the characteristics of the yogi; but they too should be careful. It is âwoman and goldâ alone that is the obstacle; it makes them deviate from the path of yoga and drags them into worldliness. Perhaps they have some desire for enjoyment. After fulfilling their desire, they again direct their minds to God and thus recover their former state of mind, fit for the practise of yoga.

âHave you ever seen the spring trap for fish, called the âsatkÄ-kalâ?â

M: âNo, sir, I havenât seen it.â

MASTER: âThey use it in our part of the country. One end of a bamboo pole is fastened in the ground, and the other is bent over with a catch. From this end a line with a hook hangs over the water, with bait tied to the hook. When the fish swallows the bait, suddenly the bamboo jumps up and regains its upright position.

âAgain, take a pair of scales, for example. If a weight is placed on one side, the lower needle moves away from the upper one. The lower needle is the mind, and the upper one, God. The meeting of the two is yoga.

âUnless the mind becomes steady there cannot be yoga. It is the wind of worldliness that always disturbs the mind, which may be likened to a candle-flame. If that flame doesnât move at all, then one is said to have attained yoga.

âÂ âWoman and goldâ alone is the obstacle to yoga. Always analyse what you see. What is there in the body of a woman? Only such things as blood, flesh, fat, entrails, and the like. Why should one love such a body?

âSometimes I used to assume a rÄjasic mood in order to practise renunciation. Once I had the desire to put on a gold-embroidered robe, wear a ring on my finger, and smoke a hubble-bubble with a long pipe. Mathur Babu procured all these things for me. I wore the gold-embroidered robe and said to myself after a while, âMind! This is what is called a gold-embroidered robe.â Then I took it off and threw it away. I couldnât stand the robe any more. Again I said to myself, âMind! This is called a shawl, and this a ring, and this, smoking a hubble-bubble with a long pipe.â I threw those things away once for all, and the desire to enjoy them never arose in my mind again.â

It was almost dusk. The Master and M. stood talking alone near the door on the southeast verandah.

MASTER (to M.): âThe mind of the yogi is always fixed on God, always absorbed in the Self. You can recognize such a man by merely looking at him. His eyes are wide open, with an aimless look, like the eyes of the mother bird hatching her eggs. Her entire mind is fixed on the eggs, and there is a vacant look in her eyes. Can you show me such a picture?â

M: âI shall try to get one.â

As evening came on, the temples were lighted up. Sri Ramakrishna was seated on his small couch, meditating on the Divine Mother. Then he chanted the names of God. Incense was burnt in the room, where an oil lamp had been lighted. Sounds of conch-shells and gongs came floating on the air as the evening worship began in the temple of KÄli. The light of the moon flooded all the quarters. The Master again spoke to M.

MASTER: âPerform your duties in an unselfish spirit. The work that VidyÄsÄgar is engaged in is very good. Always try to perform your duties without desiring any result.â

M: âYes, sir. But may I know if one can realize God while performing oneâs duties? Can âRÄmaâ and âdesireâ coexist? The other day I read in a Hindi couplet: âWhere RÄma is, there desire cannot be; where desire is, there RÄma cannot be.â â

MASTER: âAll, without exception, perform work. Even to chant the name and glories of God is work, as is the meditation of the non-dualist on âI am Heâ. Breathing is also an activity. There is no way of renouncing work altogether. So do your work, but surrender the result to God.â

M: âSir, may I make an effort to earn more money?â

MASTER: âIt is permissible to do so to maintain a religious family. You may try to increase your income, but in an honest way. The goal of life is not the earning of money, but the service of God. Money is not harmful if it is devoted to the service of God.â

M: âHow long should a man feel obliged to do his duty toward his wife and children?â

MASTER: âAs long as they feel pinched for food and clothing. But one need not take the responsibility of a son when he is able to support himself. When the young fledgling learns to pick its own food, its mother pecks it if it comes to her for food.â

M: âHow long must one do oneâs duty?â

MASTER: âThe blossom drops off when the fruit appears. One doesnât have to do oneâs duty after the attainment of God, nor does one feel like doing it then.

âIf a drunkard takes too much liquor he cannot retain consciousness. If he takes only two or three glasses, he can go on with his work. As you advance nearer and nearer to God, He will reduce your activities little by little. Have no fear.

âFinish the few duties you have at hand, and then you will have peace. When the mistress of the house goes to bathe after finishing her cooking and other household duties, she wonât come back, however you may shout after her.â

M: âSir, what is the meaning of the realization of God? What do you mean by God-vision? How does one attain it?â

MASTER: âAccording to the Vaishnavas the aspirants and the seers of God may be divided into different groups. These are the pravartaka, the sÄdhaka, the siddha, and the siddha of the siddha. He who has just set foot on the path may be called a pravartaka. He may be called a sÄdhaka who has for some time been practising spiritual disciplines, such as worship, japa, meditation, and the chanting of Godâs name and glories. He may be called a siddha who has known from his inner experience that God exists. An analogy is given in the VedÄnta to explain this. The master of the house is asleep in a dark room. Someone is groping in the darkness to find him. He touches the couch and says, âNo, it is not he.â He touches the window and says, âNo, it is not he.â He touches the door and says, âNo, it is not he.â This is known in the VedÄnta as the process of âNeti, netiâ, âNot this, not thisâ. At last his hand touches the masterâs body and he exclaims, âHere he is!â In other words, he is now conscious of the âexistenceâ of the master. He has found him, but he doesnât yet know him intimately.

âThere is another type, known as the siddha of the siddha, the âsupremely perfectâ. It is quite a different thing when one talks to the master intimately, when one knows God very intimately through love and devotion. A siddha has undoubtedly attained God, but the âsupremely perfectâ has known God very intimately.

âBut in order to realize God, one must assume one of these attitudes: ÅÄnta, dÄsya, sakhya, vÄtsalya, or madhur.

âÅÄnta, the serene attitude. The rishis of olden times had this attitude toward God. They did not desire any worldly enjoyment. It is like the single-minded devotion of a wife to her husband. She knows that her husband is the embodiment of beauty and love, a veritable Madan.

âDÄsya, the attitude of a servant toward his master. HanumÄn had this attitude toward RÄma. He felt the strength of a lion when he worked for RÄma. A wife feels this mood also. She serves her husband with all her heart and soul. A mother also has a little of this attitude, as YaÅodÄ had toward Krishna.

âSakhya, the attitude of friendship. Friends say to one another, âCome here and sit near me.â ÅridÄma and other friends sometimes fed Krishna with fruit, part of which they had already eaten, and sometimes climbed on His shoulders.

âVÄtsalya, the attitude of a mother toward her child. This was YaÅodÄâs attitude toward Krishna. The wife, too, has a little of this. She feeds her husband with her very life-blood, as it were. The mother feels happy only when the child has eaten to his heartâs content. YaÅodÄ would roam about with butter in her hand, in order to feed Krishna.

âMadhur, the attitude of a woman toward her paramour. RÄdhÄ had this attitude toward Krishna. The wife also feels it for her husband. This attitude includes all the other four.â

M: âWhen one sees God does one see Him with these eyes?â

MASTER: âGod cannot be seen with these physical eyes. In the course of spiritual discipline one gets a âlove bodyâ, endowed with âlove eyesâ, âlove earsâ, and so on. One sees God with those âlove eyesâ. One hears the voice of God with those âlove earsâ. One even gets a sexual organ made of love.â

At these words M. burst out laughing. The Master continued, unannoyed, âWith this âlove bodyâ the soul communes with God.â

M. again became serious.

MASTER: âBut this is not possible without intense love of God. One sees nothing but God everywhere when one loves Him with great intensity. It is like a person with jaundice, who sees everything yellow. Then one feels, âI am verily He.â

âA drunkard, deeply intoxicated, says, âVerily I am KÄli!â The gopis, intoxicated with love, exclaimed, âVerily I am Krishna!â

âOne who thinks of God, day and night, beholds Him everywhere. It is like a manâs seeing flames on all sides after he has gazed fixedly at one flame for some time.â

âBut that isnât the real flameâ, flashed through M.âs mind.

Sri Ramakrishna, who could read a manâs inmost thought, said: âOne doesnât lose consciousness by thinking of Him who is all Spirit, all Consciousness. Shivanath once remarked that too much thinking about God confounds the brain. Thereupon I said to him, âHow can one become unconscious by thinking of Consciousness?â â

M: âYes, sir, I realize that. It isnât like thinking of an unreal object. How can a man lose his intelligence if he always fixes his mind on Him whose very nature is eternal Intelligence?â

MASTER (with pleasure): âIt is through Godâs grace that you understand that. The doubts of the mind will not disappear without His grace. Doubts do not disappear without Self-realization.

âBut one need not fear anything if one has received the grace of God. It is rather easy for a child to stumble if he holds his fatherâs hand; but there can be no such fear if the father holds the childâs hand. A man does not have to suffer any more if God, in His grace, removes his doubts and reveals Himself to him. But this grace descends upon him only after he has prayed to God with intense yearning of heart and practised spiritual discipline. The mother feels compassion for her child when she sees him running about breathlessly. She has been hiding herself; now she appears before the child.â

âBut why should God make us run about?â thought M.

Immediately Sri Ramakrishna said: âIt is His will that we should run about a little. Then it is great fun. God has created the world in play, as it were. This is called MahÄmÄyÄ, the Great Illusion. Therefore one must take refuge in the Divine Mother, the Cosmic Power Itself. It is She who has bound us with the shackles of illusion. The realization of God is possible only when those shackles are severed.â

The Master continued: âOne must propitiate the Divine Mother, the Primal Energy, in order to obtain Godâs grace. God Himself is MahÄmÄyÄ, who deludes the world with Her illusion and conjures up the magic of creation, preservation, and destruction. She has spread this veil of ignorance before our eyes. We can go into the inner chamber only when She lets us pass through the door. Living outside, we see only outer objects, but not that Eternal Being, Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute. Therefore it is stated in the PurÄna that deities like BrahmÄ praised MahÄmÄyÄ for the destruction of the demons Madhu and Kaitabha.

âÅakti alone is the root of the universe. That Primal Energy has two aspects: vidyÄ and avidyÄ. AvidyÄ deludes. AvidyÄ conjures up âwoman and goldâ, which casts the spell. VidyÄ begets devotion, kindness, wisdom, and love, which lead one to God. This avidyÄ must be propitiated, and that is the purpose of the rites of Åakti worship.1

âThe devotee assumes various attitudes toward Åakti in order to propitiate Her: the attitude of a handmaid, a âheroâ, or a child. A heroâs attitude is to please Her even as a man pleases a woman through intercourse.

âThe worship of Åakti is extremely difficult. It is no joke. I passed two years as the handmaid and companion of the Divine Mother. But my natural attitude has always been that of a child toward its mother. I regard the breasts of any woman as those of my own mother.

âWomen are, all of them, the veritable images of Åakti. In northwest India the bride holds a knife in her hand at the time of marriage; in Bengal, a nut-cutter. The meaning is that the bridegroom, with the help of the bride, who is the embodiment of the Divine Power, will sever the bondage of illusion. This is the âheroicâ attitude. I never worshipped the Divine Mother that way. My attitude toward Her is that of a child toward its mother.

âThe bride is the very embodiment of Åakti. Havenât you noticed, at the marriage ceremony, how the groom sits behind like an idiot? But the brideâshe is so bold!

âAfter attaining God one forgets His external splendour, the glories of His creation. One doesnât think of Godâs glories after one has seen Him. The devotee, once immersed in Godâs Bliss, doesnât calculate any more about outer things. When I see Narendra, I donât need to ask him: âWhatâs your name? Where do you live?â Where is the time for such questions? Once a man asked HanumÄn which day of the fortnight it was. âBrother,â said HanumÄn, âI donât know anything of the day of the week, or the fortnight, or the position of the stars. I think of RÄma alone.â â

October 16, 1882

It was Monday, a few days before the DurgÄ PujÄ, the festival of the Divine Mother. Sri Ramakrishna was in a very happy state of mind, for Narendra was with him. Narendra had brought two or three young members of the BrÄhmo SamÄj to the temple garden. Besides these, Rakhal, Ramlal, Hazra, and M. were with the Master.

Narendra had his midday meal with Sri Ramakrishna. Afterwards a temporary bed was made on the floor of the Masterâs room so that the disciples might rest awhile. A mat was spread, over which was placed a quilt covered with a white sheet. A few cushions and pillows completed the simple bed. Like a child, the Master sat near Narendranath on the bed. He talked with the devotees in great delight. With a radiant smile lighting his face, and his eyes fixed on Narendra, he was giving them various spiritual teachings, interspersing these with incidents from his own life.

MASTER: âAfter I had experienced samÄdhi, my mind craved intensely to hear only about God. I would always search for places where they were reciting or explaining the sacred books, such as the BhÄgavata, the MahÄbhÄrata, and the AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana. I used to go to Krishnakishore to hear him read the AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana.

âWhat tremendous faith Krishnakishore had! Once, while at VrindÄvan, he felt thirsty and went to a well. Near it he saw a man standing. On being asked to draw a little water for him, the man said: âI belong to a low caste, sir. You are a brÄhmin. How can I draw water for you?â Krishnakishore said: âTake the name of Åiva. By repeating His holy name you will make yourself pure.â The low-caste man did as he was told, and Krishnakishore, orthodox brÄhmin that he was, drank that water. What tremendous faith!

âOnce a holy man came to the bank of the Ganges and lived near the bathing-ghÄt at ÄriÄdaha, not far from Dakshineswar. We thought of paying him a visit. I said to Haladhari: âKrishnakishore and I are going to see a holy man. Will you come with us?â Haladhari replied, âWhat is the use of seeing a mere human body, which is no better than a cage of clay?â Haladhari was a student of the GÄ«tÄ and VedÄnta philosophy, and therefore referred to the holy man as a mere âcage of clayâ. I repeated this to Krishnakishore. With great anger he said: âHow impudent of Haladhari to make such a remark! How can he ridicule as a âcage of clayâ the body of a man who constantly thinks of God, who meditates on RÄma, and has renounced all for the sake of the Lord? Doesnât he know that such a man is the embodiment of Spirit?â He was so upset by Haladhariâs remarks that he would turn his face away from him whenever he met him in the temple garden, and stopped speaking to him.

âOnce Krishnakishore asked me, âWhy have you cast off the sacred thread?â In those days of God-vision I felt as if I were passing through the great storm of ÄÅwin,2 and everything had blown away from me. No trace of my old self was left. I lost all consciousness of the world. I could hardly keep my cloth on my body, not to speak of the sacred thread! I said to Krishnakishore, âAh, you will understand if you ever happen to be as intoxicated with God as I was.â

âAnd it actually came to pass. He too passed through a God-intoxicated state, when he would repeat only the word âOmâ and shut himself up alone in his room. His relatives thought he was actually mad, and called in a physician. Ram KavirÄj of NÄtÄgore came to see him. Krishnakishore said to the physician, âCure me, sir, of my malady, if you please, but not of my Om.â (All laugh.)

âOne day I went to see him and found him in a pensive mood. When I asked him about it, he said: âThe tax-collector was here. He threatened to dispose of my brass pots, my cups, and my few utensils, if I didnât pay the tax; so I am worried.â I said: âBut why should you worry about it? Let him take away your pots and pans. Let him arrest your body even. How will that affect you? For your nature is that of Kha!â (Narendra and the others laugh.) He used to say to me that he was the Spirit, all-pervading as the sky. He had got that idea from the AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana. I used to tease him now and then, addressing him as âKhaâ. âIn that state of God-intoxication I used to speak out my mind to all. I was no respecter of persons. Even to men of position I was not afraid to speak the truth.

âOne day Jatindra3 came to the garden of Jadu Mallick. I was there too. I asked him: âWhat is the duty of man? Isnât it our duty to think of God?â Jatindra replied: âWe are worldly people. You donât remember his truthfulness, his forbearance, his patience, his discrimination, his dispassion, his devotion to God.â I was about to say many more things, when Hriday stopped my mouth. After a little while Jatindra left the place, saying he had some other business to attend to.

âMany days later I went with Captain to see RÄjÄ4 Sourindra Tagore. As soon as I met him, I said, âI canât address you as âRÄjÄâ, or by any such title, for I should be telling a lie.â He talked to me a few minutes, but even so our conversation was interrupted by the frequent visits of Europeans and others. A man of rÄjasic temperament, Sourindra was naturally busy with many things. Jatindra, his eldest brother, had been told of my coming, but he sent word that he had a pain in his throat and couldnât go out.

âOne day, in that state of divine intoxication, I went to the bathing-ghÄt on the Ganges at BarÄnagore. There I saw Jaya Mukherji repeating the name of God; but his mind was on something else. I went up and slapped him twice on the cheeks.

âAt one time RÄni Rasmani was staying in the temple garden. She came to the shrine of the Divine Mother, as she frequently did when I worshipped KÄli, and asked me to sing a song or two. âWhen one gets into such a state of mind, one doesnât enjoy any conversation but that about God. I used to weep when I heard people talk about worldly matters. When I accompanied Mathur Babu on a pilgrimage, we spent a few days in Benares at Raja Babuâs house. One day I was seated in the drawing-room with Mathur Babu, Raja Babu, and others. The Master asked the devotees, especially Narendra, to rest awhile, and he himself lay down on the smaller couch.

Late in the afternoon Narendra sang. Rakhal, Latu,5 M., Hazra, and Priya, Narendraâs BrÄhmo friend, were present. The singing was accompanied by the drum:

After this song Narendra sang:

Now Narendra and the devotees began to sing kirtan, accompanied by the drum and cymbals. They moved round and round the Master as they sang:

At last Narendra himself was playing on the drums, and he sang with the Master, full of joy:

With beaming face chant the sweet name of God â¦

When the music was over, Sri Ramakrishna held Narendra in his arms a long time and said, âYou have made us so happy today!â The flood-gate of the Masterâs heart was open so wide, that night, that he could hardly contain himself for joy. It was eight oâclock in the evening. Intoxicated with divine love, he paced the long verandah north of his room. Now and then he could be heard talking to the Divine Mother. Suddenly he said in an excited voice, âWhat can you do to me?â Was the Master hinting that mÄyÄ was helpless before him, since he had the Divine Mother for his support?

Narendra, M., and Priya were going to spend the night at the temple garden. This pleased the Master highly, especially since Narendra would be with him. The Holy Mother,6 who was living in the nahabat, had prepared the supper. Surendra7 bore the greater part of the Masterâs expenses. The meal was ready, and the plates were set out on the southeast verandah of the Masterâs room.

Near the east door of his room Narendra and the other devotees were gossiping.

NARENDRA: âHow do you find the young men nowadays?â

M: âThey are not bad; but they donât receive any religious instruction.â

NARENDRA: âBut from my experience I feel they are going to the dogs. They smoke cigarettes, indulge in frivolous talk, enjoy foppishness, play truant, and do everything of that sort. I have even seen them visiting questionable places.â

While the devotees were enjoying their meal, Åri Ramakrishna stood by and watched them with intense delight. That night the Masterâs joy was very great.

After supper the devotees rested on the mat spread on the floor of the Masterâs room. They began to talk with him. It was indeed a mart of joy. The Master asked Narendra to sing the song beginning with the line: âIn Wisdomâs firmament the moon of Love is rising full.â

When the song was over, the Master walked up and down the northeast verandah, where Hazra was seated with M. The Master sat down there. He asked a devotee, âDo you ever have dreams?â

DEVOTEE: âYes, sir. The other day I dreamt a strange dream. I saw the whole world enveloped in water. There was water on all sides. Shortly before midnight Narendra and the other devotees lay down on a bed made on the floor of the Masterâs room.

In the mean time the morning service had begun in the temples of KÄli and RÄdhÄkÄnta. Sounds of conch-shells and cymbals were carried on the air. Narendra and the other devotees finished their morning duties and came to the Master. With a sweet smile on his lips Sri Ramakrishna was standing on the northeast verandah, close to his own room.

NARENDRA: âWe noticed several sannyÄsis belonging to the sect of NÄnak in the Panchavati.â

As they sat there the Master looked at them with evident delight. He then began to talk with them. Narendra asked about spiritual discipline.

The sannyÄsis belonging to the sect of NÄnak entered the room and greeted the Master, saying, âNamo NÄrÄyanÄya.â10 Sri Ramakrishna asked them to sit down.

MASTER: âNothing is impossible for God. Nobody can describe His nature in words. Everything is possible for Him. There lived at a certain place two yogis who were practising spiritual discipline. The sage NÄrada was passing that way one day. Realizing who he was, one of the yogis said: âYou have just come from God Himself. What is He doing now?â NÄrada replied, âWhy, I saw Him making camels and elephants pass and repass through the eye of a needle.â At this the yogi said: âIs that anything to wonder at? Everything is possible for God.â But the other yogi said: âWhat? Making elephants pass through the eye of a needleâis that ever possible? You have never been to the Lordâs dwelling-place.â â

At nine oâclock in the morning, while the Master was still sitting in his room, Manomohan arrived from Konnagar with some members of his family. In answer to Sri Ramakrishnaâs kind inquiries, Manomohan explained that he was taking them to Calcutta. The Master said: âToday is the first day of the Bengali month, an inauspicious day for undertaking a journey. I hope everything will be well with you.â With a smile he began to talk of other matters.

When Narendra and his friends had finished bathing in the Ganges, the Master said to them earnestly: âGo to the Panchavati and meditate there under the banyan-tree. Shall I give you something to sit on?â

About half past ten Narendra and his BrÄhmo friends were meditating in the Panchavati. After a while Sri Ramakrishna came to them. M., too, was present.

The Master said to the BrÄhmo devotees: âIn meditation one must be absorbed in God. By merely floating on the surface of the water, can you reach the gems lying at the bottom of the sea?â

Then he sang:

Taking the name of KÄli, dive deep down, O mind,

Into the heartâs fathomless depths,

Where many a precious gem lies hid.

But never believe the bed of the ocean bare of gems

If in the first few dives you fail;

With firm resolve and self-control

Dive deep and make your way to Mother KÄliâs realm.

Down in the ocean depths of heavenly Wisdom lie

The wondrous pearls of Peace, O mind;

And you yourself can gather them,

If you but have pure love and follow the scripturesâ rule.

Within those ocean depths, as well,

Six alligators11 lurkâlust, anger, and the restâ

Swimming about in search of prey.

The very smell of it will shield you from their jaws.

Upon the ocean bed lie strewn

Plunge in, says RÄmprasÄd, and gather up handfuls there!

Narendra and his friends came down from their seats on the raised platform of the Panchavati and stood near the Master. He returned to his room with them. The Master continued: âWhen you plunge in the water of the ocean, you may be attacked by alligators. But they wonât touch you if your body is smeared with turmeric. There are no doubt six alligatorsâlust, anger, avarice, and so onâwithin you, in the âheartâs fathomless depthsâ. But protect yourself with the turmeric of discrimination and renunciation, and they wonât touch you.

âWhat can you achieve by mere lecturing and scholarship without discrimination and dispassion? God alone is real, and all else is unreal. God alone is substance, and all else is nonentity. That is discrimination.

âFirst of all set up God in the shrine of your heart, and then deliver lectures as much as you like. How will the mere repetition of âBrahmaâ profit you if you are not imbued with discrimination and dispassion? It is the empty sound of a conch-shell.

âThere lived in a village a young man named Padmalochan. People used to call him âPodoâ, for short. In this village there was a temple in a very dilapidated condition. It contained no image of God. AÅwattha and other plants sprang up on the ruins of its walls. Bats lived inside, and the floor was covered with dust and the droppings of the bats. The people of the village had stopped visiting the temple. One day after dusk the villagers heard the sound of a conch-shell from the direction of the temple. They thought perhaps someone had installed an image in the shrine and was performing the evening worship. One of them softly opened the door and saw Padmalochan standing in a corner, blowing the conch. No image had been set up. The temple hadnât been swept or washed. And filth and dirt lay everywhere. Then he shouted to Podo:

You have set up no image here,

Within the shrine, O fool!

Blowing the conch, you simply make

Confusion worse confounded.

Day and night eleven bats

Scream there incessantlyâ¦.

âThere is no use in merely making a noise if you want to establish the Deity in the shrine of your heart, if you want to realize God. First of all purify the mind. In the pure heart God takes His seat. One cannot bring the holy image into the temple if the droppings of bats are all around. The eleven bats are our eleven organs: five of action, five of perception, and the mind.

âFirst of all invoke the Deity, and then give lectures to your heartâs content. First of all dive deep. Plunge to the bottom and gather up the gems. Then you may do other things. But nobody wants to plunge. People are without spiritual discipline and prayer, without renunciation and dispassion. They learn a few words and immediately start to deliver lectures. It is difficult to teach others. Only if a man gets a command from God, after realizing Him, is he entitled to teach.â

Thus conversing, the Master came to the west end of the verandah. M. stood by his side. Sri Ramakrishna had repeated again and again that God cannot be realized without discrimination and renunciation. This made M. extremely worried. He had married and was then a young man of twenty-eight, educated in college in the Western way. Having a sense of duty, he asked himself, âDo discrimination and dispassion mean giving up âwoman and goldâ?â He was really at a loss to know what to do.

M. (to the Master): âWhat should one do if oneâs wife says: âYou are neglecting me. I shall commit suicide.â?â

MASTER (in a serious tone): âGive up such a wife if she proves an obstacle in the way of spiritual life. Let her commit suicide or anything else she likes. The wife that hampers her husbandâs spiritual life is an ungodly wife.â

Immersed in deep thought, M. stood leaning against the wall. Narendra and the other devotees remained silent a few minutes. The Master exchanged several words with them; then, suddenly going to M., he whispered in his ear: âBut if a man has sincere love for God, then all come under his controlâthe king, wicked persons, and his wife. Sincere love of God on the husbandâs part may eventually help the wife to lead a spiritual life. If the husband is good, then through the grace of God the wife may also follow his example.â

This had a most soothing effect on M.âs worried mind. All the while he had been thinking: âLet her commit suicide. What can I do?â

M. (to the Master): âThis world is a terrible place indeed.â

MASTER (to the devotees): âThat is the reason Chaitanya said to his companion NityÄnanda, âListen, brother, there is no hope of salvation for the worldly-minded.â â

On another occasion the Master had said to M. privately: âYes, there is no hope for a worldly man if he is not sincerely devoted to God. But he has nothing to fear if he remains in the world after realizing God. Nor need a man have any fear whatever of the world if he attains sincere devotion by practising spiritual discipline now and then in solitude. Chaitanya had several householders among his devotees, but they were householders in name only, for they lived unattached to the world.â

It was noon. The worship was over, and food offerings had been made in the temple. The doors of the temple were shut. Sri Ramakrishna sat down for his meal, and Narendra and the other devotees partook of the food offerings from the temple.

Sunday, October 22, 1882

It was the day of VijayÄ, the last day of the celebration of the worship of DurgÄ, when the clay image is immersed in the water of a lake or river.

About nine oâclock in the morning M. was seated on the floor of the Masterâs room at Dakshineswar, near Sri Ramakrishna, who was reclining on the small couch. Rakhal was then living with the Master, and Narendra and Bhavanath visited him frequently. Baburam had seen him only once or twice.

MASTER: âDid you have any holiday during the DurgÄ PujÄ?â

M: âYes, sir. I went to Keshabâs house every day for the first three days of the worship.â

MASTER: âIs that so?â

M: âI heard there a very interesting interpretation of the DurgÄ PujÄ.â

MASTER: âPlease tell me all about it.â

M: âKeshab Sen held daily morning prayers in his house, lasting till ten or eleven. During these prayers he gave the inner meaning of the DurgÄ PujÄ. He said that if anyone could realize the Divine Mother, that is to say, could install Mother DurgÄ in the shrine of his heart, then Lakshmi, Sarasvati, KÄrtika, and GaneÅa12 would come there of themselves. Lakshmi means wealth, Sarasvati knowledge, KÄrtika strength, and GaneÅa success. By realizing the Divine Mother within oneâs heart, one gets all these without any effort whatever.â

Sri Ramakrishna listened to the description, questioning M. now and then about the prayers conducted by Keshab. At last he said to M.: âDonât go hither and thither. Come here alone. Those who belong to the inner circle of my devotees will come only here. Boys like Narendra, Bhavanath, and Rakhal are my very intimate disciples. They are not to be thought lightly of. Feed13 them one day. What do you think of Narendra?â

M: âI think very highly of him, sir.â

MASTER: âHavenât you observed his many virtues? He is not only well versed in music, vocal and instrumental, but he is also very learned. Besides, he has controlled his passions and declares he will lead a celibate life. He has been devoted to God since his very boyhood.

âHow are you getting along with your meditation nowadays? What aspect of God appeals to your mindâwith form or without form?â

M: âSir, now I canât fix my mind on God with form. On the other hand, I canât concentrate steadily on God without form.â

M. sat in silence. After a few minutes he asked the Master: âWhat does one feel while thinking of God without form? MASTER: âYou see, one must practise spiritual discipline to understand this correctly. Suppose there are treasures in a room. âYou must practise discipline.

âThe jnÄnis think of God without form. They donât accept the Divine Incarnation. âKabirdÄs was strongly inclined to the formless God. At the mention of Krishnaâs name he would say: âWhy should I worship Him? M. (smiling): âYou are as infinite as He of whom we have been talking. Truly, no one can fathom your depth.â

MASTER (smiling): âAh! I see you have found it out. Let me tell you one thing. One should follow various paths. One should practise each creed for a time. M: âThat is true, sir.â

MASTER: âThere are two classes of yogis: the bahudakas and the kutichakas. The bahudakas roam about visiting various holy places and have not yet found peace of mind. âI had to practise each religion for a timeâHinduism, IslÄm, Christianity. Furthermore, I followed the paths of the ÅÄktas, Vaishnavas, and VedÄntists. I realized that there is only one God toward whom all are travelling; but the paths are different.

âWhile visiting the holy places, I would sometimes suffer great agony. Once I went with Mathur to Raja Babuâs drawing-room in Benares. âIn the dusk I would walk on the bank of the JamunÄ when the cattle returned along the sandy banks from their pastures. At the very sight of those cows the thought of Krishna would flash in my mind. I would run along like a madman, crying: âOh, where is Krishna? Where is my Krishna?â

âI went to ÅyÄmakunda and RÄdhÄkunda14 in a palanquin and got out to visit the holy Mount Govardhan. At the very sight of the mount I was overpowered with divine emotion and ran to the top. He had warned the bearers to be careful about me.

âGangÄmÄyi became very fond of me in VrindÄvan. She was an old woman who lived all alone in a hut near the Nidhuvan. âGangÄmÄyi used to experience trances. At such times a great crowd would come to see her. One day, in a state of ecstasy, she climbed on Hridayâs shoulders.

âI didnât want to leave her and return to Calcutta. Everything was arranged for me to stay with her. I was to eat double-boiled rice, and we were to have our beds on either side of the cottage. About eleven oâclock the Master took his meal, the offerings from the temple of KÄli. After taking his noonday rest he resumed his conversation with the devotees. Every now and then he uttered the holy word âOmâ or repeated the sacred names of the deities.

After sunset the evening worship was performed in the temples. Since it was the day of VijayÄ, the devotees first saluted the Divine Mother and then took the dust15 of the Masterâs feet.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# THE MASTER AND KESHAB

I T WAS FRIDAY, the day of the Lakshmi PujÄ. Keshab Chandra Sen had arranged a boat trip on the Ganges for Sri Ramakrishna.

The white steeple of the KÄli temple, the tree-tops of the Panchavati, and the silhouette of pine-trees stood high against the blue autumn sky. The gardens between the two nahabats were filled with fragrant flowers, and along the bank of the Ganges were rows of flowering plants. The blue sky was reflected in the brown water of the river, the sacred Ganges, associated with the most ancient traditions of Äryan civilization. The outer world appeared soft and serene, and the hearts of the BrÄhmo devotees were filled with peace.

Sri Ramakrishna was in his room talking with Vijay and Haralal. Some disciples of Keshab entered. Bowing before the Master, they said to him: âSir, the steamer has arrived. Keshab Babu has asked us to take you there.â A small boat was to carry the Master to the steamer. No sooner did he get into the boat than he lost outer consciousness in samÄdhi. Vijay was with him.

M. was among the passengers. As the boat came alongside the steamer, all rushed to the railing to have a view of Sri Ramakrishna. Keshab became anxious to get him safely on board. With great difficulty the Master was brought back to consciousness of the world and taken to a cabin in the steamer. Still in an abstracted mood, he walked mechanically, leaning on a devotee for support. Keshab and the others bowed before him, but he was not aware of them. Inside the cabin there were a few chairs and a table. He was made to sit on one of the chairs, Keshab and Vijay occupying two others. Some devotees were also seated, most of them on the floor, while many others had to stand outside. They peered eagerly through the door and windows. Sri Ramakrishna again went into deep samÄdhi and became totally unconscious of the outer world.

As the air in the room was stuffy because of the crowd of people, Keshab opened the windows. He was embarrassed to meet Vijay, since they had differed on certain principles of the BrÄhmo SamÄj and Vijay had separated himself from Keshabâs organization, joining another society.

The BrÄhmo devotees looked wistfully at the Master. Gradually he came back to sense consciousness; but the divine intoxication still lingered. He said to himself in a whisper: âMother, why have You brought me here? They are hedged around and not free. Can I free them?â Did the Master find that the people assembled there were locked within the prison walls of the world? Did their helplessness make the Master address these words to the Divine Mother?

Sri Ramakrishna was gradually becoming conscious of the outside world. Nilmadhav of GhÄzipur and a BrÄhmo devotee were talking about PÄvhÄri BÄbÄ. Another BrÄhmo devotee said to the Master: âSir, these gentlemen visited PÄvhÄri BÄbÄ. He lives in GhÄzipur. He is a holy man like yourself.â The Master could hardly talk; he only smiled. The devotee continued, âSir, PÄvhÄri BÄbÄ keeps your photograph in his room.â Pointing to his body the Master said with a smile, âJust a pillow-case.â

The Master continued: âBut you should remember that the heart of the devotee is the abode of God. He dwells, no doubt, in all beings, but He especially manifests Himself in the heart of the devotee. A landlord may at one time or another visit all parts of his estate, but people say he is generally to be found in a particular drawing-room. The heart of the devotee is the drawing-room of God.

âHe who is called Brahman by the jnÄnis is known as Ätman by the yogis and as BhagavÄn by the bhaktas. The same brÄhmin is called priest, when worshipping in the temple, and cook, when preparing a meal in the kitchen. The jnÄni, sticking to the path of knowledge, always reasons about the Reality, saying, âNot this, not thisâ. Brahman is neither âthisâ nor âthatâ; It is neither the universe nor its living beings. Reasoning in this way, the mind becomes steady. Then it disappears and the aspirant goes into samÄdhi. This is the Knowledge of Brahman. It is the unwavering conviction of the jnÄni that Brahman alone is real and the world illusory. All these names and forms are illusory, like a dream. What Brahman is cannot be described. One cannot even say that Brahman is a Person. This is the opinion of the jnÄnis, the followers of VedÄnta philosophy.

âBut the bhaktas accept all the states of consciousness. They take the waking state to be real also. They donât think the world to be illusory, like a dream. They say that the universe is a manifestation of Godâs power and glory. God has created all theseâsky, stars, moon, sun, mountains, ocean, men, animals. They constitute His glory. He is within us, in our hearts. Again, He is outside. The most advanced devotees say that He Himself has become all thisâthe twenty-four cosmic principles, the universe, and all living beings. The devotee of God wants to eat sugar, not to become sugar. (All laugh.)

âDo you know how a lover of God feels? His attitude is: âO God, Thou art the Master, and I am Thy servant. Thou art the Mother, and I am Thy child.â Or again: âThou art my Father and Mother. Thou art the Whole, and I am a part.â He doesnât like to say, âI am Brahman.â

âThe yogi seeks to realize the ParamÄtman, the Supreme Soul. His ideal is the union of the embodied soul and the Supreme Soul. He withdraws his mind from sense-objects and tries to concentrate it on the ParamÄtman. Therefore, during the first stage of his spiritual discipline, he retires into solitude and with undivided attention practises meditation in a fixed posture.

âBut the Reality is one and the same. The difference is only in name. He who is Brahman is verily Ätman, and again, He is the BhagavÄn. He is Brahman to the followers of the path of knowledge, ParamÄtman to the yogis, and BhagavÄn to the lovers of God.â

The steamer had been going toward Calcutta; but the passengers, with their eyes fixed on the Master and their ears given to his nectar-like words, were oblivious of its motion. Dakshineswar, with its temples and gardens, was left behind. The paddles of the boat churned the waters of the Ganges with a murmuring sound. But the devotees were indifferent to all this. Spellbound, they looked on a great yogi, his face lighted with a divine smile, his countenance radiating love, his eyes sparkling with joyâa man who had renounced all for God and who knew nothing but God. Unceasing words of wisdom flowed from his lips.

MASTER: âThe jnÄnis, who adhere to the non-dualistic philosophy of VedÄnta, say that the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction, the universe itself and all its living beings, are the manifestations of Åakti, the Divine Power.1 If you reason it out, you will realize that all these are as illusory as a dream. Brahman alone is the Reality, and all else is unreal. Even this very Åakti is unsubstantial, like a dream.

âBut though you reason all your life, unless you are established in samÄdhi, you cannot go beyond the jurisdiction of Åakti. Even when you say, âI am meditatingâ, or âI am contemplatingâ, still you are moving in the realm of Åakti, within Its power.

âThus Brahman and Åakti are identical. If you accept the one, you must accept the other. It is like fire and its power to burn. If you see the fire, you must recognize its power to burn also. You cannot think of fire without its power to burn, nor can you think of the power to burn without fire. You cannot conceive of the sunâs rays without the sun, nor can you conceive of the sun without its rays.

âWhat is milk like? Oh, you say, it is something white. You cannot think of the milk without the whiteness, and again, you cannot think of the whiteness without the milk.

âThus one cannot think of Brahman without Åakti, or of Åakti without Brahman. One cannot think of the Absolute without the Relative, or of the Relative without the Absolute.

âThe Primordial Power is ever at play.2 She is creating, preserving, and destroying in play, as it were. This Power is called KÄli. KÄli is verily Brahman, and Brahman is verily KÄli. It is one and the same Reality. When we think of It as inactive, that is to say, not engaged in the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction, then we call It Brahman. But when It engages in these activities, then we call It KÄli or Åakti. The Reality is one and the same; the difference is in name and form.

âIt is like water, called in different languages by different names, such as âjalâ, âpÄniâ, and so forth. There are three or four ghÄts on a lake. The Hindus, who drink water at one place, call it âjalâ. The MussalmÄns at another place call it âpÄniâ. And the English at a third place call it âwaterâ. All three denote one and the same thing, the difference being in the name only. In the same way, some address the Reality as âÄllÄhâ, some as âGodâ, some as âBrahmanâ, some as âKÄliâ, and others by such names as âRÄmaâ, âJesusâ, âDurgÄâ, âHariâ.â

KESHAB (with a smile): âDescribe to us, sir, in how many ways KÄli, the Divine Mother, sports in this world.â

MASTER (with a smile): âOh, She plays in different ways. It is She alone who is known as MahÄ-KÄli, Nitya-KÄli, ÅmaÅÄna-KÄli, RakshÄ-KÄli, and ÅyÄmÄ-KÄli. MahÄ-KÄli and Nitya-KÄli are mentioned in the Tantra philosophy. When there were neither the creation, nor the sun, the moon, the planets, and the earth, and when darkness was enveloped in darkness, then the Mother, the Formless One, MahÄ-KÄli, the Great Power, was one with MahÄ-KÄla, the Absolute.

âÅyÄmÄ-KÄli has a somewhat tender aspect and is worshipped in the Hindu households. She is the Dispenser of boons and the Dispeller of fear. People worship RakshÄ-KÄli, the Protectress, in times of epidemic, famine, earthquake, drought, and flood. ÅmaÅÄna-KÄli is the embodiment of the power of destruction. She resides in the cremation ground, surrounded by corpses, jackals, and terrible female spirits. From Her mouth flows a stream of blood, from Her neck hangs a garland of human heads, and around Her waist is a girdle made of human hands.

âAfter the destruction of the universe, at the end of a great cycle, the Divine Mother garners the seeds for the next creation. She is like the elderly mistress of the house, who has a hotchpotch-pot in which she keeps different articles for household use. (All laugh.)

âOh, yes! Housewives have pots like that, where they keep âsea-foamâ,3 blue pills, small bundles of seeds of cucumber, pumpkin, and gourd, and so on. They take them out when they want them. In the same way, after the destruction of the universe, my Divine Mother, the Embodiment of Brahman, gathers together the seeds for the next creation. After the creation the Primal Power dwells in the universe itself. She brings forth this phenomenal world and then pervades it. In the Vedas creation is likened to the spider and its web. The spider brings the web out of itself and then remains in it. God is the container of the universe and also what is contained in it.

âIs KÄli, my Divine Mother, of a black complexion? She appears black because She is viewed from a distance; but when intimately known She is no longer so. The sky appears blue at a distance; but look at it close by and you will find that it has no colour. The water of the ocean looks blue at a distance, but when you go near and take it in your hand, you find that it is colourless.â

The Master became intoxicated with divine love and sang:

Is KÄli, my Mother, really black?

The Naked One, of blackest hue,

Lights the Lotus of the Heartâ¦ .

The Master continued: âBondage and liberation are both of Her making. By Her mÄyÄ worldly people become entangled in âwoman and goldâ, and again, through Her grace they attain their liberation. She is called the Saviour, and the Remover of the bondage that binds one to the world.â

Then the Master sang the following song4 in his melodious voice:

In the worldâs busy market-place, O ÅyÄmÄ, Thou art flying kites;

High up they soar on the wind of hope, held fast by mÄyÄâs string.

Their frames are human skeletons, their sails of the three gunas made;

But all their curious workmanship is merely for ornament.

Upon the kite-strings Thou hast rubbed the mÄnjÄ-paste5 of world-liness,

So as to make each straining strand all the more sharp and strong.

Out of a hundred thousand kites, at best but one or two break free;

And Thou dost laugh and clap Thy hands, O Mother, watching them!

On favouring winds, says RÄmprasÄd, the kites set loose will speedily

Be borne away to the Infinite, across the sea of the world.

The Master said: âThe Divine Mother is always playful and sportive. This universe is Her play. She is self-willed and must always have Her own way. She is full of bliss. She gives freedom to one out of a hundred thousand.â

A BRÄHMO DEVOTEE: âBut, sir, if She likes, She can give freedom to all. Why, then, has She kept us bound to the world?â

MASTER: âThat is Her will. She wants to continue playing with Her created beings. In a game of hide-and-seek6 the running about soon stops if in the beginning all the players touch the âgrannyâ. If all touch her, then how can the game go on? That displeases her. Her pleasure is in continuing the game. Therefore the poet said:

Out of a hundred thousand kites, at best but one or two break free;

And Thou dost laugh and clap Thy hands, O Mother, watching them!

âIt is as if the Divine Mother said to the human mind in confidence, with a sign from Her eye, âGo and enjoy the world.â How can one blame the mind? The mind can disentangle itself from worldliness if, through Her grace, She makes it turn toward Herself. Only then does it become devoted to the Lotus Feet of the Divine Mother.â

Whereupon Sri Ramakrishna, taking upon himself, as it were, the agonies of all householders, sang a song complaining to the Divine Mother:

Mother, this is the grief that sorely grieves my heart,

That even with Thee for Mother, and though I am wide awake,

There should be robbery in my house.

Many and many a time I vow to call on Thee,

Yet when the time for prayer comes round, I have forgotten.

Now I see it is all Thy trick.

As Thou hast never given, so Thou receivest naught;

Am I to blame for this, O Mother? Hadst Thou but given,

Surely then Thou hadst received;

Out of Thine own gifts I should have given to Thee.

Glory and shame, bitter and sweet, are Thine alone;

This world is nothing but Thy play.

Then why, O Blissful One, dost Thou cause a rift in it?

Says RÄmprasÄd: Thou hast bestowed on me this mind,

And with a knowing wink of Thine eye
