Only for Thy bhaktasâ sake dost Thou assume Thy various forms;

But when Thy devoteeâs five senses merge in the five elements,

Mother, it is Thyself alone that he beholds as formless Truth.

As Ramlal sang the lines:

Above, in the throat, is the sixteen-petalled lotus flower, of smoky hue;

Within the petals of this flower there lies concealed a subtle space,

Transcending which, one sees at length the universe in Space dissolve,

the Master said to M.: âListen. This is known as the vision of SatchidÄnanda, the Formless Brahman. The Kundalini, rising above the ViÅuddha chakra, enables one to see everything as ÄkÄÅa.â

M: âYes, sir.â

MASTER: âOne attains the Absolute by going beyond the universe and its created beings conjured up by mÄyÄ. By passing beyond the NÄda one goes into samÄdhi. By repeating âOmâ one goes beyond the NÄda and attains samÄdhi.â

Adhar served Sri Ramakrishna with fruits and sweets. The Master left for Jadu Mallickâs house.

Sri Ramakrishna entered the room in Jaduâs house where the Divine Mother was worshipped. He stood before the image, which had been decorated with flowers, garlands, and sandal-paste, and which radiated a heavenly beauty and splendour. Lights were burning before the pedestal. A priest was seated before the image. The Master asked one of his companions to offer a rupee in the shrine, according to the Hindu custom.

Sri Ramakrishna stood a long time with folded hands before the blissful image, the devotees standing behind him. Gradually he went into samÄdhi, his body becoming motionless and his eyes fixed.

With a long sigh he came back to the world of the senses and said, still intoxicated with divine fervour, âMother, good-bye.â But he could not leave the place. He remained standing there. Addressing Ramlal, he said: âPlease sing that song. Then I shall be all right.â

Ramlal sang:

O Mother, Consort of Åiva, Thou hast deluded this worldâ¦ .

The Master went to the drawing-room with the devotees. Every now and then he said, âO Mother, please dwell in my heart!â Jadu was sitting in the drawing-room with his friends. The Master sat down, still in an ecstatic mood, and sang:

O Mother, ever blissful as Thou art,

Do not deprive Thy worthless child of bliss! â¦

Finishing the song, he said to Jadu, still in a state of divine fervour: âWell, sir, what shall I sing? Shall I sing âMother, am I Thine eight-months childâ?â

He sang:

Mother, am I Thine eight-months child?4 Thy red eyes cannot frighten me!

My riches are Thy Lotus Feet, which Åiva holds upon His breast;

Yet, when I seek my heritage, I meet with excuses and delays.

A deed of gift I hold in my heart, attested by Thy Husband Åiva;

I shall sue Thee, if I must, and with a single point shall win.

If Thou dost oppose me, Thou wilt learn what sort of motherâs son I am.

This bitterly contested suit between the Mother and Her sonâ

What sport it is! says RÄmprasÄd. I shall not cease tormenting Thee

Till Thou Thyself shalt yield the fight and take me in Thine arms at last.

Coming down nearly to a normal state, the Master said, âI shall take some of the Divine Motherâs prasÄd.â Then he ate a little of it.

Jadu Mallick was sitting near him with several friends, among whom were a few of his flatterers.

MASTER (with a smile): âWell, why do you keep these buffoons with you?â

JADU (with a smile): âSuppose they are. Wonât you redeem them?â

MASTER (smiling): âThe water of the Ganges cannot purify a wine-jar.â

Jadu had promised the Master that he would arrange a recital of the Chandi in his house. Some time had elapsed, but he had not yet kept his promise.

MASTER: âWell, what about the recital of the Chandi?â

JADU: âI have been busy with many things; I havenât been able to arrange it.â

MASTER: âHow is that? A man gives his word and doesnât take it back! âThe words of a man are like the tusks of the elephant: they come out but do not go back.â A man must be true to his word. What do you say?â

JADU (with a smile): âYou are right.â

MASTER: âYou are a shrewd man. You do a thing after much calculation. You are like the brÄhmin who selects a cow that eats very little, supplies plenty of dung, and gives much milk.â (All laugh.)

After a time he said to Jadu: âI now understand your nature. It is half warm and half cold. You are devoted to God and also to the world.â

The Master and his devotees were served by Jadu with sweets and fruit, and then the party left for the home of Khelat Ghosh.

Khelat Ghoshâs house was a big mansion, but it looked deserted. As the Master entered the house he fell into an ecstatic mood. M., Ramlal, and a few other devotees were with him. Their host was Khelat Ghoshâs brother-in-law. He was an old man, a Vaishnava. His body was stamped with the name of God, according to the Vaishnava custom, and he carried in his hand a small bag containing his rosary. He had visited the Master, now and then, at Dakshineswar. But most of the Vaishnavas held narrow religious views; they criticized the VedÄntists and the followers of the Åiva cult. Sri Ramakrishna soon began to speak.

MASTER: âIt is not good to feel that oneâs own religion alone is true and all others are false. God is one only, and not two. Different people call on Him by different names: some as ÄllÄh, some as God, and others as Krishna, Åiva, and Brahman. It is like the water in a lake. Some drink it at one place and call it âjalâ, others at another place and call it âpÄniâ, and still others at a third place and call it âwaterâ. The Hindus call it âjalâ, the Christians âwaterâ, and the MussalmÄns âpÄniâ. But it is one and the same thing. Opinions are but paths. Each religion is only a path leading to God, as rivers come from different directions and ultimately become one in the one ocean.

âThe Truth established in the Vedas, the PurÄnas, and the Tantras is but one SatchidÄnanda. In the Vedas It is called Brahman, in the PurÄnas It is called Krishna, RÄma, and so on, and in the Tantras It is called Åiva. The one SatchidÄnanda is called Brahman, Krishna, and Åiva.â

The devotees were silent.

A VAISHNAVA DEVOTEE: âSir, why should one think of God at all?â

MASTER: âIf a man really has that knowledge,5 then he is indeed liberated though living in a body.

âNot all, by any means, believe in God. They simply talk. The worldly-minded have heard from someone that God exists and that everything happens by His will; but it is not their inner belief.

âDo you know what a worldly manâs idea of God is like? It is like the childrenâs swearing by God when they quarrel. They have heard the word while listening to their elderly aunts quarrelling.

âIs it possible for all to comprehend God? God has created the good and the bad, the devoted and the impious, the faithful and the sceptical. The wonders that we see all exist in His creation. In one place there is more manifestation of His Power, in another less. The sunâs light is better reflected by water than by earth, and still better by a mirror. Again, there are different levels among the devotees of God: superior, mediocre, and inferior. All this has been described in the GÄ«tÄ.â

VAISHNAVA: âTrue, sir.â

MASTER: âThe inferior devotee says, âGod exists, but He is very far off, up there in heaven.â The mediocre devotee says, âGod exists in all beings as life and consciousness.â The superior devotee says: âIt is God Himself who has become everything; whatever I see is only a form of God. It is He alone who has become mÄyÄ, the universe, and all living beings. Nothing exists but God.â â

VAISHNAVA: âDoes anyone ever attain that state of mind?â

MASTER: âOne cannot attain it unless one has seen God. But there are signs that a man has had the vision of God. A man who has seen God sometimes behaves like a madman: he laughs, weeps, dances, and sings. Sometimes he behaves like a child, a child five years oldâguileless, generous, without vanity, unattached to anything, not under the control of any of the gunas, always blissful. Sometimes he behaves like a ghoul: he doesnât differentiate between things pure and things impure; he sees no difference between things clean and things unclean. And sometimes he is like an inert thing, staring vacantly: he cannot do any work; he cannot strive for anything.â

Was the Master making a veiled reference to his own states of mind?

MASTER (to the Vaishnava devotee): âThe feeling of âThee and Thineâ is the outcome of Knowledge; âI and mineâ comes from ignorance. Knowledge makes one feel: âO God, Thou art the Doer and I am Thy instrument. O God, to Thee belongs allâbody, mind, house, family, living beings, and the universe. All these are Thine. Nothing belongs to me.â

âAn ignorant person says, âOh, God is thereâvery far off.â The man of Knowledge knows that God is right here, very near, in the heart; that He has assumed all forms and dwells in all hearts as their Inner Controller.â

Sunday, July 22, 1883

Taking advantage of the holiday, many householder devotees visited Sri Ramakrishna in his room at the Dakshineswar temple garden. The young devotees, mostly students, generally came on week-days. Sometimes the Master asked his intimate disciples to come on a Tuesday or a Saturday, days that he considered very auspicious for special religious instruction. Adhar, Rakhal, and M. had come from Calcutta in a hired carriage.

Sri Ramakrishna had enjoyed a little rest after his midday meal. The room had an atmosphere of purity and holiness. On the walls hung pictures of gods and goddesses, among them one of Christ rescuing the drowning Peter. Outside the room were plants laden with fragrant flowers, and the Ganges could be seen flowing toward the south. The Master was seated on the small couch, facing the north, and the devotees sat on mats and carpets spread on the floor. All eyes were directed toward him. Mani Mallick, an old BrÄhmo devotee about sixty-five years of age, came to pay his respects to the Master. He had returned a few months earlier from a pilgrimage to Benares and was recounting his experiences to Sri Ramakrishna.

MANI MALLICK: âA monk whom I met in Benares said that no religious experience is possible without the control of the sense-organs. Nothing could be achieved by merely crying, âGod! God!â â

MASTER: âDo you understand the views of teachers like him? According to them, one must first practise spiritual discipline: self-restraint, self-control, forbearance, and the like. Their aim is to attain NirvÄna. They are followers of VedÄnta. They constantly discriminate, saying, âBrahman alone is real, and the world illusory.â But this is an extremely difficult path. If the world is illusory, then you too are illusory. The teacher who gives the instruction is equally illusory. His words, too, are as illusory as a dream.

âBut this experience is beyond the reach of the ordinary man. Do you know what it is like? If you burn camphor nothing remains. When wood is burnt at least a little ash is left. Finally, after the last analysis, the devotee goes into samÄdhi. Then he knows nothing whatsoever of âIâ, âyouâ, or the universe.

âPadmalochan was a man of deep wisdom. He had great respect for me, though at that time I constantly repeated the name of the Divine Mother. He was the court pundit of the MahÄrÄjÄ of Burdwan. Once he came to Calcutta and went to live in a garden house near KÄmÄrhÄti. I felt a desire to see him and sent Hriday there to learn if the pundit had any vanity. I was told that he had none. Then I met him. Though a man of great knowledge and scholarship, he began to weep on hearing me sing RÄmprasÄdâs devotional songs. We talked together a long while; conversation with nobody else gave me such satisfaction. He said to me, âGive up the desire for the company of devotees; otherwise people of all sorts will come to you and make you deviate from your spiritual ideal.â Once he entered into a controversy, by correspondence, with UtshavÄnanda, Vaishnavcharanâs guru. He told me an interesting incident. Once a meeting was called to decide which of the two deities, Åiva or BrahmÄ, was the greater. Unable to come to any decision, the pundits at last referred the matter to Padmalochan. With characteristic guilelessness he said: âHow do I know? Neither I nor any of my ancestors back to the fourteenth generation have seen Åiva or BrahmÄ.â About the renunciation of âwoman and goldâ, he said to me one day: âWhy have you given up those things? Such distinctions as âThis is money and that is clayâ are the outcome of ignorance.â What could I say to that? I replied: âI donât know all these things, my dear sir. But for my part, I cannot relish such things as money and the like.â

âThere was a pundit who was tremendously vain. He did not believe in the forms of God. But who can understand the inscrutable ways of the Divine? God revealed Himself to him as the Primal Power. This vision made the pundit unconscious for a long time. After regaining partial consciousness he uttered only the sound âKÄ! KÄ! KÄ!â He could not fully pronounce âKÄliâ.â

A DEVOTEE: âSir, you met Pundit VidyÄsÄgar. What did you think of him?â

MASTER: âVidyÄsÄgar has both scholarship and charity, but he lacks inner vision. Gold lies hidden within him. Had he but found it out, his activities would have been reduced; finally they would have stopped altogether. Had he but known that God resides in his heart, his mind would have been directed to God in thought and meditation. Some persons must perform selfless work a long time before they can practise dispassion and direct their minds to the spiritual ideal and at last be absorbed in God.

âThe activities that VidyÄsÄgar is engaged in are good. Charity is very noble. There is a great deal of difference between dayÄ, compassion, and mÄyÄ, attachment. DayÄ is good, but not mÄyÄ. MÄyÄ is love for oneâs relativesâoneâs wife, children, brother, sister, nephew, father, and mother. But dayÄ is the same love for all created beings without any distinction.â

M: âIs dayÄ also a bondage?â

MASTER: âYes, it is. But that concept is something far beyond the ordinary man. DayÄ springs from sattva. Sattva preserves, rajas creates, and tamas destroys. But Brahman is beyond the three gunas. It is beyond Prakriti.

âNone of the three gunas can reach Truth; they are like robbers, who cannot come to a public place for fear of being arrested. Sattva, rajas, and tamas are like so many robbers.

âListen to a story. Once a man was going through a forest, when three robbers fell upon him and robbed him of all his possessions. One of the robbers said, âWhatâs the use of keeping this man alive?â So saying, he was about to kill him with his sword, when the second robber interrupted him, saying: âOh, no! What is the use of killing him? Tie him hand and foot and leave him here.â The robbers bound his hands and feet and went away. After a while the third robber returned and said to the man: âAh, I am sorry. Are you hurt? I will release you from your bonds.â After setting the man free, the thief said: âCome with me. I will take you to the public highway.â After a long time they reached the road. Then the robber said: âFollow this road. Over there is your house.â At this the man said: âSir, you have been very good to me. Come with me to my house.â âOh, no!â the robber replied. âI canât go there. The police will know it.â

âThis world itself is the forest. The three robbers prowling here are sattva, rajas, and tamas. It is they that rob a man of the Knowledge of Truth. Tamas wants to destroy him. Rajas binds him to the world. But sattva rescues him from the clutches of rajas and tamas. Under the protection of sattva, man is rescued from anger, passion, and the other evil effects of tamas. Further, sattva loosens the bonds of the world. But sattva also is a robber. It cannot give him the ultimate Knowledge of Truth, though it shows him the road leading to the Supreme Abode of God. Setting him on the path, sattva tells him: âLook yonder. There is your home.â Even sattva is far away from the Knowledge of Brahman.

âWhat Brahman is cannot be described. Even he who knows It cannot talk about It. There is a saying that a boat, once reaching the âblack watersâ of the ocean, cannot come back.

âOnce four friends, in the course of a walk, saw a place enclosed by a wall. The wall was very high. They all became eager to know what was inside. One of them climbed to the top of the wall. What he saw on looking inside made him speechless with wonder. He only cried, âAh! Ah!â and dropped in. He could not give any information about what he saw. The others, too, climbed the wall, uttered the same cry, âAh! Ah!â, and jumped in. Now who could tell what was inside?

âSages like Jadabharata and DattÄtreya, after realizing Brahman, could not describe It. A manâs âIâ completely disappears when he goes into samÄdhi after attaining the Knowledge of Brahman. That is why RÄmprasÄd sang, addressing his mind:

If you should find the task too hard,

Call upon RÄmprasÄd for help.

The mind must completely merge itself in Knowledge. But that is not enough. âRÄmprasÄdâ, that is, the principle of âIâ, must vanish too. Then alone does one get the Knowledge of Brahman.â

A DEVOTEE: âSir, is it possible then that Åukadeva did not have the ultimate Knowledge?â

MASTER: âAccording to some people, Åukadeva only saw and touched the Ocean of Brahman; he did not dive into It. That is why he could return to the world and impart religious instruction. According to others, he returned to the world of name and form, after attaining the Knowledge of Brahman, for the purpose of teaching others. He had to recite the BhÄgavata to King Parikshit and had to teach people in various ways; therefore God did not destroy his âIâ altogether. God kept in him the âego of Knowledgeâ.â

DEVOTEE: âCan one keep up an organization after attaining the Knowledge of Brahman?â

MASTER: âOnce I talked to Keshab Sen about the Knowledge of Brahman. He asked me to explain it further. I said, âIf I proceed further, then you wonât be able to preserve your organization and following.â âThen please stop here!â replied Keshab. (All laugh.) But still I said to Keshab: â âIâ and âmineâ indicate ignorance. Without ignorance one cannot have such a feeling as âI am the doer; these are my wife, children, possessions, name and fameâ.â Thereupon Keshab said, âSir, if one gave up the âIâ, nothing whatsoever would remain.â I reassured him and said: âI am not asking you to give up all of the âIâ. You should give up only the âunripe Iâ. The âunripe Iâ makes one feel: âI am the doer. These are my wife and children. I am a teacher.â Renounce this âunripe Iâ and keep the âripe Iâ, which will make you feel that you are the servant of God, His devotee, and that God is the Doer and you are His instrument.â â

DEVOTEE: âCan the âripe Iâ form an organization?â

MASTER: âI said to Keshab Sen that the âIâ that says, âI am a leader, I have formed this party, I am teaching peopleâ, is the âunripe Iâ. It is very difficult to preach religion. It is not possible to do so without receiving the commandment of God. The permission of God is necessary. Åukadeva had a command from God to recite the BhÄgavata. If, after realizing God, a man gets His command and becomes a preacher or teacher, then that preaching or teaching does no harm. His âIâ is not âunripeâ; it is âripeâ.

âI asked Keshab to give up this âunripe Iâ. The ego that feels, âI am the servant of God and lover of Godâ does not injure one. I said to him: âYou have been constantly talking of your organization and your followers. But people also go away from your organization.â Keshab answered: âIt is true, sir. After staying in it several years, people go to another organization. What is worse, on deserting me they abuse me right and left.â âWhy donât you study their nature?â I said. âIs there any good in making anybody and everybody a disciple?â

âI said to Keshab further: âYou should accept the Divine Mother, the Primal Energy. Brahman is not different from Its Åakti. What is Brahman is also Åakti. As long as a man remains conscious of the body, he is conscious of duality. It is only when a man tries to describe what he sees that he finds duality.â Keshab later on recognized KÄli.

âOne day when Keshab was here with his disciples, I said to him that I would like to hear him preach. He delivered a lecture in the chÄndni. Then we all sat by the bathing-ghÄt and had a long conversation. I said to him: âIt is BhagavÄn alone who in one form appears as bhakta, and in another as the BhÄgavata. Please repeat âBhÄgavataâBhaktaâBhagavÄnâ.â Keshab and his disciples repeated the words. Then I asked him to repeat âGuruâKrishnaâVaishnavaâ. Thereupon Keshab said: âSir, I should not go so far now. People will say that I have become an orthodox Hindu.â

âIt is extremely difficult to go beyond the three gunas. One cannot reach that state without having realized God. Man dwells in the realm of mÄyÄ. MÄyÄ does not permit him to see God. It has made him a victim of ignorance.

âOnce Hriday brought a bull-calf here. I saw, one day, that he had tied it with a rope in the garden, so that it might graze there. I asked him, âHriday, why do you tie the calf there every day?â âUncle.â he said, âI am going to send this calf to our village. When it grows strong I shall yoke it to the plough.â As soon as I heard these words I was stunned to think: âHow inscrutable is the play of the divine mÄyÄ! KÄmÄrpukur and Sihore6 are so far away from Calcutta! This poor calf must go all that way. Then it will grow, and at length it will be yoked to the plough. This is indeed the world! This is indeed mÄyÄ!â I fell down unconscious. Only after a long time did I regain consciousness.â

It was three or four oâclock in the afternoon. M. found Sri Ramakrishna seated on the couch in an abstracted mood. After some time he heard him talking to the Divine Mother. The Master said, âO Mother, why hast Thou given him only a particle?â Remaining silent a few moments, he added: âI understand it, Mother. That little bit will be enough for him and will serve Thy purpose. That little bit will enable him to teach people.â

Did the Master thus transmit spiritual powers to his disciples? Did he thus come to know that his disciples, after him, would go out into the world as teachers of men?

Rakhal was in the room. Sri Ramakrishna was still in a state of partial consciousness when he said to Rakhal: âYou were angry with me, werenât you? Do you know why I made you angry? There was a reason. Only then would the medicine work. The surgeon first brings an abscess to a head. Only then does he apply a herb so that it may burst and dry up.â

After a pause he went on: âYes, I have found Hazra to be like a piece of dry wood. Then why does he live here? This has a meaning too. The play is enlivened by the presence of trouble-makers like JatilÄ and KutilÄ.

(To M.) âOne must accept the forms of God. Do you know the meaning of the image of JagaddhÄtri? She is the Bearer of the Universe. Without Her support and protection the universe would fall from its place and be destroyed. The Divine Mother, JagaddhÄtri, reveals Herself in the heart of one who can control the mind, which may be compared to an elephant.â

RAKHAL: âThe mind is a mad elephant.â

MASTER: âTherefore the lion, the carrier of the Divine Mother, keeps it under control.â7

It was dusk. The evening service began in the temples. Sri Ramakrishna was chanting the names of the gods and goddesses. He was seated on the small couch, with folded hands, and became absorbed in contemplation of the Divine Mother. The world outside was flooded with moonlight, and the devotees inside the Masterâs room sat in silence and looked at his serene face.

In the mean time Govinda of BelghariÄ and some of his friends had entered the room. Sri Ramakrishna was still in a semi-conscious state. After a few minutes he said to the devotees: âTell me your doubts. I shall explain everything.â

Govinda and the other devotees looked thoughtful.

GOVINDA: âRevered sir, why does the Divine Mother have a black complexion?â8

MASTER: âYou see Her as black because you are far away from Her. Go near and you will find Her devoid of all colour. The water of a lake appears black from a distance. Go near and take the water in your hand, and you will see that it has no colour at all. Similarly, the sky looks blue from a distance. But look at the atmosphere near you; it has no colour. The nearer you come to God, the more you will realize that He has neither name nor form. If you move away from the Divine Mother, you will find Her blue, like the grass-flower. Is ÅyÄmÄ male or female? A man once saw the image of the Divine Mother wearing a sacred thread.9 He said to the worshipper: âWhat? You have put the sacred thread on the Motherâs neck!â The worshipper said: âBrother, I see that you have truly known the Mother. But I have not yet been able to find out whether She is male or female; that is why I have put the sacred thread on Her image.â

âThat which is ÅyÄmÄ is also Brahman. That which has form, again, is without form. That which has attributes, again, has no attributes. Brahman is Åakti; Åakti is Brahman. They are not two. These are only two aspects, male and female, of the same Reality, Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute.â

GOVINDA: âWhat is the meaning of âyogamÄyÄâ?â

MASTER: âIt signifies the yoga, or union, of Purusha10 and Prakriti.11 Whatever you perceive in the universe is the outcome of this union. Take the image of Åiva and KÄli. KÄli stands on the bosom of Åiva; Åiva lies under Her feet like a corpse; KÄli looks at Åiva. All this denotes the union of Purusha and Prakriti. Purusha is inactive; therefore Åiva lies on the ground like a corpse. Prakriti performs all Her activities in conjunction with Purusha. Thus She creates, preserves, and destroys. That is also the meaning of the conjoined images of RÄdhÄ and Krishna. On account of that union, again, the images are slightly inclined toward each other.

âTo denote this union, Sri Krishna wears a pearl in His nose, RÄdhÄ a blue stone in hers. RÄdhÄ has a fair complexion, bright as the pearl. Sri Krishnaâs is blue. For this reason RÄdhÄ wears the blue stone. Further, Krishnaâs apparel is yellow, and RÄdhÄâs blue.

âWho is the best devotee of God? It is he who sees, after the realization of Brahman, that God alone has become all living beings, the universe, and the twenty-four cosmic principles. One must discriminate at first, saying âNot this, not thisâ, and reach the roof. After that one realizes that the steps are made of the same materials as the roof, namely, brick, lime, and brick-dust. The devotee realizes that it is Brahman alone that has become all theseâthe living beings, the universe, and so on.

âMere dry reasoningâI spit on it! I have no use for it! (The Master spits on the ground.)

âWhy should I make myself dry through mere reasoning? May I have unalloyed love for the Lotus Feet of God as long as the consciousness of âIâ and âyouâ remains with me!

(To Govinda) âSometimes I say, âThou art verily I, and I am verily Thou.â Again I feel, âThou art Thou.â Then I do not find any trace of âIâ. It is Åakti alone that becomes flesh as God Incarnate. According to one school of thought, RÄma and Krishna are but two waves in the Ocean of Absolute Bliss and Consciousness.

âChaitanya, Consciousness, is awakened after Advaita-jnÄna, the Knowledge of the non-dual Brahman. Then one perceives that God alone exists in all beings as Consciousness. After this realization comes Änanda, Bliss. Advaita, Chaitanya, and NityÄnanda.12

(To M.) âLet me ask you not to disbelieve in the forms of God. Have faith in Godâs forms. Meditate on that form of God which appeals to your mind.

(To Govinda) âThe fact is that one does not feel the longing to know or see God as long as one wants to enjoy worldly objects. The child forgets everything when he plays with his toys. Try to cajole him away from play with a sweetmeat; you will not succeed. He will eat only a bit of it. When he relishes neither the sweetmeat nor his play, then he says, âI want to go to my mother.â He doesnât care for the sweetmeat any more. If a man whom he doesnât know and has never seen says to the child, âCome along; I shall take you to your motherâ, the child follows him. The child will go with anyone who will carry him to his mother.

âThe soul becomes restless for God when one is through with the enjoyment of worldly things. Then a person has only one thoughtâhow to realize God. He listens to whatever anyone says to him about God.â

M. (to himself): âAlas! The soul becomes restless for God only when one is through with the enjoyment of worldly things.â

August 18, 1883

Sri Ramakrishna was at Balaram Boseâs house in Calcutta. He was explaining the mystery of Divine Incarnation to the devotees.

MASTER: âIn order to bring people spiritual knowledge, an Incarnation of God lives in the world in the company of devotees, cherishing an attitude of love for God. It is like going up and coming down the stairs after having once reached the roof. In order to reach the roof, other people should follow the path of devotion, as long as they have not attained Knowledge and become free of desire. The roof can be reached only when all desires are done away with. The shopkeeper does not go to bed before finishing his accounts. He goes to sleep only when his accounts are finished.

(To M.) âA man will certainly succeed if he will take the plunge. Success is sure for such a man.

âWell, what do you think of the worship conducted by Keshab, Shivanath, and the other BrÄhmo leaders?â

M: âThey are satisfied, as you say, with describing the garden, but they seldom speak of seeing the Master of the garden. Describing the garden is the beginning and end of their worship.â

MASTER: âYou are right. Our only duty is to seek the Master of the garden and speak to Him. The only purpose of life is to realize God.â

Sri Ramakrishna then went to Adharâs house. After dusk he sang and danced in Adharâs drawing-room. M., Rakhal, and other devotees were present. After the music he sat down, still in an ecstatic mood. He said to Rakhal: âThis religious fervour13 is not like rain in the rainy season, which comes in torrents and goes in torrents. It is like an image of Åiva that has not been set up by human hands but is a natural one that has sprung up, as it were, from the bowels of the earth. The other day you left Dakshineswar in a temper. I prayed to the Divine Mother to forgive you.â

The Master was still in an abstracted mood and said to Adhar, âMy son, meditate on the Deity whose name you chanted.â With these words he touched Adharâs tongue with his finger and wrote something on it. Did the Master thereby impart spirituality to Adhar?

1 GaurÄnga and NityÄnanda.

2 At one time NityÄnanda was beaten by the ruffians JagÄi and MÄdhÄi, who later were converted to spiritual life by his love.

4 A premature child is generally weak and fearful.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# THE MASTER AND M.

August 19, 1883

IT WAS SUNDAY, the first day after the full moon. Sri Ramakrishna was resting after his noon meal. The midday offering had been made in the temples, and the temple doors were closed.

In the early afternoon the Master sat up on the small couch in his room. M. prostrated himself before him and sat on the floor. The Master was talking to him on the philosophy of VedÄnta.

MASTER (to M.): âSelf-Knowledge is discussed in the AshtÄvakra SamhitÄ. The non-dualists say, âSohamâ, that is, âI am the Supreme Self.â This is the view of the sannyÄsis of the VedÄntic school. But this is not the right attitude for householders, who are conscious of doing everything themselves. That being so, how can they declare, âI am That, the actionless Supreme Selfâ? According to the non-dualists the Self is unattached. Good and bad, virtue and vice, and the other pairs of opposites, cannot in any way injure the Self, though they undoubtedly afflict those who have identified themselves with their bodies. Smoke soils the wall, certainly, but it cannot in any way affect ÄkÄÅa, space. Following the VedÄntists of this class, Krishnakishore used to say, âI am Khaâ, meaning ÄkÄÅa. Being a great devotee, he could say that with some justification; but it is not becoming for others to do so.

âBut to feel that one is a free soul is very good. By constantly repeating, âI am free, I am freeâ, a man verily becomes free. On the other hand, by constantly repeating, âI am bound, I am boundâ, he certainly becomes bound to worldliness. The fool who says only, âI am a sinner, I am a sinnerâ, verily drowns himself in worldliness. One should rather say: âI have chanted the name of God. How can I be a sinner? How can I be bound?â

(To M.) âYou see, I am very much depressed today. Hriday has written me that he is very ill. Why should I feel dejected about it? Is it because of mÄyÄ or dayÄ?â

M. could not find suitable words for a reply, and remained silent.

MASTER: âDo you know what mÄyÄ is? It is attachment to relativesâparents, brother and sister, wife and children, nephew and niece. DayÄ means love for all created beings. Now what is this, my feeling about Hriday? Is it mÄyÄ or dayÄ? But Hriday did so much for me: he served me whole-heartedly and nursed me when I was ill. But later he tormented me also. The torment became so unbearable that once I was about to commit suicide by jumping into the Ganges from the top of the embankment. But he did much to serve me. Now my mind will be at rest if he gets some money. But whom shall I ask for it? Who likes to speak about such things to our rich visitors?â

At two or three oâclock in the afternoon Adhar Sen and Balaram arrived. After saluting Sri Ramakrishna, they sat on the floor and asked him if he was well. The Master said, âYes, I am well physically, but a little troubled in mind.â He did not refer to Hriday and his troubles.

The conversation turned to the Goddess SimhavÄhini.

MASTER: âYes, I visited the Goddess. She is worshipped by one of the branches of the Mallick family of Calcutta. This branch of the family is now in straitened circumstances, and the house they live in is dilapidated. The walls and floor are spotted with moss and pigeon-droppings, and the cement and plaster are crumbling. But other branches of the Mallick family are well off. This branch has no signs of prosperity. (To M.) Well, what does that signify?â

M. remained silent.

MASTER: âThe thing is that everyone must reap the result of his past karma. One must admit the influence of tendencies inherited from past births and the result of the prÄrabdha karma. Nevertheless, in that dilapidated house I saw the face of the Goddess radiating a divine light. One must believe in the Divine Presence in the image.

âOnce I went to Vishnupur. The rÄjÄ of that place has several fine temples. In one of them there is an image of the Divine Mother, called Mrinmayi.1 There are several lakes near the temple, known as the LÄlbÄndh, KrishnabÄndh, and so on. In the water of one of the lakes I could smell the ointments that women use for their hair. How do you explain that? I didnât know at that time that the woman devotees offer ointments to the Goddess Mrinmayi while visiting Her temple. Near the lake I went into samÄdhi, though I had not yet seen the image in the temple. In that state I saw the divine form from the waist up, rising from the water.â

In the mean time other devotees had arrived. Someone referred to the political revolution and civil war in KÄbul. A devotee said that Yakub KhÄn, the Ämir of Afghanistan, had been deposed. He told the Master that the Ämir was a great devotee of God.

MASTER: âBut you must remember that pleasure and pain are the characteristics of the embodied state. In Kavi Kankanâs Chandi it is written that KÄluvir was sent to prison and a heavy stone placed on his chest. Yet KÄlu was born as a result of a boon from the Divine Mother of the Universe. Thus pleasure and pain are inevitable when the soul accepts a body. Again, take the case of Srimanta, who was a great devotee. Though his mother, KhullanÄ, was very much devoted to the Divine Mother, there was no end to his troubles. He was almost beheaded. There is also the instance of the wood-cutter who was a great lover of the Divine Mother. She appeared before him and showed him much grace and love; but he had to continue his profession of wood-cutting and earn his livelihood by that arduous work. Again, while Devaki, Krishnaâs mother, was in prison, she had a vision of God Himself endowed with four hands, holding mace, discus, conch-shell, and lotus. But with all that she couldnât get out of prison.â

M: âWhy speak only of getting out of prison? This body is the source of all our troubles. Devaki should have been freed from the body.â

MASTER: âThe truth is that one must reap the result of the prÄrabdha karma. The body remains as long as the results of past actions do not completely wear away. Once a blind man bathed in the Ganges and as a result was freed from his sins. But his blindness remained all the same. (All laugh.) It was because of his evil deeds in his past birth that he had to undergo that affliction.â

M: âYes, sir. The arrow that has already left the bow is beyond our control.â

MASTER: âHowever much a bhakta may experience physical joy and sorrow, he always has knowledge and the treasure of divine love. This treasure never leaves him. Take the PÄndava brothers for instance. Though they suffered so many calamities, they did not lose their God-Consciousness even once. Where can you find men like them, endowed with so much knowledge and devotion?â

Just then Narendra and Colonel Viswanath Upadhyaya entered the room. Narendra was then twenty-two years old and studying in college. They saluted the Master and sat down. The Master requested Narendra to sing. The tÄnpurÄ hung on the west wall of the room. The devotees fixed their eyes on Narendra as he began to tune the drums.

MASTER (to Narendra): âThe drums donât sound as well as before.â

CAPTAIN: âThey are now full. Therefore they are quiet, like a vessel filled with water. Or they are like a holy man, who remains silent when his heart is full of God-Consciousness.â

MASTER: âBut what about sages like NÄrada?â

CAPTAIN: âThey talked because they were moved by the sufferings of others.â

MASTER: âYou are right. After attaining samÄdhi, NÄrada, Åukadeva, and others came down a few steps, as it were, to the plane of normal consciousness and broke their silence out of compassion for the sufferings of others and to help them.â

Narendra began to sing:

Oh, when will dawn for me that day of blessedness

When He who is all Good, all Beauty, and all Truth,

Will light the inmost shrine of my heart?

When shall I sink at last, ever beholding Him,

Into that Ocean of Delight? â¦

No sooner had the Master heard a few words of the song than he went into deep samÄdhi. He sat with folded hands, facing the east. His body was erect and his mind completely bereft of worldly consciousness. His breath had almost stopped. With unwinking eyes he sat motionless as a picture on a canvas. His mind had dived deep into the Ocean of Godâs Beauty.

Narendra left the room and went to the east verandah, where Hazra was seated on a blanket, with a rosary in his hand. They fell to talking. Other devotees arrived. The Master came down from samÄdhi and looked around. He could not find Narendra. The tÄnpurÄ was lying on the floor. He noticed that the earnest eyes of the devotees were riveted on him.

MASTER (referring to Narendra): âHe has lighted the fire. Now it doesnât matter whether he stays in the room or goes out.

(To Captain and the other devotees) âAttribute to yourselves the bliss of God-Consciousness; then you too will experience ineffable joy. The bliss of God-Consciousness always exists in you. It is only hidden by the veiling and projecting power of mÄyÄ.2 The less you are attached to the world, the more you love God.â

CAPTAIN: âThe farther you proceed toward your home in Calcutta, the farther you leave Benares behind. Again, the farther you proceed toward Benares, the farther behind you leave your home.â

MASTER: âAs RÄdhÄ advanced toward Krishna, she could smell more and more of the sweet fragrance of His body. The nearer you approach to God, the more you feel His love. As the river approaches the ocean it increasingly feels the flow of the tides.

âThe jnÄni experiences God-Consciousness within himself; it is like the upper Ganges, flowing in only one direction. To him the whole universe is illusory, like a dream; he is always established in the Reality of Self. But with the lover of God the case is different. His feeling does not flow in only one direction. He feels both the ebb-tide and the flood-tide of divine emotion. He laughs and weeps and dances and sings in the ecstasy of God. The lover of God likes to sport with Him. In the Ocean of God-Consciousness he sometimes swims, sometimes goes down, and sometimes rises to the surfaceâlike pieces of ice in the water. (Laughter.)

âThe jnÄni seeks to realize Brahman. But the ideal of the bhakta is the Personal Godâa God endowed with omnipotence and with the six treasures. Yet Brahman and Åakti are, in fact, not different. That which is the Blissful Mother is, again, Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute. They are like the gem and its lustre. When one speaks of the lustre of the gem, one thinks of the gem; and again, when one speaks of the gem, one refers to its lustre. One cannot conceive of the lustre of the gem without thinking of the gem, and one cannot conceive of the gem without thinking of its lustre.

âExistence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute is one, and one only. But It is associated with different limiting adjuncts on account of the different degrees of Its manifestation. That is why one finds various forms of God. The devotee sings, âO my Divine Mother, Thou art all these!â Wherever you see actions, like creation, preservation, and dissolution, there is the manifestation of Åakti. Water is water whether it is calm or full of waves and bubbles. The Absolute alone is the Primordial Energy, which creates, preserves, and destroys. Thus it is the same âCaptainâ, whether he remains inactive or performs his worship or pays a visit to the Governor General. Only we designate him by different names at different times.â

CAPTAIN: âYes, sir, that is so.â

MASTER: âI said those words to Keshab Sen.â

CAPTAIN: âKeshab is not an orthodox Hindu. He adopts manners and customs according to his own whim. He is a well-to-do gentleman and not a holy man.â

MASTER (to the other devotees): âCaptain forbids me to go to see Keshab.â

CAPTAIN: âBut, sir, you act as you will. What can I do?â

MASTER (sharply): âWhy shouldnât I go to see Keshab? You feel at ease when you go to the Governor Generalâs house,3 and for money at that. Keshab thinks of God and chants His name. Isnât it you who are always saying that God Himself has become the universe and all its living beings? Doesnât God dwell in Keshab also?â

With these words the Master left the room abruptly and went to the northeast verandah. Captain and the other devotees remained, waiting for his return. M. accompanied the Master to the verandah, where Narendra was talking with Hazra. Sri Ramakrishna knew that Hazra always indulged in dry philosophical discussions. Hazra would say: âThe world is unreal, like a dream. Worship, food offerings to the Deity, and so forth, are only hallucinations of the mind. The aim of spiritual life is to meditate on oneâs own real Self.â Then he would repeat, âI am He.â But, with all that, he had a soft corner in his heart for money, material things, and peopleâs attention.

Sri Ramakrishna smiled and said to Hazra and Narendra, âHello! What are you talking about?â

NARENDRA (smiling): âOh, we are discussing a great many things. They are rather too deep for others.â

MASTER (with a smile): âBut Pure Knowledge and Pure Love are one and the same thing. Both lead the aspirants to the same goal. The path of love is much the easier.â

Narendra quoted a song:

O Mother, make me mad with Thy love!

What need have I of knowledge or reason?

Narendra said to M. that he had been reading a book by Hamilton, who wrote: âA learned ignorance is the end of philosophy and the beginning of religion.â

MASTER (to M.): âWhat does that mean?â

Narendra explained the sentence in Bengali. The Master beamed with joy and said in English, âThank you! Thank you!â Everyone laughed at the charming way he said these words. They knew that his English vocabulary consisted of only half a dozen words.

It was almost dusk when most of the devotees, including Narendra, took leave of the Master. Sri Ramakrishna went out and looked at the Ganges for a few minutes from the west porch. Two priests were bathing in preparation for the evening worship. Young men of the village were strolling in the garden or standing on the concrete embankment, gazing at the murmuring river. Others, perhaps more thoughtful, were walking about in the solitude of the Panchavati.

It became dark. The maidservant lighted the lamp in Sri Ramakrishnaâs room and burnt incense. The evening worship began in the twelve temples of Åiva and in the shrines of Krishna and KÄli.

As it was the first day after the full moon, the moonlight soon flooded the tops of the trees and temples, and touched with silver the numberless waves of the sacred river.

The Master returned to his room. After bowing to the Divine Mother, he clapped his hands and chanted the sweet names of God. A number of holy pictures hung on the walls of the room. Among others, there were pictures of Dhruva, PrahlÄda, KÄli, RÄdhÄ-Krishna, and the coronation of RÄma. The Master bowed low before the pictures and repeated the holy names. Then he repeated the holy words, âBrahmaâÄtmÄâBhagavÄn; BhÄgavataâBhaktaâBhagavÄn; BrahmaâÅakti, ÅaktiâBrahma; Veda, PurÄna, Tantra, GÄ«tÄ, GÄyatri.â Then he said: âI have taken refuge at Thy feet, O Divine Mother; not I, but Thou. I am the machine and Thou art the Operatorâ, and so on.

While the Master was meditating in this fashion on the Divine Mother, a few devotees, coming in from the garden, gathered in his room. Sri Ramakrishna sat down on the small couch. He said to the devotees: âNarendra, Bhavanath, Rakhal, and devotees like them belong to the group of the nityasiddhas; they are eternally free. Religious practice on their part is superfluous. Look at Narendra. He doesnât care about anyone. One day he was going with me in Captainâs carriage. Captain wanted him to take a good seat, but Narendra didnât even look at him. He is independent even of me. He doesnât tell me all he knows, lest I should praise his scholarship before others. He is free from ignorance and delusion. He has no bonds. He is a great soul. He has many good qualities. He is expert in music, both as a singer and player, and is also a versatile scholar. Again, he keeps his passions under control and says that he will never marry. There is a close friendship between Narendra and Bhavanath; they are just like man and woman. Narendra doesnât come here very often. That is good, for I am overwhelmed by his presence.â

Monday, August 20, 1883

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on his bed, inside the mosquito net, meditating. It was about eight oâclock in the evening. M. was sitting on the floor with his friend Hari Babu. Hari, a young man of twenty-eight, had lost his wife about eleven years before and had not married a second time. He was much devoted to his parents, brothers, and sisters.

Hazra was living at Dakshineswar. Rakhal lived with the Master, though now and then he stayed at Adharâs house. Narendra, Bhavanath, Adhar, M., Ram, Manomohan, and other devotees visited the Master almost every week.

Hriday, Sri Ramakrishnaâs nephew, was ill in his home in the country. The Master was worried about him. One of the devotees had sent him a little money, but the Master did not know it.

When Sri Ramakrishna came out of the mosquito net and sat on the small couch, the devotees saluted him.

MASTER (to M.): âI was meditating inside the net. It occurred to me that meditation, after all, was nothing but the imagining of a form, and so I did not enjoy it. One gets satisfaction if God reveals Himself in a flash. Again, I said to myself, âWho is it that meditates, and on whom does he meditate?â â

M: âYes, sir. You said that God Himself has become everythingâthe universe and all living beings. Even he who meditates is God.â

MASTER: âWhat is more, one cannot meditate unless God wills it. One can meditate when God makes it possible for one to do so. What do you say?â

M: âTrue, sir. You feel like that because there is no âIâ in you. When there is no ego, one feels like that.â

MASTER: âBut it is good to have a trace of ego, which makes it possible for a man to feel that he is the servant of God. As long as a man thinks that it is he who is doing his duties, it is very good for him to feel that God is the Master and he Godâs servant. When one is conscious of doing work, one should establish with God the relationship of servant and Master.â

M. was always reflecting on the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

MASTER (to M.): âLike the ÄkÄÅa, Brahman is without any modification. It has become manifold because of Åakti. Again, Brahman is like fire, which itself has no colour. The fire appears white if you throw a white substance into it, red if you throw a red, black if you throw a black. The three gunasâsattva, rajas, and tamasâbelong to Åakti alone. Brahman Itself is beyond the three gunas. What Brahman is cannot be described. It is beyond words. That which remains after everything is eliminated by the VedÄntic process of âNot this, not thisâ, and which is of the nature of Bliss, is Brahman.

âSuppose the husband of a young girl has come to his father-in-lawâs house and is seated in the drawing-room with other young men of his age. The girl and her friends are looking at them through the window. Her friends do not know her husband and ask her, pointing to one young man, âIs that your husband?â âNoâ, she answers, smiling. They point to another young man and ask if he is her husband. Again she answers no. They repeat the question, referring to a third, and she gives the same answer. At last they point to her husband and ask, âIs he the one?â She says neither yes nor no, but only smiles and keeps quiet. Her friends realize that he is her husband.

âOne becomes silent on realizing the true nature of Brahman.

(To M.) âWell, why do I talk so much?â

M: âYou talk in order to awaken the spiritual consciousness of the devotees. You once said that when an uncooked luchi is dropped into boiling ghee it makes a sizzling noise.â

The Master began to talk to M. about Hazra.

MASTER: âDo you know the nature of a good man? He never troubles others. He doesnât harass people. The nature of some people is such that when they go to a feast they want special seats. A man who has true devotion to God never makes a false step, never gives others trouble for nothing.

âIt is not good to live in the company of bad people. A man should stay away from them and thus protect himself. (To M.) Isnât that so?â

M: âYes, sir. The mind sinks far down in the company of the wicked. But it is quite different with a hero, as you say.â

MASTER: âHow is that?â

M: âWhen a fire is feeble it goes out when even a small stick is thrown into it; but a blazing fire is not affected even if a plantain-tree is thrown into it. The tree itself is burnt to ashes.â

The Master asked M. about his friend Hari Babu.

M: âHe has come here to pay you his respects. He lost his wife long ago.â

MASTER (to Hari): âWhat kind of work do you do?â

M: âNothing in particular. But at home he takes good care of his parents and his brothers and sisters.â

MASTER (with a smile): âHow is that? You are like âElder, the pumpkin-cutterâ. You are neither a man of the world nor a devotee of God. That is not good. You must have seen the sort of elderly man who lives in a family and is always ready, day or night, to entertain the children. He sits in the parlour and smokes the hubble-bubble. With nothing in particular to do, he leads a lazy life. Now and again he goes to the inner court and cuts a pumpkin; for, since women do not cut pumpkins, they send the children to ask him to come and do it. That is the extent of his usefulnessâhence his nickname, âElder, the pumpkin-cutterâ.

âYou must do âthisâ as well as âthatâ. Do your duties in the world, and also fix your mind on the Lotus Feet of the Lord. Read books of devotion like the BhÄgavata or the life of Chaitanya when you are alone and have nothing else to do.â

It was about ten oâclock. Sri Ramakrishna finished a light supper of farina pudding and one or two luchis. After saluting him, M. and his friend took their leave.

Friday, September 7, 1883

Sri Ramakrishna and M. were talking in the Masterâs room at half past seven in the evening. No one else was present.

MASTER: âThe other day I went to Calcutta. As I drove along the streets in the carriage, I observed that everyoneâs attention was fixed on low things. Everyone was brooding over his stomach and running after nothing but food. Everyoneâs mind was turned to âwoman and goldâ. I saw only one or two with their attention fixed on higher things, with their minds turned to God.â

M: âThe present age has aggravated this stomach-worry. Trying to imitate the English, people have turned their attention to more luxuries; therefore their wants have also increased.â

MASTER: âWhat do the English think about God?â

M: âThey believe in a formless God.â

MASTER: âThat is also one of our beliefs.â

For a time Master and disciple remained silent. Then Sri Ramakrishna began to describe his experiences of Brahman.

He put a few grains of rice into everybodyâs mouth. I too tasted a little.

âAnother day I saw rice, vegetables, and other food-stuff, and filth and dirt as well, lying around. Suddenly the soul came out of my body and, like a flame, touched everything. It was like a protruding tongue of fire and tasted everything once, even the excreta. It was revealed to me that all these are one Substance, the non-dual and indivisible Consciousness.

âAnother day4 it was revealed to me that I had devoteesâmy intimate companions, my very own. Thereafter I would climb to the roof of the kuthi as soon as the bells and the conch-shells of the evening service sounded in the temples, and cry out with a longing heart: âOh, where are you all? Come here! I am dying to see you!â

(To M.) âWell, what do you think of these visions?â

M: âGod sports through you. This I have realized, that you are the instrument and God is the Master. God has created other beings as if with a machine, but yourself with His own hands.â

Both remained silent for some time.

M: âWhy should your visions not be real? If they are unreal, then the world is still more unreal; for there is only one mind that is the instrument of perception. Your pure mind sees those visions, and our ordinary minds see worldly objects.â

M. was silent. He said to himself: âThe Master referred to âthe sun at dawnâ and âthe tree unrecognizable by manâ. Did he mean an Incarnation of God? Is this the play of God through man? Is the Master himself an Incarnation? Was this why he cried to the devotees from the roof of the kuthi: âWhere are you? Come to me!â?â

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the steps of the southeast verandah of the KÄli temple. Rakhal, M., and Hazra were with him. He talked light-heartedly about his boyhood days.

When it was dusk he returned to his room and sat down on the small couch. Soon he went into samÄdhi and in that state began to talk to the Divine Mother. Again he spoke to Her, perhaps praying about an intimate disciple: âMother, please make him stainless. Well, Mother, why have You given him only a particle?â Remaining silent a moment, he said: âOh, I see. That will be enough for Your work.â

In the same state he said, addressing the devotees: âThat which is Brahman is verily Åakti. I address That, again, as the Mother. Some of the devotees wondered, âIs Sri Ramakrishna an Incarnation of God, like Krishna, Chaitanya, and Christ?â

Sunday, September 9, 1883

As the conversation went on, several Bengali gentlemen entered the room and, after saluting the Master, sat down. One of them was already known to Sri Ramakrishna. Wonât you admit the injunctions of Åiva? Åiva Himself is the author of the Tantra, which prescribes various disciplines, including the âheroicâ.â I said to him: âBut, my dear sir, I donât know. I donât like these ideas. To me every woman is a mother.â

âAchalananda did not support his own children. He said to me, âGod will support them.â I said nothing. But this is the way I felt about it: âWho will support your children? âThere was once a goldsmith whose tongue suddenly turned up and stuck to his palate. He looked like a man in samÄdhi. He became completely inert and remained so a long time. (All laugh.)

âThese are physical things and have nothing to do with God. There was a man who knew eighty-two postures and talked big about yoga-samÄdhi. But inwardly he was drawn to âwoman and goldâ. Was it for your aunt?â7 âNo,â said Ramlal, âit is meant for you.â I said to him, âGo and return the money at once, or I shall have no peace of mind.â Ramlal returned the money early in the morning and I felt relieved.

âOnce a rich man came here and said to me: âSir, you must do something so that I may win my lawsuit. I have heard of your reputation and so I have come here.â âMy dear sir,â I said to him, âyou have made a mistake. I am not the person you are looking for; Achalananda is your man.â

The visiting gentlemen took leave of the Master after saluting him. When they had departed, Sri Ramakrishna smiled and said to M., âYou can never make a thief listen to religion. (All laugh.)

âWell, what do you think of Narendra?â

M: âHe is splendid.â

MASTER: âYes, faith. What tremendous faith Krishnakishore had! He used to say: âI have spoken the name of God once. That is enough. How can I remain a sinner? What will one gain by speaking the name of NÄrÄyana only once?â At these remarks Krishnakishoreâs anger knew no bounds. The next time he came to this garden to pick flowers he wouldnât even look at Haladhari.

M: âYes, sir. That is true.â

MASTER: âI see people coming to the Ganges to bathe. They talk their heads off about everything under the sun. The widowed aunt says: âWithout me they cannot perform the DurgÄ PujÄ. I have to look after even the smallest detail. Again, I have to supervise everything when there is a marriage festival in the family, even the bed of the bride and groom.â â

M: âWhy should we blame them? How else will they pass the time?â

MASTER (with a smile): âSome people have their shrine rooms in their attics. The women arrange the offerings and flowers and make the sandal-paste. But, while doing so, they never say a word about God. The burden of the conversation is: âWhat shall we cook today? I couldnât get good vegetables in the market. Sri Ramakrishna and M. were now conversing alone.

M: âSir, if it is God Himself who has become everything, then why do people have so many different feelings?â

MASTER: âUndoubtedly God exists in all beings as the All-pervading Spirit, but the manifestations of His Power are different in different beings. In some places there is a manifestation of the power of Knowledge; in others, of the power of ignorance. In some places there is a greater manifestation of power than in others. Donât you see that among human beings there are cheats and gamblers, to say nothing of men who are like tigers. I think of them as the âcheat Godâ, the âtiger Godâ.â

M. (with a smile): âWe should salute them from a distance. If we go near the âtiger Godâ and embrace him, he may devour us.â

MASTER: âHe and His Power, Brahman and Its Powerânothing else exists but this. In a hymn to RÄma, NÄrada said: âO RÄma, You are Åiva, and SÄ«tÄ is Bhagavati; You are BrahmÄ, and SÄ«tÄ is BrahmÄni; You are Indra, and SÄ«tÄ is IndrÄni; You are NÄrÄyana, and SÄ«tÄ is Lakshmi. O RÄma, You are the symbol of all that is masculine, and SÄ«tÄ of all that is feminine.â â

Sri Ramakrishna reflected a moment and said softly: âShall I tell you what it is like? It is like waterâ¦ . One understands all this through spiritual discipline.

âBelieve in the form of God. It is only after attaining BrahmajnÄna that one sees non-duality, the oneness of Brahman and Its Åakti. Brahman and Åakti are identical, like fire and its power to burn. When a man thinks of fire, he must also think of its power to burn. Again, when he thinks of the power to burn, he must also think of fire. Further, Brahman and Åakti are like milk and its whiteness, water and its wetness.

âBut there is a stage beyond even BrahmajnÄna. After jnÄna comes vijnÄna. He who is aware of knowledge is also aware of ignorance. The sage VaÅishtha was stricken with grief at the death of his hundred sons. If a thorn has entered your foot, get another thorn and with its help take out the first; then throw away the second also.â

Householders should go into solitude now and then, to practise spiritual discipline in order to cultivate devotion to God; they should renounce mentally. But the sannyÄsi should renounce both mentally and physically.

âI once said to Keshab, âHow can a typhoid patient be cured if he remains in a room where a pitcher of water and a jar of pickles are kept?â Now and then one should live in solitude.â

A DEVOTEE: âSir, what do you think of the NavavidhÄn? It seems to me like a hotchpotch of everything.â

MASTER: âSome say it is a modern thing. That sets me wondering: âThen is the God of the BrÄhmo SamÄj a new God?â The BrÄhmos speak of their cult as the NavavidhÄn, as a New Dispensation. Well, it may be so. Who knows? There are six systems of philosophy; so perhaps it is like one of these.

âBut do you know where those who speak of the formless God make their mistake? It is where they say that God is formless only, and that those who differ with them are wrong.

âBut I know that God is both with and without form. And He may have many more aspects. It is possible for Him to be everything.

(To Ishan) âThe ChitÅakti, MahÄmÄyÄ, has become the twenty-four cosmic principles. One day as I was meditating, my mind wandered away to RashkÄâs house. He is a scavenger. I said to my mind, âStay there, you rogue!â The Divine Mother revealed to me that the men and women in this house were mere masks; inside them was the same Divine Power, Kundalini, that rises up through the six spiritual centres of the body.

âIs the Primal Energy man or woman? Once at KÄmÄrpukur I saw the worship of KÄli in the house of the Lahas. They put a sacred thread11 on the image of the Divine Mother. One man asked, âWhy have they put the sacred thread on the Motherâs person?â The master of the house said: âBrother, I see that you have rightly understood the Mother. But I do not yet know whether the Divine Mother is male or female.â

âIt is said that MahÄmÄyÄ swallowed Åiva. When the six centres in Her were awakened, Åiva came out through Her thigh. Then Åiva created the Tantra philosophy.

âTake refuge in the ChitÅakti, the MahÄmÄyÄ.â

ISHAN: âPlease bestow your grace on me.â

MASTER: âSay to God with a guileless heart, âO God, reveal Thyself to me.â And weep. Pray to God, âO God, keep my mind away from âwoman and goldâ.â And dive deep. Can a man get pearls by floating or swimming on the surface? He must dive deep.

âOne must get instruction from a guru. Once a man was looking for a stone image of Åiva. Someone said to him: âGo to a certain river. There you will find a tree. Near it is a whirlpool. Dive into the water there, and you will find the image of Åiva.â So I say that one must get instruction from a teacher.â

ISHAN: âThat is true, sir.â

MASTER: âIt is SatchidÄnanda that comes to us in the form of the guru. If a man is initiated by a human guru, he will not achieve anything if he regards his guru as a mere man. The guru should be regarded as the direct manifestation of God. Only then can the disciple have faith in the mantra given by the guru. Once a man has faith he achieves all. The Åudra Ekalavya learnt archery in the forest before a clay image of Drona. He worshipped the image as the living Drona; that by itself enabled him to attain mastery in archery.

âDonât mix intimately with brÄhmin pundits. Their only concern is to earn money. I have seen brÄhmin priests reciting the Chandi while performing the swastyayana. It is hard to tell whether they are reading the sacred book or something else. They turn half the pages without reading them. (All laugh.)

âA nail-knife suffices to kill oneself. One needs sword and shield to kill others. That is the purpose of the ÅÄstras.

âOne doesnât really need to study the different scriptures. If one has no discrimination, one doesnât achieve anything through mere scholarship, even though one studies all the six systems of philosophy. Call on God, crying to Him secretly in solitude. He will give all that you need.â

Sri Ramakrishna had heard that Ishan was building a house on the bank of the Ganges for the practice of spiritual discipline. He asked Ishan eagerly: âHas the house been built? Let me tell you that the less people know of your spiritual life, the better it will be for you. Devotees endowed with sattva meditate in a secluded corner or in a forest, or withdraw into the mind. Sometimes they meditate inside the mosquito net.â

Now and then Ishan invited Hazra to his house. Hazra had a craze for outward purity. Sri Ramakrishna often discouraged him in this.

MASTER (to Ishan): âLet me tell you another thing. Donât be over-fastidious about outward purity. Once a sÄdhu felt very thirsty. A water-carrier was carrying water in his skin water-bag, and offered the water to the holy man. The sÄdhu asked if the skin was clean. The carrier said: âRevered sir, my skin bag is perfectly clean. But inside your skin are all sorts of filthy things. That is why I can ask you to drink water from my skin. It wonât injure you.â By âyour skinâ, the carrier meant the body, the belly, and so forth.

âHave faith in the name of God. Then you wonât need even to go to holy places.â

Sri Ramakrishna sang, intoxicated with divine fervour:

Why should I go to GangÄ or GayÄ, to KÄÅi, KÄnchi, or PrabhÄs,

So long as I can breathe my last with KÄliâs name upon my lips? â¦

Ishan remained silent.

MASTER (to Ishan): âTell me if you have any more doubts.â

ISHAN: âYou said everything when you spoke of faith.â

MASTER: âGod can be realized by true faith alone. And the realization is hastened if you believe everything about God. The cow that picks and chooses its food gives milk only in dribblets, but if she eats all kinds of plants, then her milk flows in torrents.

âOnce I heard a story. A man heard the command of God that he should see his Ideal Deity in a ram. He at once believed it. It is God who exists in all beings.

âA guru said to his disciple, âIt is RÄma alone who resides in all bodies.â The disciple was a man of great faith. One day a dog snatched a piece of bread from him and started to run away. He ran after the dog, with a jar of butter in his hand, and cried again and again: âO RÄma, stand still a minute. That bread hasnât been buttered.â

âWhat tremendous faith Krishnakishore had! He used to say, âBy chanting âOm Krishna, Om RÄmaâ, one gets the result of a million sandhyÄs.â Once he said to me secretly, âI donât like the sandhyÄ and other devotions any more; but donât tell anyone.â

âSometimes I too feel that way. The Mother reveals to me that She Herself has become everything. One day I was coming from the pine-grove toward the Panchavati. A dog followed me. I stood still for a while near the Panchavati. The thought came to my mind that the Mother might say something to me through that dog.

âYou were absolutely right when you said that through faith alone one achieves all.â

ISHAN: âBut we are householders.â

MASTER: âWhat if you are? Through His grace even the impossible becomes possible. RÄmprasÄd sang, âThis world is a mere framework of illusion.â Another man composed a song by way of reply:

This very world is a mansion of mirth;

Here I can eat, here drink and make merry.

Janakaâs might was unsurpassed;

What did he lack of the world or the Spirit?

Holding to one as well as the other,

He drank his milk from a brimming cup!

âOne should first realize God through spiritual discipline in solitude, and then live in the world. Only then can one be a King Janaka. What can you achieve otherwise?

âFurther, take the case of Åiva. He has everythingâKÄrtika, GaneÅa, Lakshmi, and Sarasvati. Still, sometimes He dances in a state of divine fervour, chanting the name of RÄma, and sometimes He is absorbed in samÄdhi.â
