âCan everyone, by the mere wish, develop Knowledge and Love at the same time? It depends on the person. One bamboo is more hollow than another. Is it possible for all to comprehend the nature of God? Can a one-seer pot hold five seers of milk?â

M: âBut what about the grace of God? Through His grace a camel can pass through the eye of a needle.â

MASTER: âBut is it possible to obtain Godâs grace just like that? A beggar may get a penny, if he asks for it. But suppose he asks you right off for his train fare. How about that?â

M. stood silent. The Master, too, remained silent. Suddenly he said: âYes, it is true. Through the grace of God some may get both jnÄna and bhakti.â

M. saluted the Master and went back to the bel-tree.

At midday, finding that M. had not yet returned, Sri Ramakrishna started toward the bel-tree; but on reaching the Panchavati he met M. carrying his prayer carpet and water-jug. M. saluted the Master.

Sri Ramakrishna said to M: âI was coming to look for you. Because of your delay I thought you might have scaled the wall and run away. I watched your eyes this morning and felt apprehensive lest you should go away like Narayan Shastri. Then I said to myself: âNo, he wonât run away. He thinks a great deal before doing anything.â â

The same night the Master talked to M., Rakhal, Latu, Harish, and a few other devotees.

MASTER (to M.): âSome people give a metaphysical interpretation of the VrindÄvan episode of Sri Krishnaâs life. What do you say about it?â

M: âThere are various opinions. What if there are? You have told us the story of Bhishmadevaâs weeping, on his bed of arrows, because he could not understand anything of Godâs ways.

âAgain, you have told us that HanumÄn used to say: âI donât know any thing about the day of the week, the position of the stars, and so forth. I only meditate on RÄma.â

âFurther, you have said to us that in the last analysis there are two things only: Brahman and Its Power. You have also said that, after the attainment of BrahmajnÄna, a man realizes these two to be One, the One that has no two.â

MASTER: âYes, that is true. Your ideal is to reach the goal. You may reach it by going either through a thorny forest or along a good road.

âDiverse opinions certainly exist. NangtÄ used to say that the monks could not be feasted because of the diversity of their views. Once a feast was arranged for the sannyÄsis. Monks belonging to many sects were invited. Everyone claimed that his sect should be fed first, but no conclusion could be arrived at. At last they all went away and the food had to be given to the prostitutes.â

M: âTotapuri was indeed a great soul.â

MASTER: âBut Hazra says he was an ordinary man. Thereâs no use in discussing these things. Everyone says that his watch alone gives the correct time.

âYou see, Narayan Shastri developed a spirit of intense renunciation. He was a great scholar. He gave up his wife and went away. A man attains yoga when he completely effaces âwoman and goldâ from his mind. With some, the characteristics of the yogi are well marked.

âI shall have to tell you something of the six centres. The mind of the yogi passes through these, and he realizes God through His grace. Have you heard of the six centres?â

M: âThese are the âseven planesâ of the VedÄnta.â

MASTER: âNot the VedÄnta, but the Vedas. Do you know what the six centres are like? They are the âlotusesâ in the subtle body. The yogis see them. They are like the fruits and leaves of a wax tree.â

M: âYes, sir. The yogis can perceive them. I have read that there is a kind of glass through which a tiny object looks very big. Likewise, through yoga one can see those subtle lotuses.â

Following Sri Ramakrishnaâs direction, M. spent the night in the hut at the Panchavati. In the early hours of the morning he was singing alone:

I am without the least benefit of prayer and austerity, O Lord!

I am the lowliest of the lowly; make me pure with Thy hallowed touch.

One by one I pass my days in hope of reaching Thy Lotus Feet,

But Thee, alas, I have not foundâ¦ .

Suddenly M. glanced toward the window and saw the Master standing there. Sri Ramakrishnaâs eyes became heavy with tears as M. sang the line:

I am the lowliest of the lowly; make me pure with Thy hallowed touch.

M. sang again:

I shall put on the ochre robe and ear-rings made of conch-shell;

Thus, in the garb of a yogini, from place to place I shall wander,

Till I have found my cruel Hariâ¦ .

M. saw that the Master was walking with Rakhal.

Friday, December 21, 1883

In the morning the Master and M. were conversing alone under the bel-tree. The Master told him many secrets of spiritual discipline, exhorting him to renounce âwoman and goldâ. He further said that the mind at times becomes oneâs guru.

After his midday meal the Master went to the Panchavati wearing a beautiful yellow robe. Two or three Vaishnava monks were there, clad in the dress of their sect.

In the afternoon a monk belonging to the sect of NÄnak arrived. He was a worshipper of the formless God. Sri Ramakrishna asked him to meditate as well on God with form. The Master said to him: âDive deep; one does not get the precious gems by merely floating on the surface. God is without form, no doubt; but He also has form. By meditating on God with form one speedily acquires devotion; then one can meditate on the formless God. It is like throwing a letter away, after learning its contents, and then setting out to follow its instructions.â

Saturday, December 22, 1883

Rakhal, Harish, M., and Latu had been staying with Sri Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar. About nine oâclock in the morning the Master was sitting with them on the southeast verandah of his room, when Balaramâs father and Devendra Ghosh of ÅyÄmpukur arrived.

A DEVOTEE: âSir, how does one obtain love for God?â

MASTER: âGo forward. The king dwells beyond the seven gates. You can see him only after passing through all the gates.

âAt the time of the installation of AnnapurnÄ at ChÄnak, I said to Dwarika Babu: âLarge fish live in the deep water of a big lake. Throw some spiced bait into the water; then the fish will come, attracted by its smell; now and then they will make the water splash. Devotion and ecstatic love are like the spiced bait.

âGod sports in the world as man. He incarnates Himself as manâas in the case of Krishna, RÄma, and Chaitanya. Once I said to Keshab: âThe greatest manifestation of God is in man. There are small holes in the balk of a field, where crabs and fish accumulate in the rainy season. If you want to find them you must seek them in the holes. If you seek God, you must seek Him in the Incarnations.â

âThe Divine Mother of the Universe manifests Herself through this three-and-a-half cubit man. There is a song that says:

O Mother, what a machine is this that Thou hast made!

What pranks Thou playest with this toy

Three and a half cubits high! â¦

âOne needs spiritual practice in order to know God and recognize Divine Incarnations. Big fish live in the large lake, but to see them one must throw spiced bait in the water. There is butter in milk, but one must churn the milk to get it. There is oil in mustard-seed, but one must press the seed to extract the oil.â

DEVOTEE: âHas God form, or is He formless?â

MASTER: âWait, wait! First of all you must go to Calcutta; then only will you know where the MaidÄn, the Asiatic Society, and the Bengal Bank are located. If you want to go to the brÄhmin quarter of Khardaha, you must first of all go to Khardaha.

âWhy should it not be possible to practise the discipline of the formless God? But it is very difficult to follow that path. One cannot follow it without renouncing âwoman and goldâ. There must be complete renunciation, both inner and outer. You cannot succeed in this path if you have the slightest trace of worldliness.

âIt is easy to worship God with form. But it is not as easy as all that.

âOne should not discuss the discipline of the Impersonal God or the path of knowledge with a bhakta. Through great effort perhaps he is just cultivating a little devotion. You will injure it if you explain away everything as a mere dream.

âKabir was a worshipper of the Impersonal God. He did not believe in Åiva, KÄli, or Krishna. He used to make fun of them and say that KÄli lived on the offerings of rice and banana, and that Krishna danced like a monkey when the gopis clapped their hands. (All laugh.)

âOne who worships God without form perhaps sees at first the deity with ten arms, then the deity with four arms, then the Baby Krishna with two arms. At last he sees the Indivisible Light and merges in It.

âIt is said that sages like DattÄtreya and Jadabharata did not return to the relative plane after having the vision of Brahman. According to some people, Åukadeva tasted only a drop of that Ocean of Brahman-Consciousness. He saw and heard the rumbling of the waves of that Ocean, but he did not dive into It.

âA brahmachÄri once said to me, âOne who goes beyond KedÄr cannot keep his body alive.â Likewise, a man cannot preserve his body after attaining BrahmajnÄna.1 The body drops off in twenty-one days.

âThere was an infinite field beyond a high wall. Four friends tried to find out what was beyond the wall. Three of them, one after the other, climbed the wall, saw the field, burst into loud laughter, and dropped to the other side. These three could not give any information about the field. Only the fourth man came back and told people about it. He is like those who retain their bodies, even after attaining BrahmajnÄna, in order to teach others. Divine Incarnations belong to this class.

âPÄrvati was born as the daughter of King HimÄlaya. After Her birth She revealed to the king Her various divine forms. The father said: âWell, Daughter, You have shown me all these forms. That is nice. But You have another aspect, which is Brahman. Please show me that.â âFather,â replied PÄrvati, âif you seek the Knowledge of Brahman, then renounce the world and live in the company of holy men.â But King HimÄlaya insisted. Thereupon PÄrvati revealed Her Brahman-form, and immediately the king fell down unconscious.

âAll that I have just said belongs to the realm of reasoning. Brahman alone is real and the world illusoryâthat is reasoning. And everything but Brahman is like a dream. But this is an extremely difficult path. To one who follows it even the divine play in the world becomes like a dream and appears unreal; his âIâ also vanishes. The followers of this path do not accept the Divine Incarnation. It is a very difficult path. The lovers of God should not hear much of such reasoning.

âThat is why God incarnates Himself as man and teaches people the path of devotion. He exhorts people to cultivate self-surrender to God. Following the path of devotion, one realizes everything through His graceâboth Knowledge and Supreme Wisdom.

âGod sports in this world. He is under the control of His devotee. âÅyÄmÄ, the Divine Mother, is Herself tied by the cord of the love of Her devotee.â

âSometimes God becomes the magnet and the devotee the needle, and sometimes the devotee becomes the magnet and God the needle. The devotee attracts God to him. God is the Beloved of His devotee and is under his control.

âAccording to one school, the gopis of VrindÄvan, like YaÅodÄ, had believed in the formless God in their previous births; but they did not derive any satisfaction from this belief. That is why later on they enjoyed so much bliss in the company of Sri Krishna in the VrindÄvan episode of His life. One day Krishna said to the gopis: âCome along. I shall show you the Abode of the Eternal. Let us go to the JamunÄ for a bath.â As they dived into the water of the river, they at once saw Goloka. Next they saw the Indivisible Light. Thereupon YaÅodÄ exclaimed: âO Krishna, we donât care for these things any more. We would like to see You in Your human form. I want to take You in my arms and feed You.â

âSo the greatest manifestation of God is through His Incarnations. The devotee should worship and serve an Incarnation of God as long as He lives in a human body. âAt the break of day He disappears into the secret chamber of His House.â

âNot all, by any means, can recognize an Incarnation of God. Assuming a human body, the Incarnation falls a victim to disease, grief, hunger, thirst, and all such things, like ordinary mortals. RÄma wept for SÄ«tÄ. âBrahman weeps, entrapped in the snare of the five elements.â

âIt is said in the PurÄna that God, in His Incarnation as the Sow, lived happily with His young ones even after the destruction of HiranyÄksha.2 As the Sow, He nursed them and forgot all about His abode in heaven. At last Åiva killed the sow body with his trident, and God, laughing aloud, went to His own abode.â

In the afternoon Bhavanath arrived. Rakhal, M., Harish, and other devotees were in the room.

MASTER (to Bhavanath): âTo love an Incarnation of Godâthat is enough. Ah, what ecstatic love the gopis had for Krishna!â

Sri Ramakrishna began to sing, assuming the attitude of the gopis:

O Krishna! You are the Soul of my soulâ¦ .

Then he sang:

I am not going home, O friend,

For there it is hard for me to chant my Krishnaâs nameâ¦ .

And again:

O Friend, that day I stood at my door as You were going to the woodsâ¦ .

Continuing, the Master said: âWhen Krishna suddenly disappeared in the act of dancing and playing with the gopis, they were beside themselves with grief. Looking at a tree, they said: âO tree, you must be a great hermit. You must have seen Krishna. Otherwise, why do you stand there motionless, as if absorbed in samÄdhi?â Looking at the earth covered with green grass, they said: âO earth, you must have seen Krishna. Otherwise, why does your hair stand on end? You must have enjoyed the thrill of His touch.â Looking at the mÄdhavi creeper, they said, âO mÄdhavi, give us back our MÄdhava!â The gopis were intoxicated with ecstatic love for Krishna. Akrura came to VrindÄvan to take Krishna and BalarÄma to MathurÄ. When they mounted the chariot, the gopis clung to the wheels. They would not let the chariot move.â

Saying this, Sri Ramakrishna sang, assuming the attitude of Akrura:

Hold not, hold not the chariotâs wheels!

Is it the wheels that make it move?

The Mover of its wheels is Krishna,

By whose will the worlds are movedâ¦ .

MASTER: âÂ âIs it the wheels that make it move?â âBy whose will the worlds are moved.â âThe driver moves the chariot at his Masterâs bidding.â I feel deeply touched by these lines.â

Sunday, December 23, 1883

At nine oâclock in the morning Sri Ramakrishna was seated on the southwest porch of his room, with Rakhal, Latu, M., Harish, and some other devotees. M. had now been nine days with the Master at Dakshineswar. Earlier in the morning Manomohan had arrived from Konnagar on his way to Calcutta. Hazra, too, was present.

A Vaishnava was singing. Referring to one of the songs, Sri Ramakrishna said: âI didnât enjoy that song very much. The songs of the earlier writers seem to me to have more of the right spirit. Once I sang for NangtÄ at the Panchavati: âTo arms! To arms, O man! Death storms your house in battle array.â I sang another: âO Mother, I have no one else to blame: Alas! I sink in the well these very hands have dug.â

âNangtÄ, the VedÄntist, was a man of profound knowledge. The song moved him to tears though he didnât understand its meaning. Padmalochan also wept when I sang the songs of RÄmprasÄd about the Divine Mother. And he was truly a great pundit.â

After the midday meal Sri Ramakrishna rested a few minutes in his room. M. was sitting on the floor. The Master was delighted to hear the music that was being played in the nahabat. He then explained to M. that Brahman alone has become the universe and all living beings.

MASTER: âReferring to a certain place, someone once said to me: âNobody sings the name of God there. It has no holy atmosphere.â No sooner did he say this than I perceived that it was God alone who had become all living beings. They appeared as countless bubbles or reflections in the Ocean of SatchidÄnanda.

âAgain, I find sometimes that living beings are like so many pills made of Indivisible Consciousness. Once I was on my way to Burdwan from KÄmÄrpukur. At one place I ran to the meadow to see how living beings are sustained. I saw ants crawling there. It appeared to me that every place was filled with Consciousness.â

Hazra entered the room and sat on the floor.

MASTER: âAgain, I perceive that living beings are like different flowers with various layers of petals. They are also revealed to me as bubbles, some big, some small.â

While describing in this way the vision of different divine forms, the Master went into an ecstatic state and said, âI have become! I am here!â Uttering these words he went into samÄdhi. His body was motionless. He remained in that state a long time and then gradually regained partial consciousness of the world. He began to laugh like a boy and pace the room. His eyes radiated bliss as if he had seen a wondrous vision. His gaze was not fixed on any particular object, and his face beamed with joy. Still pacing the room, the Master said: âI saw the paramahamsa who stayed under the banyan tree walking thus with just such a smile. Am I too in that state of mind?â

He sat on the small couch and engaged in conversation with the Divine Mother.

MASTER: âI donât even care to know. Mother, may I have pure love for Thy Lotus Feet!

(To M.) âOne attains this state immediately after freeing oneself of all grief and desire.

(To the Divine Mother) âMother, Thou hast done away with my worship. Please see, Mother, that I donât give up all desire. Mother, the paramahamsa is but a child. Doesnât a child need a mother? Therefore Thou art the Mother and I am the child. How can the child live without the Mother?â

Sri Ramakrishna was talking to the Divine Mother in a voice that would have melted even a stone. Again he addressed Her, saying: âMere knowledge of Advaita! I spit on it! Thou dost exist as long as Thou dost keep the ego in me. The paramahamsa is but a child. Doesnât a child need a mother?â

M. sat there speechless and looked at the divine manifestation in the Master. He said to himself: âThe Master is an ocean of mercy that knows no motive. He has kept himself in the state of a paramahamsa that he might, as teacher, awaken the spiritual consciousness of myself and other earnest souls.â

M. further thought: âThe Master says, âAdvaitaâChaitanyaâNityÄnandaâ; that is to say, through the knowledge of the Non-dual Brahman one attains Consciousness and enjoys Eternal Bliss. The Master has not only attained the knowledge of non-duality but is in a state of Eternal Bliss. He is always drunk with ecstatic love for the Mother of the Universe.â

With folded hands Hazra looked at the Master and said every now and then: âHow blessed you are! How blessed you are!â

MASTER (to Hazra): âBut you have hardly any faith; you simply live here to add to the play, like JatilÄ and KutilÄ.â

In the afternoon M. paced the temple garden alone. He was deeply absorbed in the thought of the Master and was pondering the Masterâs words concerning the attainment of the exalted state of the paramahamsa, after the elimination of grief and desire. M. said to himself: âWho is this Sri Ramakrishna, acting as my teacher? Has God embodied Himself for our welfare? The Master himself says that no one but an Incarnation can come down to the phenomenal plane from the state of nirvikalpa samÄdhi.â

Monday, December 24, 1883

At eight oâclock in the morning Sri Ramakrishna and M. were talking together in the pine-grove at the northern end of the temple garden. This was the eleventh day of M.âs stay with the Master.

It was winter. The sun had just risen. The river was flowing north with the tide. Not far off could be seen the bel-tree where the Master had practised great spiritual austerities. Sri Ramakrishna faced the east as he talked to his disciple and told him about the Knowledge of Brahman.

MASTER: âThe formless God is real, and equally real is God with form. NangtÄ used to instruct me about the nature of SatchidÄnanda Brahman. He would say that It is like an infinite oceanâwater everywhere, to the right, left, above, and below. Water enveloped in water. It is the Water of the Great Cause, motionless. Waves spring up when It becomes active. Its activities are creation, preservation, and destruction.

âAgain, he used to say that Brahman is where reason comes to a stop. There is the instance of camphor. Nothing remains after it is burntânot even a trace of ash.

âBrahman is beyond mind and speech. A salt doll entered the ocean to measure its depth; but it did not return to tell others how deep the ocean was. It melted in the ocean itself.

âThe rishis once said to RÄma: âO RÄma, sages like BharadvÄja may very well call you an Incarnation of God, but we cannot do that. We adore the Word-Brahman.3 We do not want the human form of God.â RÄma smiled and went away, pleased with their adoration.

âBut the Nitya and the LÄ«lÄ are the two aspects of the same Reality. As I have said before, it is like the roof and the steps leading to it. The Absolute plays in many ways: as IÅvara, as the gods, as man, and as the universe. The Incarnation is the play of the Absolute as man. Do you know how the Absolute plays as man? It is like the rushing down of water from a big roof through a pipe; the power of SatchidÄnandaânay, SatchidÄnanda Itselfâdescends through the conduit of a human form as water descends through the pipe. Only twelve sages, BharadvÄja and the others, recognized RÄma as an Incarnation of God. Not everyone can recognize an Incarnation.

âIt is God alone who incarnates Himself as man to teach people the ways of love and knowledge. Well, what do you think of me?

âOnce my father went to GayÄ. There Raghuvir said to him in a dream, âI shall be born as your son.â Thereupon my father said to Him: âO Lord, I am a poor brÄhmin. How shall I be able to serve You?â âDonât worry about itâ, Raghuvir replied. âIt will be taken care of.â

âMy sister, Hridayâs mother, used to worship my feet with flowers and sandal-paste. One day I placed my foot on her head and said to her, âYou will die in Benares.â

âOnce Mathur Babu said to me: âFather, there is nothing inside you but God. Your body is like an empty shell. It may look from outside like a pumpkin, but inside there is nothingâneither flesh nor seed. Once I saw you as someone moving with a veil on.â

(To M.) âI am shown everything beforehand. Once I saw GaurÄnga and his devotees singing kirtan in the Panchavati. I think I saw Balaram there and you too.

âI wanted to know the experiences of GaurÄnga and was shown them at ÅyÄmbÄzÄr in our native district. A crowd gathered; they even climbed the trees and the walls; they stayed with me day and night. For seven days I had no privacy whatever. Thereupon I said to the Divine Mother, âMother, I have had enough of it.â

âI am at peace now. I shall have to be born once more. Therefore I am not giving all knowledge to my companions. (With a smile) Suppose I give you all knowledge; will you then come to me again so willingly?

âI recognized you on hearing you read the Chaitanya BhÄgavat.4 You are my own. The same substance, like father and son. All of you are coming here again. When you pull one part of the kalmi creeper, all the branches come toward you. You are all relativesâlike brothers. Suppose Rakhal, Harish, and the others had gone to Puri, and you were there too. Would you live separately?

âBefore you came here, you didnât know who you were. Now you will know. It is God who, as the guru, makes one know.

âNangtÄ told the story of the tigress and the herd of goats. Once a tigress attacked a herd of goats. A hunter saw her from a distance and killed her. The tigress was pregnant and gave birth to a cub as she expired. The cub began to grow in the company of the goats. At first it was nursed by the she-goats, and later on, as it grew bigger, it began to eat grass and bleat like the goats. Gradually the cub became a big tiger; but still it ate grass and bleated. When attacked by other animals, it would run away, like the goats. One day a fierce-looking tiger attacked the herd. It was amazed to see a tiger in the herd eating grass and running away with the goats at its approach. It left the goats and caught hold of the grass-eating tiger, which began to bleat and tried to run away. But the fierce tiger dragged it to the water and said: âNow look at your face in the water. You see, you have the pot-face of a tiger; it is exactly like mine.â Next it pressed a piece of meat into its mouth. At first the grass-eating tiger refused to eat the meat. Then it got the taste of the meat and relished it. At last the fierce tiger said to the grass-eater: âWhat a disgrace! You lived with the goats and ate grass like them!â And the other was really ashamed of itself.

âEating grass is like enjoying âwoman and goldâ. To bleat and run away like a goat is to behave like an ordinary man. Going away with the new tiger is like taking shelter with the guru, who awakens oneâs spiritual consciousness, and recognizing him alone as oneâs relative. To see oneâs face rightly is to know oneâs real Self.â

Sri Ramakrishna stood up. There was silence all around, disturbed only by the gentle rustling of the pine-needles and the murmuring of the Ganges. The Master went to the Panchavati and then to his room, talking all the while with M. The disciple followed him, fascinated. At the Panchavati Sri Ramakrishna touched with his forehead the raised platform around the banyan-tree. This was the place of his intense spiritual discipline, where he had wept bitterly for the vision of the Divine Mother, where he had held intimate communion with Her, and where he had seen many divine forms.

The Master and M. passed the cluster of bakul-trees and came to the nahabat. Hazra was there. The Master said to him: âDonât eat too much, and give up this craze for outer cleanliness. People with a craze do not attain Knowledge. Follow conventions only as much as necessary. Donât go to excess.â The Master entered his room and sat on the couch.

Sri Ramakrishna was resting after his midday meal when Surendra, Ram, and other devotees arrived from Calcutta. It was about one oâclock. While M. was strolling alone under the pine-trees, Harish came there and told him that the Master wanted him in his room. Someone was going to read from the Åiva SamhitÄ, a book containing instructions about yoga and the six centres.

M. entered the room and saluted the Master. The devotees were seated on the floor, but no one was reading the book. Sri Ramakrishna was talking to the devotees.

MASTER: âThe gopis cherished ecstatic love for Krishna. There are two elements in such love: âI-nessâ and âmy-nessâ. âI-nessâ is the feeling that Krishna will be ill if âIâ do not serve Him. In this attitude the devotee does not look upon his Ideal as God.

âÂ âMy-nessâ is to feel that the Beloved is âmyâ own. The gopis had such a feeling of âmy-nessâ toward Krishna that they would place their subtle bodies under His feet lest His soles should get hurt.

âYaÅodÄ remarked: âI donât understand your ChintÄmani Krishna. To me He is simply GopÄla.â The gopis also said: âOh, where is Krishna, our Beloved? Where is Krishna, our Sweetheart?â They were not conscious of His being God.

âIt is like a small child saying âmy daddyâ. If someone says to the child, âNo, he is not your daddyâ, the child says, âYes, he is my daddy.â

âGod, incarnating Himself as man, behaves exactly like a man. That is why it is difficult to recognize an Incarnation. When God becomes man, He is exactly like man. He has the same hunger, thirst, disease, grief, and sometimes even fear. RÄma was stricken with grief for SÄ«tÄ. Krishna carried on His head the shoes and wooden stool of His father Nanda.

âIn the theatre, when an actor comes on the stage in the role of a holy man, he behaves like one, and not like the actor who is taking the part of the king. He plays his own role.

âOnce an impersonator dressed himself as a world-renouncing monk. Pleased with the correctness of his disguise, some rich people offered him a rupee. He did not accept the money but went away shaking his head. Afterwards he removed his disguise and appeared in his usual dress. Then he said to the rich people, âPlease give me the rupee.â They replied: âWhy, you went away refusing our present. Why do you ask for it now?â The man said: âBut then I was in the role of a holy man. I could not accept money.â Likewise, when God becomes man He behaves exactly like a man.

âAt VrindÄvan one sees many places associated with Krishnaâs life.â

SURENDRA: âWe were there during the holidays. Visitors were continually pestered for money. The priests and others asked for it continually. We told them that we were going to leave for Calcutta the next day, but we fled from VrindÄvan that very night.â

MASTER: âWhat is that? Shame! You said you would leave the place the next day and ran away that very day. What a shame!â

SURENDRA (embarrassed): âHere and there we saw the bÄbÄjis in the woods practising spiritual discipline in solitude.â

MASTER: âDid you give them anything?â

SURENDRA: âNo, sir.â

MASTER: âThat was not proper of you. One should give something to monks and devotees. Those who have the means should help such persons when they meet them.

âI went to VrindÄvan with Mathur Babu. The moment I came to the Dhruva GhÄt5 at MathurÄ, in a flash I saw Vasudeva crossing the JamunÄ with Krishna in his arms.

âOne evening I was taking a stroll on the beach of the river. There were small thatched huts on the beach and big plum-trees. It was the âcow-dustâ hour. The cows were returning from the pasture, raising dust with their hoofs. I saw them fording the river. Then came some cowherd boys crossing the river with their cows. No sooner did I behold this scene than I cried out, âO Krishna, where are You?â and became unconscious.

âI wanted to visit ÅyÄmakunda and RÄdhÄkunda; so Mathur Babu sent me there in a palanquin. We had a long way to go. Food was put in the palanquin. While going over the meadow I was overpowered with emotion and wept: âO Krishna, I find everything the same; only You are not here. This is the very meadow where You tended the cows.â Hriday followed me on foot. I was bathed in tears. I couldnât ask the bearers to stop the palanquin.

âAt ÅyÄmakunda and RÄdhÄkunda I saw the holy men living in small mud huts. Facing away from the road lest their eyes should fall on men, they were engaged in spiritual discipline. One should visit the âTwelve Groveâ.

âI went into samÄdhi at the sight of the image of BankuvihÄri. In that state I wanted to touch it. I did not want to visit Govindaji twice. At MathurÄ I dreamt of Krishna as the cowherd boy, Hriday and Mathur Babu had the same dream.

(To Surendra) âYou have bothâyoga and bhoga. There are different classes of sages: the brahmarshi, the devarshi, and the rÄjarshi. Åukadeva is an example of the brahmarshi. He didnât keep even one book with him. An example of the devarshi is NÄrada. Janaka was a rÄjarshi, devoted to selfless work.

âThe devotee of the Divine Mother attains dharma and moksha. He enjoys artha and kÄma as well. Once I saw you in a vision as the child of the Divine Mother. You have bothâyoga and bhoga; otherwise your countenance would look dry.

âThe man who renounces all looks dry. Once I saw a devotee of the Divine Mother at the bathing-ghÄt on the Ganges. He was eating his meal and at the same time worshipping the Mother. He looked on himself as the Motherâs child.

âBut it isnât good to have much money. I find that Jadu Mallick is drowned in worldliness. It is because he has too much money. Nabin Niyogi, too, has both yoga and bhoga. I saw him and his son waving the fan before the image of the Divine Mother at the time of the DurgÄ PujÄ.â

SURENDRA: âSir, why canât I meditate?â

MASTER: âYou remember God and think of Him, donât you?â

SURENDRA: âYes, sir. I go to sleep repeating the word âMotherâ.â

MASTER: âThat is very good. It will be enough if you remember God and think of Him.â

Sri Ramakrishna had taken Surendraâs responsibilities on himself. Why should Surendra worry about anything?

It was evening. The Master was sitting on the floor of his room with the devotees. He was talking to them about yoga and the six centres. These are described in the Åiva SamhitÄ.

MASTER: âIdÄ, PingalÄ, and SushumnÄ are the three principal nerves. All the lotuses are located in the SushumnÄ. They are formed of Consciousness, like a tree made of waxâthe branches, twigs, fruits, and so forth all of wax. The Kundalini lies in the lotus of the MulÄdhÄra. That lotus has four petals. The Primordial Energy resides in all bodies as the Kundalini. She is like a sleeping snake coiled upââof the form of a sleeping snake, having the MulÄdhÄra for Her abodeâ. (To M.) The Kundalini is speedily awakened if one follows the path of bhakti. God cannot be seen unless She is awakened. Sing earnestly and secretly in solitude:

Waken, O Mother! O Kundalini, whose nature is Bliss Eternal!

Thou art the serpent coiled in sleep, in the lotus of the MulÄdhÄra.

âRÄmprasÄd achieved perfection through singing. One obtains the vision of God if one sings with yearning heart.â

M: âGrief and distress of mind disappear if one has these experiences but once.â

MASTER: âThat is true. Distress of mind disappears for ever. I shall tell you a few things about yoga. But you see, the mother bird doesnât break the shell until the chick inside the egg is matured. The egg is hatched in the fullness of time. It is necessary to practise some spiritual discipline. The guru no doubt does everything for the disciple; but at the end he makes the disciple work a little himself. When cutting down a big tree, a man cuts almost through the trunk; then he stands aside for a moment, and the tree falls down with a crash.

âThe farmer brings water to his field through a canal from the river. He stands aside when only a little digging remains to be done to connect the field with the water. Then the earth becomes soaked and falls of itself, and the water of the river pours into the canal in torrents.

âA man is able to see God as soon as he gets rid of ego and other limitations. He sees God as soon as he is free from such feelings as âI am a scholarâ, âI am the son of such and such a personâ, âI am wealthyâ, âI am honourableâ, and so forth.

âÂ âGod alone is real and all else unreal; the world is illusoryââthat is discrimination. One cannot assimilate spiritual instruction without discrimination.

âThrough the practice of spiritual discipline one attains perfection, by the grace of God. But one must also labour a little. Then one sees God and enjoys bliss. If a man hears that a jar filled with gold is buried at a certain place, he rushes there and begins to dig. He sweats as he goes on digging. After much digging he feels the spade strike something. Then he throws away the spade and looks for the jar. At the sight of the jar he dances for joy. Then he takes up the jar and pours out the gold coins. He takes them into his hand, counts them, and feels the ecstasy of joy. Visionâtouchâenjoyment. Isnât it so?â

M: âYes, sir.â

The Master was silent a moment and then went on.

MASTER: âThose who are my own will come here even if I scold them. Look at Narendraâs nature! At first he used to abuse my Mother KÄli very much. One day I said to him sharply, âRascal! Donât come here any more.â He slowly left the room and prepared a smoke. He who is oneâs own will not be angry even if scolded. What do you say?â

M: âThat is true, sir.â

MASTER: âNarendra is perfect from his very birth. He is devoted to the ideal of the formless God.â

M. (smiling): âWhenever he comes here he brings along great excitement.â

Sri Ramakrishna smiled and said, âYes, excitement indeed.â

The following day was Tuesday, the ekÄdaÅi day of the lunar fortnight. It was eleven oâclock in the morning and the Master had not yet taken his meal. M., Rakhal, and other devotees were sitting in the Masterâs room.

MASTER (to M.): âOne should fast on the eleventh day of the lunar fortnight. That purifies the mind and helps one to develop love of God. Isnât that so?â

M: âYes, sir.â

MASTER: âBut you may take milk and puffed rice. Donât you think so?â

1 In the case of an ordinary aspirant the body drops off after he attains the Knowledge of Brahman, but this is not so in the case of a Divine Incarnation, because He is born with a special mission to teach mankind.

2 According to Hindu mythology, God incarnated Himself as a sow in order to save the world from the iniquities of the demon HiranyÄksha.

3 Om, the symbol of Brahman.

4 A life of Chaitanya.

5 A bathing-place in the JamunÄ, where, according to tradition, Vasudeva, the father of Krishna, crossed the river carrying the new-born child through a stormy night.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# M. AT DAKSHINESWAR (II)

December 26, 1883

SRI RAMAKRISHNA, accompanied by Manilal Mallick, M., and several other devotees, was in a carriage on his way to Ramâs new garden. The garden, which Ram had recently purchased, was next to Surendraâs. Ram adored the Master as an Incarnation of God. He visited Sri Ramakrishna frequently at Dakshineswar. Manilal Mallick was a member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj. The BrÄhmos do not believe in Divine Incarnations.

MASTER (to Manilal): âIn order to meditate on God, one should try at first to think of Him as free from upÄdhis, limitations. God is beyond upÄdhis. He is beyond speech and mind. But it is very difficult to achieve perfection in this form of meditation.

âBut it is easy to meditate on an IncarnationâGod born as man. Yes, God in man. The body is a mere covering. It is like a lantern with a light burning inside, or like a glass case in which one sees precious things.â

Arriving at the garden, the Master got out of the carriage and accompanied Ram and the other devotees to the sacred tulsi-grove. Standing near it, he said: âHow nice! It is a fine place. You can easily meditate on God here.â

Sri Ramakrishna sat down in the house, which stood to the south of the lake. Ram offered him a plate of fruit and sweets which he enjoyed with the devotees. After a short time he went around the garden.

Next Sri Ramakrishna proceeded toward Surendraâs garden. He walked on foot a little distance and saw a sÄdhu sitting on a couch under a tree. At once he went up to the holy man and joyfully began a conversation with him.

MASTER: âTo which order of monks do you belong? Have you any titleâGiri, Puri, or the like?â

SÄDHU: âPeople call me a paramahamsa.â

MASTER: âThat is good. âI am Åivaââthat is a good attitude. But I must tell you something else. The process of creation, preservation, and destruction that is going on day and night is due to Åakti, the Power of God. This Primal Power and Brahman are one and the same. Åakti cannot exist without Brahman, just as waves cannot exist without water. There cannot be any instrumental music without an instrument.

âAs long as God keeps us in His relative world, so long we feel that there are two. If one accepts Åakti, one accepts Brahman as well. If one is aware of night, one is also aware of day. If one is aware of knowledge, one is also aware of ignorance.

âBut there is another state in which God reveals to His devotee that Brahman is beyond both knowledge and ignorance. It cannot be described in words. What exists, exists.â

After a pleasant conversation with the sÄdhu, the Master returned to the carriage, the holy man walking with him. Sri Ramakrishna looked upon him as a friend of long acquaintance, and they walked arm in arm.

The Master arrived at Surendraâs garden. The very first thing he talked about was the sÄdhu.

MASTER: âHe is a very nice man. (To Ram) Bring him to Dakshineswar when you come. He is really a good man. There is a line in a song to the effect that a man cannot recognize a holy person unless he is holy himself.

âThe sÄdhu believes in God without form. That is good. God is both formless and endowed with form. He is many things more. The Absolute and the Relative belong to one and the same Reality. What is beyond speech and mind is born in the flesh, assuming various forms and engaging in various activities. From that one Om have sprung âOm Åivaâ, âOm KÄliâ, and âOm Krishnaâ. Suppose the master of a house has sent out a small boy of the family to invite people to a feast. All look on the boy with great fondness and affection because he is the son or grandson of a prominent man.â

The Master took refreshments at Surendraâs garden house and then set out for Dakshineswar with the devotees.

Thursday, December 27, 1883

The temple garden was filled with the sweet music of the dawn service, which mingled with the morning melody from the nahabat. Leaving his bed, Sri Ramakrishna chanted the names of God in sweet tones. Then he bowed before the pictures of the different deities in his room and went to the west porch to salute the Ganges.

Some of the devotees who had spent the night at the temple garden came to the Masterâs room and bowed before him. Rakhal was staying with the Master, and Baburam had come the previous evening. M. had been staying there two weeks.

Sri Ramakrishna said to M.: âI have been invited to Ishanâs this morning. Baburam will accompany me, and you too.â M. made ready to go with the Master.

At eight oâclock the carriage hired for the Master stood waiting in front of the nahabat. On all sides plants and trees were in flower, and the river sparkled in the sunlight of the bright winterâs day. The Master bowed once more before the pictures. Then, still chanting the name of the Divine Mother, he got into the carriage, followed by M. and Baburam. The devotees took with them Sri Ramakrishnaâs woolen shawl, woolen cap, and small bag of spices.

Sri Ramakrishna was very happy during the trip and enjoyed it like a child. About nine oâclock the carriage stopped at the door of Ishanâs house. Ishan and his relatives greeted the Master and led him to the parlour on the first floor. Shrish, Ishanâs son, was introduced to Sri Ramakrishna. The young man practised law at Alipur. He had been a brilliant student, having stood first in two of the university examinations, but he was extremely modest.

MASTER (to Shrish): âWhat is your profession?â

SHRISH: âI am practising law at Alipur.â

MASTER (to M.): âFor such a man to be a lawyer! (To Shrish) Well, have you any questions to ask? Perhaps you want to know how to live unattached in the world. Isnât that so?â

SHRISH: âUnder the pressure of duties people do many unrighteous things in the world. Further, some are engaged in good work, and some in evil. Is this due to their actions in previous births? Is that why they act this way?â

MASTER: âHow long should a man perform his duties? As long as he has not attained God. Duties drop away after the realization of God. Then one goes beyond good and evil. The flower drops off as soon as the fruit appears. The flower serves the purpose of begetting the fruit.

âHow long should a devotee perform daily devotions such as the sandhyÄ? As long as his hair does not stand on end and his eyes do not shed tears at the name of God. These things indicate that the devotee has realized God. From these one knows that he has attained pure love of God. Realizing God one goes beyond virtue and vice.

I bow my head, says PrasÄd, before desire and liberation;

Knowing the secret that KÄli is one with the highest Brahman,

I have discarded, once for all, both righteousness and sin.

âThe more you advance toward God, the less He will give you worldly duties to perform.â

SHRISH: âIt is extremely difficult to proceed toward God while leading the life of a householder.â

MASTER: âWhy so? What about the yoga of practice? At KÄmÄrpukur I have seen the women of the carpenter families selling flattened rice. Let me tell you how alert they are while doing their business. The pestle of the husking-machine that flattens the paddy constantly falls into the hole of the mortar. The woman turns the paddy in the hole with one hand and with the other holds her baby on her lap as she nurses it. In the mean time customers arrive. The machine goes on pounding the paddy, and she carries on her bargains with the customers. She says to them, âPay the few pennies you owe me before you take anything more.â You see, she has all these things to do at the same timeânurse the baby, turn the paddy as the pestle pounds it, take the flattened rice out of the hole, and talk to the buyers. This is called the yoga of practice. Fifteen parts of her mind out of sixteen are fixed on the pestle of the husking-machine, lest it should pound her hand. With only one part of her mind she nurses the baby and talks to the buyers. Likewise, he who leads the life of a householder should devote fifteen parts of his mind to God; otherwise he will face ruin and fall into the clutches of Death. He should perform the duties of the world with only one part of his mind.

âA man may lead the life of a householder after attaining Knowledge. But he must attain Knowledge first. If the milk of the mind is kept in the water of the world, they get mixed. Therefore he should turn the milk into curd and extract butter from it by churning it in solitude; then he may keep the butter in the water of the world. Therefore, you see, spiritual discipline is necessary. When the aÅwattha tree is a mere sapling, it must be enclosed by a fence; otherwise the cattle will eat it. But the fence may be taken away when the trunk grows thick and strong. Then even an elephant tied to the tree cannot harm it.

âTherefore at the beginning the aspirant should go into solitude now and then. Spiritual discipline is necessary. You want to eat rice; suppose you sit down somewhere and say, âWood contains fire and fire cooks rice.â Can saying it cook the rice? You must get two pieces of wood and by rubbing them together bring out the fire.

âBy eating siddhi one becomes intoxicated and feels happy. But suppose you havenât eaten the stuff or done anything else with it; you simply sit down somewhere and mutter, âSiddhi! siddhi!â Will that intoxicate you or make you happy?

âYou may learn a great deal from books; but it is all futile if you have no love for God and no desire to realize Him. A mere pundit, without discrimination and renunciation, has his attention fixed on âwoman and goldâ. The vulture soars very high but its eyes are fixed on the charnel-pit.

âThat alone is Knowledge through which one is able to know God. All else is futile. Well, what is your idea about God?â

SHRISH: âSir, I feel that there is an All-knowing Person. We get an indication of His Knowledge by looking at His creation. Let me give an illustration. God has made devices to keep fish and other aquatic animals alive in cold regions. As water grows colder, it gradually shrinks. But the amazing thing is that, just before turning into ice, the water becomes light and expands. In the freezing cold, fish can easily live in the water of a lake: the surface of the lake may be frozen, but the water below is all liquid. If a very cold breeze blows, it is obstructed by the ice. The water below remains warm.â

MASTER: âThat God exists may be known by looking at the universe. But it is one thing to hear of God, another thing to see God, and still another thing to talk to God. Some have heard of milk, some have seen it, and some, again, have tasted it. You feel happy when you see milk; you are nourished and strengthened when you drink it. You will get peace of mind only when you have seen God. You will enjoy bliss and gain strength only when you have talked to Him.â

SHRISH: âWe do not have time to pray to God.â

MASTER (with a smile): âThat is true. Nothing comes to pass except at the right time. Going to bed, a child said to his mother, âMother, please wake me up when I feel the call of nature.â âMy son,â said the mother, âthat urge itself will wake you up. I donât have to wake you.â

âIt is all decided beforehand by God what each one shall receive. A mother-in-law used to measure rice with a dish for her daughters-in-law. But it was not enough for them. One day the dish was broken and that made the girls happy. But the mother-in-law said to them, âChildren, you may shout and dance, but I can measure the rice with the palm of my hand.â

(To Shrish): âSurrender everything at the feet of God. What else can you do? Give Him the power of attorney. Let Him do whatever He thinks best. If you rely on a great man, he will never injure you.

âIt is no doubt necessary to practise spiritual discipline; but there are two kinds of aspirants. The nature of the one kind is like that of the young monkey, and the nature of the other kind is like that of the kitten. The young monkey, with great exertion, somehow clings to its mother. Likewise, there are some aspirants who think that in order to realize God they must repeat His name a certain number of times, meditate on Him for a certain period, and practise a certain amount of austerity. An aspirant of this kind makes his own efforts to catch hold of God. But the kitten, of itself, cannot cling to its mother. It lies on the ground and cries, âMew, mew!â It leaves everything to its mother. The mother cat sometimes puts it on a bed, sometimes on the roof behind a pile of wood. She carries the kitten in her mouth hither and thither. The kitten doesnât know how to cling to the mother. Likewise, there are some aspirants who cannot practise spiritual discipline by calculating about japa or the period of meditation. All that they do is cry to God with yearning hearts. God hears their cry and cannot keep Himself away. He reveals Himself to them.â

At noon the host wished to feed the Master and the devotees. Sri Ramakrishna was smilingly pacing the room. Now and then he exchanged a few words with the musician.

MUSICIAN: âIt is God alone who is both the âinstrumentâ and the âcauseâ. Duryodhana said to Krishna: âO Lord, Thou art seated in my heart. I act as Thou makest me act.â â

MASTER (with a smile): âYes, that is true. It is God alone who acts through us. He is the Doer, undoubtedly, and man is His instrument. But it is also true that an action cannot fail to produce its result. Your stomach will certainly burn if you eat hot chilli. It is God who has ordained that chilli will burn your stomach. If you commit a sin, you must bear its fruit. But one who has attained perfection, realized God, cannot commit sin. An expert singer cannot sing a false note. A man with a trained voice sings the notes correctly: sÄ, re, gÄ, mÄ, pÄ, dhÄ, ni.â

The meal was ready. The Master and the devotees went to the inner court, where they were treated to a generous feast.

About three oâclock in the afternoon the Master was seated again in Ishanâs drawing-room with M. and Shrish. He resumed his conversation with Shrish.

MASTER: âWhat is your attitude toward God? âI am Heâ, or âMaster and servantâ? For the householder it is very good to look on God as the Master. The householder is conscious of doing the duties of life himself. Under such conditions how can he say, âI am Heâ? To him who says, âI am Heâ the world appears to be a dream. His mind, his body, even his ego, are dreams to him. Therefore he cannot perform worldly duties. So it is very good for the householder to look on himself as the servant and on God as the Master.

âHanumÄn had the attitude of a servant. He said to RÄma: âO RÄma, sometimes I meditate on You as the whole and on myself as the part. Sometimes I feel that You are the Master and I am the servant. But when I have the Knowledge of Reality, I see that I am You and You are I.â

âIn the state of Perfect Knowledge one may feel, âI am Heâ; but that is far beyond the ordinary manâs experience.â

SHRISH: âThat is true, sir. The attitude of a servant relieves a man of all his worries. The servant depends entirely upon his master. A dog is devoted to its master. It depends upon him and is at peace.â

MASTER: âWell, what suits your tasteâGod with form or the formless Reality? But to tell you the truth, He who is formless is also endowed with form. To His bhaktas He reveals Himself as having a form. It is like a great ocean, an infinite expanse of water, without any trace of shore. Here and there some of the water has been frozen. Intense cold has turned it into ice. Just so, under the cooling influence, so to speak, of the bhaktaâs love, the Infinite appears to take a form. Again, the ice melts when the sun rises; it becomes water as before. Just so, one who follows the path of knowledgeâthe path of discriminationâdoes not see the form of God any more. To him everything is formless. The ice melts into formless water with the rise of the Sun of Knowledge. But mark this: form and formlessness belong to one and the same Reality.â

At dusk the Master was ready to start for Dakshineswar. He stood on the south porch of the drawing-room, talking to Ishan. Someone remarked that the chanting of Godâs holy name did not always produce results. Ishan said: âHow can you say that? The seeds of an aÅwattha tree are no doubt tiny, but in them lie the germs of big trees. It may take a very long time for them to grow.â

âYes, yes!â said the Master. âIt takes a long time to see the effect.â

Next to Ishanâs was his father-in-lawâs house. Sri Ramakrishna stood at the door of this house, ready to get into the carriage. Ishan and his friends stood around to bid him adieu. Sri Ramakrishna said to Ishan: âYou are living in the world as a mudfish lives in the mud. It lives in the mud but its body is not stained.

âThere are both vidyÄ and avidyÄ in this world of mÄyÄ. Who may be called a paramahamsa? He who, like a swan, can take the milk from a mixture of milk and water, leaving aside the water. He who, like an ant, can take the sugar from a mixture of sugar and sand, leaving aside the sand.â

It was evening. The Master stopped at Ramâs house on his way to Dakshineswar. He was taken to the drawing-room and there he engaged in conversation with Mahendra Goswami. Mahendra belonged to the Vaishnava sect and was Ramâs neighbour. Sri Ramakrishna was fond of him.

MASTER: âThe worshippers of Vishnu and the worshippers of Åakti will all ultimately reach one and the same goal; the ways may be different. The true Vaishnavas do not criticize the ÅÄktas.â

GOSWAMI (smiling): âÅiva and PÄrvati are our Father and Mother.â

Sri Ramakrishna, out of his stock of a dozen English words, said sweetly, âThank you!â Then he added, âYes, Father and Mother!â

GOSWAMI: âBesides, it is a sin to criticize anyone, especially a devotee of God. All sins may be forgiven, but not the sin of criticizing a devotee.â

MASTER: âBut this idea of sin does not by any means affect all. For instance, the IÅvarakotis, such as Incarnations of God, are above sin. Sri Chaitanya is an example.

âA child, walking on a narrow ridge and holding to his father, may slip into the ditch. But that can never happen if the father holds the child by the hand.

âListen. I prayed to the Divine Mother for pure love. I said to Her: âHere is Thy righteousness, here is Thy unrighteousness. Take them both and give me pure love for Thee. Here is Thy purity, here is Thy impurity. Take them both and give me pure love for Thee. O Mother, here is Thy virtue, here is Thy vice. Take them both and give me pure love for Thee.â â

MASTER: âYou should undoubtedly bow before all views. But there is a thing called unswerving devotion to one ideal. True, you should salute everyone. But you must love one ideal with your whole soul. That is unswerving devotion.

âHanumÄn could not take delight in any other form than that of RÄma. The gopis had such single-minded love for the cowherd Krishna of VrindÄvan that they did not care to see the turbaned Krishna of DwÄrakÄ.

âA wife may serve her husbandâs brothers by fetching water, or in other ways, but she cannot serve them in the way she does her husband. With him she has a special relationship.â

Ram treated the Master to sweets. Sri Ramakrishna was ready to start for Dakshineswar. He put on his woolen shawl and cap, and got into the carriage with M. and the other devotees. Ram and his friends saluted the Master.

Saturday, December 29, 1883

It was the day of the new moon, auspicious for the worship of the Divine Mother. At one oâclock in the afternoon Sri Ramakrishna got into a carriage to visit the temple of KÄli at KÄlighÄt. MASTER (to Kedar, with a smile): âWhat did you think of the sÄdhu?â

Sri Ramakrishna returned to his room. About four oâclock the door of the KÄli temple was opened, and the Master walked to the temple with the monk; M. accompanied them. Monday, December 31, 1883

At four oâclock in the afternoon the Master was sitting in his room with M., Rakhal, Latu, Harish, and other devotees.

In the evening Balaram and the other devotees returned to Calcutta. The Master remained in his room, absorbed in contemplation of the Divine Mother. After a while the sweet music of the evening worship in the temples was heard.

A little later the Master began to talk to the Mother in a tender voice that touched the heart of M., who was seated on the floor. After repeating, âHari Om! Hari Om! Om!â, the Master said: âMother, donât make me unconscious with the Knowledge of Brahman. Mother, I donât want BrahmajnÄna. I want to be merry. Wednesday, January 2, 1884

Rakhal, Latu, Harish, Ramlal, and M. had been staying with Sri Ramakrishna at the temple garden. After the TÄntrik devotee had taken his leave, Jaygopal Sen, a member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj, arrived. The Master talked with him.

MASTER (to Jaygopal): âOne should not harbour malice toward any person or any opinion. The believers in the formless God and the worshippers of God with form are all, without exception, going toward God alone. The jnÄni, the yogi, the bhaktaâall, without exception, are seeking Him alone. The follower of the path of knowledge calls Him âBrahmanâ. The yogi calls Him âÄtmanâ or âParamÄtmanâ. Jaygopal was a man of the world. Was this why the Master gave instruction suited to him?

At eight oâclock that evening the Master was sitting in his room with Rakhal and M. It was the twenty-first day of M.âs stay with Sri Ramakrishna. The Master had forbidden him to indulge in reasoning.

MASTER (to Rakhal): âIt is not good to reason too much. First comes God, and then the world. Realize God first; then you will know all about His world. (To M. and Rakhal) If first one is introduced to Jadu Mallick, then one can know everything about himâthe number of his houses, gardens, government securities, and so on. For this reason the rishi NÄrada advised VÄlmiki1 to repeat the word âmarÄâ. âMaâ means God, and ârÄâ the world. First comes God, and then the world. Krishnakishore said that the word âmarÄâ is a holy mantra because it was given to VÄlmiki by the rishi. âMaâ means God, and ârÄâ the world.

âTherefore, like VÄlmiki, one should at first renounce everything and cry to God in solitude with a longing heart. The first thing necessary is the vision of God; then comes reasoningâabout the scriptures and the world.

(To M.) âThat is why I have been telling you not to reason any more. I came from the pine-grove to say that to you. âAfter attaining God, one looks on a pundit as mere straw and dust. Padmalochan said to me: âWhat does it matter if I accompany you to a meeting at the house of a fisherman?2 With you I can dine even at the house of a pariah.â

KÄrtika and GaneÅa3 were seated near Bhagavati, who had a necklace of gems around Her neck. The Divine Mother said to them, âI will present this necklace to him who is the first to go around the universe.â Thereupon KÄrtika, without losing a moment, set out on the peacock, his carrier. âWeeping, I prayed to the Mother: âO Mother, reveal to me what is contained in the Vedas and the VedÄnta. Reveal to me what is in the PurÄna and the Tantra.â One by one She has revealed all these to me.

âYes, She has taught me everything. Oh, how many things She has shown me! One day She showed me Åiva and Åakti everywhere. Everywhere I saw the communion of Åiva and Åakti. Åiva and Åakti existing in all living thingsâmen, animals, trees, plants. I saw Them in the communion of all male and female elements.

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting in his room. M. was still staying with the Master, devoting his time to the practice of spiritual discipline. He had been spending a great part of each day in prayer and meditation under the bel-tree, where the Master had performed great austerities and had seen many wonderful visions of God.

MASTER (to M.): âDonât reason any more. In the end, reasoning only injures the aspirant. One should assume a particular attitude toward God while praying to Himâthe attitude of friend or servant or son or âheroâ.

At dusk M. was sitting at the Masterâs feet. Sri Ramakrishna had been told that Keshabâs illness had taken a turn for the worse. He was talking about Keshab and incidentally about the BrÄhmo SamÄj.

Saturday, January 5, 1884

It was the twenty-third day of M.âs stay with Sri Ramakrishna. M. had finished his midday meal about one oâclock and was resting in the nahabat when suddenly he heard someone call his name three or four times. As the Master came to the bakul-tree he spoke to M. again: âChidÄtmÄ and ChitÅakti. The Purusha is the ChidÄtmÄ and Prakriti is the ChitÅakti. They should think of themselves as companions or handmaids of the ChitÅakti, Sri RÄdhÄ. This is the whole gist of the thing.â

After dusk Sri Ramakrishna went to the KÄli temple and was pleased to see M. meditating there.

Sri Ramakrishna now came down to the normal state of mind. Rakhal and Ramlal entered the room. At the Masterâs bidding Ramlal sang:

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# THE MASTER AND HIS INJURED ARM

Where are you, Madhusudan? Come and see. My arm is broken!â

âI used to sleep in the same room with Mathur and his wife. They took care of me as if I were their own child. I was then passing through a state of divine madness. Mathur would ask me, âFather, do you hear our conversation?â âYesâ, I would reply.

âOnce Mathurâs wife became suspicious of his movements and said to him, âIf you go anywhere, he5 must accompany you.â One day Mathur went to a certain place and asked me to wait downstairs. He returned after half an hour and said to me: âCome, father, let us go now. The carriage is waiting.â When Mathurâs wife asked me about it, I reported the thing correctly. He came down after half an hour and we left the place.â Of course she understood the thing in her own way.

Sunday, February 24, 1884

Sri Ramakrishna was resting in his room after his midday meal, and Mani Mallick was sitting on the floor beside him, when M. arrived. M. saluted the Master and sat down beside Mani. The Masterâs injured arm was bandaged.

M: âI came as far as ÄlambÄzÄr in a carriage and from there I walked.â

Sri Ramakrishna began to talk to them about his health and his injured arm.

MASTER: âNow and then I become impatient about my arm. I show it to this or that man and ask him whether I shall get well again. That makes Rakhal angry. He doesnât understand my mood. Now and then I say to myself, âLet him go away.â Again I say to the Mother: âMother, where will he go? Why should he burn himself in the frying-pan of the world?â

âWell, where then is my faith in God? Once I was going to KÄmÄrpukur in a bullock-cart, when several persons came up to the cart with clubs in their hands. They looked like highwaymen. I began to chant the names of the gods. Sometimes I repeated the names of RÄma and DurgÄ, and sometimes âOm Tat Satâ, so that in case one failed another would work.

(To M.) âCan you tell me why I am so impatient?â

M: âYour mind, sir, is always absorbed in samÄdhi. You have kept a fraction of it on your body for the welfare of the devotees. Therefore you feel impatient now and then for your bodyâs safety.â

Mani Mallick told the Master about an exhibition that was being held in Calcutta. He described a beautiful image of YaÅodÄ with the Baby Krishna on her lap. Sri Ramakrishnaâs eyes filled with tears. On hearing about YaÅodÄ, the embodiment of maternal love, his spiritual consciousness was kindled and he wept.

MANILAL: âIf you were not unwell, you could visit the exhibition in the MaidÄn.â

MASTER (to M. and the others): âI shanât be able to see everything even if I go. Perhaps my eyes will fall on some certain thing and I shall become unconscious. Then I shall not be able to see the rest. I was taken to the Zoological Garden. I had to return home after seeing only the lion. Hence Jadu Mallickâs mother first suggested that I should go to the exhibition and then said I should not.â

Mani Mallick, about sixty-five years old, had been a member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj for many years, and Sri Ramakrishna gave him instruction that would agree with his mood.

MASTER: âPundit Jaynarayan had very liberal views. I visited him once and liked his attitude. But his sons wore high boots. He told me he intended to go to Benares and live there, and at last he carried out his intention; for later on he did live in Benares and die there. When one grows old one should retire, like Jaynarayan, and devote oneself to the thought of God. What do you say?â

MANILAL: âTrue, sir. I donât relish the worries and troubles of the world.â

MASTER: âGauri used to worship his wife with offerings of flowers. All women are manifestations of the Divine Mother. (To Manilal) Please tell them that little story of yours.â

MANILAL (smiling): âOnce several men were crossing the Ganges in a boat. One of them, a pundit, was making a great display of his erudition, saying that he had studied various booksâthe Vedas, the VedÄnta, and the six systems of philosophy. He asked a fellow passenger, âDo you know the VedÄnta?â âNo, revered sir.â âThe SÄmkhya and the PÄtanjala?â âNo, revered sir.â âHave you read no philosophy whatsoever?â âNo, revered sir.â The pundit was talking in this vain way and the passenger sitting in silence, when a great storm arose and the boat was about to sink. The passenger said to the pundit, âSir, can you swim?â âNoâ, replied the pundit. The passenger said, âI donât know the SÄmkhya or the PÄtanjala, but I can swim.â â

MASTER (smiling): âWhat will a man gain by knowing many scriptures? The one thing needful is to know how to cross the river of the world. God alone is real, and all else illusory.

âWhile Arjuna was aiming his arrow at the eye of the bird, Drona asked him: âWhat do you see? Do you see these kings?â âNo, sirâ, replied Arjuna. âDo you see me?â âNo.â âThe tree?â âNo.â âThe bird on the tree?â âNo.â âWhat do you see then?â âOnly the eye of the bird.â

âHe who sees only the eye of the bird can hit the mark. He alone is clever who sees that God is real and all else is illusory. What need have I of other information? HanumÄn once remarked: âI donât know anything about the phase of the moon or the position of the stars. I only contemplate RÄma.â

(To M.) âPlease buy a few fans for our use here.

(To Manilal) âLook here, pay a visit to his [meaning M.âs] father. The sight of a devotee will inspire you.

(To M.) âSince my arm was injured a deep change has come over me. I now delight only in the NaralÄ«lÄ, the human manifestation of God. Nitya and LÄ«lÄ. The Nitya is the Indivisible SatchidÄnanda, and the LÄ«lÄ, or Sport, takes various forms, such as the LÄ«lÄ as God, the LÄ«lÄ as the deities, the LÄ«lÄ as man, and the LÄ«lÄ as the universe.

âVaishnavcharan used to say that one has attained Perfect Knowledge if one believes in God sporting as man. I wouldnât admit it then. But now I realize that he was right. Vaishnavcharan liked pictures of man expressing tenderness and love.

(To Manilal) âIt is God Himself who is sporting in the form of man. It is He alone who has become Mani Mallick. The Åikhs teach: âThou art SatchidÄnanda.â

âNow and then man catches a glimpse of his real Self and becomes speechless with wonder. At such times he swims in an ocean of joy. It is like suddenly meeting a dear relative. (To M.) The other day as I was coming here in a carriage, I felt like that at the sight of Baburam. When Åiva realizes His own Self, He dances about in joy exclaiming, âWhat am I! What am I!â

âThe same thing has been described in the AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana. NÄrada said, âO RÄma, all men are Thy forms, and it is SÄ«tÄ who has become all women.â On looking at the actors in the RÄmlÄ«lÄ, I felt that NÄrÄyana Himself had taken these human forms. âWhy do people worship virgins? All women are so many forms of the Divine Mother. But Her manifestation is greatest in pure-souled virgins.

(To M.) âWhy do I become impatient when I am ill? Because the Mother has placed me in the state of a child. The child depends entirely on its mother. The child of the maidservant, when he quarrels with the child of the master, says, âI shall tell my mother.â

âI was taken to RÄdhÄbÄzÄr to be photographed. It had been arranged that I should go to Rajendra Mitraâs house that day. I heard that Keshab would be there. I planned to tell them certain things, but I forgot it all when I went to RÄdhÄbÄzÄr. I said: âO Mother, Thou wilt speak. What shall I say?â

Sunday, March 2, 1884

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the small couch in his room, listening to devotional music by Trailokya Sannyal of the BrÄhmo SamÄj. He had not yet recovered from the effects of the injury to his arm, which was still supported by a splint. Many devotees, including Narendra, Surendra, and M., were sitting on the floor.

Narendraâs father, a lawyer of the High Court of Calcutta, had passed away suddenly. He had not been able to make provision for the family, which consequently faced grave financial difficulties. Trailokya sang about the Divine Mother:

The Master again shed tears of joy. He sang some lines from a song of RÄmprasÄd:

Addressing Trailokya, the Master said: âAh! How touching your songs are! They are genuine. Only he who has gone to the ocean can fetch its water.â

The singing came to an end. The Master engaged in conversation with the devotees.

MASTER: âGod alone is the Master, and again, He is the Servant. This attitude indicates Perfect Knowledge. At first one discriminates, âNot this, not thisâ, and feels that God alone is real and all else is illusory. Afterwards the same person finds that it is God Himself who has become all thisâthe universe, mÄyÄ, and the living beings. First negation and then affirmation. This is the view held by the PurÄnas. A vilwa-fruit, for instance, includes flesh, seeds, and shell. You get the flesh by discarding the shell and seeds. But if you want to know the weight of the fruit, you cannot find it if you discard the shell and seeds. Just so, one should attain SatchidÄnanda by negating the universe and its living beings. But after the attainment of SatchidÄnanda one finds that SatchidÄnanda Itself has become the universe and the living beings. It is of one substance that the flesh and the shell and seeds are made, just like butter and buttermilk.

âIt may be asked, âHow has SatchidÄnanda become so hard?â This earth does indeed feel very hard to the touch. The answer is that blood and semen are thin liquids, and yet out of them comes such a big creature as man. Everything is possible for God. First of all reach the indivisible SatchidÄnanda, and then, coming down, look at the universe. You will then find that everything is Its manifestation. It is God alone who has become everything. The world by no means exists apart from Him.

âAll elements finally merge in ÄkÄÅa. Again, at the time of creation, ÄkÄÅa evolves into mahat and mahat into ahamkÄra. In this way the whole world-system is evolved. It is the process of involution and evolution. A devotee of God accepts everything. He accepts the universe and its created beings as well as the indivisible SatchidÄnanda.

âBut the yogiâs path is different. He does not come back after reaching the ParamÄtman, the Supreme Soul. He becomes united with It.

âThe âpartial knowerâ limits God to one object only. He thinks that God cannot exist in anything beyond that.

âThere are three classes of devotees. The lowest one says, âGod is up there.â That is, he points to heaven. The mediocre devotee says that God dwells in the heart as the âInner Controllerâ. But the highest devotee says: âGod alone has become everything. All that we perceive is so many forms of God.â Narendra used to make fun of me and say: âYes, God has become all! Then a pot is God, a cup is God!â (Laughter.)

âAll doubts disappear when one sees God. It is one thing to hear of God, but quite a different thing to see Him. A man cannot have one hundred per cent conviction through mere hearing. But if he beholds God face to face, then he is wholly convinced.

âFormal worship drops away after the vision of God. It was thus that my worship in the temple came to an end. I used to worship the Deity in the KÄli temple. It was suddenly revealed to me that everything is Pure Spirit. The utensils of worship, the altar, the door-frameâall Pure Spirit. Men, animals, and other living beingsâall Pure Spirit. Then like a madman I began to shower flowers in all directions. Whatever I saw I worshipped.

âOne day, while worshipping Åiva, I was about to offer a bel-leaf on the head of the image, when it was revealed to me that this VirÄt, this Universe, itself is Åiva. After that my worship of Åiva through the image came to an end. Another day I had been plucking flowers, when it was revealed to me that the flowering plants were so many bouquets.â

TRAILOKYA: âAh! How beautiful is Godâs creation!â

MASTER: âOh no, it is not that. It was revealed to me in a flash. I didnât calculate about it. It was shown to me that each plant was a bouquet adorning the Universal Form of God. That was the end of my plucking flowers. I look on man in just the same way. When I see a man, I see that it is God Himself who walks on earth, as it were, rocking to and fro, like a pillow floating on the waves. The pillow moves with the waves. It bobs up and down.

âThe body has, indeed, only a momentary existence. God alone is real. Now the body exists, and now it does not. Years ago, when I had been suffering terribly from indigestion, Hriday said to me, âDo ask the Mother to cure you.â I felt ashamed to speak to Her about my illness. I said to Her: âMother, I saw a skeleton in the Asiatic Society Museum. It was pieced together with wires into a human form. âWhy this desire to live? After RÄvanaâs death RÄma and Lakshmana entered his capital and saw NikashÄ, his old mother, running away. Lakshmana was surprised at this and said to RÄma, âAll her children are dead, but still life attracts her so much!â RÄma called NikashÄ to His side and said: âDonât be afraid. Why are you running away?â She replied: âRÄma, it was not fear that made me flee from You. I have been able to see all these wondrous actions of Yours simply because I am alive. âWithout desires the body cannot live. (Smiling) I had one or two desires. I prayed to the Mother, âO Mother, give me the company of those who have renounced âwoman and goldâ.â I said further: âI should like to enjoy the society of Thy jnÄnis and bhaktas. MASTER (smiling): âNo, there are still a few left. (All laugh.)

âThe body is really impermanent. When my arm was broken I said to the Mother, âMother, it hurts me very much.â At once She revealed to me a carriage and its driver. Here and there a few screws were loose. The carriage moved as the driver directed it. It had no power of its own.

Narendra was sitting on the floor in front of the Master.

MASTER (to Trailokya and the other devotees): âThe joys and sorrows of the body are inevitable. Look at Narendra. His father is dead, and his people have been put to extreme suffering. He canât find any way out of it. God places one sometimes in happiness and sometimes in misery.â

TRAILOKYA: âRevered sir, God will be gracious to Narendra.â

MASTER (with a smile): âBut when? It is true that no one starves at the temple of AnnapurnÄ in Benares; but some must wait for food till evening.

âOnce Hriday asked Sambhu Mallick for some money. Sambhu held the views of âEnglishmenâ on such matters. He said to Hriday: âWhy should I give you money? You can earn your livelihood by working. Even now you are earning something. The case of a very poor person is different. The Master spoke as if piqued because God had not yet shown His kindness to Narendra. Now and then he cast an affectionate glance at his beloved disciple.

NARENDRA: âI am now studying the views of the atheists.â

âThe ways of God are inscrutable indeed. Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows. The PÄndava brothers visited him in Krishnaâs company. Presently Bhishma burst into tears. Yet even he is bewildered by mÄyÄ and weeps at death.â âButâ, said Krishna, âBhishma isnât weeping on that account. You may ask him about it.â When asked, Bhishma said: âO Krishna, I am unable to understand anything of the ways of God. God Himself is the constant companion of the PÄndavas, and still they have no end of trouble. That is why I weep.
