âGod has revealed to me that only the ParamÄtman, whom the Vedas describe as the Pure Soul, is as immutable as Mount Sumeru, unattached, and beyond pain and pleasure. There is much confusion in this world of His mÄyÄ. One can by no means say that âthisâ will come after âthatâ or âthisâ will produce âthatâ.â

SURENDRA (smiling): âIf by giving away money in a previous birth one gets wealth in this life, then we should all give away money now.â

MASTER: âThose who have money should give it to the poor and needy. (To Trailokya) Jaygopal Sen is well-to-do. He should be charitable. That he is not so is to his discredit. There are some who are miserly even though they have money. There is no knowing who will enjoy their money afterwards.

SURENDRA: âJaygopal Babu belongs to the BrÄhmo SamÄj. I understand that now there is not one worth-while man in Keshabâs organization. Vijay Goswami, Shivanath, and other notables have organized the SÄdhÄran BrÄhmo SamÄj.â

MASTER (smiling): âGovinda Adhikari, it is said, would not keep good actors in his theatre lest they should claim a share of the profit. (All laugh.)

âThe other day I saw a disciple of Keshab. A theatrical performance was being given in Keshabâs house, and I saw the disciple dancing on the stage with a child in his arms. I understand that this man delivers âlecturesâ. He had better lecture to himself.â

Trailokya sang:

Sri Ramakrishna requested Trailokya to sing the song beginning, âO Mother, make me mad with Thy loveâ.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# RULES FOR HOUSEHOLDERS AND MONKS

Sunday, March 9, 1884

SRI RAMAKRISHNA was sitting in his room at Dakshineswar with many devotees. Among them were Mani Mallick, Mahendra KavirÄj, Balaram, M., Bhavanath, Rakhal, Latu, and Harish. The Masterâs injured arm was in a splint. In spite of the injury he was constantly absorbed in samÄdhi or instructing the devotees.

Mani Mallick and Bhavanath referred to the exhibition which was then being held near the Asiatic Museum. They said: âMany mahÄrÄjÄs have sent precious articles to the exhibitionâgold couches and the like. It is worth seeing.â

MASTER (to the devotees, with a smile): âYes, you gain much by visiting those things. You realize that those articles of gold and the other things sent by mahÄrÄjÄs are mere trash. That is a great gain in itself. When I used to go to Calcutta with Hriday, he would show me the Viceroyâs palace and say: âLook, uncle! There is the Viceroyâs palace with the big columns.â The Mother revealed to me that they were merely clay bricks laid one on top of another.

âGod and His splendour. God alone is real; the splendour has but a two-days existence. The magician and his magic. All become speechless with wonder at the magic, but it is all unreal. The magician alone is real. The rich man and his garden. People see only the garden; they should look for its rich owner.â

MANI MALLICK (to the Master): âWhat a big electric light they have at the exhibition! It makes us think how great He must be who has made such an electric light.â

MASTER (to Mani): âBut according to one view it is He Himself who has become everything. Even those who say that are He. It is SatchidÄnanda Itself that has become allâthe Creator, mÄyÄ, the universe, and living beings.â

The conversation turned to the museum.

MASTER (to the devotees): âI visited the museum once. I was shown fossils. A whole animal has become stone! Just see what an effect has been produced by company! Likewise, by constantly living in the company of a holy man one verily becomes holy.â

MANI (smiling): âHad you visited the exhibition only once, we could receive instruction for ten or fifteen years.â

MASTER (with a smile): âHow so? You mean illustrations?â

BALARAM: âNo, you shouldnât go. Your arm wonât heal if you go here and there.â

MASTER: âI should like to have two pictures. One of a yogi seated before a lighted log, and another of a yogi smoking hemp and the charcoal blazing up as he pulls. Such pictures kindle my spiritual consciousness, as an imitation fruit awakens the idea of a real one.

âThe obstacle to yoga is âwoman and goldâ. Yoga is possible when the mind becomes pure. The seat of the mind is between the eyebrows; but its look is fixed on the navel and the organs of generation and evacuation, that is to say, on âwoman and goldâ. But through spiritual discipline the same mind looks upward.

âWhat are the spiritual disciplines that give the mind its upward direction? One learns all this by constantly living in holy company. The rishis of olden times lived either in solitude or in the company of holy persons; therefore they could easily renounce âwoman and goldâ and fix their minds on God. They had no fear nor did they mind the criticism of others.

âIn order to be able to renounce, one must pray to God for the will-power to do so. One must immediately renounce what one feels to be unreal. The rishis had this will-power. Through it they controlled the sense-organs. If the tortoise once tucks in its limbs, you cannot make it bring them out even by cutting it into four pieces.

âThe worldly man is a hypocrite. He cannot be guileless. He professes to love God, but he is attracted by worldly objects. He doesnât give God even a very small part of the love he feels for âwoman and goldâ. But he says that he loves God. (To Mani Mallick) Give up hypocrisy.â

MANI: âRegarding whom, God or man?â

MASTER: âRegarding everythingâman as well as God. One must not be a hypocrite.

âHow guileless Bhavanath is! After his marriage he came to me and asked, âWhy do I feel so much love for my wife?â Alas, he is so guileless!

âIsnât it natural for a man to love his wife? This is due to the world-bewitching mÄyÄ of the Divine Mother of the Universe. A man feels about his wife that he has no one else in the world so near and dear; that she is his very own in life and death, here and hereafter.

âAgain, how much a man suffers for his wife! Still he believes that there is no other relative so near. Look at the sad plight of a husband. Perhaps he earns twenty rupees a month and is the father of three children. He hasnât the means to feed them well. His roof leaks, but he hasnât the wherewithal to repair it. He cannot afford to buy new books for his son. He cannot invest his son with the sacred thread. He begs a few pennies from his different friends.

âBut a wife endowed with spiritual wisdom is a real partner in life. She greatly helps her husband to follow the religious path. After the birth of one or two children they live like brother and sister. Both of them are devotees of GodâHis servant and His handmaid. Their family is a spiritual family. They are always happy with God and His devotees. They know that God alone is their own, from everlasting to everlasting. They are like the PÄndava brothers; they do not forget God in happiness or in sorrow.

âThe longing of the worldly-minded for God is momentary, like a drop of water on a red-hot frying-pan. The water hisses and dries up in an instant. The attention of the worldly-minded is directed to the enjoyment of worldly pleasure. Therefore they do not feel yearning and restlessness for God.

âPeople may observe the ekÄdaÅi in three ways. First, the âwaterlessâ ekÄdaÅiâthey are not permitted to drink even a drop of water. Likewise, an all-renouncing religious mendicant completely gives up all forms of enjoyment. Second, while observing the ekÄdaÅi they take milk and sandesh. Likewise, a householder devotee keeps in his house simple objects of enjoyment. Third, while observing the ekÄdaÅi they eat luchi and chakkÄ. They eat their fill. They keep a couple of loaves soaking in milk, which they will eat later on.1

âA man practises spiritual discipline, but his mind is on âwoman and goldââit is turned toward enjoyment. Therefore, in his case, the spiritual discipline does not produce the right result.

âHazra used to practise much japa and austerity here. But in the country he has his wife, children, and land. Therefore along with his spiritual discipline he carried on the business of a broker. Such people cannot be true to their word. One moment they say they will give up fish, but the next moment they break their vow.

âIs there anything that a man will not do for money? He will even compel a brÄhmin or a holy man to carry a load.

âIn my room sweets would turn bad; still I could not give them away to the worldly-minded. I could accept dirty water from others, but not even touch the jar of a worldly person.

âAt the sight of rich people Hazra would call them to him. He would give them long lectures. He would say to them: âYou see Rakhal and the other youngsters. They do not practise any spiritual discipline. They simply wander about merrily.â

âA man may live in a mountain cave, smear his body with ashes, observe fasts, and practise austere discipline; but if his mind dwells on worldly objects, on âwoman and goldâ, I say, âShame on him!â But I say that a man is blessed indeed who eats, drinks, and roams about, but who keeps his mind free from âwoman and goldâ.

(Pointing to Mani Mallick) âThere is no picture of a holy man at his house. Divine feeling is awakened through such pictures.â

MANILAL: âYes, there is. In one room there is a picture of a pious Christian woman engaged in prayer. There is another picture in which a man holds to the Hill of Faith; below is an ocean of immeasurable depth. If he gives up his hold on faith, he will drop into the bottomless water. There is still a third picture. Several virgins are keeping vigil, feeding their lamps with oil in expectation of the Bridegroom. A sleeping virgin is by their side. She will not behold the Bridegroom when He arrives. God is described here as the Bridegroom.â

MASTER (smiling): âThatâs very nice.â

MANILAL: âI have other pictures tooâone of the âTree of Faithâ and another of âSin and Virtueâ.â

MASTER (to Bhavanath): âThose are good pictures. Go to his house and see them.â

The Master remained silent a few minutes.

MASTER: âNow and then I reflect on these ideas and find that I do not like them. In the beginning of spiritual life a man should think about sin and how to get rid of it. But when, through the grace of God, devotion and ecstatic love are awakened in his heart, then he altogether forgets virtue and sin. Then he leaves the scriptures and their injunctions far behind. Thoughts of repentance and penance do not bother him at all.

âIt is like going to your destination along a winding river. This requires great effort and a long time. But when there is a flood all around, then you can go straight to your destination in a short time. Then you find the land lying under water deep as a bamboo pole.

âIn the beginning of spiritual life one goes by a roundabout way. One has to suffer a great deal. But the path becomes very easy when ecstatic love is awakened in the heart. It is like going over the paddy-field after the harvest is over. You may then walk in any direction. Before the harvest you had to go along the winding balk, but now you can walk in any direction. There may be stubble in the field, but you will not be hurt by it if you walk with your shoes on. Just so, an aspirant does not suffer if he has discrimination, dispassion, and faith in the guruâs words.â

MANILAL (to the Master): âWell, what is the rule for concentration? Where should one concentrate?â

MASTER: âThe heart is a splendid place. One can meditate there or in the SahasrÄra. These are rules for meditation given in the scriptures. But you may meditate wherever you like. Every place is filled with Brahman-Consciousness. Is there any place where It does not exist? NÄrÄyana, in Valiâs presence, covered with two steps the heavens, the earth, and the interspaces.2 Is there then any place left uncovered by God? A dirty place is as holy as the bank of the Ganges. It is said that the whole creation is the VirÄt, the Universal Form of God.

âThere are two kinds of meditation, one on the formless God and the other on God with form. But meditation on the formless God is extremely difficult. In that meditation you must wipe out all that you see or hear. You contemplate only the nature of your Inner Self. Meditating on His Inner Self, Åiva dances about. He exclaims. âWhat am I! What am I!â This is called the âÅiva yogaâ. While practising this form of meditation, one directs oneâs look to the forehead. It is meditation on the nature of oneâs Inner Self after negating the world, following the VedÄntic method of âNeti, netiâ.

âThere is another form of meditation known as the âVishnu yogaâ. The eyes are fixed on the tip of the nose. Half the look is directed inward and the other half outward. This is how one meditates on God with form. Sometimes Åiva meditates on God with form, and dances. At that time he exclaims, âRÄma! RÄma!â and dances about.â

Sri Ramakrishna then explained the sacred Word âOmâ and the true Knowledge of Brahman and the state of mind after the attainment of BrahmajnÄna.

MASTER: âThe sound Om is Brahman. The rishis and sages practised austerity to realize that Sound-Brahman. After attaining perfection one hears the sound of this eternal Word rising spontaneously from the navel.

âÂ âWhat will you gainâ, some sages ask, âby merely hearing this sound?â You hear the roar of the ocean from a distance. By following the roar you can reach the ocean. As long as there is the roar, there must also be the ocean. By following the trail of Om you attain Brahman, of which the Word is the symbol. That Brahman has been described by the Vedas as the ultimate goal. But such vision is not possible as long as you are conscious of your ego. A man realizes Brahman only when he feels neither âIâ nor âyouâ, neither âoneâ nor âmanyâ.

âThink of the sun and of ten jars filled with water. The sun is reflected in each jar. At first you see one real sun and ten reflected ones. If you break nine of the jars, there will remain only the real sun and one reflection. Each jar represents a jÄ«va. Following the reflection one can find the real sun. Through the individual soul one can reach the Supreme Soul. Through spiritual discipline the individual soul can get the vision of the Supreme Soul. What remains when the last jar is broken cannot be described.

âThe jÄ«va at first remains in a state of ignorance. He is not conscious of God, but of the multiplicity. He sees many things around him. On attaining Knowledge he becomes conscious that God dwells in all beings. Suppose a man has a thorn in the sole of his foot. He gets another thorn and takes out the first one. In other words, he removes the thorn of ajnÄna, ignorance, by means of the thorn of jnÄna, knowledge. But on attaining vijnÄna, he discards both thorns, knowledge and ignorance. Then he talks intimately with God day and night. It is no mere vision of God.

âHe who has merely heard of milk is âignorantâ. He who has seen milk has âknowledgeâ. But he who has drunk milk and been strengthened by it has attained vijnÄna.â

Thus the Master described his own state of mind to the devotees. He was indeed a vijnÄni.

MASTER (to the devotees): âThere is a difference between a sÄdhu endowed with jnÄna and one endowed with vijnÄna. The jnÄni sÄdhu has a certain way of sitting. He twirls his moustache and asks the visitor, âWell, sir! Have you any question to ask?â But the man who always sees God and talks to Him intimately has an altogether different nature. He is sometimes like an inert thing, sometimes like a ghoul, sometimes like a child, and sometimes like a madman.

âWhen he is in samÄdhi, he becomes unconscious of the outer world and appears inert. He sees everything to be full of Brahman-Consciousness; therefore he behaves like a ghoul. He is not conscious of the holy and the unholy. He does not observe any formal purity. To him everything is Brahman. He is not aware of filth as such. Even rice and other cooked food after a few days become like filth.

âAgain, he is like a madman. People notice his ways and actions and think of him as insane. Or sometimes he is like a childâno bondage, no shame, no hatred, no hesitation, or the like.

âOne reaches this state of mind after having the vision of God. When a boat passes by a magnetic hill, its screws and nails become loose and drop out. Lust, anger, and the other passions cannot exist after the vision of God.

âOnce a thunderbolt struck the KÄli temple. I noticed that it flattened the points of the screws.

âIt is no longer possible for the man who has seen God to beget children and perpetuate the creation. When a grain of paddy is sown it grows into a plant; but a grain of boiled paddy does not germinate.

âHe who has seen God retains his âIâ only in name. No evil can be done by that âIâ. It is a mere appearance, like the mark left on the coconut tree by its branch. The branch has fallen off. Only the mark remains.

âI said to Keshab Sen, âGive up the ego that makes you feel, âI am the doer; I am teaching people.â â Keshab said to me, âSir, then I cannot keep the organization.â Thereupon I said to him, âGive up the âwicked egoâ.â One doesnât have to renounce the ego that makes one feel, âI am the servant of God; I am His devotee.â One doesnât develop the âdivine egoâ as long as one retains the âwicked egoâ. If a man is in charge of the store-room, the master of the house doesnât feel responsible for it.

(To the devotees) âYou see, my nature is changing on account of this injury to my arm. It is being revealed to me that there is a greater manifestation of God in man than in other created beings. God is telling me, as it were: âI dwell in men. Be merry with men.â Among men God manifests Himself in a still greater degree in pure-souled devotees. That is why I feel great longing for Narendra, Rakhal, and other such youngsters.

âOne often sees small holes along the edge of a lake. Fish and crabs accumulate there. Just so, there is a greater accumulation of divinity in man. It is said that man is greater than the ÅÄlagrÄm. Man is NÄrÄyana Himself. If God can manifest Himself through an image, then why not through man also?

âGod is born as man for the purpose of sporting as man. RÄma, Krishna, and Chaitanya are examples. By meditating on an Incarnation of God one meditates on God Himself.â

Bhagavan Das, a BrÄhmo devotee, arrived.

MASTER (to Bhagavan Das): âThe Eternal Religion, the religion of the rishis, has been in existence from time out of mind and will exist eternally. There exist in this SanÄtana Dharma all forms of worshipâworship of God with form and worship of the Impersonal Deity as well. It contains all pathsâthe path of knowledge, the path of devotion, and so on. Other forms of religion, the modern cults, will remain for a few days and then disappear.â

March 23, 1884

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting in his room after his midday meal, with Rakhal, Ram, and some other devotees. He was not quite well. The injured arm was still bandaged.

But in spite of his illness, his room was a veritable mart of joy and he the centre of it. Devotees thronged there daily to see the Master. Spiritual talk went on incessantly, and the very air of the room vibrated with bliss. Sometimes the Master would sing the name and glories of God, and sometimes he would go into samÄdhi, the devotees being amazed at the ease with which the Master freed himself from the consciousness of the body.

RAM: âThere is talk of Narendraâs marrying Mr. R. Mitraâs daughter. Narendra has been offered a large dowry.â

MASTER (smiling): âYes, Narendra may thus become a leader of society or something like that. He will be an outstanding man, whatever career he follows.â

The Master did not much encourage the conversation about Narendra.

MASTER (to Ram): âWell, can you tell me why I become so impatient when I am ill? Sometimes I ask this man and sometimes that man how I may be cured. You see, one must either believe everyone or no one at all.

âIt is God Himself who has become the physicians. Therefore one must believe all of them. But one cannot have faith in them if one thinks of them as mere men.

âSambhu was fearfully delirious. Dr. Sarvadhikari said that the delirium was due to the strong medicine. Haladhari asked the doctor to feel his pulse. The doctor said: âLet me see your eyes. Oh, it is an enlargement of the spleen!â Haladhari said he had nothing of the sort. But Dr. Madhu gives good medicine.â

RAM: âThe medicine by itself does no good, though it greatly helps nature.â

MASTER: âIf that is so, why does opium cause constipation?â

Ram referred to Keshab Senâs death.

RAM: âYou were quite right. You said that a gardener uncovers the roots of a good rose-plant so that it may absorb the dew and grow stronger and healthier. The words of a holy man have been fulfilled.â

MASTER: âI donât know about that. I wasnât calculating when I said it. It is you who say that.â

RAM: âThe BrÄhmos have published something about you in their magazine.â

MASTER: âPublished about me? Why? Why should they write now? I eat and drink and make merry. I donât know anything else.

âI once asked Keshab, âWhy have you written about me?â He said that it would bring people here. But man cannot teach by his own power. One cannot conquer ignorance without the power of God.

âAt one time two men were engaged to wrestle. One of them was HanumÄn Singh and the other a MussalmÄn from the Punjab. The MussalmÄn was a strong, stout man. He had eaten lustily of butter and meat for fifteen days before the day of the wrestling-match, and even on that day. All thought he would be the victor. HanumÄn Singh, on the other hand, clad in a dirty cloth, had eaten sparingly for some days before the day of the match and devoted himself to repeating the holy name of MahÄvir.3 On the day of the match he observed a complete fast. All thought that he would surely be defeated. But it was he who won, while the man who had feasted for fifteen days lost the fight.

âWhat is the use of printing and advertising? He who teaches men gets his power from God. None but a man of renunciation can teach others. I am the greatest of all fools!â (All laugh.)

A DEVOTEE: âThen how is it that the Vedas and the VedÄnta, and many things besides, come out of your mouth?â

MASTER (smiling): âDuring my boyhood I could understand what the sÄdhus read at the Lahasâ house at KÄmÄrpukur, although I would miss a little here and there. If a pundit speaks to me in Sanskrit I can follow him, but I cannot speak it myself.

âTo realize God is the one goal of life. While aiming his arrow at the mark, Arjuna said, âI see only the eye of the bird and nothing elseânot the kings, not the trees, not even the bird itself.â

âThe realization of God is enough for me. What does it matter if I donât know Sanskrit?

âThe grace of God falls alike on all His children, learned and illiterateâwhoever longs for Him. The father has the same love for all his children. Suppose a father has five children. One calls him âBÄbÄâ, some âBÄâ, and some âPÄâ. These last cannot pronounce the whole word. Does the father love those who address him as âBÄbÄâ more than those who call him âPÄâ? The father knows that these last are simply too young to say âBÄbÄâ correctly.

âSince this injury to my arm a change has been coming over my mind. I have been feeling much inclined to the NaralÄ«lÄ. It is God Himself who plays about as human beings. If God can be worshipped through a clay image, then why not through a man?

âOnce a merchant was shipwrecked. He floated to the shore of Ceylon, where Vibhishana was the king of the monsters. Vibhishana ordered his servants to bring the merchant to him. At the sight of him Vibhishana was overwhelmed with joy and said: âAh! He looks like my RÄma. The same human form!â He adorned the merchant with robes and jewels, and worshipped him. When I first heard this story, I felt such joy that I cannot describe it.

âVaishnavcharan said to me, âIf a person looks on his beloved as his Ishta, he finds it very easy to direct his mind to God.â The men and women of a particular sect4 at ÅyÄmbÄzÄr, near KÄmÄrpukur, say to each other, âWhom do you love?â âI love so-and-so.â âThen know him to be your God.â When I heard this, I said to them: âThat is not my way. I look on all women as my mother.â I found out that they talked big but led immoral lives. The women then asked me if they would have salvation. âYes,â I said, âif you are absolutely faithful to one man and look on him as your God. But you cannot be liberated if you live with five men.â â

RAM: âI understand that Kedar Babu has recently visited the KartÄbhajÄsâ place.â

MASTER: âHe gathers honey from various flowers. (To Ram, Nityagopal, and the others) If a devotee believes one hundred per cent that his Chosen Ideal is God, then he attains God and sees Him.

âPeople of bygone generations had tremendous faith. What faith Haladhariâs father had! Once he was on the way to his daughterâs house when he noticed some beautiful flowers and vilwa-leaves. He gathered them for the worship of the Family Deity and walked back five or six miles to his own house.

âOnce a theatrical troupe in the village was enacting the life of RÄma. When Kaikeyi asked RÄma to go into exile in the forest, Haladhariâs father, who had been watching the performance, sprang up. He went to the actor who played Kaikeyi, crying out, âYou wretch!â, and was about to burn the actorâs face with a torch. He was a very pious man. After finishing his ablutions he would stand in the water and meditate on the Deity, reciting the invocation: âI meditate on Thee, of red hue and four facesâ, while tears streamed down his cheeks.

âWhen my father walked along the lanes of the village wearing his wooden sandals, the shopkeepers would stand up out of respect and say, âThere he comes!â When he bathed in the HÄldÄrpukur, the villagers would not have the courage to get into the water. Before bathing they would inquire if he had finished his bath.

âWhen my father chanted the name of Raghuvir, his chest would turn crimson. This also happened to me. When I saw the cows at VrindÄvan returning from the pasture, I was transported into a divine mood and my body became red.

âVery strong was the faith of the people in those days. One hears that God used to dance then, taking the form of KÄli, while the devotee clapped his hands keeping time.â

A hathayogi was staying in the hut at the Panchavati. Ramprasanna, the son of Krishnakishore of ÄriÄdaha, and several other men had become his devotees. The yogi needed twenty-five rupees a month for his milk and opium; so Ramprasanna had requested Sri Ramakrishna to speak to his devotees about the yogi and get some money. The Master said to several devotees: âA hathayogi has come to the Panchavati. Go and visit him. See what sort of man he is.â

A young man of twenty-seven or twenty-eight, known as ThÄkur DÄdÄ, entered the room with a few friends and saluted the Master. He lived at BarÄnagore and was the son of a brÄhmin pundit. He was practising the kathakatÄ5 in order to earn money to meet his familyâs expenses. At one time he had been seized with the spirit of renunciation and had gone away from his family. Even now he practised spiritual discipline at home.

MASTER: âHave you come on foot? Where do you live?â

DÄDÄ: âYes, sir, I have walked from home. I live at BarÄnagore.â

MASTER: âHave you come here for any particular purpose?â

DÄDÄ: âI have come here to visit you. I pray to God. But why do I suffer now and then from worries? For a few days I feel very happy. Why do I feel restless afterwards?â

MASTER: âI see. Things have not been fitted quite exactly. The machine works smoothly if the mechanic fits the cogs of the wheels correctly. In your case there is an obstruction somewhere.â

DÄDÄ: âYes, sir. That must be so.â

MASTER: âAre you initiated?â

DÄDÄ: âYes, sir.â

MASTER: âDo you have faith in your mantra?â

A friend of ThÄkur DÄdÄ said that the latter could sing well. The Master asked him to sing.

ThÄkur DÄdÄ sang:

MASTER: âAh, what a nice song! âFountain-head of Blissâ! âFruit of Truthâ! âLaugh and dance and weep and singâ! Your song tastes very sweet to me. Why should you worry?

âPleasure and pain are inevitable in the life of the world. One suffers now and then from a little worry and trouble. A man living in a room full of soot cannot avoid being a little stained.â

DÄDÄ: âPlease tell me what I should do now.â

Mahimacharan entered the room and saluted the Master. Sri Ramakrishna said to him: âAh! He has sung a nice song. Please sing it again.â ThÄkur DÄdÄ repeated the song.

MASTER (to Mahima): âPlease recite that verse, the one about devotion to Hari.â

Mahimacharan recited, quoting from the NÄrada PancharÄtra:

What need is there of penance if God is worshipped with love?

What is the use of penance if God is not worshipped with love?

MASTER: âRecite that part alsoââObtain from Him the love of Godâ.â

Mahima recited:

O Brahman! O my child! Cease from practising further penances.

Hasten to Åankara, the Ocean of Heavenly Wisdom;

Which snaps in twain the shackles that bind you to the world.

MASTER: âYes, Åankara will bestow the love of God.â

MAHIMA: âOne who is free from bondage is the eternal Åiva.â

MASTER: âShame, hatred, fear, hesitationâthese are the shackles. What do you say?â

MAHIMA: âYes, sir. And also the desire to conceal, and shrinking before praise.â

MASTER: âThere are two signs of knowledge. First, an unshakable buddhi. No matter how many sorrows, afflictions, dangers, and obstacles one may be faced with, oneâs mind does not undergo any change. It is like the blacksmithâs anvil, which receives constant blows from the hammer and still remains unshaken. And second, manlinessâvery strong grit. If lust and anger injure a man, he must renounce them once for all. If a tortoise once tucks in its limbs, it wonât put them out again though you may cut it into four pieces. (To ThÄkur DÄdÄ and the others) There are two kinds of renunciation: intense and feeble. Feeble renunciation is a slow process; one moves in a slow rhythm. Intense renunciation is like the sharp edge of a razor. It cuts the bondage of mÄyÄ easily and at once.

âOne farmer labours for days to bring water from the lake to his field. But his efforts are futile because he has no grit. Another farmer, after labouring for two or three days, takes a vow and says, âI will bring water into my field today, and not till then will I go home.â He puts aside all thought of his bath or his meal. He labours the whole day and feels great joy when in the evening he finds water entering his field with a murmuring sound. Then he goes home and says to his wife: âNow give me some oil. I shall take my bath.â After finishing his bath and his meal he lies down to sleep with a peaceful mind.

âA certain woman said to her husband: âSo-and-so has developed a spirit of great dispassion for the world, but I donât see anything of the sort in you. He has sixteen wives. He is giving them up one by one.â The husband, with a towel on his shoulder, was going to the lake for his bath. He said to his wife: âYou are crazy! He wonât be able to give up the world. Is it ever possible to renounce bit by bit? I can renounce. Look! Here I go.â He didnât stop even to settle his household affairs. He left home just as he was, the towel on his shoulder, and went away. That is intense renunciation.

âThere is another kind of renunciation, called âmarkatavairÄgyaâ, âmonkey renunciationâ. A man, harrowed by distress at home, puts on an ochre robe and goes away to Benares. For many days he does not send home any news of himself. Then he writes to his people: âDonât be worried about me. I have got a job here.â

âThere is always trouble in family life. The wife may be disobedient. Perhaps the husband earns only twenty rupees a month. He hasnât the means to perform the ârice-eating ceremonyâ for his baby. He cannot educate his son. The house is dilapidated. The roof leaks and he hasnât the money to repair it.

âTherefore when the youngsters come here I ask them whether they have anyone at home. (To Mahima) Why should householders renounce the world? What great troubles the wandering monks pass through! The wife of a certain man said to him: âYou want to renounce the world? Why? You will have to beg morsels from eight different homes. But here you get all your food at one place. Isnât that nice?â

âWandering monks, while searching for a sadÄvrata,6 may have to go six miles out of their way. I have seen them travelling along the regular road after their pilgrimage to Puri and making a detour to find an eating-place.

âYou are leading a householderâs life. That is very good. It is like fighting from a fort. There are many disadvantages in fighting in an open field. So many dangers, too. Bullets may hit you.

âBut one should spend some time in solitude and attain Knowledge. Then one can lead the life of a householder. Janaka lived in the world after attaining Knowledge. When you have gained it, you may live anywhere. Then nothing matters.â

MAHIMA: âSir, why does a man become deluded by worldly objects?â

MASTER: âIt is because he lives in their midst without having realized God. Man never succumbs to delusion after he has realized God. The moth no longer enjoys darkness if it has once seen the light.

âTo be able to realize God, one must practise absolute continence. Sages like Sukadeva are examples of an urdhvaretÄ.7 Their chastity was absolutely unbroken. There is another class, who previously have had discharges of semen but who later on have controlled them. A man controlling the seminal fluid for twelve years develops a special power. He grows a new inner nerve called the nerve of memory. Through that nerve he remembers all, he understands all.

âLoss of semen impairs the strength. But it does not injure one if one loses it in a dream. That semen one gets from food. What remains after nocturnal discharge is enough. But one must not know a woman.

âThe semen that remains after nocturnal discharge is very ârefinedâ. The Lahas kept jars of molasses in their house. Every jar had a hole in it. After a year they found that the molasses had crystallized like sugar candy. The unnecessary watery part had leaked out through the hole.

âA sannyÄsi must absolutely renounce woman. You are already involved; but that doesnât matter.

âA sannyÄsi must not look even at the picture of a woman. But this is too difficult for an ordinary man. SÄ, re, gÄ, mÄ, pÄ, dhÄ, ni are the seven notes of the scale. It is not possible to keep your voice on âniâ a long time.

âTo lose semen is extremely harmful for a sannyÄsi. Therefore he must live so carefully that he will not have to see the form of a woman. He must keep himself away from a woman even if she is a devotee of God. It is injurious for him to look even at the picture of a woman. He will lose semen in a dream, if not in the waking state.

âA sannyÄsi may have control over his senses, but to set an example to mankind he should not talk with women. He must not talk to one very long, even if she is a devotee of God.

âLiving as a sannyÄsi is like observing the ekadaÅi without drinking even a drop of water. There are two other ways of observing the day. You may eat fruit or take luchi and curry. With the luchi and curry you may also take slices of bread soaked in milk. (All laugh.)

(Smiling) âAbsolute fasting is not possible for you.

âOnce I saw Krishnakishore eating luchi and curry on an ekÄdaÅi day. I said to Hriday, âHridu, I want to observe Krishnakishoreâs ekÄdaÅi!â (All laugh.) And so I did one day. I ate my fill. The next day I had to fast.â (Laughter.)

The devotees who had gone to the Panchavati to visit the hathayogi came back.

MASTER (addressing them): âWell, what do you think of him? I dare say you have measured him with your own tape.â

Sri Ramakrishna saw that very few of the devotees were willing to give money to the hathayogi.

MASTER: âYou donât like a sÄdhu if you have to give him money. Rajendra Mitra draws a salary of eight hundred rupees a month. He had been to AllÄhÄbÄd to see the kumbhamelÄ. I asked him, âWell, what kind of sÄdhus did you see at the fair?â Rajendra said: âI didnât find any very great sÄdhu there. I noticed one, it is true. But even he accepted money.â

âI say to myself, âIf no one gives money to a sÄdhu, then how will he feed himself?â There is no collection plate here; therefore all come. And I say to myself: âAlas! They love their money. Let them have it.â â

The Master rested awhile. A devotee sat on the end of the small couch and gently stroked his feet. The Master said to him softly: âThat which is formless again has form. One should believe in the forms of God also. By meditating on KÄli the aspirant realizes God as KÄli. Next he finds that the form merges in the Indivisible Absolute. That which is the Indivisible SatchidÄnanda is verily KÄli.â

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the semicircular porch west of his room, talking with Mahima and other devotees about the hathayogi. The talk drifted to Ramprasanna, the son of Krishnakishore. The Master was fond of the young man.

MASTER: âRamprasanna roams about aimlessly. The other day he came here and sat in the room, but he did not speak a word. He pressed his nostrils with his fingers, practising prÄnÄyÄma. I offered him something to eat, but he wouldnât take it. On another occasion I had asked him to sit by me. He squatted on the floor placing one leg upon the other. He was rather discourteous to Captain. I weep at his motherâs suffering.

(To Mahima) âRamprasanna asked me to speak to you about the hathayogi. The yogiâs daily expenses are six and a half ÄnnÄs. But he wonât tell you about it himself.â

MAHIMA: âWho will listen to him even if he does?â

Mani Sen of PÄnihÄti entered the room with several friends, one of whom was a physician. Mani asked the Master about his injured arm. The doctor did not approve of the medicine prescribed by Pratap Mazumdar. The Master said to him: âWhy should you say that? Pratap is no fool.â

Suddenly Latu cried out, âOh! The medicine bottle has dropped and broken.â

It was not yet dusk. The Master, seated on the couch, was talking to M. Mahimacharan was on the semicircular porch engaged in a loud discussion of the scriptures with the physician friend of Mani Sen. Sri Ramakrishna heard it and with a smile said to M.: âThere! He is delivering himself. That is the characteristic of rajas. It stimulates the desire to âlectureâ and to show off oneâs scholarship. But sattva makes one introspective. It makes one hide oneâs virtues. But I must say that Mahima is a grand person. He takes such delight in spiritual talk.â

Adhar entered the room, saluted the Master, and sat by M.âs side. He had not come for the past few days.

MASTER: âHello! Why havenât you come all these days?â

ADHAR: âSir, I have been busy with so many things. I had to attend a conference of the school committee and various other meetings.â

MASTER: âSo you completely lost yourself in schools and meetings and forgot everything else?â

ADHAR: âEverything else was hidden away in a corner of my mind. How is your arm?â

MASTER: âJust look. It is not yet healed. I have been taking medicine prescribed by Pratap.â

After a time the Master suddenly said to Adhar: âLook here. All these are unrealâmeetings, school, office, and everything else. God alone is the Substance, and all else is illusory. One should worship God with oneâs whole mind.â

Adhar sat without speaking a word.

MASTER: âAll else is illusory. This moment the body is and the next moment it is not. One must make haste to worship God.8

âBut you donât have to renounce everything. Live in the world the way the tortoise does. The tortoise roams about in the water but keeps its eggs on land. Its whole mind is on the eggs.

âWhat a nice state of mind Captain has developed! He looks like a rishi when he is seated to perform worship. He performs the Ärati with lighted camphor and recites beautiful hymns. When he rises from his seat after finishing the worship, his eyes are swollen from emotion, as if bitten by ants. Besides, he always devotes himself to the study of the sacred books, such as the GÄ«tÄ and the BhÄgavata. Once I used one or two English words before him, and that made him angry. He said, âEnglish-educated people are profane.â â

After a while Adhar said humbly to the Master: âSir, you havenât been to our place for a long time. The drawing-room smells worldly and everything else appears to be steeped in darkness.â

The Master was deeply touched by these words of his devotee. He suddenly stood up and blessed M. and Adhar in an ecstatic mood, touching their heads and hearts. In a voice choked with love the Master said: âI look upon you as NÄrÄyana Himself. You are indeed my own.â

Mahimacharan entered the room.

MASTER (to Mahima): âWhat I said about aspirants practising continence is true. Without chastity one cannot assimilate these teachings.

âOnce a man said to Chaitanya: âYou give the devotees so much instruction. Why donât they make much progress?â Chaitanya said: âThey dissipate their powers in the company of women. That is why they cannot assimilate spiritual instruction. If one keeps water in a leaky jar, the water escapes little by little through the leak.â â

Mahima and the other devotees remained silent. After a time Mahima said, âPlease pray to God for us that we may acquire the necessary strength.â

MASTER: âBe on your guard even now. It is difficult, no doubt, to check the torrent in the rainy season. But a great deal of water has gone out. If you build the embankment now it will stand.â

1 This observance is an ekÄdaÅi in name only, since the observer fills his stomach with delicious food. By avoiding rice and a few cooked articles, he keeps to the letter of the law.

Vali granted the boon. With two steps the Lord covered the earth, the heavens, and the interspaces. Vali was forced to place his own head before the Lord for the third step. This curbed his pride.

Gradually they should idealize their love by looking upon each other as divine, eventually realizing that their physical love is also the love of God. This is very difficult to realize.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# A DAY AT DAKSHINESWAR

Saturday, April 5, 1884

IT WAS ABOUT EIGHT OâCLOCK in the morning when M. arrived at the temple garden and found Sri Ramakrishna seated on the small couch in his room. A few devotees were sitting on the floor. The Master was talking to them. Prankrishna Mukherji was there.

Prankrishna belonged to an aristocratic family and lived in the northern part of Calcutta. He held a high post in an English business firm. He was very much devoted to Sri Ramakrishna and, though a householder, derived great pleasure from the study of VedÄnta philosophy. He was a frequent visitor at the temple garden. Once he invited the Master to his house in Calcutta and held a religious festival. Every day, early in the morning, he bathed in the holy water of the Ganges. Whenever it was convenient, he would come to Dakshineswar in a hired country boat.

That morning he had hired a boat and invited M. to accompany him to Dakshineswar. The boat had hardly left shore when the river became choppy. M. had become frightened and begged Prankrishna to put him back on land. In spite of assurances, M. had kept saying: âYou must put me ashore. I shall walk to Dakshineswar.â And so M. came on foot and found Sri Ramakrishna talking to Prankrishna and the others.

MASTER (to Prankrishna): âBut there is a greater manifestation of God in man. You may ask, âHow is it possible for God to be incarnated as a man who suffers from hunger, thirst, and the other traits of an embodied being, and perhaps also from disease and grief?â The reply is, âEven Brahman weeps, entrapped in the snare of the five elements.â

âDonât you know how RÄma had to weep, stricken with grief for SÄ«tÄ? Further, it is said that the Lord incarnated Himself as a sow in order to kill the demon HiranyÄksha. HiranyÄksha was eventually killed, but God would not go back to His abode in heaven. He enjoyed His sowâs life. He had given birth to several young ones and was rather happy with them. The gods said among themselves: âWhat does this mean? The Lord doesnât care to return to heaven!â They all went to Åiva and laid the matter before him. Åiva came down and urged the Lord to leave the sow body and return to heaven. But the sow only suckled her young ones. (Laughter.) Then Åiva destroyed the sow body with his trident, and the Lord came out laughing aloud and went back to His own abode.â

PRANKRISHNA (to the Master): âSir, what is the AnÄhata sound?â

MASTER: âIt is a spontaneous sound constantly going on by itself. It is the sound of the Pranava, Om. It originates in the Supreme Brahman and is heard by yogis. People immersed in worldliness do not hear it. A yogi alone knows that this sound originates both from his navel and from the Supreme Brahman resting on the Ocean of Milk.â1

PRANKRISHNA: âSir, what is the nature of the life after death?â

MASTER: âKeshab Sen also asked that question. As long as a man remains ignorant, that is to say, as long as he has not realized God, so long will he be born. But after attaining Knowledge he will not have to come back to this earth or to any other plane of existence.

âThe potter puts his pots in the sun to dry. Havenât you noticed that among them there are both baked and unbaked ones? When a cow happens to walk over them, some of the pots get broken to pieces. The broken pots that are already baked, the potter throws away, since they are of no more use to him. But the soft ones, though broken, he gathers up. He makes them into a lump and out of this forms new pots. In the same way, so long as a man has not realized God, he will have to come back to the Potterâs hand, that is, he will have to be born again and again.

âWhat is the use of sowing a boiled paddy grain? It will never bring forth a shoot. Likewise, if a man is boiled in the fire of Knowledge, he will not be used for new creation. He is liberated.

âAccording to the PurÄnas, the bhakta and the BhagavÄn are two separate entities. âIâ am one and âYouâ are another. The body is a plate, as it were, containing the water of mind, intelligence, and ego. Brahman is like the sun. It is reflected in the water. Therefore the devotee sees the divine form.

âAccording to the VedÄnta, Brahman alone is real and all else is mÄyÄ, dreamlike and unsubstantial. The ego, like a stick, lies across the Ocean of SatchidÄnanda. (To M.) Listen to what I am saying. When this ego is taken away, there remains only one undivided Ocean of SatchidÄnanda. But as long as the stick of ego remains, there is an appearance of two: here is one part of the water and there another part. Attaining the Knowledge of Brahman one is established in samÄdhi. Then the ego is effaced.

âBut ÅankarÄchÄrya retained the âego of Knowledgeâ2 in order to teach men. (To Prankrishna) But there are signs that distinguish the man of Knowledge. Some people think they have Knowledge. What are the characteristics of Knowledge? A jnÄni cannot injure anybody. He becomes like a child. If a steel sword touches the philosopherâs stone, it is transformed into gold. Gold can never cut. It may seem from the outside that a jnÄni also has anger or egotism, but in reality he has no such thing.

âFrom a distance a burnt string lying on the ground may look like a real one; but if you come near and blow at it, it disappears altogether. The anger and egotism of a jnÄni are mere appearances; they are not real.

âA child has no attachment. He makes a play house, and if anyone touches it, he will jump about and cry. The next moment he himself will break it. This moment he may be very attached to his cloth. He says: âMy daddy has given it to me. I wonât part with it.â But the next moment you can cajole him away from it with a toy. He will go away with you, leaving the cloth behind.

âThese are the characteristics of a jnÄni. Perhaps he has many luxuries at homeâcouch, chairs, paintings, and equipage. But any day he may leave all these and go off to Benares.

âAccording to VedÄnta the waking state, too, is unreal. Once a woodcutter lay dreaming, when someone woke him up. Greatly annoyed, he said: âWhy have you disturbed my sleep? I was dreaming that I was a king and the father of seven children. The princes were becoming well versed in letters and military arts. I was secure on my throne and ruled over my subjects. Why have you demolished my world of joy?â âBut that was a mere dreamâ, said the other man. âWhy should that bother you?â âFool!â said the wood-cutter. âYou donât understand. My becoming a king in the dream was just as real as is my being a wood-cutter. If being a wood-cutter is real, then being a king in a dream is real also.â â

Prankrishna always talked about jnÄna. Was this why the Master described the state of the jnÄni? Now he proceeded to describe the state of the vijnÄni.

MASTER: âJnÄna is the realization of Self through the process of âNeti, netiâ, âNot this, not thisâ. One goes into samÄdhi through this process of elimination and realizes the Ätman.

âBut vijnÄna means Knowledge with a greater fullness. Some have heard of milk, some have seen milk, and some have drunk milk. He who has merely heard of it is âignorantâ. He who has seen it is a jnÄni. But he who has drunk it has vijnÄna, that is to say, a fuller knowledge of it. After having the vision of God one talks to Him as if He were an intimate relative. That is vijnÄna.

âFirst of all you must discriminate, following the method of âNeti, netiâ: âHe is not the five elements, nor the sense-organs, nor the mind, nor the intelligence, nor the ego. He is beyond all these cosmic principles.â You want to climb to the roof; then you must eliminate and leave behind all the steps, one by one. The steps are by no means the roof. But after reaching the roof you find that the steps are made of the same materialsâbrick, lime, and brick-dustâas the roof. It is the Supreme Brahman that has become the universe and its living beings and the twenty-four cosmic principles. That which is Ätman has become the five elements. You may ask why the earth is so hard, if it has come out of Ätman? All is possible through the will of God. Donât you see that bone and flesh are made from blood and semen? How hard âsea-foamâ3 becomes!

âAfter attaining vijnÄna one can live in the world as well. Then one clearly realizes that God Himself has become the universe and all living beings, that He is not outside the world.

(To Prankrishna) âThe fact is that one must have the âspiritual eyeâ. You will develop that eye as soon as your mind becomes pure. Take for instance the KumÄri PujÄ. I worshipped a virgin. The girl, to be sure, had all her human imperfections; still I regarded her as the Divine Mother Herself.

âOn one side is the wife and on the other the son. Love is bestowed on both, but in different ways. Therefore it comes to this, that everything depends upon the mind. The pure mind acquires a new attitude. Through that mind one sees God in this world. Therefore one needs spiritual discipline.

âYes, spiritual discipline is necessary. You should know that a man becomes easily attached to a woman. A woman naturally loves a man, and a man also naturally loves a woman. Therefore both fall speedily from their spiritual ideal. But it also must be said that there is a great advantage in leading the life of a householder. In case of urgent necessity a man may live with his wife.

(Smiling) âWell, M., why are you smiling?â

M. (to himself): âThe Master makes this much allowance for householders since they cannot renounce everything. Is complete and absolute continence impossible for a householder?â

The hathayogi who had been living in the Panchavati entered the room. He was in the habit of taking milk and opium. He did not eat rice or other food and had no money to buy the milk and opium. The Master had talked with him in the Panchavati. The hathayogi had told Rakhal to ask the Master to make some provision for him, and Sri Ramakrishna had promised to speak about it to the visitors from Calcutta.

HATHAYOGI (to the Master): âWhat did you say to Rakhal about me?â

MASTER: âI said that I would ask some rich visitors to help you. Butâ(to Prankrishna) you, perhaps, do not like these yogis?â

Prankrishna remained silent. The hathayogi left the room and the conversation went on.

MASTER (to Prankrishna and the others): âIf a man leads a householderâs life he must have unflagging devotion to truth. God can be realized through truth alone. Formerly I was very particular about telling the truth, though now my zeal has abated a little. If I said, âI shall batheâ, then I would get into the water of the Ganges, recite the mantra, and sprinkle a little water over my head. But still there would remain some doubt in me as to whether my bath was complete. Once I went to Ramâs house in Calcutta. I happened to say, âI shall not take any luchi.â When I sat down for the meal I felt hungry. But I had said I would not eat the luchi; so I had to fill my stomach with sweets. (All laugh.)

âBut my zeal for truthfulness has abated a little now. Once I said I would go to the pine-grove, but then I felt I had no particular urge to go. What was to be done? I asked Ram4 about it. He said I didnât have to go. Then I reasoned to myself: âWell, everyone is NÄrÄyana. So Ram, too, is NÄrÄyana. Why shouldnât I listen to him? The elephant is NÄrÄyana no doubt, but the mÄhut is NÄrÄyana too. Since the mÄhut asked me not to go near the elephant, then why shouldnât I obey him?â Through reasoning like this my zeal for truthfulness is slightly less strong now than before.

âI find a change coming over me. Years ago Vaishnavcharan said to me, âOne attains Perfect Knowledge when one sees God in man.â Now I see that it is God alone who is moving about in various forms: as a holy man, as a cheat, as a villain. Therefore I say, âNÄrÄyana in the guise of the sÄdhu, NÄrÄyana in the guise of the cheat, NÄrÄyana in the guise of the villain, NÄrÄyana in the guise of the lecher.â

âNow my problem is how I can feed all of you. I want to feed everyone. So I keep one at a time with me and feed him.â

Prankrishna (looking at M. and smiling): âA fine man, indeed! (To the Master) He would not let us go till we put him ashore.â

MASTER (smiling): âWhy? What happened?â

PRANKRISHNA: âHe was in our boat. Seeing that the river was slightly rough, he insisted on being put ashore. (To M.) How did you come?â

M. (smiling): âOn foot.â

Sri Ramakrishna laughed.

PRANKRISHNA (to the Master): âSir, I am thinking now of giving up my work. One who is involved in activity cannot accomplish anything. (Pointing to his companion) I am training him to do my work. After I resign, he will relieve me. Work has become intolerable.â

MASTER: âYes, work is very troublesome. It is now good for you to meditate on God for a few days in solitude. No doubt you say that you would like to give up your work. Captain said the same thing. Worldly people talk that way; but they donât succeed in carrying out their intention.

âThere are many pundits who speak words of wisdom. But they merely talk; they donât live up to them. They are like vultures, which soar very high but keep their gaze fixed on the charnel-pit. What I mean is that these pundits are attached to the world, to âwoman and goldâ. If I hear that pundits are practising discrimination and dispassion, then I fear them. Otherwise I look upon them as mere goats and dogs.â

Prankrishna saluted the Master and took his leave. He said to M., âWill you come with us?â

M: âNo, sir! Catch me going with you again! Good-bye.â

Prankrishna laughed and said, âI see you wonât come in the boat.â

M. took a little stroll near the Panchavati and bathed in the river. Then he went to the temples of RÄdhÄkÄnta and KÄli and prostrated himself before the images. He said to himself: âI have heard that God has no form. Then why do I bow before these images? Is it because Sri Ramakrishna believes in gods and goddesses with form? I donât know anything about God, nor do I understand Him. The Master believes in images; then why shouldnât I too, who am so insignificant a creature, accept them?â

M. looked at the image of KÄli. He saw that the Divine Mother holds in Her two left hands a manâs severed head and a sword. With Her two right hands She offers boons and reassurance to Her devotees. In one aspect She is terrible, and in another She is the ever affectionate Mother of Her devotees. The two ideals are harmonized in Her. She is compassionate and affectionate to Her devotees, to those who are submissive and helpless. It is also true that She is terrible, the âConsort of Deathâ. She alone knows why She assumes two aspects at the same time.

M. remembered this interpretation of KÄli given by the Master. He said to himself, âI have heard that Keshab accepted KÄli in Sri Ramakrishnaâs presence. Is this, as Keshab used to say, the Goddess, all Spirit and Consciousness, manifesting Herself through a clay image?â

M. returned to the Masterâs room and sat on the floor. Sri Ramakrishna offered him some fruit and sweets to eat. On account of trouble in the family, M. had recently rented a house in another section of Calcutta near his school, his father and brothers continuing to live in the ancestral home. But Sri Ramakrishna wanted him to return to his own home, since a joint family affords many advantages to one leading a religious life. Once or twice the Master had spoken to M. to this effect, but unfortunately he had not yet returned to his family. Sri Ramakrishna referred to the matter again.

MASTER: âTell me that you are going to your ancestral home.â

M: âI can never persuade myself to enter that place.â

MASTER: âWhy? Your father is making over the whole house.â

M: âI have suffered too much there. I can by no means make up my mind to go there.â

MASTER: âWhom do you fear?â

M: âAll of them.â

MASTER (seriously): âIsnât that like your being afraid to get into the boat?â

The midday worship and the offering of food in the temples were over. The bells, gongs, and cymbals of the Ärati were being played, and the temple garden was filled with joyful activity. Beggars, sÄdhus, and guests hurried to the guest-house for the noonday meal, carrying leaf or metal plates in their hands. M. also took some of the prasÄd from the KÄli temple.

Sri Ramakrishna had been resting awhile after his meal when several devotees, including Ram and Girindra, arrived. They sat down after saluting the Master. The conversation turned to the New Dispensation Church of Keshab Chandra Sen.

RAM (to the Master): âSir, I donât think the NavavidhÄn has done people any good. If Keshab Babu himself was a genuine man, why are his disciples left in such a plight? I donât think there is anything at all in the New Dispensation. It is like rattling some potsherds in a room and then locking it up. People may take it to be the jingling of coins, but inside there is nothing but potsherds. Outsiders donât know what is inside.â

MASTER: âThere must be some substance in it. Otherwise, why should so many people respect Keshab? Why isnât Shivanath honoured as much as Keshab? Such a thing cannot happen without the will of God.

âBut a man cannot act as an ÄchÄrya without renouncing the world. People wonât respect him. They will say: âOh, he is a worldly man. He secretly enjoys âwoman and goldâ himself but tells us that God alone is real and the world unsubstantial, like a dream.â Unless a man renounces everything his teachings cannot be accepted by all. Some worldly people may follow him. Keshab led the life of a householder; hence his mind was directed to the world also. He had to safeguard his family interests. That is why he left his affairs in such good order though he delivered so many religious lectures. What an aristocratic man he married his daughter to! Inside Keshabâs inner apartments I saw many big bedsteads. All these things gradually come to one who leads a householderâs life. The world is indeed a place for enjoyment.â

RAM: âKeshab Sen inherited those bedsteads when his ancestral property was divided. And for Keshab to take part in the division of property! Whatever you may say, sir, Vijay Babu told me that Keshab had said to him, âI am a partial manifestation of Christ and GaurÄnga. I suggest that you declare yourself as Advaita.â5 Do you know what else he said? He said that you too were a follower of the New Dispensation.â (All laugh.)

MASTER (laughing): âWho knows? But as for myself, I donât even know what the term âNew Dispensationâ means.â (Laughter.)

RAM: âKeshabâs disciples say that he was the first to harmonize jnÄna and bhakti.â

MASTER (in surprise): âHow is that? What then of the AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana? It is written there that, while praying to RÄma, NÄrada said: âO RÄma, Thou art the Supreme Brahman described in the Vedas. Thou dwellest with us as a man; Thou appearest as a man. In reality Thou art not a man; Thou art that Supreme Brahman.â RÄma said: âNÄrada, I am very much pleased with you. Accept a boon from Me.â NÄrada replied: âWhat boon shall I ask of Thee? Grant me pure love for Thy Lotus Feet, and may I never be deluded by Thy world-bewitching mÄyÄ!â The AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana is full of such statements regarding jnÄna and bhakti.â

The conversation turned to Amrita, a disciple of Keshab.

RAM: âAmrita Babu seems to be in very bad shape.â

MASTER: âYes, he looked very ill when I saw him the other day.â

RAM: âSir, let me tell you about the lectures of the New Dispensation. While the drum is being played, the members cry out, âVictory unto Keshab!â You say that âdalâ6 grows only in a stagnant pool. So Amrita said one day in the course of his sermon: âThe holy man7 has no doubt said that âdalâ grows in a stagnant pool. But, brothers, we want âdalâ, we want a sect. Really and truly, I tell you that we want a sect.â â

MASTER: âWhat nonsense! Shame on him! What kind of sermon is that?â

The conversation drifted to the desire of some people for praise.

MASTER: âThey took me to Keshabâs house to see a performance of the NimÄi-sannyÄs. I heard, that day, someone speaking of Keshab and Pratap as Chaitanya and NityÄnanda. Prasanna asked me, âWho are you then?â Keshab looked at me to see what I would say. I said to him, âI am the servant of your servant, the dust of the dust of your feet.â Keshab said with a smile, âYou canât catch him!â â

RAM: âSometimes Keshab used to say you were John the Baptist.â

A DEVOTEE: âBut Keshab also said you were the Chaitanya of the nineteenth century [said in English].â

MASTER: âWhat does that mean?â

DEVOTEE: âThat Chaitanya has been incarnated again in the present century of the Christian era, and that you are he.â

MASTER (absent-mindedly): âWhat of it? Can you tell me now how my arm can be cured? This arm is worrying me so much.â

They talked about Trailokyaâs music. Trailokya sang devotional songs in Keshabâs BrÄhmo SamÄj.

MASTER: âAh! How nice his songs are!â

RAM: âDo you think they are genuine?â

MASTER: âYes, they are. Otherwise, why should I be so drawn to them?â

RAM: âHe has composed his songs by borrowing your ideas. While conducting the worship Keshab Sen described your feelings and realizations, and Trailokya Babu composed songs accordingly. Take this song, for instance:

There is an overflow of Joy in the market-place of Love;

He saw you enjoying divine bliss in the company of devotees and wrote songs like this.â

MASTER (with a smile): âStop! Donât torment me any more. Why should I be involved in all this?â (All laugh.)

GIRINDRA: âThe BrÄhmos say that the Paramahamsadeva has no faculty for organization [said in English].â

MASTER: âWhat does that mean?â

M: âThat you donât know how to lead a sect; that your intellect is rather dull. They say things like that.â (All laugh.)

MASTER (to Ram): âNow tell me why my arm was hurt. Stand up and deliver a lecture on that. (Laughter.)

âThe BrÄhmos insist that God is formless. Suppose they do. It is enough to call on Him with sincerity of heart. If the devotee is sincere, then God, who is the Inner Guide of all, will certainly reveal to the devotee His true nature.

âBut it is not good to say that what we ourselves think of God is the only truth and what others think is false; that because we think of God as formless, therefore He is formless and cannot have any form; that because we think of God as having form, therefore He has form and cannot be formless. Can a man really fathom Godâs nature?

âThis kind of friction exists between the Vaishnavas and the ÅÄktas. The Vaishnava says, âMy KeÅava is the only Saviourâ, whereas the ÅÄkta insists, âMy Bhagavati is the only Saviour.â

âOnce I took Vaishnavcharan to Mathur Babu. Now, Vaishnavcharan was a very learned Vaishnava and an orthodox devotee of his sect. Mathur, on the other hand, was a devotee of the Divine Mother. They were engaged in a friendly discussion when suddenly Vaishnavcharan said, âKeÅava is the only Saviour.â No sooner did Mathur hear this than his face became red with anger and he blurted out, âYou rascal!â (All laugh.) He was a ÅÄkta. Wasnât it natural for him to say that? I gave Vaishnavcharan a nudge.

âI see people who talk about religion constantly quarrelling with one another. Hindus, MussalmÄns, BrÄhmos, ÅÄktas, Vaishnavas, Åaivas, all quarrel with one another. They havenât the intelligence to understand that He who is called Krishna is also Åiva and the Primal Åakti, and that it is He, again, who is called Jesus and ÄllÄh. âThere is only one RÄma and He has a thousand names.â

âTruth is one; only It is called by different names. All people are seeking the same Truth; the variance is due to climate, temperament, and name. A lake has many ghÄts. From one ghÄt the Hindus take water in jars and call it âjalâ. From another ghÄt the MussalmÄns take water in leather bags and call it âpÄniâ. From a third the Christians take the same thing and call it âwaterâ. (All laugh.) Suppose someone says that the thing is not âjalâ but âpÄniâ, or that it is not âpÄniâ but âwaterâ, or that it is not âwaterâ but âjalâ. It would indeed be ridiculous. But this very thing is at the root of the friction among sects, their misunderstandings and quarrels. This is why people injure and kill one another, and shed blood, in the name of religion. But this is not good. Everyone is going toward God. They will all realize Him if they have sincerity and longing of heart.

(To M.) âThis is for you. All scripturesâthe Vedas, the PurÄnas, the Tantrasâseek Him alone and no one else, only that one SatchidÄnanda. That which is called SatchidÄnanda Brahman in the Vedas is called SatchidÄnanda Åiva in the Tantra. Again it is He alone who is called SatchidÄnanda Krishna in the PurÄnas.â

The Master was told that now and then Ram cooked his own food at home.

MASTER (to M.): âDo you too cook your own meals?â

M: âNo, sir.â

MASTER: âYou may try it. With your meals take a little clarified butter made from cowâs milk. That will purify your body and mind.â

A long conversation ensued about Ramâs household affairs. Ramâs father was a devout Vaishnava and worshipped Krishna daily at home. He had married a second time when Ram was quite young. Both the father and the stepmother lived with Ram at Ramâs house. But Ram was never happy with his stepmother, and this sometimes created a misunderstanding between himself and his father.

They were talking about this when Ram said, âMy father has gone to the dogs!â

MASTER (to the devotees): âDid you hear that? The father has gone to the dogs and the son is all right!â

RAM: âThere is no peace when my stepmother comes home. There is always some trouble or other. Our family is about to break up. So I say, let her live with her father.â

GIRINDRA (to Ram): âWhy donât you too keep your wife at her fatherâs home?â (Laughter.)

MASTER (smiling): âAre husband and wife like earthen pots or jars, that you may keep the pot in one place and the lid in another? Åiva in one place and Åakti in another?â

RAM: âSir, we are quite happy. But when she comes the family is broken up. If such is the caseââ

MASTER: âThen build them a separate home. That will be a different thing. You will defray their monthly expenses. How worthy of worship oneâs parents are! Rakhal asked me if he could take the food left on his fatherâs plate. âWhat do you mean?â I said. âWhat have you become that you cannot?â But it is also true that good people wonât give anyone, even a dog, the food from their plates.â

GIRINDRA: âSir, suppose oneâs parents are guilty of a terrible crime, a heinous sin?â

MASTER: âWhat if they are? You must not renounce your mother even if she commits adultery. The woman guru of a certain family became corrupt. The members of the family said that they would like to make the son of the guru their spiritual guide. But I said: âHow is that? Will you accept the shoot and give up the yam? Suppose she is corrupt; still you must regard her as your Ishta. âThough my guru visits the tavern, still to me he is the holy NityÄnanda.â â

âAre father and mother mere trifles? No spiritual practice will bear fruit unless they are pleased. Chaitanya was intoxicated with the love of God. Still, before taking to the monastic life, for how many days did he try to persuade his mother to give him her permission to become a monk! He said to her: âMother, donât worry. I shall visit you every now and then.â

(To M., reproachfully) âAnd let me say this to you. Your father and mother brought you up. You yourself are the father of several children. Yet you have left home with your wife. You have cheated your parents. You have come away with your wife and children, and you feel you have become a holy man. Your father doesnât need any money from you; otherwise I should have cried, âShame on you!â â

Everybody in the room became grave and remained silent.

MASTER: âA man has certain debts to pay: his debts to the gods and rishis, and his debts to mother, father, and wife. He cannot achieve anything without paying the debt he owes to his parents. A man is indebted to his wife as well. Harish has renounced his wife and is living here. If he had left her unprovided for, then I should have called him an abominable wretch.

âAfter attaining Knowledge you will regard that very wife as the manifestation of the Divine Mother Herself. It is written in the Chandi, âThe Goddess dwells in all beings as the Mother.â It is She who has become your mother.

âAll the women you see are only She, the Divine Mother. That is why I cannot rebuke even BrindÄ, the maidservant. There are people who spout verses from the scriptures and talk big, but in their conduct they are quite different. Ramprasanna is constantly busy procuring opium and milk for the hathayogi. He says that Manu enjoins it upon man to serve the sÄdhu. But his old mother hasnât enough to eat. She walks to the market to buy her own groceries. It makes me very angry.

âBut here you have to consider another thing. When a man is intoxicated with ecstatic love of God, then who is his father or mother or wife? His love of God is so intense that he becomes mad with it. Then he has no duty to perform. He is free from all debts. What is this divine intoxication? In this state a man forgets the world. He also forgets his own body, which is so dear to all. Chaitanya had this intoxication. He plunged into the ocean not knowing that it was the ocean. He dashed himself again and again on the ground. He was not aware of hunger, of thirst, or of sleep. He was not at all conscious of any such thing as his body.â

All at once Sri Ramakrishna exclaimed, âAh, Chaitanya!â and stood up.

MASTER (to the devotees): âChaitanya means âUndivided Consciousnessâ. Vaishnavcharan used to say that GaurÄnga was like a bubble in the Ocean of Undivided Consciousness.

(To the elder Gopal8) âDo you intend to go on a pilgrimage now?â

GOPAL: âYes, sir. I should like to wander about a little.â

RAM (to Gopal): âHe [meaning the Master] says that one becomes a kutichaka after being a bahudaka. The sÄdhu that visits many holy places is called a bahudaka. He whose craving for travel has been satiated and who sits down in one place is called a kutichaka.

âHe also tells us a parable. Once a bird sat on the mast of a ship. When the ship sailed through the mouth of the Ganges into the âblack watersâ of the ocean, the bird failed to notice the fact. When it finally became aware of the ocean, it left the mast and flew north in search of land. But it found no limit to the water and so returned. After resting awhile it flew south. There too it found no limit to the water. Panting for breath the bird returned to the mast. Again, after resting awhile, it flew east and then west. Finding no limit to the water in any direction, at last it settled down on the mast of the ship.â

MASTER (to the elder Gopal and the other devotees): âAs long as a man feels that God is âthereâ, he is ignorant. But he attains Knowledge when he feels that God is âhereâ.

âA man wanted a smoke. He went to a neighbourâs house to light his charcoal. It was the dead of night and the household was asleep. After he had knocked a great deal, someone came down to open the door. At sight of the man he asked, âHello! Whatâs the matter?â The man replied: âCanât you guess? You know how fond I am of smoking. I have come here to light my charcoal.â The neighbour said: âHa! Ha! You are a fine man indeed! You took the trouble to come and do all this knocking at the door! Why, you have a lighted lantern in your hand!â (All laugh.)

âWhat a man seeks is very near him. Still he wanders about from place to place.â

RAM: âSir, I now realize why a guru asks some of his disciples to visit the four principal holy places of the country. Once having wandered about, the disciple discovers that it is the same here as there. Then he returns to the guru. All this wandering is only to create faith in the guruâs words.â

After this conversation had come to an end, Sri Ramakrishna extolled Ramâs virtues.

MASTER (to the devotees): âHow many fine qualities Ram possesses! How many devotees he serves and looks after! (To Ram) Adhar told me that you showed him great kindness.â

Adhar, a beloved householder devotee of the Master, had recently arranged some religious music at his house. The Master and many devotees had been present. But Adhar had forgotten to invite Ram, who was a very proud man and had complained about it to his friends. So Adhar had gone to Ramâs house to express his regret for the mistake.

RAM: âIt wasnât really Adharâs mistake. I have come to know that Rakhal is to blame. Rakhal was given chargeââ

MASTER: âYou mustnât find fault with Rakhal. Heâs a mere child. Even now you can bring out his motherâs milk by squeezing his throat.â

RAM: âSir, why should you speak that way? It was such an occasion!â

MASTER: (interrupting): âAdhar simply didnât remember to invite you. He is absent-minded. The other day he went with me to Jadu Mallickâs house. As we took our leave, I said to him, âYou havenât offered anything to the Goddess in the chapel.â âSir,â he said, âI didnât know one should.â

(To Ram) âSuppose he didnât invite you to his house. Why such a fuss about going to a place where the name of the Lord was sung? One may go unasked to participate in religious music. One doesnât have to be invited.â

1 According to Hindu mythology, after the dissolution of the universe and before the next creation, the Supreme Lord rests on the Ocean of the Great Cause, also called the âOcean of Milkâ.

2 The ego illumined and purified by the Knowledge of God. Following the method of discrimination, the jnÄni, in samÄdhi, merges his ego in Brahman. This apparent ego is called the âego of Knowledgeâ. A bhakta, following the path of love, realizes his eternal relationship with God. He too keeps an appearance of individuality on the relative plane. This ego has none of the characteristics of the worldly ego and is called the âego of Devotionâ.
