The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# PUNDIT SHASHADHAR

Wednesday, June 25, 1884

I T WAS THE DAY of the RathayÄtrÄ, the Car Festival of the Hindus. At Ishanâs invitation Sri Ramakrishna went to his house in Calcutta. For some time the Master had had a desire to meet Pundit Shashadhar TarkachudÄmani, who had been staying with one of Ishanâs neighbours. So it was decided that he would visit the pundit in the afternoon.

A few devotees, including Hazra, accompanied the Master to Ishanâs house. Ishan had invited one or two brÄhmin scholars and a devotee who followed the TÄntrik method of worship. Shrish and Ishanâs other sons were also present.

The Master noticed that the TÄntrik worshipper had a vermilion mark on his forehead, and smilingly said, âI see he is branded.â

After a while M. and Narendra arrived and bowed before Sri Ramakrishna. The Master had previously informed M. that he would be at Ishanâs house.

The Master joked about the delay in serving their meal. One of the scholars quoted a Sanskrit verse about the anxiety created in peopleâs minds by the pangs of hunger. Proceeding to explain the verse he said: âThe study of philosophy is indeed edifying, but poetry is more fascinating than philosophy. People listening to good poems think of the study of philosophy âVedÄnta, NyÄya, SÄmkhya, and so forthâas dry and insipid. Again, music is more attractive than poetry. Music melts even a heart of stone. But a beautiful woman has an even greater attraction for a manâs heart than music. Such a woman, passing by, diverts a manâs attention from both poetry and music. But when a man feels the pangs of hunger, everything elseâpoetry, music, and womanâappears as of no consequence. Thus hunger is the most arresting thing.â

The Master remarked with a smile, âThe pundit is witty.â

Soon Narendra began to sing. A few moments later the Master went upstairs for a little rest. M. and Shrish accompanied him. M. introduced Shrish to the Master, saying: âHe is a scholar and a man of peaceful nature. We were fellow students in our boyhood. Now he is a lawyer.â

MASTER: âIt is a pity that such a man should practise law.â

M: âYes, sir. It was a mistake on his part.â

MASTER: âI know a few lawyers. One of them shows me great respect. He is a straightforward man. (To Shrish) What is your idea about the most essential thing in life?â

SHRISH: âGod exists and He alone does everything. But the attributes we ascribe to Him are not the right ones. How can a man conceive of Him? His nature is infinite.â

MASTER: âWhat need is there of your counting the number of trees and branches in an orchard? You have come to the orchard to eat mangoes. Do that and be happy. The aim of human birth is to love God. Realize that love and be at peace.

âSuppose you have entered a tavern for a drink. Is it necessary for you to know how many gallons of wine there are in the tavern? One glass is enough for you. What need is there of your knowing the infinite qualities of God? You may discriminate for millions of years about Godâs attributes and still you will not know them.â

The Master remained silent a few minutes. A brÄhmin pundit came into the room.

MASTER (to M.): âThere is no substance whatsoever in the worldly life. The members of Ishanâs family are good; so he has some peace here. Suppose his sons had been lewd, disobedient, and addicted to drink and other vices. Then there would have been no end to his troubles. One very seldom comes across such a religious family, in which all the members are devoted to God. I have seen only two or three such families. Generally one finds quarrels, misunderstanding, jealousy, and friction. Besides, there are disease, grief, and poverty in the world. Seeing this condition, I prayed to the Divine Mother, âO Mother, turn my mind at once from the world to God.â

âLook at Narendraâs troubles. His father is dead and the members of his family are starving. He has been trying his utmost to secure a position, but he has not yet found one. Just see how unsettled his mind is!

(To M.) âYou used to come to Dakshineswar very frequently. But why have you become such a rare visitor? Perhaps you have become particularly friendly with your wife. Is it true? Why should I blame you? The influence of âwoman and goldâ is everywhere. Therefore I pray, âO Divine Mother, please donât make me a worldly man if I am to be born again in a human body.â â

BRÄHMIN SCHOLAR: âWhy should you say that, sir? The scriptures extol the life of a householder.â

MASTER: âYes, that is true. But it is very difficult to lead the true life of a householder. (To M.) How wrong of us! They are singing, especially Narendra, and we have left the room.â

About four oâclock in the afternoon the Master left in a carriage for the house where Pundit Shashadhar was staying. As soon as Sri Ramakrishna got into the carriage he went into samÄdhi. His physical frame was very tender as a result of the austerities he had undergone during the long years of his spiritual discipline and his constant absorption in God-Consciousness. The Master would suffer from the slightest physical discomfort and even from the vibration of worldly thoughts around him. Once Keshab Chandra Sen had said that Sri Ramakrishna, Christ, and Sri Chaitanya belonged to a delicate species of humanity that should be kept in a glass case and protected from the vulgar contact of the world.

It was the rainy season, and a fine drizzle of rain had made the road muddy. The sky was overcast. The devotees followed the carriage on foot. As the carriage stopped in front of the house, the host and his relatives welcomed the Master and took him upstairs to the drawing-room. There the Master met the pundit.

Pundit Shashadhar, a man of fair complexion and no longer young, had a string of rudrÄksha beads around his neck. He was one of the renowned Sanskrit scholars of his timeâa pillar of orthodox Hinduism, which had reasserted itself after the first wave of Christianity and Western culture had passed over Hindu society. His clear exposition of the Hindu scriptures, his ringing sincerity, and his stirring eloquence had brought back a large number of the educated young Hindus of Bengal to the religion of their forefathers.

The pundit saluted the Master with reverence. Narendra, Rakhal, Ram, Hazra, and M., who had come with the Master, seated themselves in the room as near the Master as they could, anxious not to miss one of his words.

At the sight of the pundit the Master again went into samÄdhi. After a while, still remaining in that state, he looked at the pundit and said with a smile, âVery well, very well.â Then, addressing the pundit, the Master said, âTell me how you give lectures.â

PUNDIT: âSir, I try to explain the teachings of the Hindu scriptures.â

MASTER: âFor the Kaliyuga the path of devotion described by NÄrada is best. Where can people find time now to perform their duties according to the scriptural injunctions? Nowadays the decoctions of roots and herbs of the orthodox Hindu physicians cannot be given to a fever patient. By the time that kind of medicine begins its slow process of curing, the patient is done for. Therefore only a drastic medicine like the allopathic âfever mixtureâ is effective now. You may ask people to practise scriptural rites and rituals; but, when prescribing the rituals, remove the âhead and tailâ.1 I tell people not to bother about the elaborate rituals of the sandhyÄ as enjoined in the scriptures. I say that it will be enough for them to repeat the GÄyatri alone. If you must give instruction about scriptural ceremonies, do so only to a very few, like Ishan.

âYou may deliver thousands of lectures, but they wonât make the slightest impression on worldly people. Can one drive a nail into a stone wall? The point of the nail will sooner break than make a dent in the stone. What will you gain by striking the tough skin of the crocodile with a sword? The sÄdhuâs water-bowl, made from the shell of a bitter gourd, may visit the four principal holy places of India with its owner, but it will still remain as bitter as ever. Your lectures are not helping worldly people very much; and you will realize this by and by. The calf cannot stand on its legs all at once. Now it drops to the ground and now it stands up. So it learns to stand firmly on its legs and walk.

âYou cannot distinguish a lover of God from a worldly person. It isnât your fault, of course. When the first onrush of the gale shakes the trees, it is impossible to distinguish one tree from anotherâthe mango from the tamarind, for instance.

âWithout having realized God one cannot give up rituals altogether. How long should one practise the sandhyÄ and other forms of ritualistic worship? As long as one does not shed tears of joy at the name of God and feel a thrill in oneâs body. You will know that your ritualistic worship has come to an end when your eyes become filled with tears as you repeat âOm RÄmaâ. Then you do not have to continue your sandhyÄ or other rituals.

âWhen the fruit appears the blossom drops off. Love of God is the fruit, and rituals are the blossom. When the daughter-in-law of the house becomes pregnant, she cannot do much work. Her mother-in-law gradually lessens her duties in the house. When her time arrives she does practically nothing. And after the child is born her only work is to play with it. She doesnât do any household duties at all. The sandhyÄ merges in the GÄyatri, the GÄyatri in Om, and Om in samÄdhi. It is like the sound of a bell: tâaâm. The yogi, by following in the trail of the sound Om, gradually merges himself in the Supreme Brahman. His sandhyÄ and other ritualistic duties disappear in samÄdhi. Thus the duties of the jnÄni come to an end.â

As the Master talked of samÄdhi, he himself went into that state. His face radiated a heavenly light. Bereft of outer consciousness, he could not utter another word. His gaze was indrawn and transfixed in communion with the Self. After a long time the Master began to recognize the world around him and said, like a child, âI shall have a drink of water.â Whenever after samÄdhi the Master asked for a drink of water, his devotees knew that he was gradually becoming conscious of the outer world.

Still lingering in the state of ecstasy, he said to the Divine Mother: âO Mother, the other day You showed me Pundit Iswar Chandra VidyÄsÄgar. Then I told You that I should like to see another pundit, and so You have brought me here.â

Looking at the pundit, he said: âMy child, add a little more to your strength. Practise spiritual discipline a few days more. You have hardly set your foot on the tree, yet you expect to lay hold of a big cluster of fruit. But, of course, you are doing all this for the welfare of others.â With these words he bowed his head before the pundit.

The Master continued: âWhen I first heard about you, I inquired whether you were merely erudite or whether you had discrimination and renunciation. A pundit who doesnât know how to discriminate between the Real and the unreal is no pundit at all.

âThere is no harm in teaching others if the preacher has a commission from the Lord. Nobody can confound a preacher who teaches people after having received the command of God. âWhen the lamp is lighted the moths come in swarms. They donât have to be invited. In the same way, the preacher who has a commission from God need not invite people to hear him. He doesnât have to announce the time of his lectures. He possesses such irresistible attraction that people come to him of their own accord. What will you be pleased to accept?â In that case I say to them: âGo away. I donât care for these. I donât want anything.â

âDoes the magnet say to the iron, âCome near me?â That is not necessary. Because of the attraction of the magnet, the iron rushes to it.

âSuch a preacher may not be a scholarly person, but donât conclude from that that he has any lack of wisdom. Does book-learning make one wise? âCan a preacher ever lack knowledge if but once he is favoured with a benign glance from the Divine Mother? Therefore I ask you whether you have received any commission from God.â

HAZRA: âOh yes, he must have it. (To the pundit) Isnât it true, sir?â

MASTER: âWhat will a man accomplish by mere lectures without the commission from God? Once a BrÄhmo preacher said in the course of his sermon, âFriends, how much I used to drink!â and so on. âA high government official from BarisÄl once said to me, âSir, if you begin the work of preaching, I too shall gird my loins.â I told him the story of peopleâs dirtying the bank of the HÄldÄrpukur and of its being stopped only when a constable, armed with authority from the government, put up a notice prohibiting it.

âTherefore I say to you, dive deep in God-Consciousness.â

Saying this, the Master began to sing in an ecstasy of love for God:

If you descend to the uttermost depths,

The Master continued: âOne does not die if one sinks in this Ocean. This is the Ocean of Immortality. Once I said to Narendra: âGod is the Ocean of Bliss. Tell me if you want to plunge into It. Just imagine there is some syrup in a cup and that you have become a fly. âThere are innumerable pathways leading to the Ocean of Immortality. The essential thing is to reach the Ocean. It doesnât matter which path you follow. âWhat is jnÄnayoga? The jnÄni seeks to realize Brahman. He discriminates, saying, âNot this, not thisâ. âTo follow jnÄnayoga in this age is also very difficult. First, a manâs life depends entirely on food. Second, he has a short span of life. A thorn enters your flesh, blood flows from the wound, and you suffer very badly from the pain; but nevertheless if you are a jnÄni you must be able to say: âWhy, there is no thorn in my flesh at all. Nothing is the matter with me.â

âTherefore bhaktiyoga is prescribed for this age. By following this path one comes to God more easily than by following the others. One can undoubtedly reach God by following the paths of jnÄna and karma, but they are very difficult paths.

âBhaktiyoga is the religion for this age. But that does not mean that the lover of God will reach one goal and the philosopher and worker another. It means that if a person seeks the Knowledge of Brahman he can attain It by following the path of bhakti, too. God, who loves His devotee, can give him the Knowledge of Brahman if He so desires.

âBut the bhakta wants to realize the Personal God endowed with form and talk to Him. He seldom seeks the Knowledge of Brahman. But God, who does everything at His pleasure, can make His devotee the heir to His infinite glories if it pleases Him. He gives His devotee both the Love of God and the Knowledge of Brahman. If one is able somehow to reach Calcutta, one can see the MaidÄn and the museum and other places too. The thing is how to reach Calcutta.

âBy realizing the Divine Mother of the Universe, you will get Knowledge as well as Devotion. You will get both. In bhÄva samÄdhi you will see the form of God, and in nirvikalpa samÄdhi you will realize Brahman, the Absolute Existence-Knowledge-Bliss. In nirvikalpa samÄdhi ego, name, and form do not exist.

âA lover of God prays to the Divine Mother: âO Mother, I am very much afraid of selfish actions. Such actions have desires behind them, and if I perform them I shall have to reap their fruit. But it is very difficult to work in a detached spirit. I shall certainly forget Thee, O Mother, if I involve myself in selfish actions. Therefore I have no use for them. May my actions, O Divine Mother, be fewer every day till I attain Thee. May I perform, without attachment to the results, only what action is absolutely necessary for me. May I have great love for Thee as I go on with my few duties. May I not entangle myself in new work so long as I do not realize Thee. But I shall perform it if I receive Thy command. Otherwise not.â â

PUNDIT: âHow far did you go in visiting the sacred places?â

MASTER: âOh, I visited a few places. (With a smile) But Hazra went farther and also climbed higher. He visited Hrishikesh, but I didnât go so far or so high.

âYou must have noticed kites and vultures soaring very high in the sky; but their eyes are always fixed on the charnel-pits. Do you know the meaning of âcharnel-pitsâ? It is âwoman and goldâ.

âWhat is the use of making pilgrimages if you can attain love of God remaining where you are? I have been to Benares and noticed the same trees there as here. The same green tamarind-leaves!

âPilgrimage becomes futile if it does not enable you to attain love of God. Love of God is the one essential and necessary thing. Do you know the meaning of âkites and vulturesâ? There are many people who talk big and who say that they have performed most of the duties enjoined in the scriptures. But with all that their minds are engrossed in worldliness and deeply preoccupied with money, riches, name, fame, creature comforts, and such things.â

PUNDIT: âIt is true, sir. Going on a pilgrimage is like seeking diamonds and gems, while discarding the precious stone that is worn by NÄrÄyana Himself on His breast.â

MASTER: âI want you to remember this. You may impart thousands of instructions to people, but they will not bear fruit except in proper time. On going to bed, a child said to his mother, âMother, please wake me up when I feel the call of nature.â The mother said: âDonât worry about it, my child. That call will wake you up itself.â (All laugh.) One feels yearning for God at the proper time.

âThere are three classes of physicians. The physicians of one class feel the patientâs pulse and go away, merely prescribing medicine. As they leave the room they simply ask the patient to take the medicine. They are the poorest class of physicians. Likewise, there are teachers who only give instruction, but do not stop to see whether their teachings have produced a good or bad effect. They do not think at all about the disciple.

âThere are physicians of another class, who prescribe medicine and ask the patient to take it. If the patient is unwilling to follow their directions, they reason with him. They are the mediocre physicians. Likewise, there are mediocre teachers. They give instruction to the student and, further, try to persuade him in various ways to follow the instruction.

âLastly, there are the physicians of the highest class. If the patient does not respond to their gentle persuasion, they even exert force upon him. If necessary, they press their knees on the patientâs chest and force the medicine down his throat. Likewise, there are teachers of the highest class, who even exert force to direct the mind of the pupil toward God.â

PUNDIT: âSir, if there are such superior teachers as you have described, then why should you say that one does not get the Knowledge of God until the right time comes?â

MASTER: âYou are right. But what will the physician do if the medicine runs out of the patientâs mouth and doesnât reach his stomach? In such a case even the best physician canât do anything.

âThe teacher should judge the fitness of the student before giving him instruction. But you donât discriminate in your instruction. When a young man comes to me for instruction, first of all I ask him about his relatives at home. Suppose he has lost his father; suppose his father has left some debts for him. How can such a person direct his mind to God? Are you listening to me?â

PUNDIT: âYes, sir. I am paying attention to every word.â

MASTER: âOne day some Åikh soldiers came to the temple garden at Dakshineswar. I met them in front of the KÄli temple. One of them referred to God as very compassionate. âIndeed!â I said. âIs that true? But how do you know?â He answered, âBecause, sir, God gives us food and takes every care of us.â I said: âWhy should that surprise you? God is the Father of us all. Who will look after the child if the father doesnât? Do you mean to say that the people of the neighbouring village should look after the child?â

NARENDRA: âThen shouldnât we call God kind?â

MASTER: âHave I forbidden you to? What I mean is that God is our very own. He is not a stranger to us.â

PUNDIT: âPriceless words!â

MASTER(to Narendra): âI listened to your singing, but I didnât enjoy it. So I left the room. Your mind is now set on seeking a job, and therefore your song sounded dull.â

Narendra flushed. He felt ashamed of himself and remained silent.

The Master asked for a drink of water. A glass of water had been placed near him, but he could not take it. He asked for some fresh water. Later it was found that a man of immoral character had touched the first glass.

PUNDIT(to Hazra): âYou live in his company day and night. You must be very happy.â

MASTER (with a smile): âThis is indeed a great occasion for me. Today I have seen the crescent moon of the second day of the bright fortnight. (All laugh.) Do you know why I referred to the moon of the second day? SÄ«tÄ once said to RÄvana, âYou are the full moon and RÄma is the crescent moon of the second day of the bright fortnight.â RÄvana did not understand the meaning of these words. He thought SÄ«tÄ was flattering him and became exceedingly happy. But SÄ«tÄ meant that RÄvana had reached the fullest limit of his power and prosperity, and that thenceforth he would wane like the full moon. RÄma, on the other hand, was like the moon of the second day. He would wax day by day.â

The Master was about to take his leave. The pundit and his friends bowed low before him.

It was not yet dusk, and Sri Ramakrishna returned to Ishanâs house with the devotees. The Master took his seat in the drawing-room with Ishan and his sons, a pundit, and a few devotees.

MASTER (smiling, to Ishan): âI said to Pundit Shashadhar: âYou have hardly set your foot on the tree, and yet you aspire to lay hold of a big bunch of fruit. First of all practise some spiritual discipline. Then you may teach others.â â

ISHAN: âEvery preacher thinks that he enlightens others. The glow-worm also may think that it illumines the world. Imagining this to be the glow-wormâs feeling, someone said to it: âO glow-worm, how can you bring light to the world? You only reveal the intensity of the darkness.â â

MASTER (with a smile): âBut Shashadhar is not just a scholar. He also has a little discrimination and dispassion.â

A pundit who was present said to Sri Ramakrishna, âYou are indeed a great soul.â

MASTER: âYou may say that about sages like NÄrada, PrahlÄda, or Åukadeva. I am like your son.

âOf course, in one sense your words are true. It is said that in one respect the devotee of God is greater than God Himself, because he carries God in his heart. (All rejoice.) It is said in the Vaishnava books: âA devotee regards himself as a higher, and God as a lower, being.â YaÅodÄ, the mother of Krishna, was about to fetter Krishna, who was God Incarnate, with chains! She believed that no one but herself could take care of Krishna.

âSometimes God acts as the magnet and the devotee as the needle. God attracts the devotee to Himself. Again, sometimes the devotee acts as the magnet and God as the needle. Such is the attraction of the devotee that God comes to him, unable to resist his love.â

The Master was about to leave for Dakshineswar. Ishan and the other devotees stood around him while he gave Ishan various words of advice.

MASTER: âA devotee who can call on God while living a householderâs life is a hero indeed. God thinks: âHe who has renounced the world for My sake will surely pray to Me. He must serve Me. Is there anything very remarkable about it? People will cry shame on him if he fails to do so. But he is blessed indeed who prays to Me in the midst of his worldly duties. He is trying to find Me, overcoming a great obstacleâpushing away, as it were, a huge block of stone weighing a ton. Such a man is a real hero.â â

PUNDIT: âYou are right, sir. The scripture says the same thing. There is in the MahÄbhÄrata the story of the âpious hunterâ and the âchaste womanâ. Once a hermit was disturbed in his meditation by a crow. When he cast an angry glance at the bird, it was reduced to ashes. The hermit said to himself: âI have destroyed the crow by a mere glance. I must have made great progress in spiritual life.â One day he went to a womanâs house to beg his food. She was devoted to her husband and served him day and night; she provided him with water to wash his feet and even dried them with her hair. When the hermit knocked at her door for alms, she was serving her husband and could not open the door at once. The hermit, in a fit of anger, began to curse her. The chaste woman answered from the inner apartments: âI am not your crow. Wait a few minutes, sir. After finishing my service to my husband I shall give you my attention.â The hermit was very much surprised to find that this simple woman was aware of his having burnt the crow to ashes. He wanted her to give him spiritual instruction. At her bidding he went to the âpious hunterâ at Benares. This hunter sold meat, but he also served his parents day and night as embodiments of God. The hermit said to himself in utter amazement: âWhy, he is a butcher and a worldly man! How can he give me the Knowledge of Brahman?â But the hunter was a knower of Brahman and had acquired divine knowledge through the performance of his worldly duties. The hermit was illumined by the instruction of the âpious hunterâ.â

The Master was about to take his leave. He was standing at the door of the next house, where Ishanâs father-in-law lived. Ishan and the other devotees stood by the Master. They were waiting to bid him good-bye. Sri Ramakrishna said to Ishan: âLive in the world like an ant. The world contains a mixture of truth and untruth, sugar and sand. Be an ant and take the sugar.

âAgain, the world is a mixture of milk and water, the bliss of God-Consciousness and the pleasure of sense-enjoyment. Be a swan and drink the milk, leaving the water aside.

âLive in the world like a waterfowl. The water clings to the bird, but the bird shakes it off. Live in the world like a mudfish. The fish lives in the mud, but its skin is always bright and shiny.

âThe world is indeed a mixture of truth and make-believe. Discard the make-believe and take the truth.â

Sri Ramakrishna got into the carriage and left for Dakshineswar.

1 The non-essential parts. The allusion is to the head and tail of fish, which are non-essential.

2 A noted wrestler of the time.

3 Breathing exercises as prescribed in rÄjayoga.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# ADVICE TO PUNDIT SHASHADHAR

Monday, June 30, 1884

SRI RAMAKRISHNA was in his room, sitting on a mat spread on the floor. Pundit Shashadhar and a few devotees were with him on the mat, and the rest sat on the bare floor. Surendra, Baburam, M., Harish, Latu, Hazra, and others were present. It was about four oâclock in the afternoon.

Sri Ramakrishna had met Pundit Shashadhar six days before in Calcutta, and now the pundit had come to Dakshineswar to visit the Master. Bhudar Chattopadhyaya and his elder brother, the punditâs hosts, were with him.

The pundit was a follower of the path of jnÄna. The Master was explaining this path to him. He said: âNityÄ and LÄ«lÄ are the two aspects of one and the same Reality. He who is the Indivisible SatchidÄnanda has assumed different forms for the sake of His LÄ«lÄ.â As he described the nature of the Ultimate Reality the Master every now and then became unconscious in samÄdhi. While he talked he was intoxicated with spiritual fervour. He said to the pundit: âMy dear sir, Brahman is immutable and immovable, like Mount Sumeru. But He who is âimmovableâ can also âmoveâ.â

The Master was in ecstasy. He began to sing in his melodious voice:

Who is there that can understand what Mother KÄli is?

Even the six darÅanas are powerless to reveal Herâ¦ .

He went on:

Is Mother merely a simple woman, born as others are born?

Only by chanting Her holy name

Does Åiva survive the deadly poison.1

She it is who creates the worlds, She who preserves and destroys,

With a mere wink of Her wondrous eyes;

She holds the universe in Her womb.

Seeking a shelter at Her feet, the gods themselves feel safe;

And MahÄdeva, God of Gods,

Lies prostrate underneath Her feet.

Again he sang:

Is Mother only Åivaâs wife? To Her must needs bow down

The all-destroying King of Death!

Naked She roams about the world, slaying Her demon foes,

Or stands erect on Åivaâs breast.

Her feet upon Her Husbandâs form! What a strange wife She makes!

My Motherâs play, declares PrasÄd, shatters all rules and laws:

Strive hard for purity, O mind,

And understand my Motherâs ways.

And again:

I drink no ordinary wine, but Wine of Everlasting Bliss,

As I repeat my Mother KÄliâs name;

It so intoxicates my mind that people take me to be drunk! â¦

And again:

Can everyone have the vision of ÅyÄmÄ? Is KÄliâs treasure for everyone?

Oh, what a pity my foolish mind will not see what is true!

Even with all His penances, rarely does Åiva Himself behold

The mind-bewitching sight of Mother ÅyÄmÄâs crimson feet.

To him who meditates on Her the riches of heaven are poor indeed;

If ÅyÄmÄ casts Her glance on him, he swims in Eternal Bliss.

The prince of yogis, the king of the gods, meditate on Her feet in vain;

Yet worthless KamalÄkÄnta yearns for the Motherâs blessed feet!

The Masterâs ecstatic mood gradually relaxed. He stopped singing and sat in silence. After a while he got up and sat on the small couch.

Pundit Shashadhar was charmed with his singing. Very humbly he said to Sri Ramakrishna, âAre you going to sing any more?â

A little later the Master sang again:

High in the heaven of the Motherâs feet, my mind was soaring like a kite,

When came a blast of sinâs rough wind that drove it swiftly toward the earth. â¦

Then he sang:

Once for all, this time, I have thoroughly understood;

From One2 who knows it well, I have learnt the secret of bhÄva.

A man has come to me from a country where there is no night,

And now I cannot distinguish day from night any longer;

Rituals and devotions have all grown profitless for me.

My sleep is broken; how can I slumber any more?

For now I am wide awake in the sleeplessness of yoga.

O Divine Mother, made one with Thee in yoga-sleep3 at last,

My slumber I have lulled asleep for evermore.

I bow my head, says PrasÄd, before desire and liberation;

Knowing the secret that KÄli is one with the highest Brahman,

I have discarded, once for all, both righteousness and sin.

Sri Ramakrishna continued:

I have surrendered my soul at the fearless feet of the Mother;

Am I afraid of Death any more?

Unto the tuft of hair on my head

Is tied the almighty mantra, Mother KÄliâs name.

My body I have sold in the market-place of the world

And with it have bought Sri DurgÄâs name.

As Sri Ramakrishna sang the line, âAnd with it have bought Sri DurgÄâs nameâ, the tears flowed from Pundit Shashadharâs eyes. The Master went on with the song:

Deep within my heart I have planted the name of KÄli,

The Wish-fulfilling Tree of heaven;

When Yama, King of Death, appears,

To him I shall open my heart and show it growing there.

I have cast out from me my six unflagging foes;4

Ready am I to sail lifeâs sea,

Crying, âTo DurgÄ, victory!â

Again he sang:

Dwell, O mind, within yourself;

Enter no otherâs home.

If you but seek there, you will find

All you are searching for. â¦

And again:

Though I5 am never loath to grant salvation,

I hesitate indeed to grant pure love.

Whoever wins pure love surpasses all;

He is adored by men;

He triumphs over the three worldsâ¦ .

The pundit had studied the Vedas and the other scriptures. He loved to discuss philosophy. The Master, seated on the couch, cast his benign look on the pundit and gave him counsel through parables.

MASTER (to the pundit): âThere are many scriptures like the Vedas. But one cannot realize God without austerity and spiritual discipline. âGod cannot be found in the six systems, the Vedas, or the Tantra.â

âBut one should learn the contents of the scriptures and then act according to their injunctions. A man lost a letter. He couldnât remember where he had left it. He began to search for it with a lamp. After two or three people had searched, the letter was at last found. The message in the letter was: âPlease send us five seers of sandesh and a piece of wearing-cloth.â The man read it and then threw the letter away. There was no further need of it; now all he had to do was to buy the five seers of sandesh and the piece of cloth.

âBetter than reading is hearing, and better than hearing is seeing. One understands the scriptures better by hearing them from the lips of the guru or of a holy man. Then one doesnât have to think about their non-essential part. HanumÄn said: âBrother, I donât know much about the phase of the moon or the position of the stars. I just contemplate RÄma.â

âBut seeing is far better than hearing. Then all doubts disappear. It is true that many things are recorded in the scriptures; but all these are useless without the direct realization of God, without devotion to His Lotus Feet, without purity of heart. The almanac forecasts the rainfall of the year. But not a drop of water will you get by squeezing the almanac. No, not even one drop.

âHow long should one reason about the texts of the scriptures? So long as one does not have direct realization of God. How long does the bee buzz about? As long as it is not sitting on a flower. No sooner does it light on a flower and begin to sip honey than it keeps quiet.

âBut you must remember another thing. One may talk even after the realization of God. But then one talks only of God and of Divine Bliss. It is like a drunkardâs crying, âVictory to the Divine Mother!â He can hardly say anything else on account of his drunkenness. You can notice, too, that a bee makes an indistinct humming sound after having sipped the honey from a flower.

âThe jnÄni reasons about the world through the process of âNeti, netiâ, âNot this, not thisâ. Reasoning in this way, he at last comes to a state of Bliss, and that is Brahman. What is the nature of a jnÄni? He behaves according to scriptural injunctions.

âOnce I was taken to ChÄnak and saw some sÄdhus there. Several of them were sewing. (All laugh.) At the sight of us they threw aside their sewing. They sat straight, crossing their legs, and conversed with us. (All laugh.)

âBut jnÄnis will not talk about spiritual things without being asked. They will inquire, at first, about such things as your health and your family.

âBut the nature of the vijnÄni is different. He is unconcerned about anything. Perhaps he carries his wearing-cloth loose under his arm, like a child; or perhaps the cloth has dropped from his body altogether.

âThe man who knows that God exists is called a jnÄni. A jnÄni is like one who knows beyond a doubt that a log of wood contains fire. But a vijnÄni is he who lights the log, cooks over the fire, and is nourished by the food. The eight fetters have fallen from the vijnÄni. He may keep merely the appearance of lust, anger, and the rest.â

PUNDIT: âÂ âThe knots of his heart are cut asunder; all his doubts are destroyed.â â

MASTER: âYes. Once a ship sailed into the ocean. Suddenly its iron joints, nails, and screws fell out. The ship was passing a magnetic hill, and so all its iron was loosened.

âI used to go to Krishnakishoreâs house. Once, when I was there, he said to me, âWhy do you chew betel-leaf?â I said: âIt is my sweet pleasure. I shall chew betel-leaf, look at my face in the mirror, and dance naked among a thousand girls.â6 Krishnakishoreâs wife scolded him and said: âWhat have you said to Ramakrishna? You donât know how to talk to people.â

âIn this state, passions like lust and anger are burnt up, though nothing happens to the physical body. It looks just like any other body; but the inside is all hollow and pure.â

A DEVOTEE: âDoes the body remain even after the realization of God?â

MASTER: âThe body survives with some so that they may work out their prÄrabdha karma or work for the welfare of others. By bathing in the Ganges a man gets rid of his sin and attains liberation. But if he happens to be blind, he doesnât get rid of his blindness. Of course, he escapes future births, which would otherwise be necessary for reaping the results of his past sinful karma. His present body remains alive as long as its momentum7 is not exhausted; but future births are no longer possible. The wheel moves as long as the impulse that has set it in motion lasts. Then it comes to a stop. In the case of such a person, passions like lust and anger are burnt up. Only the body remains alive to perform a few actions.â

PUNDIT: âThat is called samskÄra.â

MASTER: âThe vijnÄni always sees God. That is why he is so indifferent about the world. He sees God even with his eyes open. Sometimes he comes down to the LÄ«lÄ from the Nitya, and sometimes he goes up to the Nitya from the LÄ«lÄ.â

PUNDIT: âI donât understand that.â

MASTER: âThe jnÄni reasons about the world through the process of âNeti, netiâ, and at last reaches the Eternal and Indivisible SatchidÄnanda. He reasons in this manner: âBrahman is not the living beings; It is neither the universe nor the twenty-four cosmic principles.â As a result of such reasoning he attains the Absolute. Then he realizes that it is the Absolute that has become all thisâthe universe, its living beings, and the twenty-four cosmic principles.

âMilk sets into curd, and the curd is churned into butter. After extracting the butter one realizes that butter is not essentially different from buttermilk and buttermilk not essentially different from butter. The bark of a tree goes with the pith and the pith goes with the bark.â

PUNDIT (smiling, to Bhudar): âDid you understand that? It is very difficult.â

MASTER: âIf there is butter, there must be buttermilk also. If you think of butter, you must also think of buttermilk along with it; for there cannot be any butter without buttermilk. Just so, if you accept the Nitya, you must also accept the LÄ«lÄ. It is the process of negation and affirmation. You realize the Nitya by negating the LÄ«lÄ. Then you affirm the LÄ«lÄ, seeing in it the manifestation of the Nitya. One attains this state after realizing Reality in both aspects: Personal and Impersonal. The Personal is the embodiment of Chit, Consciousness; and the Impersonal is the Indivisible SatchidÄnanda.

âBrahman alone has become everything. Therefore to the vijnÄni this world is a âmansion of mirthâ. But to the jnÄni it is a âframework of illusionâ. RÄmprasÄd described the world as a âframework of illusionâ. Another man said to him by way of retort:

This very world is a mansion of mirth;

Here I can eat, here drink and make merry.

O physician,8 you are a fool!

You see only the surface of things.

Janakaâs might was unsurpassed;

What did he lack of the world or the Spirit?

Holding to one as well as the other,

He drank his milk from a brimming cup!

âThe vijnÄni enjoys the Bliss of God in a richer way. Some have heard of milk, some have seen it, and some have drunk it. The vijnÄni has drunk milk, enjoyed it, and been nourished by it.â

The Master remained silent a few moments and then asked Pundit Shashadhar to have a smoke. The pundit went to the southeast verandah to smoke. Soon he came back to the room and sat on the floor with the devotees. Seated on the small couch, the Master continued the conversation.

MASTER (to the pundit): âLet me tell you something. There are three kinds of Änanda, joy: the joy of worldly enjoyment, the joy of worship, and the Joy of Brahman. The joy of worldly enjoyment is the joy of âwoman and goldâ, which people always enjoy. The joy of worship one enjoys while chanting the name and glories of God. And the Joy of Brahman is the joy of God-vision. After experiencing the joy of God-vision the rishis of olden times went beyond all rules and conventions.

âChaitanyadeva used to experience three spiritual states: the inmost, the semi-conscious, and the conscious. In the inmost state he would see God and go into samÄdhi. He would be in the state of jada samÄdhi. In the semi-conscious state he would be partially conscious of the outer world. In the conscious state he could sing the name and glories of God.â

HAZRA (to the pundit): âSo your doubts are now solved.â

MASTER (to the pundit): âWhat is samÄdhi? It is the complete merging of the mind in God-Consciousness. The jnÄni experiences jada samÄdhi, in which no trace of âIâ is left. The samÄdhi attained through the path of bhakti is called âchetana samÄdhiâ. In this samÄdhi there remains the consciousness of âIââthe âIâ of the servant-and-Master relationship, of the lover-and-Beloved relationship, of the enjoyer-and-Food relationship. God is the Master; the devotee is the servant. God is the Beloved; the devotee is the lover. God is the Food, and the devotee is the enjoyer. âI donât want to be sugar. I want to eat it.â â

PUNDIT: âWhat will happen if God dissolves all of the âIâ, if He changes the enjoyer himself into sugar?â

MASTER (smiling): âCome, come! Tell me what is in your mind. But donât the scriptures mention NÄrada, Sanaka, SanÄtana, Sananda, and SanatkumÄra?â

PUNDIT: âYes, sir. They do.â

MASTER: âThough they were jnÄnis, yet they kept the âIâ of the bhakta. Havenât you read the BhÄgavata?â

PUNDIT: âI have read only part of it, not the whole.â

MASTER: âPray to God. He is full of compassion. Will He not listen to the words of His devotee? He is the Kalpataru. You will get whatever you desire from Him.â

PUNDIT: âI havenât thought deeply about these things before. But now I understand.â

MASTER: âGod keeps a little of âIâ in His devotee even after giving him the Knowledge of Brahman. That âIâ is the âI of the devoteeâ, the âI of the jnÄniâ. Through that âIâ the devotee enjoys the infinite play of God.

âThe pestle9 was almost worn out with rubbing. Only a little was left. That fell into the underbrush and brought about the destruction of the lunar race, the race of the Yadus. The vijnÄni retains the âI of the devoteeâ, the âI of the jnÄniâ, in order to taste the Bliss of God and teach people.

âThe rishis of old had timid natures. They were easily frightened. Do you know their attitude? It was this: âLet me somehow get my own salvation; who cares for others?â A hollow piece of drift-wood somehow manages to float; but it sinks if even a bird sits on it. But NÄrada and sages of his kind are like a huge log that not only can float across to the other shore but can carry many animals and other creatures as well. A steamship itself crosses the ocean and also carries people across.

âTeachers like NÄrada belong to the class of the vijnÄni. They were much more courageous than the other rishis. They are like an expert satrancha-player. You must have noticed how he shouts, as he throws the dice: âWhat do I want? Six? No, five! Here is five!â And every time he throws the dice he gets the number he wants. He is such a clever player! And while playing he even twirls his moustaches.

âA mere jnÄni trembles with fear. He is like an amateur satrancha-player. He is anxious to move his pieces somehow to the safety zone, where they wonât be overtaken by his opponent. But a vijnÄni isnât afraid of anything. He has realized both aspects of God: Personal and Impersonal. He has talked with God. He has enjoyed the Bliss of God.

âIt is a joy to merge the mind in the Indivisible Brahman through contemplation. And it is also a joy to keep the mind on the LÄ«lÄ, the Relative, without dissolving it in the Absolute.

âA mere jnÄni is a monotonous person. He always analyses, saying: âIt is not this, not this. The world is like a dream.â But I have âraised both my handsâ. Therefore I accept everything.

âListen to a story. Once a woman went to see her weaver friend. The weaver, who had been spinning different kinds of silk thread, was very happy to see her friend and said to her: âFriend, I canât tell you how happy I am to see you. Let me get you some refreshments.â She left the room. The woman looked at the threads of different colours and was tempted. She hid a bundle of thread under one arm. The weaver returned presently with the refreshments and began to feed her guest with great enthusiasm. But, looking at the thread, she realized that her friend had taken a bundle. Hitting upon a plan to get it back, she said: âFriend, it is so long since I have seen you. This is a day of great joy for me. I feel very much like asking you to dance with me.â The friend said, âSister, I am feeling very happy too.â So the two friends began to dance together. When the weaver saw that her friend danced without raising her hands, she said: âFriend, let us dance with both hands raised. This is a day of great joy.â But the guest pressed one arm to her side and danced raising only the other. The weaver said: âHow is this, friend? Why should you dance with only one hand raised? Dance with me raising both hands. Look at me. See how I dance with both hands raised.â But the guest still pressed one arm to her side. She danced with the other hand raised and said with a smile, âThis is all I know of dancing.â â

The Master continued: âI donât press my arm to my side. Both my hands are free. I am not afraid of anything. I accept both the Nitya and the LÄ«lÄ, both the Absolute and the Relative.

âI said to Keshab Sen that he would not be able to realize God without renouncing the ego. He said, âSir, in that case I should not be able to keep my organization together.â Thereupon I said to him: âI am asking you to give up the âunripe egoâ, the âwicked egoâ. But there is no harm in the âripe egoâ, the âchild egoâ, the âservant egoâ, the âego of Knowledgeâ.â

âThe worldly manâs ego, the âignorant egoâ, the âunripe egoâ, is like a thick stick. It divides, as it were, the water of the Ocean of SatchidÄnanda. But the âservant egoâ, the âchild egoâ, the âego of Knowledgeâ, is like a line on the water. One clearly sees that there is only one expanse of water. The dividing line makes it appear that the water has two parts, but one clearly sees that in reality there is only one expanse of water.

âÅankarÄchÄrya kept the âego of Knowledgeâ in order to teach people. God keeps in many people the âego of a jnÄniâ or the âego of a bhaktaâ even after they have attained BrahmajnÄna. HanumÄn, after realizing God in both His Personal and His Impersonal aspect, cherished toward God the attitude of a servant, a devotee. He said to RÄma: âO RÄma, sometimes I think that You are the whole and I am a part of You. Sometimes I think that You are the Master and I am Your servant. And sometimes, RÄma, when I contemplate the Absolute, I see that I am You and You are I.â

âYaÅodÄ became grief-stricken at being separated from Krishna, and called on RÄdhÄ. RÄdhÄ saw YaÅodÄâs suffering and revealed herself to her as the divine Åakti, which was her real nature. She said to YaÅodÄ: âKrishna is ChidÄtmÄ, Absolute Consciousness, and I am ChitÅakti, the Primal Power. Ask a boon of Me.â YaÅodÄ said: âI donât want BrahmajnÄna. Please grant me only this: that I may see the form of GopÄla in my meditation; that I may always have the company of Krishnaâs devotees; that I may always serve the devotees of God; that I may always chant Godâs name and glories.â

âOnce the gopis felt a great desire to see the forms of the Lord. So Krishna asked them to dive into the water of the JamunÄ. No sooner did they dive into the water than they all arrived at Vaikuntha. There they saw the form of the Lord endowed with His six celestial splendours. But they did not like it. They said to Krishna: âWe want to see GopÄla and serve Him. Please grant us that boon alone. We donât want anything else.â

âBefore His departure for MathurÄ, Krishna wanted to give the Knowledge of Brahman to the gopis. He said to them: âI dwell both inside and outside all beings. Why should you see only one form of Mine?â The gopis cried in chorus: âO Krishna, do You want to go away from us? Is that why You are instructing us in BrahmajnÄna?â

âDo you know the attitude of the gopis? It is this: âWe are RÄdhÄâs and RÄdhÄ is ours.â â10

A DEVOTEE: âDoes this âIâ of the devotee never disappear altogether?â

MASTER: âYes, it disappears at times. Then one attains the Knowledge of Brahman and goes into samÄdhi. I too lose it, but not for all the time. In the musical scale there are seven notes: sÄ, re, gÄ, mÄ, pÄ, dhÄ, and ni. But one cannot keep oneâs voice on âniâ a long time. One must bring it down again to the lower notes. I pray to the Divine Mother, âO Mother, do not give me BrahmajnÄna.â Formerly believers in God with form used to visit me a great deal. Then the modern BrahmajnÄnis11 began to arrive. During that period I used to remain unconscious in samÄdhi most of the time. Whenever I regained consciousness, I would say to the Divine Mother, âO Mother, please donât give me BrahmajnÄna.â â

PUNDIT: âDoes God listen to our prayers?â

MASTER: âGod is the Kalpataru, the Wish-fulfilling Tree. You will certainly get whatever you ask of Him. But you must pray standing near the Kalpataru. Only then will your prayer be fulfilled. But you must remember another thing. God knows our inner feeling. A man gets the fulfilment of the desire he cherishes while practising sÄdhanÄ. As one thinks, so one receives. A magician was showing his tricks before a king. Now and then he exclaimed: âCome confusion! Come delusion! O King, give me money! Give me clothes!â Suddenly his tongue turned upward and clove to the roof of his mouth. He experienced kumbhaka. He could utter neither word nor sound, and became motionless. People thought he was dead. They built a vault of bricks and buried him there in that posture. After a thousand years someone dug into the vault. Inside it people found a man seated in samÄdhi. They took him for a holy man and worshipped him. When they shook him his tongue was loosened and regained its normal position. The magician became conscious of the outer world and cried, as he had a thousand years before: âCome confusion! Come delusion! O King, give me money! Give me clothes!â

âI used to weep, praying to the Divine Mother, âO Mother, destroy with Thy thunderbolt my inclination to reason.â â

PUNDIT: âThen you too had an inclination to reason?â

MASTER: âYes, once.â

PUNDIT: âThen please assure us that we shall get rid of that inclination too. How did you get rid of yours?â

MASTER: âOh, somehow or other.â

Sri Ramakrishna was silent awhile. Then he went on with his conversation.

MASTER: âGod is the Kalpataru. One should pray standing near It. Then one will get whatever one desires.

âHow many things God has created! Infinite is His universe. But what need have I to know about His infinite splendours? If I must know these, let me first realize Him. Then God Himself will tell me all about them. What need have I to know how many houses and how many government securities Jadu Mallick possesses? All that I need is somehow to converse with Jadu Mallick. I may succeed in seeing him by jumping over a ditch or through a petition or after being pushed about by his gate-keeper. Once I get a chance to talk to him, then he himself will tell me all about his possessions if I ask him. If one becomes acquainted with the master, then one is respected by his officers too. (All laugh.)

âThere are some who do not care to know the splendours of God. What do I care about knowing how many gallons of wine there are in the tavern? One bottle is enough for me. Why should I desire the knowledge of Godâs splendours? I am intoxicated with the little wine I have swallowed.

âBoth bhaktiyoga and jnÄnayoga are paths by which you can realize God. Whatever path you may follow, you will certainly realize Him. The path of bhakti is an easy one. The path of knowledge and discrimination is very difficult. Why should one reason so much to know which path is the best? I talked about this with Vijay for many days. Once I told him about a man who used to pray, âO God, reveal to me who and what You are.â

âThe path of knowledge and discrimination is difficult indeed. PÄrvati, the Divine Mother, revealed Her various forms to Her father and said, âFather, if you want BrahmajnÄna, then live in the company of holy men.â

âBrahman cannot be described in words. It is said in the RÄma GÄ«tÄ that Brahman has only been indirectly hinted at by the scriptures. When one speaks about the âcowherd village on the Gangesâ, one indirectly states that the village is situated on the bank of the Ganges.

âWhy shouldnât a man be able to realize the formless Brahman? But it is extremely difficult. He cannot if he has even the slightest trace of worldliness. He can be directly aware of Brahman in his inmost consciousness only when he renounces all sense-objectsâform, taste, smell, touch, and soundâand only when his mind completely stops functioning. And then, too, he knows only this much of Brahmanâthat It exists.â

Quoting from an Upanishad, the pundit said, âIt is to be experienced only as Existence.â

MASTER: âIn order to realize God a devotee should make use of a particular attitudeâthe attitude of a âheroâ or a friend or a handmaid or a child.â

MANI MALLICK: âOnly then can one feel attached to God.â

MASTER: âFor many days I cherished the feeling that I was a companion of the Divine Mother. I used to say: âI am the handmaid of Brahmamayi, the Blissful Mother. O companions of the Divine Mother, make me the Motherâs handmaid! I shall go about proudly, saying, âI am Brahmamayiâs handmaid!â â

âSome souls realize God without practising any spiritual discipline. They are called nityasiddha, eternally perfect. Those who have realized God through austerity, japa, and the like, are called sÄdhanasiddha, perfect through spiritual discipline. Again, there are those called kripÄsiddha, perfect through divine grace. These last may be compared to a room kept dark a thousand years, which becomes light the moment a lamp is brought in.

âThere is also a class of devotees, the hathÄtsiddha, that is to say, those who have suddenly attained God-vision. Their case is like that of a poor boy who has suddenly found favour with a rich man. The rich man marries his daughter to the boy and along with her gives him land, house, carriage, servants, and so forth.

âThere is still another class of devotees, the svapnasiddha, who have had the vision of God in a dream.â

SURENDRA (smiling): âLet us go to sleep then. We shall wake and find ourselves babus, aristocrats.â

MASTER (tenderly): âYou are already a babu. When the letter âÄâ is joined to the letter âkaâ, âkaâ becomes âkÄâ. It is futile to add another âÄâ. If you add it, you will still have the same âkÄâ. (All laugh.)

âThe nityasiddha is in a class apart. He is like arani wood.12 A little rubbing produces fire. You can get fire from it even without rubbing. The nityasiddha realizes God by practising slight spiritual discipline and sometimes without practising any at all. But he does practise spiritual discipline after realizing God. He is like the gourd or pumpkin vineâfirst fruit, then flower.â

The pundit smiled at this illustration.

MASTER: âThere is the instance of PrahlÄda. He was a nityasiddha. While writing the letter âkaâ he shed a stream of tears.â13

The Master was pleased with the punditâs humility. He praised him to the devotees.

MASTER: âHe has such a nice nature. You find no difficulty in driving a nail into a mud wall. But its point breaks if you try to drive it against a stone; and still it will not pierce it. There are people whose spiritual consciousness is not at all awakened even though they hear about God a thousand times. They are like a crocodile, on whose hide you cannot make any impression with a sword.â

PUNDIT: âBut one can hurt a crocodile by throwing a spear into its belly.â (All laugh.)

MASTER (smiling): âWhat good is there in reading a whole lot of scriptures? What good is there in the study of philosophy? What is the use of talking big? In order to learn archery one should first aim at a banana tree, then at a reed, then at a wick, and last at a flying bird. At the beginning one should concentrate on God with form.

âThen there are devotees who are beyond the three gunas. They are eternally devoted to God, like NÄrada. These devotees behold Krishna as Chinmaya, all Spirit, His Abode as Chinmaya, His devotee as Chinmaya. To them God is eternal, His Abode is eternal, His devotee is eternal.

âThose who reason and speculate following the process of âNeti, netiâ do not accept the Incarnation of God. Hazra says well that Divine Incarnation is only for the bhakta, and not for the jnÄni, because the jnÄni is quite contented with his ideal, âI am Heâ.â

Sri Ramakrishna and the devotees remained silent awhile. The pundit resumed the conversation.

PUNDIT: âSir, how does one get rid of callousness? Laughter makes me think of muscles and nerves. Grief makes me think of the nervous system.â

MASTER (smiling): âThat is why Narayan Shastri used to say, âThe harmful effect of the study of the scriptures is that it encourages reasoning and arguing.â â

PUNDIT: âIs there no way for us then?â

MASTER: âYes, there is the path of discrimination. In a song occurs the line: âAsk her son Discrimination about the Truth.â

âThe way lies through discrimination, renunciation, and passionate yearning for God. Unless a man practises discrimination, he cannot utter the right words. One time, after expounding religion at great length, Pundit Samadhyayi said, âGod is dry.â He reminded me of the man who once said, âMy uncleâs cow-shed is full of horses.â Now, does anyone keep horses in a cow-shed? (With a smile) You have become like a chÄnÄbarÄ14 fried in butter. Now it will be good for you, and for others as well, if you are soaked in syrup a few days. Just a few days.â

PUNDIT (smiling): âThe sweetmeat is over-fried. It has become charred.â

MASTER (with a laugh): âNo! No! It is brown as a cockroach. Just the right colour.â

HAZRA: âThe sweetmeat is well cooked. It has become spongy. Now it will soak up the syrup nicely.â

MASTER: âYou see, there is no need to read too much of the scriptures. If you read too much you will be inclined to reason and argue. NangtÄ used to teach me thus: What you get by repeating the word âGÄ«tÄâ ten times is the essence of the book. In other words, if you repeat âGÄ«tÄâ ten times it is reversed into âtÄgiâ, which indicates renunciation.

âYes, the way to realize God is through discrimination, renunciation, and yearning for Him. What kind of yearning? One should yearn for God as the cow, with yearning heart, runs after its calf.â

PUNDIT: âThe same thing is said in the Vedas: âO God, we call on Thee as the cow lows for the calf.â â

MASTER: âAdd your tears to your yearning. And if you can renounce everything through discrimination and dispassion, then you will be able to see God. That yearning brings about God-intoxication, whether you follow the path of knowledge or the path of devotion. The sage DurvÄsÄ was mad with the Knowledge of God.

âThere is a great deal of difference between the knowledge of a householder and that of an all-renouncing sannyÄsi. The householderâs knowledge is like the light of a lamp, which illumines only the inside of a room. He cannot see anything, with the help of such knowledge, except his own body and his immediate family. But the knowledge of the all-renouncing monk is like the light of the sun. Through that light he can see both inside and outside the room. Chaitanyadevaâs knowledge had the brilliance of the sunâthe sun of Knowledge. Further, he radiated the soothing light of the moon of Devotion. He was endowed with bothâthe Knowledge of Brahman and ecstatic love of God.

(To the pundit) âOne can attain spiritual consciousness through both affirmation and negation. There is the positive path of love and devotion, and there is the negative path of knowledge and discrimination. You are preaching the path of knowledge. But that creates a very difficult situation: there the guru and the disciple do not see each other. Åukadeva went to Janaka for instruction about the Knowledge of Brahman. Janaka said to him: âYou must pay me the guruâs fee beforehand. When you attain the Knowledge of Brahman you wonât pay me the fee, because the knower of Brahman sees no difference between the guru and the disciple.â

âBoth negation and affirmation are ways to realize one and the same goal. Infinite are the opinions and infinite are the ways. But you must remember one thing. The injunction is that the path of devotion described by NÄrada is best suited to the Kaliyuga. According to this path, first comes bhakti; then bhÄva, when bhakti is mature. Higher than bhÄva are mahÄbhÄva and prema. An ordinary mortal does not attain mahÄbhÄva and prema. He who has achieved these has realized the goal, that is to say, has attained God.â

PUNDIT: âIn expounding religion one has to use a great many words.â

MASTER: âWhile preaching, eliminate the âhead and tailâ, that is to say, emphasize only the essentials.â

The pundit and Mani Mallick became engaged in conversation. Mani was a member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj. The pundit argued vehemently about the good and bad sides of the SamÄj. Sri Ramakrishna was seated on the small couch and looked on, smiling. Presently he remarked: âThis is the tÄmasic aspect of sattva, the attitude of a hero. This is necessary. One should not hold oneâs tongue at the sight of injustice and untruth. Suppose a bad woman wants to drag you from the path of righteousness. You must then assume the heroic attitude and say: âWhat? You witch! You dare injure my spiritual life? I shall cut your body in two right now.â â

With a smile Sri Ramakrishna said to the pundit: âMani Mallick has been following the tenets of the BrÄhmo SamÄj a long time. You canât convert him to your views. Is it an easy thing to destroy old tendencies? Once there lived a very pious Hindu who always worshipped the Divine Mother and chanted Her name. When the MussalmÄns conquered the country, they forced him to embrace IslÄm. They said to him: âYou are now a MussalmÄn. Say âÄllÄhâ. From now on you must repeat only the name of ÄllÄh.â With great difficulty he repeated the word âÄllÄhâ, but every now and then blurted out âJagadambÄâ.15 At that the MussalmÄns were about to beat him. Thereupon he said to them: âI beseech you! Please do not kill me. I have been trying my utmost to repeat the name of ÄllÄh, but our JagadambÄ has filled me up to the throat. She pushes out your ÄllÄh.â (All laugh.)

(To the pundit) âPlease donât say anything to Mani Mallick. You must know that there are different tastes. There are also different powers of digestion. God has made different religions and creeds to suit different aspirants. By no means all are fit for the Knowledge of Brahman. Therefore the worship of God with form has been provided.

âThe mother brings home a fish for her children. She curries part of the fish, part she fries, and with another part she makes pilau. By no means all can digest the pilau. So she makes fish soup for those who have weak stomachs. Further, some want pickled or fried fish. There are different temperaments. There are differences in the capacity to comprehend.â

All sat in silence. Sri Ramakrishna said to the pundit, âGo and visit the temples and take a stroll in the garden.â It was about half past five in the afternoon. The pundit left the room with his friends and several of the devotees.

After a while the Master went with M. toward the bathing-ghÄt on the Ganges. He said to M., âBaburam now says, âWhat shall I gain by study?â â On the bank of the river he met the pundit and said to him, âArenât you going to the KÄli temple?â The pundit said: âYes, sir. Let us go together.â

With a smiling face Sri Ramakrishna proceeded to the temple through the courtyard. He said to the pundit, âListen to a song.â

He sang:

Is KÄli, my Mother, really black?

The Naked One, of blackest hue,

Lights the Lotus of the Heartâ¦ .

As he was going through the courtyard, he quoted to the pundit from a song:

Lighting the lamp of Knowledge in the chamber of your heart,

Behold the face of the Mother, Brahmanâs Embodiment.

They came to the temple. Sri Ramakrishna saluted the Divine Mother, touching the ground with his forehead.

Red hibiscus flowers and vilwa-leaves adorned the Motherâs feet. Her three eyes radiated love for Her devotees. Two of Her hands were raised as if to give them boons and reassurance; the other two hands held symbols of death. She was clothed in a sÄri of Benares silk and was decked with ornaments.

Referring to the image, one of the party remarked, âI heard it was made by the sculptor Nabin.â The Master answered: âYes, I know. But to me She is the Embodiment of Spirit.â

As Sri Ramakrishna was coming back to his room with the devotees, he said to Baburam, âCome with us.â M. also joined them.

It was dusk. The Master was sitting on the semicircular porch west of his room. Baburam and M. sat near him. He was in a mood of partial ecstasy.

Rakhal was not then living with Sri Ramakrishna, and therefore the Master was having difficulties about his personal service. Several devotees lived with him, but he could not bear the touch of everyone during his spiritual moods. He hinted to Baburam: âDo stay with me. It will be very nice. In this mood I cannot allow others to touch me.â

The pundit entered the Masterâs room after visiting the temples. The Master said to him from the porch, âTake some refreshments.â The pundit said that he had not yet performed his evening devotions. At once Sri Ramakrishna stood up and sang in an exalted mood:

Why should I go to GangÄ or GayÄ, to KÄÅi, KÄnchi, or PrabhÄs,

So long as I can breathe my last with KÄliâs name upon my lips?

What need of rituals has a man, what need of devotions any more,

If he repeats the Motherâs name at the three holy hours? â¦

Intoxicated with ecstatic love, the Master said: âHow long should one perform devotions? So long as oneâs mind does not merge in God while repeating Om.â

PUNDIT: âThen let me eat the refreshments. I shall perform the devotions later on.â

MASTER: âNo, I donât want to obstruct the current of your life. It is not good to renounce anything before the proper time arrives. When the fruit ripens, the flower drops off of itself. One shouldnât forcibly tear off the green branch of a coconut tree. That injures the tree.â

Surendra was about to leave. He invited his friends into his carriage. The Master, still in an ecstatic mood, said, âDonât take more people than your horse can draw.â Surendra took leave of Sri Ramakrishna. The pundit left the room to perform his worship. M. and Baburam saluted the Master. They were about to leave for Calcutta. Sri Ramakrishna was still in an ecstatic mood.

MASTER (to M.): âI cannot utter a word now. Stay a few minutes.â

M. again took his seat and waited for the Masterâs command. Sri Ramakrishna motioned to Baburam to take a seat and asked him to fan him a little. M. also took part in rendering this personal service to the Master.

The pundit entered the room with his friends. He had finished his devotions and was ready to eat the refreshments. One of his companions asked the Master: âShall we succeed in spiritual life? Please tell us what our way is.â

Donât eat any food of the ÅrÄddha ceremony.16 Live in the world like an unchaste woman. She performs her household duties with great attention, but her mind dwells day and night on her paramour. Perform your duties in the world but keep your mind always fixed on God.â

The pundit finished eating his refreshments.

MASTER (to the pundit): âYou have read the GÄ«tÄ, no doubt. It says that there is a special power of God in the man who is honoured and respected by all.â

The pundit quoted the verse from the GÄ«tÄ.

MASTER: âOne cannot but admit the manifestation of power. VidyÄsÄgar once asked me, âHas God given more power to some than to others?â I said to him: âCertainly. Otherwise, how can one man kill a hundred? If there is no special manifestation of power, then why is Queen Victoria so much honoured and respected? Donât you admit it?â He agreed with me.â

The pundit and his friends saluted the Master and were about to take their leave. Sri Ramakrishna said to the pundit: âCome again. One hemp-smoker rejoices in the company of another hemp-smoker. The pundit left the room. With a smile the Master said: âHe has become âdilutedâ even in one day. Did you notice how modest he was? And he accepted everything I said.â

Moonlight flooded the semicircular porch. Sri Ramakrishna was still seated there. M. was about to leave.

M: âYes, sir. Let me say good-bye.â

Thursday, July 3, 1884

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting in Balaram Boseâs house in Calcutta. It was the day of the âReturn Car Festivalâ. The Lord of the Universe was worshipped in Balaramâs house as JagannÄth. There was a small car in the house for use during the Car Festival.

Balaramâs father was a pious Vaishnava who devoted most of his time to prayer and meditation in his garden house at VrindÄvan. He also studied devotional books and enjoyed the company of devotees. Balaram had brought his father to Calcutta to meet the Master.

MASTER (to Balaramâs father and the others): âThe BhaktamÄla is one of the Vaishnava books. It is a fine book. It describes the lives of the various Vaishnava devotees. But it is one-sided. At one place the author found peace of mind only after compelling Bhagavati, the Divine Mother, to take Her initiation according to the Vaishnava discipline.

âOnce I spoke highly of Vaishnavcharan to Mathur and persuaded him to invite Vaishnavcharan to his house. Mathur welcomed him with great courtesy. He fed his guest from silver plates. Then do you know what happened? Vaishnav said in front of Mathur, âYou will achieve nothing whatsoever in spiritual life unless you accept Krishna as your Ideal.â Mathur was a follower of the ÅÄkta cult and a worshipper of the Divine Mother. âI understand that the BhÄgavata also contains some statements like that. I hear that it is said there that trying to cross the ocean of the world without accepting Krishna as the Ideal Deity is like trying to cross a great sea by holding to the tail of a dog. Each sect magnifies its own view.

âThe ÅÄktas, too, try to belittle the Vaishnavas. The Vaishnavas say that Krishna alone is the Helmsman to take one across the ocean of the world. The ÅÄktas retort: âOh, yes! We agree to that. Our Divine Mother is the Empress of the Universe. Why should She bother about a ferry-boat? Therefore She has engaged that fellow Krishna for the purpose.â (All laugh.)

âBesides, how vain people are about their own sects! There are weavers in the villages near KÄmÄrpukur. Many of them are Vaishnavas and like to talk big. They say: âWhich Vishnu does he worship? The Preserver? Oh, we wouldnât touch him!â Or: âWhich Åiva are you talking about? We accept the ÄtmÄrÄma Åiva.â Or again, âPlease explain to us which Hari you worship.â They spin their yarn and indulge in talk like that.

âRatiâs mother, RÄni Katyayaniâs favourite confidante, is a follower of Vaishnavcharan. She is a bigoted Vaishnava. She used to visit me very frequently, and none could outdo her in devotion. One day she noticed me eating the prasÄd from the KÄli temple. Since then I havenât seen even her shadow.

âHe is indeed a real man who has harmonized everything. Most people are one-sided. But I find that all opinions point to the One. All viewsâthe ÅÄkta, the Vaishnava, the VedÄntaâhave that One for their centre. He who is formless is, again, endowed with form. It is He who appears in different forms. âThe attributeless Brahman is my Father. God with attributes is my Mother. Whom shall I blame? Whom shall I praise? âHe who is described in the Vedas is also described in the Tantras and the PurÄnas. All of them speak about the one SatchidÄnanda. The Nitya and the LÄ«lÄ are the two aspects of the one Reality. It is described in the Vedas as âOm SatchidÄnanda Brahmanâ, in the Tantras as âOm SatchidÄnanda Åivaâ, the ever-pure Åiva, and in the PurÄnas as âOm SatchidÄnanda Krishnaâ. All the scriptures, the Vedas, the PurÄnas, and the Tantras, speak only of one SatchidÄnanda. It is stated in the Vaishnava scriptures that it is Krishna Himself who has become KÄli.â

Sri Ramakrishna went to the porch for a few minutes and then returned. As he was going out, Vishvambarâs daughter, six or seven years old, saluted him. On returning to the room, the Master began talking to the little girl and her companions, who were of the same age.

THE CHILD (to the Master): âI saluted you and you didnât even notice it.â

The child said, âI swear I donât sing.â When the Master pressed her again, she said, âShould you press me when I said âI swearâ?â The Master was very happy with the children and sang light and frivolous songs to entertain them.

He sang:

MASTER (to the devotees): âThe paramahamsa is like a five-year-old child. He sees everything filled with Consciousness. At one time I was staying at KÄmÄrpukur when Shivaram17 was four or five years old. One day he was trying to catch grasshoppers near the pond. The leaves were moving. To stop their rustling he said to the leaves: âHush! Hush! I want to catch a grasshopper.â Another day it was stormy. It rained hard. Shivaram was with me inside the house. âThe paramahamsa is like a child. He cannot distinguish between a stranger and a relative. He isnât particular about worldly relationships. One day Shivaram said to me, âUncle, are you my fatherâs brother or his brother-in-law?â

âThe paramahamsa is like a child. He doesnât keep any track of his whereabouts. He sees everything as Brahman. He is indifferent to his own movements. âSometimes the paramahamsa behaves like a madman. When I experienced that divine madness I used to worship my own sexual organ as the Åiva-phallus. But I canât do that now. Haladhari followed him and asked: âWho are you? Are you a purnajnÄni?â18 The madman whispered, âSh! Yes, I am a purnajnÄni.â My heart began to palpitate as Haladhari told me about it. Sri Ramakrishna began to talk with M. Other devotees, too, were present.

MASTER (to M.): âHow do you feel about Shashadhar?â

Sri Ramakrishna danced with the devotees. The musician and his party joined the Master in the music and dancing. Soon the whole verandah was filled with people. Shashadhar and the devotees listened to these words with rapt attention.
