The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# THE DURGÄ PUJÄ FESTIVAL

Friday, September 26, 1884

SRI RAMAKRISHNA had come to Calcutta. It was the first day of the DurgÄ PujÄ, the great religious festival, and the Hindus of the metropolis were celebrating it. The Master intended to visit the image of the Divine Mother at Adharâs house. He also wanted to see Shivanath, the BrÄhmo devotee.

It was about midday. Umbrella in hand, M. was pacing the foot-path in front of the BrÄhmo SamÄj temple. Two hours had passed but the Master had not yet appeared. Now and then M. sat down on the steps of Dr. Mahalnavishâs dispensary and watched the joy and mirth of the people, young and old, who were celebrating the PujÄ.

A little after three the Masterâs carriage drove up. As soon as Sri Ramakrishna stepped out he saluted the temple of the BrÄhmo SamÄj with folded hands. Hazra and a few other devotees were with him. M. bowed before the Master and took the dust of his feet. The Master told him that he was going to Shivanathâs house. A few minutes later several members of the BrÄhmo SamÄj came and took him to Shivanathâs. But Shivanath was not at home. Shortly afterwards Vijay Goswami, Mahalnavish, and several other BrÄhmo leaders greeted the Master and took him inside the BrÄhmo temple.

Sri Ramakrishna was in a happy mood. He was given a seat below the altar. There the BrÄhmo devotees sang their devotional music. Vijay and the BrÄhmo devotees sat in front of the Master.

MASTER (to Vijay, with a smile): âI was told that you had put up a âsignboardâ here that people belonging to other faiths are not allowed to come in. Narendra, too, said to me: âYou shouldnât go to the BrÄhmo SamÄj. You had better visit Shivanathâs house.â

âBut I say that we are all calling on the same God. Jealousy and malice need not be. Some say that God is formless, and some that God has form. I say, let one man meditate on God with form if he believes in form, and let another meditate on the formless Deity if he does not believe in form. What I mean is that dogmatism is not good. It is not good to feel that my religion alone is true and other religions are false. The correct attitude is this: My religion is right, but I do not know whether other religions are right or wrong, true or false. I say this because one cannot know the true nature of God unless one realizes Him. Kabir used to say: âGod with form is my Mother, the Formless is my Father. Which shall I blame? Which shall I praise? The two pans of the scales are equally heavy.â

âHindus, MussalmÄns, Christians, ÅÄktas, Åaivas, Vaishnavas, the BrahmajnÄnis of the time of the rishis, and you, the BrahmajnÄnis of modern times, all seek the same object. A mother prepares dishes to suit the stomachs of her children. Suppose a mother has five children and a fish is bought for the family. She doesnât cook pilau or kÄliÄ for all of them. All have not the same power of digestion; so she prepares a simple stew for some. But she loves all her children equally.

âDo you know my attitude? I love all the preparations of fish. I have a womanly nature. (All laugh.) I feel myself at home with every dishâfried fish, fish cooked with turmeric powder, pickled fish. And further, I equally relish rich preparations like fish-head, kÄliÄ, and pilau. (All laugh.)

âDo you know what the truth is? God has made different religions to suit different aspirants, times, and countries. All doctrines are only so many paths; but a path is by no means God Himself. Indeed, one can reach God if one follows any of the paths with whole-hearted devotion. Suppose there are errors in the religion that one has accepted; if one is sincere and earnest, then God Himself will correct those errors. Suppose a man has set out with a sincere desire to visit JagannÄth at Puri and by mistake has gone north instead of south; then certainly someone meeting him on the way will tell him: âMy good fellow, donât go that way. Go to the south.â And the man will reach JagannÄth sooner or later.

âIf there are errors in other religions, that is none of our business. God, to whom the world belongs, takes care of that. Our duty is somehow to visit JagannÄth. (To the BrÄhmos) The view you hold is good indeed. You describe God as formless. That is fine. One may eat a cake with icing, either straight or sidewise. It will taste sweet either way.

âBut dogmatism is not good. You have no doubt heard the story of the chameleon. A man entered a wood and saw a chameleon on a tree. He reported to his friends, âI have seen a red lizard.â He was firmly convinced that it was nothing but red. Another person, after visiting the tree, said, âI have seen a green lizard.â He was firmly convinced that it was nothing but green. But the man who lived under the tree said: âWhat both of you have said is true. But the fact is that the creature is sometimes red, sometimes green, sometimes yellow, and sometimes has no colour at all.â

âGod has been described in the Vedas as both with attributes and without. You describe Him as without form only. That is one-sided. But never mind. If you know one of His aspects truly, you will be able to know His other aspects too. God Himself will tell you all about them. (Pointing to two or three BrÄhmo devotees) Those who come to your SamÄj know both this gentleman and that.â

Vijay still belonged to the SÄdhÄran BrÄhmo SamÄj. He was a salaried preacher of that organization but could not obey all its rules and regulations. He mixed with those who believed in God with form. This was creating a misunderstanding between him and the BrÄhmo authorities. Many BrÄhmos disapproved of his conduct. The Master suddenly looked at Vijay and began to talk to him.

MASTER (to Vijay, smiling): âI understand that they have been finding fault with you for mixing with those who believe in God with form. Is that true? He who is a devotee of God must have an understanding that cannot be shaken under any conditions. He must be like the anvil in a blacksmithâs shop. It is constantly being struck by the hammer; still it is unshaken. Bad people may abuse you very much and speak ill of you; but you must bear with them all if you sincerely seek God. Isnât it possible to think of God in the midst of the wicked? Just think of the rishis of ancient times. They used to meditate on God in the forest, surrounded on all sides by tigers, bears, and other ferocious beasts. Wicked men have the nature of tigers and bears. They will pursue you to do you an injury.

âOne must be careful about these few things. First, an influential man who has much money and many men under his control. He can injure you if he wants; you must be careful while talking to him; perhaps you may have to approve what he says. Second, a dog. When it chases you or barks at you, you must stand still, talk to it gently, and pacify it. Third, a bull. If it runs after you with lowered horns, you must calm it with a gentle voice. Fourth, a drunkard. If you arouse his anger, he will abuse you, naming fourteen generations of your family. You should say to him: âHello uncle! How are you?â Then he will be mightily pleased and sit by you and smoke.

âIn the presence of a wicked person I become alert. If such a man asks me whether I have a pipe for smoking, I say, âYes, I have.â Some people have the nature of a snake: they will bite you without warning. You have to discriminate a great deal in order to avoid the bite; otherwise your passion will be stirred up to such an extent that you will feel like doing injury in return. The companionship of a holy man is greatly needed now and then. It enables one to discriminate between the Real and the unreal.â

VIJAY: âI have no time, sir. I am entangled in my duties here.â

MASTER: âYou are a religious teacher. Others have holidays, but not so a religious teacher. When the manager of an estate brings order to one part of it, the landlord sends him to another part. So you have no leisure.â (All laugh.)

VIJAY (with folded hands): âSir, please give me your blessing.â

MASTER: âNow you are talking like an ignorant person. It is God alone who blesses.â

VIJAY: âRevered sir, please give us some instruction.â

The Master glanced around the BrÄhmo temple and said with a smile, âThis is nice tooâa mixture of crystals and syrup.1 There are crystals, and there is syrup too.

âI have scored too many points and am therefore out of the game. (All laugh.) Do you know the game called ânaxâ? It is a game of cards, and anyone scoring above seventeen is out of the game. Those who score fewer pointsâsay five, seven, or tenâare clever. I have scored too many and am out of the game.

âOnce Keshab Sen gave a lecture at his house. I was present. Many people were there. The ladies were seated behind the screen. Keshab, in the course of his talk, said, âO God, please bless us that we may dive and disappear altogether in the river of bhakti.â I said to Keshab with a smile: If you disappear altogether in the river of bhakti, then what will be the fate of those behind the screen? By all means dive into the river, but you had better come back to dry land now and then. Donât disappear in the river altogether.â At these words Keshab and the others burst out laughing.

âNever mind. One can realize God in the world, too, if only one is sincere. âIâ and âmineââthat is ignorance. But, âO God! Thou and Thineââthat is knowledge.

âLive in the world like a maidservant in a rich manâs house. She performs all the household duties, brings up her masterâs child, and speaks of him as âmy Hariâ. But in her heart she knows quite well that neither the house nor the child belongs to her. She performs all her duties, but just the same her mind dwells on her native place. Likewise, do your worldly duties but fix your mind on God. And know that house, family, and son do not belong to you; they are Godâs. You are only His servant.

âI ask people to renounce mentally. I do not ask them to give up the world. If one lives in the world unattached and seeks God with sincerity, then one is able to attain Him.

(To Vijay) âThere was a time when I too would meditate on God with my eyes closed.2 Then I said to myself: âDoes God exist only when I think of Him with my eyes closed? Doesnât He exist when I look around with my eyes open?â Now, when I look around with my eyes open, I see that God dwells in all beings. He is the Indwelling Spirit of allâmen, animals and other living beings, trees and plants, sun and moon, land and water.

âWhy do I seek Shivanath? He who meditates on God for many days has substance in him, has divine power in him. Further, he who sings well, plays well on a musical instrument, or has mastered any one art, has in him real substance and the power of God. This is the view of the GÄ«tÄ. It is said in the Chandi that he who is endowed with physical beauty has in him substance and the power of God. (To Vijay) Ah, what a beautiful nature Kedar has! No sooner does he come to me than he bursts into tears. His eyes are always red and swim in tears, like a chÄnÄbarÄ in syrup.â

VIJAY: âAt Dacca he is constantly talking about you. He is always eager to see you.â

Sri Ramakrishna was about to depart. The BrÄhmo devotees bowed low before him and he returned their salute. Then, getting into the carriage, he set out for Adharâs house to see the image of the Divine Mother.

Sunday, September 28, 1884

It was the day of the MahÄshtami, the most auspicious day of the worship of DurgÄ, the Divine Mother. At Adharâs invitation Sri Ramakrishna had come to Calcutta to see the holy image at his house. Before going there he went to Ramâs. Many devotees, including Narendra, Baburam, M., Niranjan, Vijay, Kedar, Ram, and Surendra, were present. Balaram and Rakhal were still at VrindÄvan.

MASTER (looking at Vijay and Kedar, with a smile): âThis is a nice reunion today. You two have the same spiritual mood. (To Vijay) Well, what about Shivanath? Did youâ?â

VIJAY: âYes, sir, he heard that you had been to his house. I havenât seen him, but I sent him word. He knows about it.â

MASTER (to Vijay and the others): âFour desires have come into my mind. I shall eat fish curry cooked with egg-plant. I shall visit Shivanath. The devotees will repeat the name of Hari over their beads, and I shall watch them. And the TÄntrik devotees will drink consecrated wine, eight ÄnnÄsâ worth, on the ashtami3 day, and I shall watch them and salute them.â

Narendra was seated in front of the Master. He was about twenty-two years old. While Sri Ramakrishna was talking thus his eyes fell upon his beloved disciple. At once the Master stood up and went into samÄdhi. He placed one foot on Narendraâs knee. He was in a deep spiritual mood, his eyes unblinking, his mind completely unconscious of the outer world. After a long time he came down to the relative plane of consciousness; but he still appeared dazed, for the intoxication of divine bliss had not altogether left him. Speaking to himself in that ecstatic state, he repeated the name of God. He said: âSatchidÄnanda! SatchidÄnanda! SatchidÄnanda! Shall I repeat that? No, it is the day of the Divine Mother, the Giver of the bliss of divine inebriation. O Mother, full of the bliss of divine inebriation! SÄ, re, gÄ, mÄ, pÄ, dhÄ, ni. It is not good to keep the voice on ni.â It is not possible to keep it there very long. I shall keep it on the next lower note.

âThere are different planes of consciousness: the gross, the subtle, the causal, and the Great Cause. Entering the MahÄkÄrana, the Great Cause, one becomes silent; one cannot utter a word.

âBut an IÅvarakoti, after attaining the Great Cause, can come down again to the lower planes. Incarnations of God, and others like them, belong to the class of the IÅvarakotis. They climb up, and they can also come down. They climb to the roof, and they can come down again by the stairs and move about on a lower floor. It is a case of negation and affirmation.4 There is, for instance, the seven-storey palace of a king. Strangers have access only to the lower apartments; but the prince, who knows the palace to be his own, can move up and down from floor to floor. There is a kind of rocket that throws out sparks in one pattern and then seems to go out. After a moment it makes another pattern, and then still another. There is no end to the patterns it can make. But there is another kind of rocket that, when it is lighted, makes only a dull sound, throws out a few sparks, and then goes out altogether. Like this second kind, an ordinary jÄ«va, after much spiritual effort, can go to a higher plane; but he cannot come down to tell others his experiences. After much effort he may go into samÄdhi; but he cannot climb down from that state or tell others what he has seen there.

âThere is a class of devotees, the nityasiddhas, the ever-perfect. From their very birth they seek God. They do not enjoy anything of the world. The Vedas speak of the homÄ bird. It lives very high in the sky. There the mother bird lays her egg. She lives so high that the egg falls for many days. While falling it is hatched. The chick continues to fall. That also goes on for many days. In the mean time the chick develops eyes. Coming near the earth, it becomes conscious of the world. It realizes it will meet certain death if it hits the ground. Then it gives a shrill cry and shoots up toward its mother. The earth means death, and it frightens the young bird; it then seeks its mother. She dwells high up in the sky, and the young bird shoots straight up in that direction. It doesnât look anywhere else.

âThose who are born as the companions of an Incarnation of God are eternally perfect. For some of them that birth is the last.

(To Vijay) âYou have bothâyoga and bhoga. King Janaka also had yoga and bhoga. Therefore he is called a rÄjarshi, both king and seer. NÄrada was a devarshi, and Åukadeva a brahmarshi. Yes, Sukadeva was a brahmarshi. He was not a mere jnÄni; he was the very embodiment of JnÄna, Divine Knowledge. Whom do I call a jnÄni? A man who has attained Knowledge and has done so after much effort. Sukadeva was the very image of Knowledge, in other words, a form of concentrated Knowledge. He attained Knowledge spontaneously, without any labour.â

Saying this, Sri Ramakrishna came down to the normal mood. Then he talked freely with the devotees. The Master asked Kedar to sing.

Kedar sang:

How shall I open my heart, O friend?

It is forbidden me to speak,

I am about to die, for lack of a kindred soul

To understand my miseryâ¦ .

Kedar sang several other songs. After the music the Master again talked to the devotees. Nandalal, Keshabâs nephew, was also present with a few BrÄhmo friends. They were sitting near the Master.

MASTER (to Vijay and the other devotees): âA man brought a bottle of consecrated wine for me; but I couldnât even touch it.â

VIJAY: âAh!â

MASTER: âI become intoxicated at the mere thought of God. I donât have to take any wine. I feel drunk at the very sight of the charanÄmrita.5 I feel as if I had drunk five bottles of liquor. When a person attains such a state he cannot help discriminating about food.â

NARENDRA: âAs regards food, one should take whatever comes.â

MASTER: âWhat you say applies only to a particular state of the aspirantâs mind. No food can harm a jnÄni. According to the GÄ«tÄ, the jnÄni himself does not eat; his eating is an offering to the Kundalini. But that does not apply to a bhakta. The present state of my mind is such that I cannot eat any food unless it is first offered to God by a brÄhmin priest. Formerly my state of mind was such that I would enjoy inhaling the smell of burning corpses, carried by the wind from the other side of the Ganges. It tasted very sweet to me. But nowadays I cannot eat food touched by anybody and everybody. No, I cannot. But once in a while I do. One day I was taken to see a performance of a play at Keshabâs house. They gave me luchi and curries to eat. I didnât know whether the food was handed to me by a washerman or a barber; but I ate quite a little. (All laugh.) Rakhal had asked me to eat.

(To Narendra) âWith you it is all right. You are in âthisâ as well as in âthatâ.6 You can eat everything now. (To the devotees) Blessed is he who feels longing for God, though he eats pork. But shame on him whose mind dwells on âwoman and goldâ, though he eats the purest foodâboiled vegetables, rice, and ghee.

âOnce I had a desire to eat dÄl cooked in a blacksmithâs house. From my childhood I had heard the blacksmiths say, âDo the brÄhmins know how to cook?â I ate the dÄl, but it smelt of the blacksmith. (All laugh.)

âI received the ÄllÄh mantra7 from Govinda Rai. Rice was cooked for me with onions8 in the kuthi. I ate some. I ate curry in Mani Mallickâs garden house, but I felt a kind of repulsion to it.

âWhen I went to KÄmÄrpukur, Ramlalâs father was frightened. He thought I might eat at any and every house. He was frightened to think I might be expelled from the caste; so I couldnât stay long. I came away.

âBoth the Vedas and the PurÄnas describe pure food and conduct. But what the Vedas and the PurÄnas ask people to shun as impure is extolled by the Tantra as good.

âOh, what a state of mind I passed through! I would open my mouth, touching, as it were, heaven and the nether world with my jaws, and utter the word âMÄâ. I felt that I had seized the Mother, like a fisherman dragging fish in his net. Let me recite a song:

This time I shall devour Thee utterly, Mother KÄli!

For I was born under an evil star,

And one so born becomes, they say, the eater of his mother.

Thou must devour me first, or I myself shall eat Thee up;

One or the other it must be.

I shall besmear my hands with black,9 and with black my face;

With black I shall besmear the whole of my body.

And when Death seizes me, with black I shall besmear his face.

O Mother, I shall eat Thee up but not digest Thee;

I shall install Thee in my heart

And make Thee offerings with my mind.

You may say that by eating KÄli I shall embroil myself

With KÄla,10 Her Husband, but I am not afraid;

Braving His anger, I shall chant my Motherâs name.

To show the world that RÄmprasÄd is KÄliâs rightful son,

Come what may, I shall eat Thee upâThee and Thy retinueâ

Or lose my life attempting it.

âI almost became madâsuch was my longing for God.â

Narendra began to sing:

O Mother, make me mad with Thy love!

What need have I of knowledge or reason? â¦

Listening to the song, the Master again went into samÄdhi. Coming down to the normal plane, he assumed the attitude of GirirÄni11 and sang the Ägamani. He sang, intoxicated with divine love:

Tell me, my UmÄ, how have you fared, alone in the Strangerâs house? â¦

He said to the devotees, âToday is the MahÄshtami. The Mother has come; that is why I feel such an awakening of spiritual emotion.â

KEDAR: âLord, you are here. Are you different from the Divine Mother?â

Sri Ramakrishna looked in another direction and sang in an absent-minded mood:

Ah, friend! I have not found Him yet, whose love has driven me madâ¦ .

Again he became ecstatic and sang of the Divine Mother. As he sang, Vijay suddenly stood up crying the name of Hari. Sri Ramakrishna, full of divine love, began to dance with Vijay and the other devotees.

The music was over. The Master, Vijay, Narendra, and the other devotees sat down. All eyes were fixed on Sri Ramakrishna, who began conversing with the devotees. He asked about their health. Kedar spoke to him humbly in a soft, sweet voice. Narendra, Chunilal, Ram, M., and Harish were sitting by the Master.

KEDAR (humbly): âHow can I get rid of my dizziness?â

MASTER (tenderly): âOne gets that. I have had it myself. Use a little almond oil. I have heard that it cures dizziness.â

KEDAR: âI shall, sir.â

Surendra stood near Sri Ramakrishna. He was in the habit of drinking and often went to excess. This had worried the Master greatly, but he had not asked Surendra to give up drinking altogether. It was dusk. Regaining partial consciousness, the Master sang:

Behold my Mother playing with Åiva, lost in an ecstasy of joy!

Then he chanted the name of Hari, clapping his hands occasionally. In a sweet voice he said: âHari! Hari! O mind, chant the name of Hari! Sing the name of Hari!â Then he chanted: âRÄma! RÄma RÄma! RÄma!â

Ramchandra Dutta came in and stood near him.

Supper was ready on the roof. Sri Ramakrishna and the devotees were taken there and sumptuously fed. Later the Master went to Adharâs house with M., Niranjan, and others. Monday, September 29, 1884

It was the third day of the DurgÄ PujÄ. The Master had been awake in his room at Dakshineswar since early morning. The morning worship in the KÄli temple was over and the orchestra had played the morning melodies in the nahabat. BrÄhmins and gardeners, basket in hand, were plucking flowers for the worship of the Divine Mother. Bhavanath, Baburam, Niranjan, and M. had spent the night at Dakshineswar, sleeping on the porch of the Masterâs room. As soon as they awoke they saw Sri Ramakrishna dancing in an ecstatic mood. He was chanting: âVictory to Mother DurgÄ! Hallowed be the name of DurgÄ!â He was naked and looked like a child as he chanted the name of the Blissful Mother. The devotees sat on their beds and with unwinking eyes watched Sri Ramakrishnaâs spiritual mood. Hazra was living at the temple garden. Latu was also living there to render the Master personal service. Rakhal was still at VrindÄvan. Narendra visited Sri Ramakrishna now and then. He was expected that day.

The devotees washed their faces. The Master took his seat on a mat on the north verandah. Bhavanath and M. sat beside him. Other devotees were coming in and out of the room.

MASTER (to Bhavanath): âThe truth is that ordinary men cannot easily have faith. But an IÅvarakotiâs faith is spontaneous. PrahlÄda burst into tears while writing the letter âkaâ.12 It reminded him of Krishna. It is the nature of jÄ«vas to doubt. They say yes, no doubt, butâ

âHazra can never be persuaded to believe that Brahman and Åakti, that Åakti and the Being endowed with Åakti, are one and the same. When the Reality appears as Creator, Preserver, and Destroyer, we call It Åakti; when It is inactive, we call It Brahman. But really It is one and the same thingâindivisible. Fire naturally brings to mind its power to burn; and the idea of burning naturally brings to mind the idea of fire. It is impossible to think of the one without the other.

âSo I prayed to the Divine Mother: âO Mother! Hazra is trying to upset the views of this place.13 Either give him right understanding or take him from here.â The next day he came to me and said, âYes, I agree with you.â He said that God exists everywhere as All-pervading Consciousness.â

BHAVANATH (smiling): âDid what Hazra said really make you suffer so much?â

MASTER: âYou see, I am now in a different mood. I canât shout and carry on heated discussions with people. I am not in a mood now to argue and quarrel with Hazra. Hriday said to me at Jadu Mallickâs garden house, âUncle, donât you want to keep me with you?â14 âNo,â I said, âI am no longer in a mood to get into heated arguments with you.â

âWhat is knowledge and what is ignorance? A man is ignorant so long as he feels that God is far away. He has knowledge when he knows that God is here and everywhere.

âWhen a man has true knowledge he feels that everything is filled with Consciousness. At KÄmÄrpukur I used to talk to Shibu,15 who was then a lad four or five years old. When the clouds rumbled and lightning flashed, Shibu would say to me: âThere, uncle! Theyâre striking matches again!â (All laugh.) One day I noticed him chasing grasshoppers by himself. The leaves rustled in the near-by trees. âHush! Hush!â he said to the leaves. âI want to catch the grasshoppers.â He was a child and saw everything throbbing with consciousness. One cannot realize God without the faith that knows no guile, the simple faith of a child.

âAh, what a state of mind I passed through! One day something bit me while I was sitting in the grass. I was afraid it might have been a snake, and I didnât know what to do. I had heard that if a snake bites you again immediately after its first bite, it takes back its own venom. At once I set out to discover the hole so that I might let the snake bite me again. While I was searching, a man said to me, âWhat are you doing?â After listening to my story, he said, âBut the snake must bite in the very same place it has bitten before.â Thereupon I went away. Perhaps I had been bitten by a scorpion or some other insect.

âI had heard from Ramlal that the autumn chill was good for oneâs health. Ramlal had quoted a verse to support it. One day, as I was returning from Calcutta in a carriage, I stuck my head out of the window so that I might get all the chill. Then I fell ill.â (All laugh.)

Sri Ramakrishna entered his room and sat down. His legs were a little swollen. He asked the devotees to feel his legs and see whether or not the pressure of their fingers made dimples. Dimples did appear with the pressure, but the devotees said that it was nothing.

Hazra entered the room and sat down. The Master talked awhile about different things and then said to Hazra: âYou see, many people were at Ramâs house yesterday. Vijay, Kedar, and others were there. But why did I feel so deeply stirred at the sight of Narendra? I found that Kedar belonged to the realm of Divine Inebriation.â

Presently Narendra arrived, and Sri Ramakrishna was exceedingly happy. Narendra saluted the Master and began to talk with Bhavanath and others in the room. M. was seated near by. A long mat was spread on the floor. While talking, Narendra lay on it flat on his stomach. The Master looked at him and suddenly went into samÄdhi. He sat on Narendraâs back in an ecstatic mood.

Bhavanath sang:

Sri Ramakrishna came down from the plane of samÄdhi. He sang:

Hazra was sitting on the northeast verandah counting the beads of his rosary. The Master went and sat in front of him, taking the rosary in his own hands.

It was about noon. The gong and the bells announced the worship and offering in the various temples. The brÄhmins, the Vaishnavas, and the beggars went to the guest-house to have their midday meal. The devotees were engaged in a game of golokdhÄm.18 Hazra joined them. The Master stood by, watching them play. M. and Kishori reached âheavenâ. Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the small couch in his room. Narendra, Baburam, Bhavanath, and M. were sitting on the floor. Narendra referred to various religious sectsâthe GhoshpÄrÄ, PanchanÄmi, and others. Sri Ramakrishna described their views and condemned their immoral practices. MASTER (to Narendra): âYou need not listen to these things. The bhairavas and the bhairavis of the TÄntrik sect also follow this kind of discipline. (To Narendra and the others) âLet me tell you this. I regard woman as my mother; I regard myself as her son. This is a very pure attitude. There is no danger in it. âThere are various paths to reach God. Each view is a path. It is like reaching the KÄli temple by different roads. But it must be said that some paths are clean and some dirty. It is good to travel on a clean path.

âNo one else is here, and you are my own people. Let me tell you something. I have come to the final realization that God is the Whole and I am a part of Him, that God is the Master and I am His servant. Furthermore, I think every now and then that He is I and I am He.â

The devotees listened to these words in deep silence.

BHAVANATH (humbly): âI feel disturbed if I have a misunderstanding with someone. I feel that in that case I am not able to love all.â

âWhen I attain God I shall attain everything. BHAVANATH (smiling): âThis is the shrewd calculation of a business man.â

Hazra was sitting on the verandah.

A DEVOTEE: âCanât God fulfil a devoteeâs desire?â

âWhen I went to VrindÄvan I felt no desire to return to Calcutta. It was arranged that I should live with GangÄmÄ.22 Everything was settled. Sri Ramakrishna had set out from Dakshineswar for Adharâs house in Calcutta. Narayan and Gangadhar were with him. In the carriage, in an ecstatic mood, he said: âShall I count the beads? He asked Kedar and Vijay to bless Narayan and Baburam that they might have devotion to God. MASTER (to Kedar and the other devotees): âIt is good that I have met you all here; otherwise perhaps you would have come to the KÄli temple to see me. Through the will of God, however, we have met here.â

Sri Ramakrishna smiled. Vaishnavcharan began a kirtan about RÄdhÄ and Krishna. When the music was nearing its end, with the union of RÄdhÄ and Krishna, the Master began to dance with ecstatic fervour. The devotees danced and sang around him. After the music they all sat down. The Master said to Vijay, referring to Vaishnavcharan, âHe sings very well.â He asked the musician to sing the song about Sri Chaitanya, beginning with the line, âThe beautiful GaurÄnga, the youthful dancer, fair as molten gold.â

The Master and the musician sang again and again the following lines from the song:

Kedar and several devotees stood up. They were about to return home. Kedar saluted the Master and bade him good-bye.

Just then Adhar came in to take the Master to the dining-room, for the meal was ready. Sri Ramakrishna stood up and said, addressing Kedar and Vijay: âCome. Come with me.â They followed him and partook of the dinner together with the other devotees.

Yogendra, the editor of a Bengali paper, the BangavÄsi, entered the room. The conversation turned to the Personal God and God without form.

The Master sang:

A mendicant has come to us, ever absorbed in divine moodsâ¦ .

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# THE MASTER IN VARIOUS MOODS

Thursday, October 2, 1884

SRI RAMAKRISHNA was sitting in his room at Dakshineswar. Latu, Ramlal, Harish, and Hazra were living with him at the temple garden. Baburam spent a day or two with him now and then.

Manilal Mallick, Priya Mukherji and his relative Hari, a bearded BrÄhmo devotee from Shibpur, and several MÄrwÄri devotees from Calcutta were in the Masterâs room. Manilal was an old member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj.

MASTER (to Manilal and the others): âIt is wise to salute a person mentally. What need is there of touching his feet? Mental salutation doesnât embarrass anybody.

âThe attitude that my religion alone is right and all other religions are false is not good. I see that God Himself has become all these: men, images, and ÅÄlagrÄm. I see one alone in all these; I do not see two. I see only one.

âMany people think that their opinion alone is right and othersâ opinions are wrong; that they alone have won and others have lost. But a person who has gone forward may be detained by some slight obstacle, and someone who has been lagging behind may then steal a march on him. In the game of golokdhÄm one may advance a great deal, but still somehow oneâs piece may fail to reach the goal.

âTriumph or defeat is in the hands of God. We cannot understand His ways. You must have noticed that the green coconut remains high in the tree and is exposed to the sun, but still its milk is cool. On the other hand the pÄniphal1 remains in the water, but when eaten it heats the body.

âLook at the body of man. The head is the root, and it is at the top.â

MANILAL: âWhat then is our duty?â

MASTER: âTo remain somehow united with God. There are two ways: karmayoga and manoyoga. Householders practise yoga through karma, the performance of duty. There are four stages of life: brahmacharya, gÄrhasthya, vÄnaprastha, and sannyÄs. SannyÄsis must renounce those karmas which are performed with special ends in view; but they should perform the daily obligatory karmas, giving up all desire for results. SannyÄsis are united with God by such karmas as the acceptance of the staff, the receiving of alms, going on pilgrimage, and the performance of worship and japa.

âIt doesnât matter what kind of action you are engaged in. You can be united with God through any action provided that, performing it, you give up all desire for its result.

âThere is the other path: manoyoga. A yogi practising this discipline doesnât show any outward sign. He is inwardly united with God. Take Jadabharata and Åukadeva, for instance. There are many other yogis of this class, but these two are well known. They shave neither hair nor beard.

âAll actions drop away when a man reaches the stage of the paramahamsa. He always remembers the ideal and meditates on it. He is always united with God in his mind. If he ever performs an action it is to teach men.

âA man may be united with God either through action or through inwardness of thought, but he can know everything through bhakti. Through bhakti one spontaneously experiences kumbhaka. The nerve currents and breathing calm down when the mind is concentrated. Again, the mind is concentrated when the nerve currents and breathing calm down. Then the buddhi, the discriminating power, becomes steady. The man who achieves this state is not himself aware of it.

âOne can attain everything through bhaktiyoga. I wept before the Mother and prayed, âO Mother, please tell me, please reveal to me, what the yogis have realized through yoga and the jnÄnis through discrimination.â And the Mother has revealed everything to me. She reveals everything if the devotee cries to Her with a yearning heart. She has shown me everything that is in the Vedas, the VedÄnta, the PurÄnas, and the Tantra.â

MANILAL: âAnd what about hathayoga?â

MASTER: âThe hathayogis identify themselves with their bodies. They practise internal washing and similar disciplines, and devote themselves only to the care of the body. Their ideal is to increase longevity. They serve the body day and night. That is not good.

âWhat is your duty? You should renounce âwoman and goldâ mentally. You cannot look on the world as crow-droppings.

âChaitanyadeva said that the duties of householders were kindness to living beings, service to the Vaishnavas, and the chanting of Godâs holy name.

âKeshab Sen once said about me: âNow he asks us to hold to bothâGod and the world. But one day he will sting us.â No, that is not true. Why should I sting?â

MANI MALLICK: âBut, sir, you do.â

MASTER (smiling): âHow so? You are a householder. Why should you renounce?

âBut the renunciation of the world is needful for those whom God wants to be teachers of men. One who is an ÄchÄrya should give up âwoman and goldâ; otherwise people will not take his advice. It is not enough for him to renounce only mentally; he should also renounce outwardly. Only then will his teaching bear fruit. Otherwise people will think, âThough he asks us to give up âwoman and goldâ, he enjoys them himself in secret.â

âA physician prescribed medicine for a patient and said to him, âCome another day and Iâll give you directions about diet.â The physician had several jars of molasses in his room that day. The patient lived very far away. He visited the physician later and the physician said to him: âBe careful about your food. âI have seen the ÄchÄrya of the Ädi BrÄhmo SamÄj. I understand that he has married for the second or third time. He has grown-up children. And such men are teachers! âOnce Mahendra KavirÄj of Sinthi gave five rupees to Ramlal. I didnât know about it. When Ramlal told me about the money, I asked him, âFor whom was the money given?â He said it was for me. âThere was a low-caste woman named Bhagi Teli in our part of the country. She had many disciples and devotees. (To Manilal) âKeshab Senâs mother came here the other day. The young boys of her family sang the name of Hari. She went around them clapping her hands. MANILAL: âRamkamal Sen, Keshab Babuâs grandfather, was a devotee of God. He used to sit in a tulsi-grove and repeat Godâs holy name. Pyarimohan, Keshabâs father, was also a Vaishnava devotee.â

MASTER: âThe son could not have been so devoted to God if the father had not been like that. Look at Vijay. Then the Master sang:

He continued: âYou cannot make a pot without first carefully preparing the clay. The pot will crack if the clay contains particles of sand or stone. That is why the potter first prepares the clay by removing the sand and stones.

Sri Ramakrishna was worrying, like a child, because he thought his legs were slightly swollen. Mahendra KavirÄj of Sinthi entered the room and saluted the Master.

âI was told that the autumn dew was good. One day, while coming from Calcutta, I stuck my head out of the carriage and exposed it to the damp air. (All laugh.)

(To Mahendra of Sinthi) âThat pundit from Sinthi is very good. He holds a title for his scholarship. He respects me. I said to him, âYou have read a great deal; but give up the vanity that you are a scholar.â That made him very happy. I discussed VedÄnta with him.

(To M.) âThat which is Pure Ätman is unattached. MÄyÄ, or avidyÄ, is in It. In mÄyÄ there are three gunas: sattva, rajas, and tamas. These three gunas also exist in the Pure Ätman. Prakriti, the Primal Energy, is the cause of all these. Brahman, Pure Ätman, is the Cause of the cause.

(To the bearded BrÄhmo devotee from Shibpur) âAre you a BrÄhmo?â

The MÄrwÄri devotees from BurrabÄzÄr entered the room and saluted the Master. He began to praise them.

DEVOTEE: âWe read the scriptures. Why is it that we canât assimilate them?â

âThe hand bleeds when it touches a thorny plant. Suppose you bring such a plant and repeat, sitting near it: âThere! The plant is burning.â Will that burn the plant? âAs long as you live inside the house of mÄyÄ, as long as there exists the cloud of mÄyÄ, you do not see the effect of the Sun of Knowledge. (To the MÄrwÄri devotee) âThe rules for a sannyÄsi are extremely hard. He cannot have the slightest contact with âwoman and goldâ. He must not accept money with his own hands, and he must not even allow it to be left near him.

It is also impossible for me to keep it near me.â He was a very clever fellow. He said: âThen you too have the idea of acceptance and rejection. In that case you havenât attained Perfect Knowledge.â âMy dear sir,â I said, âI havenât yet gone that far.â (All laugh.) Lakshminarayan then wanted to leave the money with Hriday. I said to him: âThat will not do. If you leave it with Hriday, then I shall instruct him to spend it as I wish. If he does not comply, I shall be angry. The very contact of money is bad. No, you canât leave it with Hriday.â Wonât an object kept near a mirror be reflected in it?â

DEVOTEE: âRevered sir, is a man liberated only when he dies on the bank of the Ganges?â

MASTER: âIt is the Knowledge of God alone that gives liberation. The jnÄni will certainly attain liberation wherever he may die, whether in the charnel-pit or on the bank of the Ganges. But the bank of the Ganges is prescribed for a bound soul.â

DEVOTEE: âRevered sir, why does a man dying in Benares become liberated?â

MASTER: âA person dying in Benares sees the vision of Åiva. Åiva says to him: âThis is My aspect with form, My embodiment in mÄyÄ. I assume this form for the sake of the devotees. Now look. I am merging in the indivisible SatchidÄnanda!â Uttering these words, Åiva withdraws His form and enables the dying person to see Brahman.

âThe PurÄnas say that even a chandÄla endowed with love of God achieves liberation. According to this school the name of God is enough to liberate a soul. There is no need of such things as worship, sacrifice, the discipline of Tantra, and the recitation of mantras.

âBut the teachings of the Vedas are different. According to the Vedas none but a brÄhmin can be liberated. Further, the worship is not accepted by the gods unless the mantras are recited correctly. One must perform sacrifice, worship, and so on, according to scriptural injunction. But where is the time in the Kaliyuga to perform the Vedic rituals? Therefore in the Kaliyuga the path of devotion prescribed by NÄrada is best. The path of karma is very difficult. Karma becomes a cause of bondage unless it is performed in a spirit of detachment. Further, the life of man nowadays depends on food. He has no time to observe the rituals enjoined by the scriptures. The patient dies if he tries to cure his fever by taking the decoction of herbs prescribed by the orthodox native physicians. Therefore he should take a modern âfever mixtureâ.

âAccording to NÄrada the devotee should sing the name and glories of God. The path of karma is not the right one for the Kaliyuga. Bhaktiyoga is the right path. Do your duties in the world as long as you need them to reap the fruit of the actions of your past lives. But you must develop love for God and be passionately attached to Him. The singing of the name and glories of God destroys the effect of past action.

âYou donât have to perform duties all your life. As you develop unalloyed love and longing for God, your duties become fewer and fewer. After the realization of God they completely drop away. When the young daughter-in-law is pregnant, her mother-in-law lessens her duties. After the birth of the child she doesnât have to do any household work.â

Several young men from the village of Dakshineswar entered the room and saluted Sri Ramakrishna. It was about four oâclock in the afternoon. They sat down and began to talk with the Master.

YOUNG MAN: âSir, what is Knowledge?â

MASTER: âIt is to know that God is the only Reality and that all else is unreal. That which is the Real is also called Brahman. It has another name: KÄla, Time. There is a saying, âO brother, how many things come into being in Time and disappear in Time!â

âThat which sports with KÄla is called KÄli. She is the Primal Energy. KÄla and KÄli, Brahman and Åakti, are indivisible.

âThat Brahman, of the nature of Reality, is eternal. It exists in past, present, and future. It is without beginning or end. It cannot be described in words. The utmost that can be said of Brahman is that It is of the very nature of Intelligence and Bliss.

âThe world is illusory; Brahman alone is real. The world is of the nature of magic. The magician is real but his magic is unreal.â

YOUNG MAN: âIf the world is of the nature of illusionâmagicâthen why doesnât one get rid of it?â

MASTER: âIt is due to the samskÄras, inborn tendencies. Repeated births in this world of mÄyÄ make one believe that mÄyÄ is real.

âLet me tell you how powerful inborn tendencies are. A prince had, in a previous birth, been the son of a washerman. While playing with his chums in his incarnation as the prince, he said to them: âStop those games. I will show you a new one. I shall lie on my belly, and you will beat the clothes on my back as the washerman does, making a swishing sound.â

âMany youngsters come here. But only a few long for God. These few are born with a spiritual tendency. They shudder at the talk of marriage. Niranjan has said from boyhood that he will not marry.

âMore than twenty years ago two young men used to come here from BarÄnagore. One was named Govinda Pal and the other Gopal Sen. They had been devoted to God since boyhood. The very mention of marriage would frighten them. Gopal used to have bhÄva samÄdhi. He would shrink from worldly people, as a mouse from a cat. One day he saw the boys of the Tagore family strolling in the garden. He shut himself in the kuthi lest he should have to talk with them.

âGopal went into samÄdhi in the Panchavati. In that state he said to me, touching my feet: âLet me go. I cannot live in this world any more. You have a long time to wait. Let me go.â I said to him, in an ecstatic mood, âYou must come again.â âVery well, I willâ, he said. A few days later Govinda came to me. âWhere is Gopal?â I asked him. He said, âHe has passed away.â

âWhat are the other youngsters about? Money, house, carriage, clothes, and finally marriage. These are the things that keep them busy. If they want to marry, at the outset they make inquiries about the girl. They want to find out for themselves whether she is beautiful.

âThere is a person who speaks much ill of me. He is always criticizing me for loving the youngsters. I love only those who are born with good tendencies, pure souls with longing for God, who do not pay any attention to money, creature comforts, and such things.

âIf married people develop love for God, they will not be attached to the world. Hirananda is married. What if he is? He will not be much attached to the world.â

Hirananda, a member of the BrÄhmo SamÄj, was a native of Sindh. He had met the Master in Calcutta and become devoted to him.

Manilal, the MÄrwÄri devotees, the BrÄhmo devotees from Shibpur, and the young men from Dakshineswar saluted Sri Ramakrishna and took their leave.

It was evening. Lamps were lighted on the south and west verandahs. A lamp was lighted in the Masterâs room also, and incense was burnt. He was repeating the name of the Divine Mother, absorbed in contemplation of Her. After a while he talked again to the devotees. There was still some time before the evening worship in the temples.

MASTER (to M.): âWhat need of the sandhyÄ has a man who thinks of God day and night?

What need of rituals has a man, what need of devotions any more,

If he repeats the Motherâs name at the three holy hours?

Rituals may pursue him close, but never can they overtake him.

Charity, vows, and giving of gifts do not appeal to Madanâs mind;

The Blissful Motherâs Lotus Feet are his whole prayer and sacrifice.

âThe sandhyÄ merges in the GÄyatri, the GÄyatri in Om. A man is firmly established in spiritual life when he goes into samÄdhi on uttering âOmâ only once.

âThere is a sÄdhu in Hrishikesh who gets up early in the morning and stands near a great waterfall. He looks at it the whole day and says to God: âAh, You have done well! Well done! How amazing!â He doesnât practise any other form of japa or austerity. At night he returns to his hut.

âWhat need is there even to bother oneâs head about whether God is formless or has a form? It is enough for a man to pray to Him, alone in solitude, weeping, âO God, reveal Yourself to me as You are.â

âGod is both inside and outside. It is He who dwells inside us. Therefore the Vedas say, âTattvamasiâThat thou art.â God is also outside us. He appears manifold through mÄyÄ; but in reality He alone exists. Therefore before describing the various names and forms of God, one should say, âOm Tat Sat.â3

âIt is one thing to learn about God from the scriptures, and quite another to see Him. The scriptures only give hints. Therefore to read a great many scriptures is not necessary. It is much better to pray to God in solitude.

âIt isnât necessary to read all of the GÄ«tÄ. One can get the essence of the GÄ«tÄ by repeating the word ten times. It becomes reversed and is then âtÄgiâ. The essence of the book is: âO man, renounce everything and worship God.â â

The Master went into an ecstatic mood while watching the evening worship of KÄli in the company of the devotees. He was in no condition even to salute the image. Very carefully he returned to his room with the devotees and sat down; he was still in an ecstatic mood. He spoke to them while in that state.

In the room was Hari, a young man about twenty years of age, who was a relative of the Mukherjis and very much devoted to the Master. He was married. At that time he was living with the Mukherjis and looking for a job.

MASTER (to Hari, in an ecstatic mood): âTake your initiation after getting your motherâs permission. (To Priya, referring to Hari) I couldnât give him the mantra though I said I would initiate him. I donât initiate people. Continue with your own meditation and japa as you have been doing.â

PRIYA: âYes, sir.â

MASTER: âAnd I am saying this to you in this state of my mind. Believe my words. You see, there is no show or deceit here. I just said to the Divine Mother in my ecstatic mood, âO Mother, may those who come here [referring to himself] through sincere attraction obtain perfection!â â

Mahendra KavirÄj of Sinthi was seated on the verandah conversing with Ramlal, Hazra, and others. The Master called to him from his room. M. went out quickly and brought Mahendra in.

MASTER (to Mahendra): âSit down and listen to my words.â

Mahendra was a little embarrassed. He sat down.

MASTER (to the devotees): âGod can be served in different ways. An ecstatic lover of God enjoys Him in different ways. Sometimes he says, âO God, You are the lotus and I am the beeâ, and sometimes, âYou are the Ocean of SatchidÄnanda and I am the fish.â Sometimes, again, the lover of God says, âI am Your dancing-girl.â He dances and sings before Him. He thinks of himself sometimes as the friend of God and sometimes as His handmaid. He looks on God sometimes as a child, as did YaÅodÄ, and sometimes as husband or sweetheart, as did the gopis.

âSometimes BalarÄma looked on Krishna as a friend; sometimes he would think he was Krishnaâs umbrella or carpet. He served Krishna in all possible ways.â

Was Sri Ramakrishna hinting at his own state of mind while thus describing the different attitudes of a lover of God?

Next he described Chaitanyaâs three spiritual moods.

MASTER: âChaitanyadeva used to experience three moods. In the inmost mood he would be absorbed in samÄdhi, unconscious of the outer world. In the semi-conscious mood he would dance in ecstasy but could not talk. In the conscious mood he would sing the glories of God.

(To the devotees) âYou are listening to my words. Try to assimilate them. When worldly people sit before a sÄdhu, for the time being they completely hide all worldly thoughts and ideas. But once away from the holy man they let them out again. You have seen a pigeon eating dried peas. You think he has digested them, but he keeps them in his crop. You can feel them there.

âAt dusk put aside all duties and pray to God. One is reminded of Him by darkness. At the approach of darkness one thinks: âI could see everything a moment ago. Who has brought about this change?â The MussalmÄns put aside all activities and say their prayers at the appointed times.â

MUKHERJI: âRevered sir, is it good to practise japa?â

MASTER: âYes. One attains God through japa. By repeating the name of God secretly and in solitude one receives divine grace. Then comes His vision. Suppose there is a big piece of timber lying under water and fastened to the land with a chain; by proceeding along the chain, link by link, you will at last touch the timber.

âHigher than worship is japa, higher than japa is meditation, higher than meditation is bhÄva, and higher than bhÄva are mahÄbhÄva and prema. Chaitanyadeva had prema. When one attains prema one has the rope to tie God.â

Hazra entered the room.

MASTER (to Hazra): âLove of God, when it is intense and spontaneous, is called rÄga-bhakti. Vaidhi-bhakti, formal devotion, depends on scriptural injunctions. It comes and it goes. But rÄga-bhakti is like a stone emblem of Åiva that has sprung up out of the bowels of the earth. One cannot find its root; they say the root goes as far as Benares. Only an Incarnation of God and His companions attain rÄga-bhakti.â

HAZRA: âAh me!â

MASTER: âOne day I was returning from the pine-grove, when I saw you telling your beads. I said to the Divine Mother: âMother, what a small-minded fellow he is! He lives here and still he practises japa with a rosary! Whoever comes here [referring to himself] will have his spiritual consciousness awakened all at once; he wonât have to bother much about japa. Go to Calcutta and you will find thousands telling their beadsâeven the prostitutes.â

(To M.) âPlease bring Naran here in a carriage. I am making the same request to Mukherji. I shall give Naran something to eat when he comes. There is great significance in feeding boys like him.â

Sunday, October 5, 1884

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting in his room after the midday meal, with M., Hazra, the elder Kali, Baburam, Ramlal, Hari, and others. Some of them sat on the floor and some stood about. On the previous day the Master had visited Keshabâs mother at her Calcutta house and had made her happy with his devotional songs.

Hazra had been living with the Master at Dakshineswar a long time. He was a little conceited about his knowledge and even criticized the Master now and then before others. Again, he would sit on the verandah of the Masterâs room and tell his beads with apparent concentration. He spoke slightingly of Chaitanya as a âmodern Incarnationâ. He would say: âGod gives not only pure devotion but also wealth. He has no lack of it. By attaining God one obtains the eight occult powers as well.â Hazra had a small debt to clear up, about one thousand rupees. He had incurred it for the building of his house and was worried about paying it.

The elder Kali had a position in an office, from which he received a small salary. He had a large family to maintain. He was devoted to the Master and visited him now and then, even absenting himself from the office.

KALI (to Hazra): âYou go about criticizing people; you are like a touchstone, testing what is pure gold and what is impure. Why do you speak so much ill of others?â

HAZRA: âWhatever I say, I say to him [meaning Sri Ramakrishna] alone.â

MASTER: âThat is so.â

Hazra began to explain TattvajnÄna.

HAZRA: âThe meaning of TattvajnÄna is the knowledge of the existence of the twenty-four tattvas, or cosmic principles.â

He was wrong about the meaning of the word.

A DEVOTEE: âWhat are they?â

M. (to the Master, smiling): âHe says that the six passions are included in the twenty-four cosmic principles.â

The word âTatâ means the Supreme Self, and the word âtvamâ, the embodied soul. One attains Supreme Knowledge, TattvajnÄna, by realizing the identity of the embodied soul and the Supreme Self.â

After a few minutes Hazra left the room and sat on the porch.

MASTER (to M. and the others): âHe [meaning Hazra] only argues. This moment perhaps he understands, but the next moment he is his old self again.

âWhen the angler hooks a big fish and finds it pulling hard, he releases the line; otherwise it will snap and the angler himself will be thrown into the water. Therefore I do not say much to him.

(To M.) âHazra said that a man could not be liberated unless he was born in a brÄhmin body. âHow is that?â I said. âOne attains liberation through bhakti alone. Åavari was the daughter of a hunter. She, RuhidÄs, and others belonged to the Åudra caste. They were liberated through bhakti alone.â âBut stillââ Hazra insisted.

âHe recognized Dhruvaâs spiritual greatness, but not as much as he recognized PrahlÄdaâs. When Latu said, âDhruva had great yearning for God from his boyhoodâ, he kept still.

âI said that there was nothing greater than the bhakti that sought no end and had no selfish motive. Hazra contradicted me. I said to him, âA wealthy man is annoyed when a petitioner comes to him. âThere he comesâ, he says angrily. âSit downâ, he says to him in an indifferent voice, and shows that he is much annoyed. He doesnât allow such a beggar to ride with him in his carriage.â

âBut Hazra said that God was not like such wealthy people of the world; did He lack wealth, that He should feel pinched to give it away? Hazra said further: âWhen rain falls from the sky, the Ganges and all the big rivers and lakes overflow with water. Small tanks, too, are filled. (To the devotees) âBut I call this impure devotion to God. Pure devotion has no desire behind it. You donât want anything from me, but you love to see me and hear my words. My mind also dwells on you. I wonder how you are and why you donât come.

âYou donât want anything of God but still you love Him. That is pure bhakti, love of God with no motive behind it. PrahlÄda had it. He sought neither kingdom nor riches; he sought Hari alone.â

M: âHazra is a chatterbox. He wonât achieve anything unless he becomes silent.â

MASTER: âNow and then he comes to me and becomes mellowed. But he is a pest; again he argues. It is very hard to get rid of egotism. You may cut down an aÅwattha tree, but the next day a sprout will spring up. As long as the roots remain, the tree will grow again.

âI said to Hazra, âDonât speak ill of anyone.â It is NÄrÄyana Himself who has assumed all these forms. One can worship even a wicked person. Havenât you observed the KumÄri PujÄ? Why should you worship a girl who has all the physical limitations of a human being? It is because she is a form of the Divine Mother. But God dwells in a special way in His devotee. The devotee is His parlour. If the gourd has a large body then it makes a good tÄnpurÄ. It gives a nice sound.â

Two monks had arrived at the temple garden in the morning. They were devoted to the study of the Bhagavad GÄ«tÄ, the VedÄnta, and other scriptures. They entered the Masterâs room, saluted him, and sat on the mat on the floor. Sri Ramakrishna was seated on the small couch. The Master spoke to the sÄdhus in HindusthÄni.

MASTER: âHave you had your meal?â

SÄDHU: âYes, sir.â

MASTER: âWhat did you eat?â

SÄDHU: âDÄl and bread. Will you take some?â

MASTER: âNo, I take only a few morsels of rice. Well, your japa and meditation must be without any desire for results. Isnât that so?â

SÄDHU: âYes, sir.â

One sÄdhu said to the other, quoting from the GÄ«tÄ: âO Arjuna, whatever action you perform, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give in charity, and whatever austerities you practise, offer everything to Me.â

(To one of the sÄdhus) âWell, sir, one should be desireless; one should renounce all desires. Isnât that so?â

SÄDHU: âYes, sir.â

They should think, âO God, You are the Master and the Lord, and I am Your servant.â People who identify themselves with the body should not have the attitude of âI am Heâ.â

The devotees in the room remained silent. Sri Ramakrishna was smiling a little, a picture of self-contentment. He appeared happy in his own Self.

One of the sÄdhus whispered in the otherâs ear: âLook! This is the state of the paramahamsa.â

Sri Ramakrishna smiled like a child. The monks left the room. The devotees were moving about in the room and on the porch.

MASTER (to M.): âDid you go to Nabin Senâs house?â

M: âYes, sir. I listened to the songs from downstairs.â
