âWhy should you be frightened? Hold fast to God. What if the world is like a forest of thorns? Put on shoes and walk on the thorns. Whom should you fear? You wonât have to play again the part of the âthiefâ in the game of hide-and-seek, once you touch the âgrannyâ.8

âKing Janaka used to fence with two swordsâthe one of Knowledge and the other of action. Nothing can frighten an expert player.

(To M.) âMy mind is still drawn to what he just recited.â

Sri Ramakrishna referred to the hymns chanted by Mahima.

Nabai Chaitanya and the other devotees began to sing. They were joined by the Master, who danced, drunk with divine love. Afterwards he said: âThis is the one thing needful, the chanting of Godâs name. All else is unreal. Love and devotion alone are real, and other things are of no consequence.â

Later Sri Ramakrishna went out in the direction of the Panchavati. He asked M. about Binode, a student in M.âs school, who now and then experienced ecstasy while thinking of God. The Master loved him dearly.

As he was returning to his room with M., he asked: âWell, some speak of me as an Incarnation of God. What do you think about it?â The Master came back to his room and sat on the small couch. He repeated the question to M. The other devotees were seated at a distance and could not follow the conversation.

MASTER: âWhat do you say?â

M: âI think so too. You are like Sri Chaitanya.â

MASTER: âIs it a full manifestation of God, or a part? Tell me how much.â

M: âI donât know, sir. But it is true that there is in you an Incarnation of the Divine Power. There is no doubt that God alone dwells in you.â

MASTER: âThat is true. Chaitanya also wanted to realize Åakti, the Divine Power.â

Narendra was engaged in a heated discussion. Ram, who had recently recovered from an illness, joined him.

MASTER (to M.): âI donât like such discussions. (To Ram) Will you stop that? You havenât been well. All right, go on softly; donât get so excited. (To M.) I donât like these discussions. I used to weep and pray to the Divine Mother saying: âO Mother, one man says it is this, while another says it is that. Do Thou tell me, O Mother, what is the truth.â â

Saturday, March 7, 1885

At three oâclock in the afternoon Sri Ramakrishna was in his room at Dakshineswar conversing happily with his devotees. Baburam, the younger Naren, Paltu, Haripada, Mohinimohan, and others were present. A young brÄhmin who had been staying with the Master a few days was also there.

The Holy Mother, Sri Ramakrishnaâs wife, was living in the nahabat. Occasionally she would come to Sri Ramakrishnaâs room to attend to his needs. Mohinimohan had brought his wife and Nabinâs mother with him to the temple garden from Calcutta. The ladies were with the Holy Mother; they were waiting for an opportunity to visit the Master when the men devotees would leave the room.

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the small couch. As he looked at the young devotees his face beamed with joy.

Rakhal was not then living at Dakshineswar with the Master. Since his return from VrindÄvan he had been living at home.

MASTER (smiling): âRakhal is now enjoying his âpensionâ. Since his return from VrindÄvan he has been staying at home. His wife is there. But he said to me that he would not accept any work even if he were offered a salary of a thousand rupees.

âRakhal would lie down here and say to me that he didnât care even for my company. He was then passing through such an exalted state.

âBhavanath is married; but he spends the whole night in spiritual conversation with his wife. The couple pass their time talking of God alone. I said to him, âHave a little fun with your wife now and then.â âWhat?â he retorted angrily. âShall we too indulge in frivolity?â â

Sri Ramakrishna began to talk about Narendra.

MASTER (to the devotees): âI havenât felt the same strong longing for the younger Naren that I felt for Narendra.

(To Haripada) âDo you go to Girish Ghoshâs house?â

HARIPADA: âYes, I go there very often. He is our neighbour.â

MASTER: âDoes Narendra, too, go there?â

HARIPADA: âYes, I see him there occasionally.â

MASTER: âWhat does he say in reply to Girish?â [Girish Ghosh spoke of Sri Ramakrishna as an Incarnation of God.]

HARIPADA: âNarendra has been defeated in the argument.â

MASTER: âNo, Narendra says, âGirish Ghosh has such strong faith; why should I contradict him?â â

The brother of Judge Anukal Mukhopadhyayaâs son-in-law was in the room. The Master asked him, âDo you know Narendra?â

BROTHER: âYes, sir. He is a very intelligent young man.â

MASTER (to the devotees): âHe must be a good man because he speaks highly of Narendra. Narendra was here the other day and sang with Trailokya Sannyal. But that day his singing seemed flat to me.â

Baburam was a student in the Entrance Class in the school where M. taught.

MASTER (to Baburam): âWhere are your books? Arenât you attending to your studies? (To M.) He wants to stick to both.9

âThat is very difficult. What will you gain by knowing God partially? VaÅishthadeva, great sage that he was, was overcome at the death of his sons. That amazed Lakshmana and he asked RÄma the reason. RÄma said: âBrother, what is there to wonder at? He who has knowledge has ignorance also. Brother, go beyond both knowledge and ignorance.â If a thorn enters the sole of your foot, you get another thorn to take out the first one. Afterwards you throw both away. Likewise, one procures the thorn of knowledge to remove the thorn of ignorance; then one goes beyond both knowledge and ignorance.â

BABURAM (smiling): âThatâs what I want.â

MASTER (smiling): âBut, my child, can you attain it by holding to both? If you want that, then come away.â

BABURAM (smiling): âTake me away from the world.â

MASTER (to M.): âRakhal lived with me, but that was different; his father agreed to it. If these boys stay here there will be trouble.

(To Baburam) âYou have no strength of mind; you havenât much courage. Just see how the younger Naren says, âI will come away for good.â â

Sri Ramakrishna came down from the small couch and sat among the youngsters on the floor. M. sat by his side.

MASTER (to M.): âI have been seeking one who has totally renounced âwoman and goldâ. When I find a young man, I think that perhaps he will live with me; but everyone raises some objection or other.

âA ghost sought a companion. It is said that a man who dies on a Saturday or Tuesday becomes a ghost. Therefore, whenever the ghost saw anybody fall from a roof or stumble and faint on the road on either of those days, he would run to him, hoping that the man, through an accidental death, would become a ghost and be his companion. But such was his ill luck that everyone revived. The poor thing could not get a companion.

âJust see, Rakhal always gives his wife as an excuse. He says, âWhat will become of her?â When I touched Narendra on the chest, he became unconscious; then he cried out: âOh, what have you done to me? Donât you know that I have a father and mother?â

âWhy has God made me lead this kind of life?10 Chaitanyadeva became a sannyÄsi so that all would salute him. Whoever salutes an Incarnation, even once, obtains liberation.â

Mohinimohan had brought a basket of sweetmeats for Sri Ramakrishna.

MASTER: âWho has brought these sweets?â

Baburam pointed to Mohinimohan.

Sri Ramakrishna touched the sweets, uttering the word âOmâ, and ate a little. Then he distributed them among the devotees. To the surprise of the others, he fed the younger Naren and a few of the boys with his own hand.

MASTER (to M.): âThis has a meaning. There is a greater manifestation of God in men of pure heart. In former years, when I used to go to KÄmÄrpukur, I would feed some of the young boys with my own hand. ChinÄ Sankhari would say, âWhy doesnât he feed us that way?â But how could I? They led an immoral life. Who would feed them?â

Sri Ramakrishna was in the happiest mood with his young and pure-souled devotees. He was seated on the small couch and was doing funny imitations of a kirtani. The devotees laughed heartily. The kirtani is dressed lavishly and covered with ornaments. She sings, standing on the floor, a coloured kerchief in her hand. Now and then she coughs to draw peopleâs attention and blows her nose, raising her nose-ring. When a respectable gentleman enters the room, she welcomes him with appropriate words, still continuing her song. Now and then she pulls her sÄri from her arms to show off her jewels.

The devotees were convulsed with laughter at this mimicry by Sri Ramakrishna. Paltu rolled on the ground. Pointing to him, the Master said to M.: âLook at that child! He is rolling with laughter.â He said to Paltu with a smile: âDonât report this to your father, or he will lose the little respect he has for me. You see, he is an âEnglishmanâ.â

MASTER (to the devotees): âThere are people who indulge in all kinds of gossip at the time of their daily devotions. As you know, one is not permitted to talk then; so they make all kinds of signs, keeping their lips closed. In order to say, âBring thisâ, âBring thatâ, they make sounds like âHuhâ, âUhuhâ. All such things they do! (Laughter.)

âAgain, there are some who bargain for fish while telling their beads. As they count the rosary, with a finger they point out the fish, indicating, âThat one, please.â They reserve all their business for that time! (Laughter.)

âThere are women who come to the Ganges for their bath and, instead of thinking of God, gossip about no end of things. âWhat jewels did you offer at the time of your sonâs marriage?âââHas so-and-so returned from her father-in-lawâs house?âââSo-and-so is seriously ill.âââSo-and-so went to see the bride; we hope that they will offer a magnificent dowry and that there will be a great feast.âââHarish always nags at me; he canât stay away from me even an hour.âââMy child, I couldnât come to see you all these days; I was so busy with the betrothal of so-and-soâs daughter.â

âYou see, they have come to bathe in the holy river, and yet they indulge in all sorts of worldly talk.â

The Master began to look intently at the younger Naren and went into samÄdhi. Did he see God Himself in the pure-souled devotee?

The devotees silently watched the figure of Sri Ramakrishna motionless in samÄdhi. A few minutes before there had been so much laughter in the room; now there was deep silence, as if no one were there. The Master sat with folded hands as in his photograph.

After a short while his mind began to come down to the relative plane. He heaved a long sigh and became aware of the outer world. He looked at the devotees and began to talk with them of their spiritual progress.

MASTER (to the younger Naren): âI have been eager to see you. You will succeed. Come here once in a while. Well, which do you preferâjnÄna or bhakti?â

THE YOUNGER NAREN: âPure bhakti.â

MASTER: âBut how can you love someone unless you know him? (Pointing to M., with a smile) How can you love him unless you know him? (To M.) Since a pure-souled person has asked for pure bhakti, it must have some meaning.

âOne does not seek bhakti of oneâs own accord without inborn tendencies. This is the characteristic of premÄ-bhakti. There is another kind of bhakti, called jnÄna-bhakti, which is love of God based on reasoning.

Sri Ramakrishna was still in the ecstatic mood. He spoke tenderly to the other devotees about their future.

(To Baburam) âWhy donât I attract you to me? It is just to avoid trouble.

(To Mohinimohan) âAs for you, you are all right. There is a little yet to be done. When that is achieved, nothing will remainâneither duty nor work nor the world itself. Is it good to get rid of everything?â

As Sri Ramakrishna spoke these words he looked at Mohini affectionately, as if scanning his inmost feelings. Was Mohini really wondering whether it would be wise to renounce all for God? After a while Sri Ramakrishna said, âGod binds the BhÄgavata pundit to the world with one tie; otherwise, who would remain to explain the sacred book? He keeps the pundit bound for the good of men. That is why the Divine Mother has kept you in the world.â

Now Sri Ramakrishna spoke to the young brÄhmin.

MASTER: âGive up knowledge and reasoning; accept bhakti. Bhakti alone is the essence. Is this the third day of your stay here?â

BRÄHMIN (with folded hands): âYes, sir.â

MASTER: âHave faith. Depend on God. Then you will not have to do anything yourself. Mother KÄli will do everything for you.

âJnÄna goes as far as the outer court, but bhakti can enter the inner court. The Pure Self is unattached. Both vidyÄ and avidyÄ are in It, but It is unattached. Sometimes there is a good and sometimes a bad smell in the air, but the air itself is unaffected.

âOnce VyÄsadeva was about to cross the JamunÄ. The gopis also were there. They wanted to go to the other side of the river to sell curd, milk, and cream. But there was no ferry at that time. They were all worried about how to cross the river, when VyÄsa said to them, âI am very hungry.â The milkmaids fed him with milk and cream. He finished almost all their food. Then VyÄsa said to the river, âO JamunÄ, if I have not eaten anything, then your waters will part and we shall walk through.â It so happened. The river parted and a pathway was formed between the waters. Following that path, the gopis and VyÄsa crossed the river. VyÄsa had said, âIf I have not eaten anythingâ. That means, the real man is Pure Ätman. Ätman is unattached and beyond Prakriti. It has neither hunger nor thirst; It knows neither birth nor death; It does not age, nor does It die. It is immutable as Mount Sumeru.

âHe who has attained this Knowledge of Brahman is a jÄ«vanmukta, liberated while living in the body. He rightly understands that the Ätman and the body are two separate things. After realizing God one does not identify the Ätman with the body. These two are separate, like the kernel and the shell of the coconut when its milk dries up. The Ätman moves, as it were, within the body. When the âmilkâ of worldly-mindedness has dried up, one gets Self-Knowledge. Then one feels that Ätman and body are two separate things. The kernel of a green almond or betel-nut cannot be separated from the shell; but when they are ripe the juice dries up and the kernel separates from the shell. After the attainment of the Knowledge of Brahman, the âmilkâ of worldly-mindedness dries up.

âBut it is extremely difficult to attain the Knowledge of Brahman. One doesnât get it by merely talking about it. Some people feign it. (Smiling) There was a man who was a great liar; but, on the other hand, he used to say he had the Knowledge of Brahman. When someone took him to task for telling lies, he said: âWhy, this world is truly like a dream. If everything is unreal, then can truth itself be real? Truth is as unreal as falsehood.â â (All laugh.)

Sri Ramakrishna sat with the devotees on the mat on the floor. He was smiling. He said to the devotees, âPlease stroke my feet gently.â They carried out his request. He said to M., âThere is great significance in this.â11 Placing his hand on his heart, the Master said, âIf there is anything here, then through this service the ignorance and illusion of the devotees will be completely destroyed.â

Suddenly Sri Ramakrishna became serious, as if about to reveal a secret.

The other day, when Harish was with me, I saw SatchidÄnanda come out of this sheath.12 It said, âI incarnate Myself in every age.â I thought that I myself was saying these words out of mere fancy. The devotees listened to these words in amazement. Some wondered whether God Himself was seated before them in the form of Sri Ramakrishna. The Master paused a moment. MASTER (to M.): âJust now I was saying to the Mother, âI cannot talk much.â I also said to Her, âMay peopleâs inner consciousness be awakened by only one touch!â You see, such is the power of YogamÄyÄ that She can cast a spell. (To M.) âWell, do you think that those who come here are realizing anything?â

(To the young devotees) âRead the BhaktichaitanyachandrikÄ by Trailokya. Ask Trailokya for a copy. He has written well about Chaitanyadeva.â

(To Paltu) âCome here now and then.â

(To Haripada) âWhy hasnât Mahendra Mukherji come here lately?â

Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the small couch talking to Mohini. Mohiniâs wife was almost mad with grief on account of her sonâs death. Sometimes she laughed and sometimes she wept. But she felt peaceful in Sri Ramakrishnaâs presence.

Sri Ramakrishna entered his room and sat on the small couch. He had been passing through an extraordinary state of mind: he could not touch any metal. Tarak was about twenty years old, and married. His parents did not allow him to come to Sri Ramakrishna. He lived mostly at his home near BowbÄzÄr. The Master was very fond of him. Tarakâs friend had a tÄmasic nature; he rather scoffed at the Master and religious ideas in general.

There is no harm in disobeying your elders for the sake of God. Vali disregarded the words of ÅukrÄchÄrya, his teacher, in order to please God. Vibhishana went against the wishes of RÄvana, his elder brother, to please RÄma. Sri Ramakrishna took Tarakâs hand into his own and seemed to feel its weight. A few moments later he said: âThere is a little crookedness in your mind; but that will go. Tarak saluted Sri Ramakrishna and took his leave. The Master lay down on the small couch. He seemed worried about Tarak. Suddenly he said to M., âWhy do I worry so much about these young boys?â M. kept still. He was thinking over a reply. The Master asked him, âWhy donât you speak?â

Mohiniâs wife entered the room and sat at one side. Sri Ramakrishna spoke to M. about Tarakâs friend.

MASTER: âWhy did Tarak bring that fellow with him?â

M: âPerhaps he wanted a companion for the road. It is a long way from Calcutta; so he brought a friend with him.â

The Master suddenly addressed Mohiniâs wife and said: âBy unnatural death one becomes an evil spirit. Beware. Make it clear to your mind. Is this what you have come to after hearing and seeing so much?â

Mohini was about to take his leave. He saluted Sri Ramakrishna. His wife also saluted the Master, who stood near the north door of the room. Mohiniâs wife spoke to him in a whisper.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# WITH THE DEVOTEES IN CALCUTTA

March 11, 1885

ON THE MORNING of Wednesday, March 11, Sri Ramakrishna and some of his disciples visited Balaram Boseâs house. Balaram was indeed blessed among the householder disciples of the Master. Sri Ramakrishna often described him as a rasaddÄr, or supplier of stores, appointed by the Divine Mother to take care of his physical needs. Balaramâs house in Calcutta had been sanctified many times by the Masterâs presence. There he frequently lost himself in samÄdhi, dancing, singing, or talking about God. Those of the Masterâs disciples and devotees who could not go to Dakshineswar visited him there and received his instruction. He often asked Balaram to invite young disciples such as Rakhal, Bhavanath, and Narendra to his house, saying: âThese pure souls are the veritable manifestations of God. To feed them is to feed God Himself. They are born with special divine attributes. By serving them you will be serving God.â And so it happened that whenever the Master was at Balaramâs house the devotees would gather there. It was the Masterâs chief vineyard in Calcutta. It was here that the devotees came to know each other intimately.

M. taught in a school in the neighbourhood. He often brought his young students to visit the Master at Balaramâs house. On this day, having learnt of Sri Ramakrishnaâs arrival, M. went there at noon during the recess hour of the school. He found the Master resting in the drawing-room after his midday meal. Several young boys were in the room. M. prostrated himself before the Master and sat by his side.

MASTER (tenderly): âHow could you come now? Have you no school work?â

M: âI have come directly from school. Just now I have no important work to do.â

A DEVOTEE: âNo, sir; he is playing truant today.â (All laugh.)

M. said to himself, âAlas! It is indeed as if some invisible power had drawn me here.â

The Master, looking a little thoughtful, asked M. to come nearer. He said, âPlease wring out my wet towel and put my coat in the sun.â Then he continued: âMy legs and feet ache. Please rub them gently.â

M. felt very happy to be given the privilege of rendering these services to the Master.

Sri Ramakrishna said to M.: âCan you tell me why I have been feeling like this the past few days? It is impossible for me to touch any metal. When I touched a metal cup I felt as if I had been stung by a horned fish. There was an excruciating pain all over my arm. But I must use a brass water-jar, and so I tried to carry it after covering it with my towel. But the moment I touched the jar I felt the same acute pain in my arm. It was an unbearable pain! At last I prayed to the Divine Mother: âO Mother, I shall never do it again. Please forgive me this time.â

âThe younger Naren often visits me. Do you think his people at home will object? He is very pure and doesnât know what carnal pleasure is.â

M: âHe is a âlarge receptacleâ.â

MASTER: âThat is true. Further, he says he remembers spiritual things after hearing them once only. He told me, âI used to weep in my boyhood because I couldnât see God.â â

The Master and M. were thus talking about the young devotee when someone reminded M. of his school.

MASTER: âWhat is the time now?â

A DEVOTEE: âIt is ten minutes to one.â

MASTER (to M.): âYou had better go now. It is getting late for you. You have left your duties. (To Latu) Where is Rakhal?â

LATU: âHe has gone home.â

MASTER: âWhat? Has he gone away without seeing me?â

After school-hours M. returned to Balaramâs house and found the Master sitting in the drawing-room, surrounded by his devotees and disciples. Among them were Girish, Suresh, Balaram, Latu, and Chunilal. The Masterâs face was beaming with a sweet smile, which was reflected in the happy faces of those in the room. M. was asked to take a seat by the Masterâs side.

MASTER (to Girish): âYou had better argue this point with Narendra and see what he has to say.â

GIRISH: âNarendra says that God is infinite; we cannot even so much as say that the things or persons we perceive are parts of God. How can Infinity have parts? It cannot.â

MASTER: âHowever great and infinite God may be, His Essence can and does manifest itself through man by His mere will. Godâs Incarnation as a man cannot be explained by analogy. One must feel it for oneself and realize it by direct perception. An analogy can give us only a little glimpse. By touching the horns, legs, or tail of a cow, we in fact touch the cow herself; but for us the essential thing about a cow is her milk, which comes through the udder. The Divine Incarnation is like the udder. God incarnates Himself as man from time to time in order to teach people devotion and divine love.â

GIRISH: âNarendra says: âIs it ever possible to know all of God? He is infinite.â â

MASTER (to Girish): âWho can comprehend everything about God? It is not given to man to know any aspect of God, great or small. And what need is there to know everything about God? It is enough if we only realize Him. And we see God Himself if we but see His Incarnation. Suppose a person goes to the Ganges and touches its water. He will then say, âYes, I have seen and touched the Ganges.â To say this it is not necessary for him to touch the whole length of the river from HÄrdwÄr to GangÄsÄgar. (Laughter.)

âIf I touch your feet, surely that is the same as touching you. (Laughter.) If a person goes to the ocean and touches but a little of its water, he has surely touched the ocean itself. Fire, as an element, exists in all things, but in wood it is present to a greater degree.â

GIRISH (smiling): âI am looking for fire. Naturally I want to go to a place where I can get it.â

MASTER (smiling): âYes, fire, as an element, is present more in wood than in any other object. If you seek God, then seek Him in man; He manifests Himself more in man than in any other thing. If you see a man endowed with ecstatic love, overflowing with prema, mad after God, intoxicated with His love, then know for certain that God has incarnated Himself through that man.

(To M.) âThere is no doubt that God exists in all things; but the manifestations of His Power are different in different beings. The greatest manifestation of His Power is through an Incarnation. Again, in some Incarnations there is a complete manifestation of Godâs Power. It is the Åakti, the Power of God, that is born as an Incarnation.â

GIRISH: âNarendra says that God is beyond our words and thought.â

MASTER: âThat is not altogether true. He is, no doubt, unknowable by this ordinary mind, but He can indeed be known by the pure mind. The mind and intellect become pure the moment they are free from attachment to âwoman and goldâ. The pure mind and pure intellect are one and the same. God is known by the pure mind. Didnât the sages and seers of olden times see God? They realized the All-pervading Consciousness by means of their inner consciousness.â

GIRISH (with a smile): âI defeated Narendra in the argument.â

MASTER: âOh, no! He said to me: âWhen Girish Ghosh has so much faith in Godâs Incarnation as man, what can I say to him? It is not proper to meddle with such faith.â â

GIRISH (with a smile): âSir, we are very free and easy with our words. But M. is sitting there with his lips shut tight. What in the world is passing through his mind? What do you say about it, sir?â

MASTER (with a laugh): âThere is a common adage that tells people to beware of the following: a man with a loose tongue, a man whose mind cannot be fathomed even by an expert diver, a man who sticks the sacred tulsi-leaf in his ears as a sign of holiness, a woman wearing a long veil to proclaim her chastity, and the cold water of a reservoir covered with green scum, by bathing in which one gets typhoid fever. These are all dangerous things. (With a smile) But it is different with M. He is a serious man.â (All laugh.)

âA man received a letter from home informing him that certain presents were to be sent to his relatives. The names of the articles were given in the letter. âIn the scriptures you will find the way to realize God. But after getting all the information about the path, you must begin to work. Only then can you attain your goal.

(To Girish) âNarendra is a boy of a very high order. He excels in everything: vocal and instrumental music and studies. Again, he has control over his sense-organs. Gradually it became dusk. The shadow of evening fell on Calcutta. For the moment the noise of the busy metropolis was stilled. Gongs and conch-shells proclaimed the evening worship in many Hindu homes. Devotees of God set aside their worldly duties and turned their minds to prayer and meditation. This joining of day and night, this mystic twilight, always created an ecstatic mood in the Master.

The devotees seated in the room looked at Sri Ramakrishna as he began to chant the sweet name of the Divine Mother. After the chanting he began to pray. What was the need of prayer to a soul in constant communion with God? Did he not rather want to teach erring mortals how to pray? Addressing the Divine Mother, he said, âO Mother, I throw myself on Thy mercy; I take shelter at Thy Hallowed Feet. I do not want bodily comforts; I do not crave name and fame; I do not seek the eight occult powers. Be gracious and grant that I may have pure love for Thee, a love unsmitten by desire, untainted by any selfish endsâa love craved by the devotee for the sake of love alone. Be gracious, Mother, and out of Thy infinite mercy grant me love for Thy Lotus Feet.â

Every word of this prayer, uttered from the depths of his soul, stirred the minds of the devotees. The melody of his voice and the childlike simplicity of his face touched their hearts very deeply.

Girish invited the Master to his house, saying that he must go there that very night.

As the Master was coming down from the second floor of Balaramâs house, he became filled with divine ecstasy. He looked as if he were drunk. As the Master and the devotees entered the lane where Girish lived, he was able to utter words. He said to Narendra: âAre you quite well, my child? NITYAGOPAL: âTarak.1 He is always with me. But sometimes he too gets on my nerves.â

Again the Master went into an ecstatic mood. Strange thoughts seemed to stir his mind and he remained speechless. After a while he said: âArt Thou come? I too am here.â Who could pretend to understand these words?

Many of his devotees were in the room: Narendra, Girish, Ram, Haripada, Chuni, Balaram, and M. Narendra did not believe that God could incarnate Himself in a human body. But Girish differed with him; he had the burning faith that from time to time the Almighty Lord, through His inscrutable Power, assumes a human body and descends to earth to serve a divine purpose.

The discussion began; but they talked in Bengali. Narendra said: âGod is Infinity. How is it possible for us to comprehend Him? He dwells in every human being. It is not the case that He manifests Himself through one person only.â

Gradually Narendra and Girish became involved in a heated discussion. If God is Infinity, how can He have parts? What did Hamilton say? What were the views of Herbert Spencer, of Tyndall, of Huxley? And so forth and so on.

MASTER (to M.): âI donât enjoy these discussions. Why should I argue at all? I clearly see that God is everything; He Himself has become all. I see that whatever is, is God. He is everything; again, He is beyond everything. I come to a state in which my mind and intellect merge in the Indivisible. MASTER: âAgain, I cannot utter a word unless I come down at least two steps from the plane of samÄdhi. Åankaraâs Non-dualistic explanation of VedÄnta is true, and so is the Qualified Non-dualistic interpretation of RÄmÄnuja.â

These threeâBrahman, the world, and living beingsâtogether constitute One. Take the instance of a bel-fruit. A man wanted to know the weight of the fruit. He separated the shell, the flesh, and the seeds. But can a man get the weight by weighing only the flesh? He must weigh flesh, shell, and seeds together. The Nitya and the LÄ«lÄ are the two aspects of one and the same Reality; therefore, according to RÄmÄnuja, Brahman is qualified by the universe and the living beings. This is the theory of Qualified Non-dualism.

(To M.) âI do see God directly. What shall I reason about? I clearly see that He Himself has become everything; that He Himself has become the universe and all living beings.

âBut without awakening oneâs own inner consciousness one cannot realize the All-pervading Consciousness. How long does a man reason? So long as he has not realized God. But mere words will not do. As for myself, I clearly see that He Himself has become everything. The inner consciousness must be awakened through the grace of God. Through this awakening a man goes into samÄdhi. He often forgets that he has a body. He gets rid of his attachment to âwoman and goldâ and does not enjoy any talk unless it is about God. The discussion came to a close. Sri Ramakrishna said to M.: âI have observed that a man acquires one kind of knowledge about God through reasoning and another kind through meditation; but he acquires a third kind of Knowledge about God when God reveals Himself to him, His devotee. Sri Ramakrishna asked Narendra to sit by his side. He tenderly inquired about his health and showed him much affection.

It was late at night. Girish asked Haripada to call a cab, for he had to go to the theatre. As Haripada was about to leave the room the Master said with a smile: âMind, a cab. Donât forget to bring one.â (All laugh.)

Narendra said in a whisper, âJust a moment ago he [meaning Girish] was calling him [meaning Sri Ramakrishna] God, an Incarnation, and now he is attracted to the theatre!â

Narendra was sitting beside the Master. The latter looked at him intently and suddenly moved closer to his beloved disciple. The Master gently stroked Narendraâs body and affectionately touched his chin, uttering sweetly the holy words, âHari Om! Hari Om! Hari Om!â He was fast becoming unconscious of the outer world. His hand was on Narendraâs foot. Still in that mood he gently stroked Narendraâs body. Slowly a change came over his mind. With folded hands he said to Narendra: âSing a song, please; then I shall be all right. How else shall I be able to stand on my own legs?â Again he became speechless. â âWoman and goldâ alone is the world. It makes one forget God.â

âJust see the bewitching power of women! I mean the women who are the embodiment of avidyÄ, the power of delusion. They fool men, as it were. They take away their inner substance. âIf a woman says to her husband, âGo thereâ, he at once stands up, ready to go. If she says, âSit down hereâ, immediately he sits down.

âA job-seeker got tired of visiting the manager in an office. He couldnât get the job. The manager said to him, âThere is no vacancy now; but come and see me now and then.â This went on for a long time, and the candidate lost all hope. One day he told his tale of woe to a friend. As evening came on, lamps were lighted in the drawing-room and on the verandah. Sri Ramakrishna bowed to the Divine Mother and began to chant the name of God. The devotees sat around and listened to his sweet chanting. They wanted to discuss with Trailokya his remarks about the Masterâs change of opinion on worldly life. Girish started the discussion.

GIRISH (to Trailokya): âYou have written that, after coming in contact with Keshab, Sri Ramakrishna changed his views about worldly life; but it isnât true.â

MASTER(to Trailokya and the other devotees): âIf a man enjoys the Bliss of God, he doesnât enjoy the world. Having tasted divine bliss, he finds the world insipid. If a man gets a shawl, he doesnât care for broadcloth.â

TRAILOKYA:âI referred to those who wanted to lead a worldly life. I didnât mean renouncers.â

MASTER:âWhat are you talking about? People talk about leading a religious life in the world. But if they once taste the bliss of God they will not enjoy anything else. Their attachment to worldly duties declines. As their spiritual joy becomes deeper, they simply cannot perform their worldly duties. More and more they seek that joy. Can worldly pleasures and sex pleasures be compared to the bliss of God? If a man once tastes that bliss, he runs after it ever afterwards. It matters very little to him then whether the world remains or disappears.

âThough the chÄtak bird is about to die of a parched throat, and around it there are seven oceans, rivers, and lakes overflowing with water, still it will not touch that water. Its throat is cracking with thirst, and still it will not drink that water. It looks up, mouth agape, for the rain to fall when the star SvÄti is in the ascendant. âTo the chÄtak bird all waters are mere dryness beside SvÄti water.â

âPeople say they will hold to both God and the world. After drinking an ounce of wine, a man may be pleasantly intoxicated and also conscious of the world; but can he be both when he has drunk a great deal more?

âAfter the bliss of God nothing else tastes good. Then talk about âwoman and goldâ stabs the heart, as it were. (Intoning) âI cannot enjoy the talk of worldly people.â When a man becomes mad for God, he doesnât enjoy money or such things.â

TRAILOKYA:âBut, sir, if a man is to remain in the world, he needs money and he must also save. He has to give in charity andââ

MASTER:âWhat? Do you mean that one must first save money and then seek God? And you talk about charity and kindness! A worldly man spends thousands of rupees for his daughterâs marriage. Yet, all the while, his neighbours are dying of starvation; and he finds it hard to give them two morsels of rice; he calculates a thousand times before giving them even that much. The people around him have nothing to eat; but what does he care about that? He says to himself: âWhat can I do? Let the rascals live or die. All I care about is that the members of my family should live well.â And they talk about doing good to others!â

TRAILOKYA:âBut, sir, there are good people in the world as well. Take the case of Pundarika VidyÄnidhi, the devotee of Chaitanya. He lived in the world.â

MASTER:âHe had drunk wine up to his neck. If he had drunk a little more, he couldnât have led a worldly life.â

Trailokya remained silent. M. said aside to Girish, âThen what he has written is not true.â

GIRISH (to Trailokya): âThen what you have written is not true.â

TRAILOKYA:âWhy so? Doesnât he [meaning Sri Ramakrishna] admit that a man can lead a spiritual life in the world?â

MASTER:âYes, he can. But such a man should first of all attain Knowledge and then live in the world. First he should realize God. Then âhe can swim in a sea of slander and not be stained.â After realizing God, a man can live in the world like a mudfish. The world he lives in after attaining God is the world of vidyÄ. In it he sees neither woman nor gold. He finds there only devotion, devotee, and God. You see, I too have a wife, and a few pots and pans in my room; I too feed a few vagabonds; I too worry about the devoteesâHabiâs mother for instanceâwhen they come here.â

A DEVOTEE(to Trailokya): âI have read in your book that you do not believe in the Incarnation of God. You said so in connection with Chaitanya.â

TRAILOKYA: âWhy, Chaitanya himself protested against the idea of Divine Incarnation. Once, in Puri, Advaita and the other devotees sang a song to the effect that Chaitanya was God. At this Chaitanya shut the door of his room. Infinite are the glories of God. As he [meaning Sri Ramakrishna] says, the devotee is the parlour of God. Suppose a parlour is very well furnished; does that mean that the master of the house has exhausted all his power and splendour in that one parlour?â

GIRISH:âHe [meaning Sri Ramakrishna] says that prema alone is the essence of God; we need the man through whom this ecstatic love of God flows. He says that the milk of the cow flows through the udder; we need the udder; we do not care for the other parts of the cowâthe legs, tail, or horns.â

TRAILOKYA:âThe milk of Godâs prema flows through an infinite number of channels. God has infinite powers.â

GIRISH:âBut what other power can stand before prema?â

GIRISH:âYes, I admit that. But there is also a thing called the power of avidyÄ.â

TRAILOKYA: âIs avidyÄ a thing? Does there exist a substance called avidyÄ? It is only a negation, as darkness is the negation of light. There is no doubt that we prize prema most: what is a drop to God is an ocean to us. But if you say that prema is the last word about God, then you limit God Himself.â

MASTER(to Trailokya and the other devotees): âYes, yes, that is true. But an ounce of wine makes me drunk. What need have I to count the gallons of wine in the tavern? What need have we to know about the infinite powers of God?â

GIRISH(to Trailokya): âDo you believe in the Incarnation of God?â

TRAILOKYA:âGod incarnates Himself through His devotees alone. There cannot be a manifestation of infinite powers. It simply isnât possible. It is impossible for any man to manifest infinite powers.â

GIRISH: âYou can serve your children as âBrahma GopÄlaâ.10 Then why isnât it possible to worship a great soul as God?â

MASTER(to Trailokya): âWhy all this bother about infinity? If I want to touch you, must I touch your entire body? If you want to bathe in the Ganges, must you touch the whole river from HÄrdwÄr down to the ocean?

â âAll troubles come to an end when the ego dies.â As long as a trace of âI-consciousnessâ remains, one is conscious of difference. Nobody knows what remains after the âIâ disappears. Nobody can express it in words. That which is remains. After the âIâ disappears one cannot say that a part manifests through this man and the rest through another. SatchidÄnanda is the ocean. The pot of âIâ is immersed in it. As long as the pot exists, the water seems to be divided into two parts: one part inside the pot and the other part outside it. But when the pot is broken there is only one stretch of water. One cannot even say that. Who would say that?â

After the discussion Sri Ramakrishna became engaged in pleasant conversation with Trailokya.

MASTER: âYou are happy. Isnât that so?â

TRAILOKYA:âBut I shall become my old self again as soon as I leave this place. Here I feel very much the awakening of spiritual consciousness.â

MASTER: âYou donât have to be afraid of walking on thorns if you are wearing shoes. You neednât be afraid of âwoman and goldâ if you know that God alone is real and all else illusory.â

It was about nine oâclock in the evening. Balaram took Trailokya to another room and gave him refreshments. Sri Ramakrishna began to tell the devotees about Trailokya and people of his views.

MASTER (to Girish, M., and the other devotees): âDo you know what these people are like? They are like a frog living in a well, who has never seen the outside world. He knows only his well; so he will not believe that there is such a thing as the world. Likewise, people talk so much about the world because they have not known the joy of God.

(To Girish) âWhy do you argue with them so much? They busy themselves with bothâthe world and God. One cannot understand the joy of God unless one has tasted it. Can anybody explain sex pleasure to a five-year-old boy? Worldly people talk about God only from hearsay. Children, hearing their old aunts quarrelling among themselves, learn to say, âThere is my Godâ, âI swear by God.â

âBut that doesnât matter. I donât blame such people. Can all comprehend the Indivisible SatchidÄnanda? Only twelve rishis could recognize RÄmachandra. All cannot recognize an Incarnation of God. Some take him for an ordinary man, some for a holy person, and only a few recognize him as an Incarnation.

âOne offers a price for an article according to oneâs capital. A rich man said to his servant: âTake this diamond to the market and let me know how different people price it. Take it, first of all, to the egg-plant seller.â The servant took the diamond to the egg-plant seller. He examined it, turning it over in the palm of his hand, and said, âBrother, I can give nine seers of egg-plants for it.â âFriend,â said the servant, âa little moreâsay, ten seers.â The egg-plant seller replied: âNo, I have already quoted above the market price. You may give it to me if that price suits you.â The servant laughed. He went back to his master and said: âSir, he would give me only nine seers of egg-plants and not one more. He said he had offered more than the market price.â The master smiled and said: âNow take it to the cloth-dealer. The other man deals only in egg-plants. What does he know about a diamond? The cloth-dealer has a little more capital. Let us see how much he offers for it.â The servant went to the cloth-dealer and said: âWill you buy this? How much will you pay for it?â The merchant said: âYes, it is a good thing. I can make a nice ornament out of it. I will give you nine hundred rupees for it.â âBrother,â said the servant, âoffer a little more and I will sell it to you. Give me at least a thousand rupees.â The cloth-dealer said: âFriend, donât press me for more. I have offered more than the market price. I cannot give a rupee more. Suit yourself.â Laughing the servant returned to his master and said: âHe wonât give a rupee more than nine hundred. He too said he had quoted above the market price.â The master said with a laugh: âNow take it to a jeweller. Let us see what he has to say.â The servant went to a jeweller. The jeweller glanced at the diamond and said at once, âI will give you one hundred thousand rupees for it.â

âThey talk of practising religion in the world. Suppose a man is shut up in a room. All the doors and windows are closed. Only a little light comes through a hole in the ceiling. Can he see the sun with that roof over his head? And what will he do with only one ray of light? âWoman and goldâ is the roof. Can he see the sun unless he removes the roof? Worldly people are shut up in a room, as it were.

âThe Incarnations of God belong to the class of the IÅvarakotis. They roam about in the open spaces. They are never imprisoned in the world, never entangled by it. Their ego is not the âthick egoâ of worldly people. The ego, the âI-consciousnessâ, of worldly people is like four walls and a roof: the man inside them cannot see anything outside. The ego of the Incarnations and other IÅvarakotis is a âthin egoâ: through it they have an uninterrupted vision of God. Take the case of a man who stands by a wall on both sides of which there are meadows stretching to infinity. If there is a hole in the wall, through it he can see everything on the other side. If the hole is a big one, he can even pass through it. The ego of the Incarnations and other IÅvarakotis is like the wall with a hole. Though they remain on this side of the wall, still they can see the endless meadow on the other side. That is to say, though they have a human body, they are always united with God. Again, if they will, they can pass through the big hole to the other side and remain in samÄdhi. And if the hole is big enough, they can go through it and come back again. That is to say, though established in samÄdhi, they can again descend to the worldly plane.â

The devotees listened breathlessly to these words about the mystery of Divine Incarnation.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

The musician arrived with his party and sat in the middle of the room. He was waiting for a sign from Sri Ramakrishna to begin the kirtan. The Master gave his permission.

MASTER (smiling): âThat was the result of his japa and austerity. You see, physical traits to a great extent influence character. Short stature and a body with dents here and there are not good traits. People with such traits take a long time to acquire spiritual knowledge.â

BHAVANATH: âLet us stop talking about these things.â

MASTER: âDonât misunderstand me. (To Narendra) You say you understand people; that is why I am telling you all this. Do you know how I look on people like Hazra? I know that just as God takes the form of holy men, so He also takes the form of cheats and rogues. (To Mahimacharan) What do you say? All are God.â

MAHIMA: âYes, sir. All are God.â

GIRISH (to the Master): âSir, what is ekÄngi prema?â

MASTER: âIt means one-sided love. For instance, the water does not seek the duck, but the duck loves water. There are other kinds of love: sÄdhÄrani, samanjasÄ, and samarthÄ. In the first, which is ordinary love, the lover seeks his own happiness; he doesnât care whether the other person is happy or not. That was ChandrÄvaliâs attitude toward Krishna. In the second, which is a compromise, both seek each otherâs happiness. This is a noble kind of love. But the third is the highest of all. Such a lover says to his beloved, âBe happy yourself, whatever may happen to me.â RÄdhÄ had this highest love. She was happy in Krishnaâs happiness. The gopis, too, had attained this exalted state.

âDo you know who the gopis were? RÄmachandra was wandering in the forest where sixty thousand rishis dwelt. They were very eager to see Him. He cast a tender glance at them. According to a certain PurÄna, they were born later on as the gopis of VrindÄvan.â

A DEVOTEE: âSir, who may be called an antaranga?â

MASTER: âLet me give an illustration. A nÄtmandir has pillars inside and outside. An antaranga is like the inside pillars. Those who always live near the guru are the antarangas.

(To Mahimacharan) âThe jnÄni wants neither a form of God nor His Incarnation. While wandering in the forest, RÄmachandra saw a number of rishis. They welcomed Him to their ÄÅrama with great love and said to Him: âO RÄma, today our life is blessed because we have seen You. But we know You as the son of DaÅaratha. BharadvÄja and other sages call You a Divine Incarnation; but that is not our view. We meditate on the Indivisible SatchidÄnanda.â RÄma was pleased with them and smiled.

âAh, what a state of mind I passed through! My mind would lose itself in the Indivisible Absolute. How many days I spent that way! I renounced bhakti and bhakta, devotion and devotee. I became inert. I could not feel the form of my own head. I was about to die. I thought of keeping Ramlalâs aunt5 near me.

âI ordered the removal of all pictures and portraits from my room. When I regained outer consciousness, when the mind climbed down to the ordinary level, I felt as if I were being suffocated like a drowning person. At last I said to myself, âIf I canât bear people, then how shall I live?â Then my mind was again directed to bhakti and bhakta. âWhat has happened to me?â I kept asking people. Bholanath6 said to me, âThis state of mind has been described in the MahÄbhÄrata.â How can a man live, on coming down from the plane of samÄdhi? Surely he requires devotion to God and the company of devotees. Otherwise, how will he keep his mind occupied?â

MAHIMACHARAN (to the Master): âSir, can a man return from the plane of samÄdhi to the plane of the ordinary world?â

MASTER (in a low voice, to Mahima): âI shall tell you privately. You are the only one fit to hear it.

âKoar Singh also asked me that question. You see, there is a vast difference between the jÄ«va and IÅvara. Through worship and austerity, a jÄ«va can at the utmost attain samÄdhi; but he cannot come down from that state. On the other hand, an Incarnation of God can come down from samÄdhi. A jÄ«va is like an officer of the king; he can go as far as the outer court of the seven-storey palace. But the kingâs son has access to all the seven floors; he can also go outside. Everybody says that no one can return from the plane of samÄdhi. In that case, how do you account for sages like Åankara and RÄmÄnuja? They retained the âego of Knowledgeâ.â

MAHIMA: âThat is true, indeed. Otherwise, how could they write books?â

MASTER: âAgain, there are the instances of sages like PrahlÄda, NÄrada, and HanumÄn. They too retained bhakti after attaining samÄdhi.â

MAHIMA: âThat is true, sir.â

MASTER: âSome people indulge in philosophical speculation and think much of themselves. Perhaps they have studied a little VedÄnta. But a man cannot be egotistic if he has true knowledge. In other words, in samÄdhi man becomes one with God and gets rid of his egotism. True knowledge is impossible without samÄdhi. In samÄdhi man becomes one with God. Then he can have no egotism.

âDo you know what it is like? Just at noon the sun is directly overhead. If you look around then, you do not see your shadow. Likewise, you will not find the âshadowâ of ego after attaining Knowledge, samÄdhi.

âBut if you see in anyone a trace of âI-consciousnessâ after the attainment of true Knowledge, then know that it is either the âego of Knowledgeâ or the âego of Devotionâ or the âservant egoâ. It is not the âego of ignoranceâ.

âAgain, jnÄna and bhakti are twin paths. Whichever you follow, it is God that you will ultimately reach. The jnÄni looks on God in one way and the bhakta looks on Him in another way. The God of the jnÄni is full of brilliance, and the God of the bhakta full of sweetness.â

Bhavanath was seated near the Master, listening to these words.

BHAVANATH (to the Master): âSir, I have a question to ask. I donât quite understand the Chandi. It is written there that the Divine Mother kills all beings. What does that mean?â

MASTER: âThis is all Her lÄ«lÄ, Her sportive pleasure. That question used to bother me too. Later I found out that all is mÄyÄ. Both creation and destruction are Godâs mÄyÄ.â

Girish conducted Sri Ramakrishna and the devotees to the roof, where the meal was served. There was a bright moon in the sky. The devotees took their seats. The Master occupied a seat in front of them. All were in a joyous mood.

Sri Ramakrishna was beside himself with joy at the sight of Narendra. The beloved disciple sat in the front row. Every now and then the Master asked how he was getting along. He had hardly finished half his meal when he came to Narendra with some water-melon sherbet and curd from his own plate. Tenderly he said to the disciple, âPlease eat this.â Then he went back to his own place.

Saturday, May 9, 1885

It was about three oâclock in the afternoon. Sri Ramakrishna sat in Balaramâs drawing-room in a happy mood. Many devotees were present. Narendra, M., Bhavanath, Purna, Paltu, the younger Naren, Girish, Ram, Binode, Dwija, and others sat around him.

Balaram was not there. He had gone to Monghyr for a change of air. His eldest daughter had invited Sri Ramakrishna and the devotees and celebrated the occasion with a feast. The Master was resting after the meal.

Again and again the Master asked M.: âAm I liberal-minded? Tell me.â

BHAVANATH (smiling): âWhy do you ask him? He will only keep quiet.â

A beggar entered the room. He wanted to sing. The devotees listened to a song or two. Narendra liked his singing and asked him to sing more.

MASTER: âStop! Stop! We donât want any more songs. Where is the money? (To Narendra) You may order the music, but who will pay?â

A DEVOTEE (smiling): âSir, the beggar may think you are an Ämir, a wealthy aristocrat, the way you are leaning against that big pillow.â (All laugh.)

MASTER (smiling): âHe may also think I am ill.â

The conversation drifted to Hazra and his egotism. For some reason he had had to go away from Dakshineswar.

NARENDRA: âHazra now admits he was egotistic.â

MASTER: âDonât believe him. He says so in order to come back to Dakshineswar. (To the devotees) Narendra always insists that Hazra is a grand person.â

NARENDRA: âEven now I say so.â

MASTER: âWhy? You have heard so much about him, and still you think so?â

NARENDRA: âHe has slight defects but many virtues.â

MASTER: âI admit that he has devotion to his ideal. He said to me, âYou donât care for me now, but later you will be seeking my company.â A goswÄmi came from SrerÄmpore. He was a descendant of Advaita GoswÄmi. He intended to spend a night or two at the temple garden. I asked him very cordially to stay. Do you know what Hazra said to me? He said, âSend him to the temple officer.â What was in his mind was that the goswÄmi might ask for milk or food, and that he might have to give him some from his own share. I said to Hazra: âNow, you rogue! Even I prostrate myself before him because he is a goswÄmi. And you, after leading a worldly life and indulging a great deal in âwoman and goldâ, have so much pride because of a little japa! Arenât you ashamed of yourself?â

âOne realizes God through sattva. Rajas and tamas take one away from Him. The scriptures describe sattva as white, rajas as red, and tamas as black. Once I asked Hazra: âTell me what you think of the people that come here. How much sattva does each one possess?â He said, âNarendra has one hundred per cent and I have one hundred and ten per cent.â âWhat about me?â I asked. And he said: âYou still have a trace of pink. You have only seventy-five per cent, I should say.â (All laugh.)

âHazra used to practise japa at Dakshineswar. While telling his beads, he would also try to do a little brokerage business. He has a debt of a few thousand rupees which he must clear up. About the brÄhmin cooks of the temple he remarked, âDo you think I talk with people of that sort?â

âThe truth is that you cannot attain God if you have even a trace of desire. Subtle is the way of dharma. If you are trying to thread a needle, you will not succeed if the thread has even a slight fibre sticking out.

âThere are people who perform japa for thirty years and still do not attain any result. Why? A gangrenous sore requires very drastic treatment. Ordinary medicine wonât cure it.

âNo matter how much sÄdhanÄ you practise, you will not realize the goal as long as you have desire. But this also is true, that one can realize the goal in a moment through the grace of God, through His kindness. Take the case of a room that has been dark a thousand years. If somebody suddenly brings a lamp into it, the room is lighted in an instant.

âSuppose a poor manâs son has fallen into the good graces of a rich person. He marries his daughter. Immediately he gets an equipage, clothes, furniture, a house, and other things.â

A DEVOTEE: âSir, how does one receive Godâs grace?â

MASTER: âGod has the nature of a child. A child is sitting with gems in the skirt of his cloth. Many a person passes by him along the road. Many of them pray to him for gems. But he hides the gems with his hands and says, turning away his face, âNo, I will not give any away.â But another man comes along. He doesnât ask for the gems, and yet the child runs after him and offers him the gems, begging him to accept them.

âOne cannot realize God without renunciation. Who will accept my words? I have been seeking a companion, a sympathetic soul who will understand my feelings. When I see a great devotee, I say to myself, âPerhaps he will accept my ideal.â But later on I find that he behaves in a different way.

âA ghost sought a companion. One becomes a ghost if one dies from an accident on a Saturday or a Tuesday. So whenever the ghost found someone who seemed to be dying from an accident on either of these days, he would run to him. He would say to himself that at last he had found his companion. But no sooner would he run to the man than he would see the man getting up. The man, perhaps, had fallen from a roof and after a few moments regained consciousness.

âOnce Mathur Babu was in an ecstatic mood. He behaved like a drunkard and could not look after his work. At this all said: âWho will look after his estate if he behaves like that? Certainly the young priest7 has cast a spell upon him.â

âDuring one of Narendraâs early visits I touched his chest and he became unconscious. Regaining consciousness, he wept and said: âOh, why did you do that to me? I have a father! I have a mother!â This âIâ and âmineâ spring from ignorance.

âA guru said to his disciple: âThe world is illusory. Come away with me.â âBut, revered sir,â said the disciple, âmy people at homeâmy father, my mother, my wifeâlove me so much. How can I give them up?â The guru said: âNo doubt you now have this feeling of âIâ and âmineâ and say that they love you; but this is all an illusion of your mind. I shall teach you a trick, and you will know whether they love you truly or not.â Saying this, the teacher gave the disciple a pill and said to him: âSwallow this at home. You will appear to be a corpse, but you will not lose consciousness. You will see everything and hear everything. Then I shall come to your house and gradually you will regain your normal state.â

âThe disciple followed the teacherâs instructions and lay on his bed like a dead person. The house was filled with loud wailing. His mother, his wife, and the others lay on the ground weeping bitterly. Just then a brÄhmin entered the house and said to them, âWhat is the matter with you?â âThis boy is deadâ, they replied. The brÄhmin felt his pulse and said: âHow is that? No, he is not dead. I have a medicine for him that will cure him completely.â The joy of the relatives was unbounded; it seemed to them that heaven itself had come down into their house. âButâ, said the brÄhmin, âI must tell you something else. Another person must take some of this medicine first, and then the boy must swallow the rest. But the other person will die. I see he has so many dear relatives here; one of them will certainly agree to take the medicine. I see his wife and mother crying bitterly. Surely they will not hesitate to take it.â

âAt once the weeping stopped and all sat quiet. The mother said: âWell, this is a big family. Suppose I die; then who will look after the family?â She fell into a reflective mood. The wife, who had been crying a minute before and bemoaning her ill luck, said: âWell, he has gone the way of mortals. I have these two or three young children. Who will look after them if I die?â

âThe disciple saw everything and heard everything. He stood up at once and said to the teacher: âLet us go, revered sir. I will follow you.â (All laugh.)

âAnother disciple said to his teacher: âRevered sir, my wife takes great care of me. It is for her sake that I cannot give up the world.â The disciple practised hathayoga. The teacher taught him, too, a trick to test his wifeâs love. One day there was a great wailing in his house. The neighbours came running and saw the hathayogi seated in a posture, his limbs paralysed and distorted. They thought he was dead. His wife fell on the ground, weeping piteously: âOh, what has befallen me? How have you provided for our future? Oh, friends, I never dreamt I should meet such a fate!â

âIn the mean time the relatives and friends had brought a cot to take the corpse out. But suddenly a difficulty arose as they started to move it. Since the body was twisted and stiff, it could not be taken out through the door. A neighbour quickly brought an axe and began to chop away the door-frame. The wife was crying bitterly, when she heard the sound of the axe. She ran to the door. âWhat are you doing, friends?â she asked, still weeping. The neighbour said, âWe canât take the body out; so we are chopping away the door-frame.â

â âPleaseâ, said the wife, âdonât do any such thing. I am a widow now; I have no one to look after me. I have to bring up these young children. If you destroy this door, I shall not be able to replace it. Friends, death is inevitable for all, and my husband cannot be called back to life. You had better cut his limbs.â The hathayogi at once stood up. The effect of the medicine had worn off. He said to his wife: âYou evil one! You want to cut off my hands and feet, do you?â So saying, he renounced home and followed his teacher. (All laugh.)

âMany women make a show of grief. Knowing beforehand that they will have to weep, they first take off their nose-rings and other ornaments, put them securely in a box, and lock it. Then they fall on the ground and weep, âO friends, what has befallen us?â â

NARENDRA: âHow can I believe, without proof, that God incarnates Himself as a man?â

GIRISH: âFaith alone is sufficient. What is the proof that these objects exist here? Faith alone is the proof.â

A DEVOTEE: âHave philosophers been able to prove that the external world exists outside us? But they say we have an irresistible belief in it.â

GIRISH (to Narendra): âYou wouldnât believe, even if God appeared before you. God Himself might say that He was God born as a man, but perhaps you would say that He was a liar and a cheat.â

The conversation turned to the immortality of the gods.

NARENDRA: âWhat is the proof of their immortality?â

GIRISH: âYou wouldnât believe it even if the gods appeared before you.â

NARENDRA: âThat the immortals existed in the past requires proof.â

M. whispered something to Paltu.

PALTU (smiling, to Narendra): âWhat need is there for the immortals to be without beginning? To be immortal one need only be without end.â

MASTER (smiling): âNarendra is the son of a lawyer, but Paltu of a deputy magistrate.â (All laugh.)

All kept silent awhile.

JOGIN (smiling): âHe [meaning the Master] doesnât accept Narendraâs words any more.â

MASTER (smiling): âOne day I remarked that the chÄtak bird doesnât drink any water except that which falls from the sky. Narendra said, âThe chÄtak drinks ordinary water as well.â Then I said to the Divine Mother, âMother, then are my words untrue?â I was greatly worried about it. Another day, later on, Narendra was here. Several birds were flying about in the room. He exclaimed, âThere! There!â âWhat is there?â I asked. He said, âThere is your chÄtak!â I found they were only bats. Since that day I donât accept what he says. (All laugh.)

âAt Jadu Mallickâs garden house Narendra said to me, âThe forms of God that you see are the fiction of your mind.â I was amazed and said to him, âBut they speak too!â Narendra answered, âYes, one may think so.â I went to the temple and wept before the Mother. âO Mother,â I said, âwhat is this? Then is this all false? How could Narendra say that?â Instantly I had a revelation. I saw ConsciousnessâIndivisible Consciousnessâand a divine being formed of that Consciousness. The divine form said to me, âIf your words are untrue, how is it that they tally with the facts?â Thereupon I said to Narendra: âYou rogue! You created unbelief in my mind. Donât come here any more.â â

The discussion continued. Narendra was arguing. He was then slightly over twenty-two years of age.

NARENDRA (to Girish, M., and the others): âHow am I to believe in the words of scripture? The MahÄnirvÄna Tantra says, in one place, that unless a man attains the Knowledge of Brahman he goes to hell; and the same book says, in another place, that there is no salvation without the worship of PÄrvati, the Divine Mother. Manu writes about himself in the ManusamhitÄ; Moses describes his own death in the Pentateuch.

âThe SÄmkhya philosophy says that God does not exist, because there is no proof of His existence. Again, the same philosophy says that one must accept the Vedas and that they are eternal.

âBut I donât say that these are not true. I simply donât understand them. Please explain them to me. People have explained the scriptures according to their fancy. Which explanation shall we accept? White light coming through a red medium appears red, through a green medium, green.â

A DEVOTEE: âThe GÄ«tÄ contains the words of God.â

MASTER: âYes, the GÄ«tÄ is the essence of all scriptures. A sannyÄsi may or may not keep with him another book, but he always carries a pocket GÄ«tÄ.â

A DEVOTEE: âThe GÄ«tÄ contains the words of Krishna.â

NARENDRA: âYes, Krishna or any fellow for that matter!â

Sri Ramakrishna was amazed at these words of Narendra.

MASTER: âThis is a fine discussion. There are two interpretations of the scriptures: the literal and the real. One should accept the real meaning aloneâwhat agrees with the words of God. There is a vast difference between the words written in a letter and the direct words of its writer. The scriptures are like the words of the letter; the words of God are direct words. I do not accept anything unless it agrees with the direct words of the Divine Mother.â

The conversation again turned to Divine Incarnation.

NARENDRA: âIt is enough to have faith in God. I donât care about what He is doing or what He hangs from. Infinite is the universe; infinite are the Incarnations.â

As Sri Ramakrishna heard the words, âInfinite is the universe; infinite are the Incarnationsâ, he said with folded hands, âAh!â

M. whispered something to Bhavanath.

BHAVANATH: âM. says: âAs long as I have not seen the elephant, how can I know whether it can pass through the eye of a needle? I do not know God; how can I understand through reason whether or not He can incarnate Himself as man?â â

MASTER: âEverything is possible for God. It is He who casts the spell. The magician swallows the knife and takes it out again; he swallows stones and bricks.â

A DEVOTEE: âThe BrÄhmos say that a man should perform his worldly duties. He must not renounce them.â

GIRISH: âYes, I saw something like that in their paper, the Sulabha SamÄchÄr. But a man cannot even finish all the works that are necessary for him in order to know God, and still he speaks of worldly duties.â

Sri Ramakrishna smiled a little, looked at M., and made a sign with his eye, as if to say, âWhat he says is right.â

M. understood that this question of performing duties was an extremely difficult one.

Purna arrived.

MASTER: âWho told you about our being here?â

PURNA: âSarada.â

MASTER (to the woman devotees): âGive him some refreshments.â

Narendra was preparing to sing. The Master and the devotees were eager to hear his music. Narendra sang:

Åiva, Thy ready thunderbolt rules over meadows, hills, and sky!

O God of Gods! O Slayer of Time! Thou the Great Void, the King of Dharma!

Åiva, Thou Blessed One, redeem me; take away my grievous sin.

He sang again:

Sweet is Thy name, O Refuge of the humble!

It falls like sweetest nectar on our ears

And comforts us, Beloved of our souls! â¦

Again:

Enamoured of the worldâs bleak wilderness.

PALTU: âWonât you sing that one?â

NARENDRA: âWhich one?â

PALTU: â âWhen I behold Thy peerless face.â â

Narendra sang:

At M.âs request Narendra sang again, M. and many of the devotees listening with folded hands:

Be drunk, O mind, be drunk with the Wine of Heavenly Bliss!

Roll on the ground and weep, chanting Hariâs sweet name! â¦

Narendra sang again:

Meditate, O my mind, on the Lord Hari,

The Stainless One, Pure Spirit through and through.

How peerless is the light that in Him shines!

How soul-bewitching is His wondrous form!

How dear is He to all His devotees! â¦

He sang another song:

Then he sang:

Upon the tray of the sky blaze bright

The lamps of sun and moon;

Like diamonds shine the glittering stars

To deck Thy wondrous formâ¦ .

He continued:

Fasten your mind, O man, on the Primal Purusha,

Who is the Cause of all causes,

The Stainless One, the Beginningless Truth.

As PrÄna He pervades the infinite universe;

The man of faith beholds Him,

Living, resplendent, the Root of allâ¦ .

At Narayanâs request Narendra sang:

Come! Come, Mother! Doll of my soul! My heartâs Delight!

In my heartâs lotus come and sit, that I may see Thy face.

Alas! sweet Mother, even from birth I have suffered much;

But I have borne it all, Thou knowest, gazing at Thee.

Open the lotus of my heart, dear Mother! Reveal Thyself there.

Then Narendra sang a song of his own choice:

In dense darkness, O Mother, Thy formless beauty sparkles;

Therefore the yogis meditate in a dark mountain caveâ¦ .

As Sri Ramakrishna heard this soul-enthralling song, he went into samÄdhi.

Narendra again sang:

Be drunk, O mind, be drunk with the Wine of Heavenly Bliss! â¦

The Master was in samÄdhi. He was sitting on a pillow, dangling his feet, facing the north and leaning against the wall. The devotees were seated around him.

In an ecstatic mood Sri Ramakrishna talked to the Divine Mother. He said: âI shall take my meal now. Art Thou come? Hast Thou found Thy lodging and left Thy baggage there and then come out?â He continued: âI donât enjoy anybodyâs company now. Why should I listen to the music, Mother? The Master was gradually regaining consciousness of the outer world. Looking at the devotees he said: âYears ago I used to be amazed to see people keeping kai fish alive in a pot of water. I would say: âHow cruel these people are! They will finally kill the fish.â But later, as changes came over my mind, I realized that bodies are like pillow-cases. It doesnât matter whether they remain or drop off.â

BHAVANATH: âThen may one injure a man without incurring sin? Kill him?â

MASTER: âYes, it is permissible if one has achieved that state of mind. But not everyone has it. It is the state of BrahmajnÄna.

âBy coming down a step or two from samÄdhi I enjoy bhakti and bhakta.

âThere exist in God both vidyÄ and avidyÄ. VidyÄmÄyÄ leads one to God, and avidyÄmÄyÄ away from Him. Knowledge, devotion, compassion, and renunciation belong to the realm of vidyÄ. With the help of these a man comes near God. One step more and he attains God, Knowledge of Brahman. In that state he clearly feels and sees that it is God who has become everything. He has nothing to give up and nothing to accept. It is impossible for him to be angry with anyone.

âOne day I was riding in a carriage. I saw two prostitutes standing on a verandah. They appeared to me to be embodiments of the Divine Mother Herself. I saluted them.

âWhen I first attained this exalted state I could not worship Mother KÄli or give Her the food offering. Haladhari and Hriday told me that on account of this the temple officer had slandered me. But I only laughed; I wasnât in the least angry. Attain BrahmajnÄna and then roam about enjoying Godâs lÄ«lÄ. A holy man came to a town and went about seeing the sights. He met another sÄdhu, an acquaintance. The latter said: âI see you are gadding about. Where is your baggage? I hope no thief has stolen it.â The first sÄdhu said: âNot at all. First I found a lodging, put my things in the room in proper order, and locked the door. Now I am enjoying the fun of the city.â â (All laugh.)

BHAVANATH: âThese are very lofty words.â

M. (to himself): âTasting Godâs lÄ«lÄ after BrahmajnÄna! Climbing down to the ordinary plane of consciousness after the attainment of samÄdhi!â

MASTER (to M. and the others): âIs it an easy thing to obtain the Knowledge of Brahman? It is not possible unless the mind is annihilated. The guru said to the disciple, âGive me your mind and I shall give you Knowledge.â In this state one enjoys only spiritual talk and the company of devotees.

(To Ram) âYou are a physician. You know that medicine works only when it mixes with the patientâs blood and becomes one with it. Likewise, in the state of BrahmajnÄna one sees God both within and without. One sees that it is God Himself who has become the body, mind, life, and soul.â

M. (to himself): âAssimilation!â

MASTER: âA man attains BrahmajnÄna as soon as his mind is annihilated. With the annihilation of the mind dies the ego, which says âIâ, âIâ. One also attains the Knowledge of Brahman by following the path of devotion. One also attains It by following the path of knowledge, that is to say, discrimination. The jnÄnis discriminate, saying, âNeti, netiâ, that is, âAll this is illusory, like a dream.â They analyse the world through the process of âNot this, not thisâ; it is mÄyÄ. When the world vanishes, only the jÄ«vas, that is to say, so many egos, remain.

âEach ego may be likened to a pot. Suppose there are ten pots filled with water, and the sun is reflected in them. How many suns do you see?â

A DEVOTEE: âTen reflections. Besides, there certainly exists the real sun.â

MASTER: âSuppose you break one pot. How many suns do you see now?â

DEVOTEE: âNine reflected suns. But there certainly exists the real sun.â

MASTER: âNo. What remains cannot be described. What is remains. How will you know there is a real sun unless there is a reflected sun? âI-consciousnessâ is destroyed in samÄdhi. A man climbing down from samÄdhi to the lower plane cannot describe what he has seen there.â

It was late in the evening. Lamps were burning in the drawing-room. Sri Ramakrishna was in a spiritual mood. The devotees sat around him.

MASTER (in the ecstatic mood): âThere is no one else here; so I am telling you this. He who from the depth of his soul seeks to know God will certainly realize Him. He must. He alone who is restless for God and seeks nothing but Him will certainly realize Him.

âThose who belong to this place8 have already come. Those who will come from now on are outsiders. Such people will come now and then. The Divine Mother will tell them: âDo this. Call on God in this way.â

âWhy doesnât manâs mind dwell on God? You see, more powerful than God is His MahÄmÄyÄ, His Power of Illusion. More powerful than the judge is his orderly. (All laugh.)

âRÄma said to NÄrada: âI am very much pleased with your prayer. Ask a boon of Me.â NÄrada replied, âO RÄma, may I have pure devotion to Your Lotus Feet, and may I not be deluded by Your world-bewitching mÄyÄ!â RÄma said, âBe it so: ask for something else.â NÄrada replied, âNo, RÄma, I do not want any other boon.â

âEveryone is under the spell of this world-bewitching mÄyÄ. When God assumes a human body, He too comes under the spell. RÄma wandered about weeping for SÄ«tÄ. âBrahman weeps entangled in the snare of the five elements.â But you must remember this: God, by His mere will, can liberate Himself from this snare.â

âCaptainâs father was a great devotee. He was a subÄdÄr in the English army. Even on the battle-field he would perform his worship at the proper time. With one hand he would worship Åiva and with the other he would wield his gun and sword.

(To M.) âNarendra now respects RÄdhikÄ very much. He says that if anyone wants to know how to love SatchidÄnanda, he can learn it from her.

âSatchidÄnanda wanted to taste divine bliss for Itself. That is why It created RÄdhikÄ. She was created from the person of SatchidÄnanda Krishna. YaÅodÄ came with Krishna in her arms to see RÄdhikÄ. Only then did she open her eyes, to behold Krishna. In a playful mood Krishna touched her eyes. (To the Assamese boy) Havenât you seen this? The pundit was about to take leave of Sri Ramakrishna.

PUNDIT: âI must go home.â

A few minutes later he saluted the Master and departed.

MASTER (to M.): âYou see how great the difference is between worldly people and the youngsters? This pundit has been worrying about money day and night. He has come to Calcutta to earn money; otherwise his people at home will have nothing to eat. So he has to knock at different doors. When will he concentrate his mind on God? âThe youngsters do not enjoy worldly peopleâs company. Rakhal used to say, âI feel nervous at the sight of the worldly-minded.â When I was first beginning to have spiritual experiences, I used to shut the doors of my room when I saw worldly people coming.

âAs a boy, at KÄmÄrpukur, I loved Ram Mallick dearly. But afterwards, when he came here, I couldnât even touch him. Ram Mallick and I were great friends during our boyhood. We were together day and night; we slept together. At that time I was sixteen or seventeen years old.
