His relatives used to come riding in palanquins. Now he has a shop at ChÄnak. I sent for him many a time; he came here the other day and spent two days. Ram said he had no children; he brought up his nephew, but the boy died. He told me this with a sigh; his eyes were filled with tears; he was grief-stricken for his nephew. The brÄhmin lady still stood near the north door. She was a widow. Her only daughter had been married to a very aristocratic man, a landlord in Calcutta with the title of RÄja. Whenever the daughter visited her she was escorted by liveried footmen. Then the motherâs heart swelled with pride. The brÄhmin lady listened to the account of Ram Mallickâs grief for his nephew. For the last few days she had been running to the Master from her home at BÄghbÄzÄr like an insane person. She was eager to know whether Sri Ramakrishna could suggest any remedy for her unquenchable grief. Sri Ramakrishna resumed the conversation.

MASTER: âA man came here the other day. He sat a few minutes and then said, âLet me go and see the âmoon-faceâ of my child.â I couldnât control myself and said: âSo you prefer your sonâs âmoon-faceâ to Godâs âmoon-faceâ! Get out, you fool!â

(To M.) âThe truth is that God alone is real and all else unreal. Men, universe, house, childrenâall these are like the magic of the magician. The magician strikes his wand and says: âCome delusion! Come confusion!â Then he says to the audience, âOpen the lid of the pot; see the birds fly into the sky.â But the magician alone is real and his magic unreal. The unreal exists for a second and then vanishes.

âÅiva was seated in KailÄÅ. His companion Nandi was near Him. Suddenly a terrific noise arose. âRevered Sir,â asked Nandi, âwhat does that mean?â Åiva said: âRÄvana is born. That is its meaning.â A few moments later another terrific noise was heard. âNow what is this noise?â Nandi asked. Åiva said with a smile, âNow RÄvana is dead.â Birth and death are like magic: you see the magic for a second and then it disappears. God alone is real and all else unreal. Water alone is real; its bubbles appear and disappear. They disappear into the very water from which they rise.

All sat in silence. The brÄhmin lady said, âMay I go home now?â The Master said to her tenderly: âDo you want to go now? It is very hot. Why now? You can go later in a carriage with the devotees.â

Because the day was so hot, a devotee gave the Master a new fan made of sandal-wood. He was very much pleased and said: âGood! Good! Om Tat Sat! KÄli!â First he fanned the pictures of the gods and goddesses, and then he fanned himself. He said to M.: âSee! Feel the breeze!â M. was highly pleased.

Captain arrived with his children.

Sri Ramakrishna said to Kishori, âPlease show the temples to the children.â He began to talk to Captain. M., Dwija, and the other devotees were sitting on the floor. Sri Ramakrishna was sitting on the small couch, facing the north. He asked Captain to sit in front of him on the same couch.

MASTER: âI was telling the devotees about youâyour devotion, worship, and Ärati.â

MASTER: âOnly the ego that is attached to âwoman and goldâ is harmful. But the ego that feels it is the servant of God does no harm to anybody. Neither does the ego of a child, which is not under the control of any guna. One moment children quarrel, and the next moment they are on friendly terms. âWith this kind of ego one is able to love SatchidÄnanda. It is impossible to get rid of the ego. Therefore it should be made to feel that it is the devotee of God, His servant. Otherwise, how can one live? How intense was the love of the gopis for Sri Krishna! (To Captain) Please tell us something about the gopis. You read the BhÄgavata so much.â

CAPTAIN: âWhen Sri Krishna lived at VrindÄvan, without any of His royal splendour, even then the gopis loved Him more than their own souls. Therefore Sri Krishna said, âHow shall I be able to pay off my debt to the gopis, who surrendered to me their allâtheir bodies, minds, and souls?â â

Captainâs words awakened intense love for Krishna in the Masterâs mind. He exclaimed, âGovinda! Govinda! Govinda!â and was about to go into an ecstatic mood. Captain was amazed and said: âHow blessed he is! How blessed he is!â

Captain and the devotees watched this love-ecstasy of Sri Ramakrishna. They sat quietly gazing at him, awaiting his return to the consciousness of the world.

A DEVOTEE: âBankim has written a life of Krishna.â

âA man said to his friend, âYesterday, as I was passing through a certain part of the city, I saw a house fall with a crash.â âWaitâ, said the friend. âLet me look it up in the newspaper.â But this incident wasnât mentioned in the paper. Sri Ramakrishna was talking thus to Captain and the devotees when Jaygopal Sen and Trailokya of the BrÄhmo SamÄj arrived. They saluted the Master and sat down. Sri Ramakrishna looked at Trailokya with a smile and continued the conversation.

MASTER: âIt is on account of the ego that one is not able to see God. In front of the door of Godâs mansion lies the stump of ego. One cannot enter the mansion without jumping over the stump.

âThere was once a man who had acquired the power to tame ghosts. One day, at his summons, a ghost appeared. The ghost said: âNow tell me what you want me to do. The moment you cannot give me any work I shall break your neck.â The man had many things to accomplish, and he had the ghost do them all, one by one. At last he could find nothing more for the ghost to do. âNowâ, said the ghost, âI am going to break your neck.â âWait a minuteâ, said the man. âI shall return presently.â He ran to his teacher and said: âRevered sir, I am in great danger. âLikewise, the ego seems to vanish this moment, but it reappears the next. Unless one renounces the ego, one does not receive the grace of God.

âSuppose there is a feast in a house and the master of the house puts a man in charge of the stores. âOnce Lakshmi and NÄrÄyana were seated in Vaikuntha, when NÄrÄyana suddenly stood up. Lakshmi had been stroking His feet. She said, âLord, where are You going?â NÄrÄyana answered: âOne of My devotees is in great danger. I must save him.â With these words He went out. But He came back immediately. Lakshmi said, âLord, why have You returned so soon?â NÄrÄyana smiled and said: âThe devotee was going along the road overwhelmed with love for Me. Some washermen were drying clothes on the grass, and the devotee walked over the clothes. At this the washermen chased him and were going to beat him with their sticks. So I ran out to protect him.â âBut why have You come back?â asked Lakshmi. NÄrÄyana laughed and said: âI saw the devotee himself picking up a brick to throw at them. (All laugh.) So I came back.â

âI said to Keshab, âYou must renounce your ego.â Keshab replied, âIf I do, how can I keep my organization together?â

âI said to him: âHow slow you are to understand! I am not asking you to renounce the âripe egoâ, the ego that makes a man feel he is a servant of God or His devotee. It doesnât harm one.â â

TRAILOKYA: âIt is very difficult to get rid of the ego. People only think they are free from it.â

MASTER: âGauri would not refer to himself as âIâ lest he should feel egotistic. He would say âthisâ instead. I followed his example and would refer to myself as âthisâ instead of âIâ. Instead of saying, âI have eaten,â I would say, âThis has eaten.â Mathur noticed it and said one day: âWhat is this, revered father? Why should you talk that way? Let them talk that way. âI said to Keshab, âSince the ego cannot be given up, let it remain as the servant, the servant of God.â PrahlÄda had two moods. Sometimes he would feel that he was God. In that mood he would say, âThou art verily I, and I am verily Thou.â But when he was conscious of his ego, he felt that God was the Master and he was His servant. After a man is firmly established in the ideal of âI am Heâ, he can live as Godâs servant. He may then think of himself as the servant of God.

(To Captain) âWhen a man attains the Knowledge of Brahman he shows certain characteristics. The BhÄgavata describes four of them: the state of a child, of an inert thing, of a madman, and of a ghoul. Sometimes the knower of Brahman acts like a five-year-old child. Sometimes he acts like a madman. Sometimes he remains like an inert thing. In this state he cannot work; he renounces all action. You may say that jnÄnis like Janaka were active. Sri Ramakrishna began to speak about the renunciation of action. But he also said that those who felt they must do their duties should do them in a detached spirit.

One needs intense tapasyÄ.

âIt is God who does everything. We are His instruments. Some Åikhs said to me in front of the KÄli temple, âGod is compassionate.â I said, âTo whom is He compassionate?â âWhy, revered sir, to all of usâ, said the Åikhs. I said: âWe are His children. Does compassion to oneâs own children mean much? A father must look after his children; or do you expect the people of the neighbourhood to bring them up?â Well, wonât those who say that God is compassionate ever understand that we are Godâs children and not someone elseâs?â

CAPTAIN: âYou are right. They donât regard God as their own.â

MASTER: âShould we not, then, address God as compassionate? Of course we should, as long as we practise sÄdhanÄ. After realizing God, one rightly feels that God is our Father or Mother. As long as we have not realized God, we feel that we are far away from Him, children of someone else.

âDuring the stage of sÄdhanÄ one should describe God by all His attributes. One day Hazra said to Narendra: âGod is Infinity. Infinite is His splendour. Do you think He will accept your offerings of sweets and bananas or listen to your music? This is a mistaken notion of yours.â Narendra at once sank ten fathoms. So I said to Hazra, âYou villain! Where will these youngsters be if you talk to them like that?â How can a man live if he gives up devotion? No doubt God has infinite splendour; yet He is under the control of His devotees. A rich manâs gate-keeper comes to the parlour where his master is seated with his friends. He stands on one side of the room. In his hand he has something covered with a cloth. He is very hesitant. The master asks him, âWell, gate-keeper, what have you in your hand?â Very hesitantly the servant takes out a custard-apple from under the cover, places it in front of his master, and says, âSir, it is my desire that you should eat this.â The Master is impressed by his servantâs devotion. âGod is under the control of His devotees. King Duryodhana was very attentive to Krishna and said to Him, âPlease have your meal here.â But the Lord went to Viduraâs hut. He is very fond of His devotees. He ate Viduraâs simple rice and greens as if they were celestial food.

âSometimes a perfect jnÄni behaves like a ghoul. He does not discriminate about food and drink, holiness and unholiness. A perfect knower of God and a perfect idiot have the same outer signs. He doesnât utter the mantras, nor does he observe the rituals.

âA man cannot renounce action as long as he desires worldly enjoyment. As long as one cherishes a desire for enjoyment, one performs action.

âA bird sat absent-mindedly on the mast of a ship anchored in the Ganges. Slowly the ship sailed out into the ocean. When the bird came to its senses, it could find no shore in any direction. It flew toward the north hoping to reach land; it went very far and grew very tired but could find no shore. What could it do? It returned to the ship and sat on the mast. After a long while the bird flew away again, this time toward the east. It couldnât find land in that direction either; everywhere it saw nothing but limitless ocean. Very tired, it again returned to the ship and sat on the mast. After resting a long while, the bird went toward the south, and then toward the west. When it found no sign of land in any direction, it came back and settled down on the mast. It did not leave the mast again, but sat there without making any further effort. It no longer felt restless or worried. Because it was free from worry, it made no further effort.â

CAPTAIN: âAh, what an illustration!â

MASTER: âWorldly people wander about to the four quarters of the earth for the sake of happiness. They donât find it anywhere; they only become tired and weary. When through their attachment to âwoman and goldâ they only suffer misery, they feel an urge toward dispassion and renunciation. Most people cannot renounce âwoman and goldâ without first enjoying it. There are two sorts of people: those who stay in one place and those who go about to many places. There are some sÄdhakas who visit many sacred places. They cannot settle down in one spot; they must drink the water of many holy places. Thus roaming about, they satisfy their unfulfilled desires. âBut what is there to enjoy in the world? âWoman and goldâ? That is only a momentary pleasure. One moment it exists and the next moment it disappears.

âThe world is like an overcast sky that steadily pours down rain: the face of the sun is seldom seen. There is mostly suffering in the world. On account of the cloud of âwoman and goldâ one cannot see the sun. Some people ask me: âSir, why has God created such a world? Is there no way out for us?â I say to them: âWhy shouldnât there be a way out? Take shelter with God and pray to Him with a yearning heart for a favourable wind, that you may have things in your favour. If you call on Him with yearning, He will surely listen to you.â

âA man had a son who was on the point of death. In a frenzy he asked remedies of different people. One of them said: âHere is a remedy: First it must rain when the star SvÄti is in the ascendant; then some of the rain must fall into a skull; then a frog must come there to drink the water, and a snake must chase it; and when the snake is about to bite the frog, the frog must hop away and the poison must fall into the skull. You should give the patient a little of the poison and rain-water from the skull.â The father set out eagerly to find the medicine when the star SvÄti was in the sky. It started raining. Fervently he said to God, âO Lord, please get a skull for me.â Searching here and there, he at last found a skull with rain-water in it. Again he prayed to God, saying, âO Lord, I beseech Thee, please help me find the frog and the snake.â Since he had great longing, he got the frog and the snake also. In the twinkling of an eye he saw a snake chasing a frog, and as it was about to bite the frog, its poison fell into the skull.

âIf one takes shelter with God and prays to Him with great longing, God will surely listen; He will certainly make everything favourable.â

CAPTAIN: âWhat an apt illustration!â

MASTER: âYes, God makes everything favourable. Perhaps the aspirant doesnât marry. Thus he is able to devote his whole attention to God. Or perhaps his brothers earn the familyâs livelihood. Or perhaps a son takes on the responsibilities of the family. Then the aspirant will not have to bother about the world; he can give one hundred per cent of his mind to God.

âBut one cannot succeed unless one renounces âwoman and goldâ. Only by renunciation is ignorance destroyed. The sunâs rays, falling on a lens, burn many objects. But if a room is dark inside, you cannot get that result. You must come out of the room to use the lens.

âBut some people live in the world even after attaining jnÄna. They see both what is inside and what is outside the room. The light of God illumines the world. Therefore with that light they can discriminate between good and bad, permanent and impermanent. The ignorant, who lead a worldly life without knowing God, are like people living in a house with mud walls. With the help of a dim light they can see the inside of the house but nothing more. But those who live in the world after having attained Knowledge and realized God, are like people living in a glass house. They see the inside of the room and also all that is outside. The light from the sun of Knowledge enters strongly into the room. They perceive everything inside the room very clearly. They know what is good and what is bad, what is permanent and what is impermanent.

âGod alone is the Doer, and we are all His instruments. Therefore it is impossible even for a jnÄni to be egotistic. The writer of a hymn to Åiva felt proud of his achievement; but his pride was dashed to pieces when Åivaâs bull bared his teeth. He saw that each tooth was a word of the hymn. Do you understand the meaning of this? These words had existed from the beginningless past. The writer had only discovered them.

âIt is not good to be a guru by profession. One cannot be a teacher without a command from God. He who says he is a guru6 is a man of mean intelligence. Havenât you seen a balance? The lighter side goes higher. He who is spiritually higher than others does not consider himself a guru.7 Everyone wants to be a teacher, but a disciple is hard to find.â

Trailokya was seated on the floor, to the north of the small couch. He was going to sing. Sri Ramakrishna said to him, âAh, how sweetly you sing!â

Trailokya sang to the accompaniment of a tÄnpurÄ:

I have joined my heart to Thee: all that exists art Thou;

Thee only have I found, for Thou art all that exists.

O Lord, Beloved of my heart! Thou art the Home of all;

Where indeed is the heart in which Thou dost not dwell?

Thou hast entered every heart: all that exists art Thou.

Whether sage or fool, whether Hindu or MussalmÄn,

Thou makest them as Thou wilt: all that exists art Thou.

Thy presence is everywhere, whether in heaven or in KaabÄ;

Before Thee all must bow, for Thou art all that exists.

From earth below to the highest heaven, from heaven to deepest earth,

I see Thee wherever I look: all that exists art Thou.

Pondering, I have understood; I have seen it beyond a doubt;

I find not a single thing that may be compared to Thee.

To JÄfar8 it has been revealed that Thou art all that exists.

He sang again:

Thou art my All in All, O Lord!âthe Life of my life, the Essence of essence;

In the three worlds I have none else but Thee to call my own.

Thou art my peace, my joy, my hope; Thou my support, my wealth, my glory;

Thou art my wisdom and my strength.

Thou art my home, my place of rest; my dearest friend, my next of kin;

My present and my future, Thou; my heaven and my salvation.

Thou art my scriptures, my commandments; Thou art my ever gracious Guru;

Thou the Spring of my boundless bliss.

Thou art the Way, and Thou the Goal; Thou the Adorable One, O Lord!

Thou art the Mother tender-hearted; Thou the chastising Father;

Thou the Creator and Protector; Thou the Helmsman who dost steer

My craft across the sea of life.

While Sri Ramakrishna listened to the songs he was overwhelmed with emotion. Again and again he said: âAh, Thou art all! Ah me! Ah me!â

The music was over. It was six oâclock in the evening. Sri Ramakrishna went to the pine-grove, M. accompanying him. Sri Ramakrishna was laughing and talking. Suddenly he said to M.: âWhy havenât you eaten any refreshments? Why havenât the others eaten either?â He was eager for the devotees to take some refreshments.

Sri Ramakrishna was to go to Calcutta in the evening. While returning from the pine-grove he said to M., âI donât know who will take me to Calcutta in his carriage.â

It was evening. A lamp was lighted in Sri Ramakrishnaâs room and incense was burnt. Lamps also were lighted in the different temples and buildings. The orchestra was playing in the nahabat. Soon the evening service would begin in the temples.

Sri Ramakrishna sat on the small couch. After chanting the names of the different deities, he meditated on the Divine Mother. The evening service was over. Sri Ramakrishna paced the room, now and then talking to the devotees. He also consulted M. about his going to Calcutta.

Presently Narendra arrived. He was accompanied by Sarat and one or two other young devotees. They all saluted the Master.

At the sight of Narendra Sri Ramakrishnaâs love overflowed. He tenderly touched Narendraâs chin as one touches a babyâs to show oneâs love. He said in a loving voice, âAh, you have come!â

The Master was standing in his room, facing the Ganges. Narendra and his young friends were talking to him, facing the east. The Master turned toward M. and said: âNarendra has come. How can I go to Calcutta now? I sent for Narendra. How can I go now? What do you think?â

M: âAs you wish, sir. Let us put it off today.â

MASTER: âAll right. We shall go tomorrow, either by boat or by carriage. (To the other devotees) It is late. Go home now.â

One by one the devotees saluted him and departed.

1 Kedar spoke of Sri Ramakrishna as an Incarnation of God.

2 NirvÄna, or total annihilation of the ego, is the ideal of the jnÄnis, the non-dualists.

3 The Master was speaking of Totapuri, whom he always referred to as âNangtÄâ, the ânaked oneâ.

4 Sri Ramakrishna.

5 The founder of the school.

6 The word means both âspiritual teacherâ and âheavinessâ.

7 The meaning is that if a man thinks of himself as âguruâ he is âheavyâ and goes down, like the heavier pan of a balance.

8 The author of the song.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# CAR FESTIVAL AT BALARAMâS HOUSE

Monday, July 13, 1885

SRI RAMAKRISHNA was sitting in Balaramâs drawing-room with the devotees. It was nine oâclock in the morning. Balaram was going to celebrate the Car Festival the following day. The Deity JagannÄth1 was worshipped daily at his house. He had a small car which would be drawn along the verandah to celebrate the festival. The Master had been specially invited for the occasion.

Sri Ramakrishna and M. were talking together. Narayan, Tejchandra, Balaram, and other devotees were in the room. The Master was talking about Purna, a lad of fifteen. He was very eager to see the boy.

MASTER (to M.): âWell, by which road will he come to see me? Please have Purna and Dwija meet each other.

âWhen two people are of the same age and have the same inner nature, I bring them together. There is a meaning in this. In this way both make progress. Have you noticed Purnaâs longing for God?â

M: âYes, sir. One day I was riding on a tram. He saw me from the roof of his house and ran down to the street. With great fervour he saluted me from the street.â

MASTER (with tears in his eyes): âAh! Ah! It is because you have helped him make the contact through which he will find out the supreme ideal of his life. One doesnât act like that unless one longs for God.

âNarendra, the younger Naren, and Purnaâthese three have a manly nature. It is not so with Bhavanath. He has a womanly nature.

âPurna is in such an exalted state that either he will very soon give up his bodyâthe body is useless after the realization of Godâor his inner nature will within a few days burst forth.

âHe has a divine natureâthe traits of a god. It makes a person less fearful of men. If you put a garland of flowers round his neck or smear his body with sandal-paste or burn incense before him, he will go into samÄdhi; for then he will know beyond the shadow of a doubt that NÄrÄyana Himself dwells in his body, that it is NÄrÄyana who has assumed the body. I have come to know about it.

âA few days after my first experience of the God-intoxicated state at Dakshineswar, a lady of a brÄhmin family arrived there. She had many good traits. No sooner was a garland put round her neck and incense burnt before her than she went into samÄdhi. A few moments later she experienced great bliss; tears streamed from her eyes. I saluted her and said, âMother, shall I succeed?â âYesâ, she replied.

âI want to see Purna once more. But how will it be possible for me? It seems he is a part.2 How amazing! Not a mere particle, but a part. Very intelligent, too. I understand that he is very clever in his studies. Therefore I have hit it right.

âBy dint of austerity, a man may obtain God as his son. By the roadside on the way to KÄmÄrpukur is Ranjit Rayaâs lake. Bhagavati, the Divine Mother, was born as his daughter. Even now people hold an annual festival there in the month of Chaitra, in honour of this divine daughter. I feel very much like going there.

âRanjit Raya was the landlord of that part of the country. Through the power of his tapasyÄ he obtained the Divine Mother as his daughter. He was very fond of her, and she too was much attached to him; she hardly left his presence. One day Ranjit Raya was engaged in the duties of his estate. He was very busy. The girl, with her childlike nature, was constantly interrupting him, saying: âFather, what is this? What is that?â Ranjit Raya tried, with sweet words, to persuade her not to disturb him, and said: âMy child, please leave me alone. I have much work to do.â But the girl would not go away. At last, absent-mindedly, the father said, âGet out of here!â On this pretext she left home. A pedlar of conch-shell articles was going along the road. From him she took a pair of bracelets for her wrists. When he asked for the price, she said that he could get the money from a certain box in her home. Then she disappeared. Nobody saw her again. In the mean time the pedlar came to the house and asked for the price of his bracelets. When she was not to be found at home, her relatives began to run about looking for her. Ranjit Raya sent people in all directions to search for her. The money owed to the pedlar was found in the box, as she had indicated. Ranjit Raya was weeping bitterly, when people came running to him and said that they had noticed something in the lake. They all ran there and saw an arm, with conch-shell bracelets on the wrist, being waved above the water. A moment afterwards it disappeared. Even now people worship her as the Divine Mother at the time of the annual festival. (To M.) All this is true.â

M: âYes, sir.â

MASTER:âNarendra now believes these things.

âPurna was born with an element of Vishnu. I worshipped him mentally with bel-leaves; but the offering was not accepted. Then I worshipped him with tulsi-leaves and sandal-paste.3 That proved to be all right. God reveals Himself in many ways: sometimes as man, sometimes in other divine forms made of Spirit. One must believe in divine forms. What do you say?â

M: âIt is true, sir.â

MASTER:âThe brÄhmani of KÄmÄrhÄti4 sees many visions. She lives all by herself in a lonely room in a garden on the bank of the Ganges. She spends her time in japa. GopÄla5 sleeps with her. (The Master gives a start.) It is not imagination, but fact. She saw that GopÄlaâs palms were red. He walks with her. She suckles Him at her breast. They talk to each other. When Narendra heard the story he wept. Formerly I too used to see many visions, but now in my ecstatic state I donât see so many. I am gradually getting over my feminine nature; I feel nowadays more like a man. Therefore I control my emotion; I donât manifest it outwardly so much.

âThe younger Naren has the nature of a man. Therefore in meditation his mind completely merges in the Ideal. He does not show emotion. Nityagopal has a feminine nature. Therefore while he is in a spiritual mood his body becomes distorted and twisted; it becomes flushed.

(To M.) âWell, people renounce grain by grain, but what a mood these youngsters are in!

âBinode said: âI have to sleep with my wife. That makes me feel very bad.â It is bad for an aspirant to sleep with his wife, whether he has intercourse with her or not. There is the friction of the body and also the physical warmth.

âWhat a state Dwija is passing through! In my presence he only sways his body and fixes his glance on me. Is that a trifling thing? If a man gathers his whole mind and fixes it on me, then, indeed, he achieves everything.

âBut what am I? It is all He. I am the machine and He is its Operator. It is God alone who exists in this [meaning his body]. That is why so many people are feeling more and more attracted to it. A mere touch is enough to awaken their spirituality. This attraction, this pull, is the attraction of God and of none else.

âTarak of BelghariÄ was going home from Dakshineswar. I clearly noticed that a flame-like thing came out of this [meaning his body] and followed him. A few days later Tarak came back to Dakshineswar. In a state of samÄdhi He who dwells in this body placed His foot on Tarakâs chest.

âWell, are there more youngsters like these?â

M: âMohit is very nice. He came to you once or twice. He is studying enough books to pass two university examinations. He has great longing for God.â

MASTER:âThat may be. But he doesnât belong to a high plane. His physical traits are not so good; he has a puggish face. But these other youngsters belong to a high plane.

âMany troubles and worries follow in the wake of a birth in a physical body. Further, if a person is cursed, he may have to be born seven times. One must be very careful. One has to assume a human body if one cherishes the slightest desire.â

A DEVOTEE: âWhat are the desires of those who are Incarnations of God?â

MASTER (smiling): âI find that I have not got rid of all my desires. Once I saw a holy man with a shawl, and I too wanted to put on one like it. Even now I have that desire. I donât know whether I shall have to be born again for it.â

BALARAM (smiling): âThen will you be born again just for a shawl?â (All laugh.)

MASTER (smiling): âOne has to keep a good desire so that one may give up the body meditating on it. There are four holy places for the sÄdhus to visit. They visit three and leave out one. Many of them leave out Puri, the place of JagannÄth, so that they can give up their bodies meditating on JagannÄth.â

A man dressed in an ochre robe entered the room and greeted the Master. Privately he was in the habit of criticizing Sri Ramakrishna; so at the sight of him Balaram laughed. Sri Ramakrishna could read a manâs mind. He said to Balaram: âNever mind. Let him say I am a cheat.â

Sri Ramakrishna was talking to Tejchandra.

MASTER: âI send for you so often. Why donât you come? If you practise meditation and prayer it will make me happy. I look on you as my own; that is why I send for you.â

TEJCHANDRA: âSir, I have to go to the office. I am very busy with my duties.â

M. (smiling): âThere was a marriage ceremony at his home and he got leave from his office for ten days.â

MASTER: âWell, well! You say you have no leisure. You told me just now that you were going to renounce the world.â

NARAYAN: âM. said to us one day that this world is a wilderness.â

MASTER (to M.): âPlease tell them that story of the disciple who became unconscious after taking the medicine. His teacher arrived at the house and said he would revive if someone else swallowed a pill that he would prescribe. The disciple would get back his life, but the man who swallowed the pill would die.

âPlease tell the other one, too, of the hathayogi who thought that his wife and children were his very own, and who feigned death with his limbs stretched out. It will do them good to hear those stories.â

It was noon. Sri Ramakrishna partook of the food that had been offered to the Family Deity, JagannÄth. The Master often used to say that the food at Balaramâs house was very pure. Afterwards he rested awhile.

Late in the afternoon Sri Ramakrishna sat with the devotees in the drawing-room of Balaramâs house. Chandra Babu, of the KartÄbhajÄ sect, and a witty brÄhmin were there. The brÄhmin was something of a buffoon; his words made everybody laugh.

About six oâclock Girishâs brother Atul and Tejchandraâs brother arrived. Sri Ramakrishna was in samÄdhi. A few minutes later he said, still in the ecstatic mood: âCan one become unconscious by meditating on Consciousness? Can one lose oneâs mind by thinking of God? God is of the very nature of Knowledge; He is of the very nature of Eternity, Purity, and Consciousness.â

Sri Ramakrishna said to the witty brÄhmin: âWhy do you waste your time with these frivolous jokes about insignificant worldly things? Direct your mind to God. If a man can calculate about salt, he can also calculate about sugar candy.â

BRÄHMIN (smiling): âPlease attract me.â

MASTER: âWhat can I do? Everything depends on your effort. Your mind is your own. Give up this trifling buffoonery and go forward toward God. You can go farther and farther along that way. The brahmachÄri asked the wood-cutter to go forward. At first the wood-cutter found a sandal-wood forest; next, a silver-mine; next, a gold-mine; and then gems and diamonds.â

BRÄHMIN: âThere is no end to this path.â

MASTER: âWhere you find peace, there is the end,â

About a new visitor Sri Ramakrishna said: âI didnât find any substance in him. He seemed worthless.â

It was dusk. Lamps were lighted in the room. Sri Ramakrishna was meditating on the Divine Mother and chanting Her name in his melodious voice. The devotees sat around him. Since Balaram was going to celebrate the Car Festival at his house the following day, Sri Ramakrishna intended to spend the night there.

After taking some refreshments in the inner apartments, Sri Ramakrishna returned to the parlour. It was about ten oâclock. The Master said to M., âPlease bring my towel from the other room.â

A bed was made for Sri Ramakrishna in the adjoining small room. About half past ten Sri Ramakrishna lay down to sleep. It was summertime. He said to M., âYou had better bring a fan.â He asked the disciple to fan him. At midnight Sri Ramakrishna woke up. He said to M., âDonât fan me any more; I feel chilly.â

Tuesday, July 14, 1885

It was the day of the Car Festival. Sri Ramakrishna left his bed very early in the morning. He was alone in the room, dancing and chanting the name of God. M. entered and saluted the Master. Other devotees arrived one by one. They saluted the Master and took seats near him. Sri Ramakrishna was longing intensely for Purna. He was talking to M. about him.

MASTER: âDid you give Purna any instruction?â

M: âI asked him to read the life of Chaitanya. He is familiar with the incidents of his life. I told him further that you ask people to stick to the truth.â

MASTER: âHow did he take it when you said about me, âHe is an Incarnation of Godâ?â

M: âI said to him, âCome with me if you want to see a person like Chaitanya.â â

MASTER: âAnything else?â

M: âAlso that remark of yours that when an elephant enters a small pool there is a great splashing of water all around; likewise, in the case of a âsmall receptacleâ, emotion overflows.

âAbout his giving up of fish, I said to him: âWhy have you done that? Your family will make a great fuss about it.â â

MASTER: âThatâs good. One should keep oneâs feelings and emotions to oneself.â

It was about half past six in the morning. M. was going to bathe in the Ganges, when suddenly tremors of an earthquake were felt. At once he returned to Sri Ramakrishnaâs room. The Master stood in the drawing-room. The devotees stood around him. They were talking about the earthquake. The shaking had been rather violent, and many of the devotees were frightened.

M: âYou should all have gone downstairs.â

MASTER: âSuch is the fate of the house under whose roof one lives; and still people are so egotistic. (To M.) Do you remember the great storm of the month of ÄÅwin?â

M: âYes, sir. I was very young at that timeânine or ten years old. I was alone in a room while the storm was raging, and I prayed to God.â

M. was surprised and said to himself: âWhy did the Master suddenly ask me about the great storm of ÄÅwin? Does he know that I was alone at that time earnestly praying to God with tears in my eyes? Does he know all this? Has he been protecting me as my guru since my very birth?â

MASTER: âIt was quite late in the day at Dakshineswar when the storm broke, but somehow they managed to cook the meals. The trees were uprooted. You see, this is the fate of the house one lives in.

âBut when one attains Perfect Knowledge, then one finds that dying and killing are one and the same thing; that is to say, both are unreal. When one is dead, one has not really died; and when one has killed another, the man is not really dead. Both the LÄ«lÄ and the Nitya belong to the same Reality. In one form It is the Absolute, and in another, the LÄ«lÄ. Even though the LÄ«lÄ is destroyed, the Nitya always exists. Water is water, whether it is still or in waves; it is the same water when the waves quiet down.â

Sri Ramakrishna sat in the drawing-room with the devotees. Mahendra Mukherji, Hari, the younger Naren, and many other devotees were there. Hari lived alone and studied VedÄnta. He was about twenty-three years old, and unmarried. Sri Ramakrishna was very fond of him. He wanted Hari to visit him frequently. But since Hari loved solitude he did not often come to the Master.

MASTER (to Hari): âWell, I havenât seen you for a long time.

âYou see, in one form He is the Absolute and in another He is the Relative. What does VedÄnta teach? Brahman alone is real and the world illusory. Isnât that so? But as long as God keeps the âego of a devoteeâ in a man, the Relative is also real. When He completely effaces the ego, then what is remains. That cannot be described by the tongue. But as long as God keeps the ego, one must accept all. By removing the outer sheaths of the plantain-tree, you reach the inner pith. As long as the tree contains sheaths, it also contains pith. So too, as long as it contains pith, it also contains sheaths. The pith goes with the sheaths and the sheaths go with the pith. In the same way, when you speak of the Nitya, it is understood that the LÄ«lÄ also exists; and when you speak of the LÄ«lÄ, it is understood that the Nitya also exists.

âIt is He alone who has become the universe, living beings, and the twenty-four cosmic principles. When He is actionless, I call Him Brahman; when He creates, preserves, and destroys, I call Him Åakti. Brahman and Åakti are not different from each other. Water is water, whether it is still or moving.

âIt is not possible to rid oneself of âI-consciousnessâ. And as long as one is aware of this âI-consciousnessâ, one cannot speak of the universe and its living beings as unreal. You cannot get the correct weight of the bel-fruit if you leave out its shell and pits.

âThe brick, lime, and brick-dust of which the stairs are made are the same brick, lime, and brick-dust of which the roof is made. The universe and its living beings exist on account of the Reality of Him who is known as Brahman.

âThe devoteesâI mean the vijnÄnisâaccept both God with form and the Formless, both the Personal God and the Impersonal. In a shoreless oceanâan infinite expanse of waterâvisible blocks of ice are formed here and there by intense cold. Similarly, under the cooling influence, so to say, of the deep love of Its worshipper, the Infinite reduces Itself to the finite and appears before the worshipper as God with form. Again, as, on the rising of the sun, the ice melts away, so, on the awakening of Knowledge, God with form melts away into the same Infinite and Formless.

âAs long as a man analyses with the mind, he cannot reach the Absolute. As long as you reason with your mind, you have no way of getting rid of the universe and the objects of the sensesâform, taste, smell, touch, and sound. When reasoning stops, you attain the Knowledge of Brahman. Ätman cannot be realized through this mind; Ätman is realized through Ätman alone. Pure Mind, Pure Buddhi, Pure Ätmanâall these are one and the same.

âJust think how many things you need to perceive an object. You need eyes; you need light; you need mind. You cannot perceive the object if you leave out any one of these three. As long as the mind functions, how can you say that the universe and the âIâ do not exist?

âWhen the mind is annihilated, when it stops deliberating pro and con, then one goes into samÄdhi, one attains the Knowledge of Brahman. You know the seven notes of the scale: sÄ, re, gÄ, mÄ, pÄ, dhÄ, ni. One cannot keep oneâs voice on âniâ very long.â

Looking at the younger Naren, Sri Ramakrishna said: âWhat will you gain by merely being intuitively aware of Godâs existence? A mere vision of God is by no means everything. You have to bring Him into your room. You have to talk to Him.

âSome have heard of milk, some have seen milk, and some have drunk milk. Some have seen the king, but only one or two can bring the king home and entertain him.â

M. went to the Ganges to take his bath. It was ten oâclock. Sri Ramakrishna was still talking with the devotees. After finishing his bath, M. returned to Balaramâs house. He saluted the Master and sat down near him.

Sri Ramakrishna was filled with intense spiritual fervour. Words of wisdom flowed from him. Now and then he narrated his profound mystical experiences to the devotees.

MASTER: âI went to Benares with Mathur Babu. Our boat was passing the ManikarnikÄ GhÄt on the Ganges, when suddenly I had a vision of Åiva. He will be able to go whenever he hears the call. But one should look after oneâs mother as long as she is alive. I used to worship my mother with flowers and sandal-paste. It is the Mother of the Universe who is embodied as our earthly mother.

âAs long as you look after your own body, you must look after your mother too. Therefore I said to Hazra: âWhen you have a cold, you procure black pepper, sugar candy, and salt. As long as you feel you must look after your body, you must look after your mother too.â

âBut it is quite different when you completely forget your body. Then God Himself assumes your responsibilities. A minor cannot look after himself; therefore a guardian is appointed for him. Chaitanyadeva, like a minor, could not look after himself.â

M. went to the Ganges to bathe.

Sri Ramakrishna was talking with the devotees in the small room in Balaramâs house. Mahendra, Balaram, Tulasi, Haripada, Girish, and other devotees were sitting on the floor. M. returned from the Ganges. After saluting the Master he took a seat near him. Sri Ramakrishna was recounting to the devotees some of his spiritual experiences.

MASTER: âOne day in the KÄli temple Haladhari and NangtÄ were reading the AdhyÄtma RÄmÄyana. Suddenly I had a vision of a river with woods on both sides. The trees and plants were green. RÄma and Lakshmana were walking along wearing their shorts. One day, in front of the kuthi, I saw Arjunaâs chariot. Sri Krishna was seated in it as the charioteer. I still remember it. Another day, while listening to kirtan at KÄmÄrpukur, I saw GaurÄnga in front of me.

âAt that time a naked person, emerging from my body, used to go about with me. I used to joke with him. He looked like a boy and was a paramahamsa. I canât describe to you all the divine forms I saw at that time. I was suffering then from indigestion, which would become worse when I saw visions; so I would try to shun these divine forms and would spit on the ground when I saw them. But they would follow me and obsess me like ghosts. I was always overwhelmed with divine ecstasy and couldnât tell the passing of day and night. On the day after such a vision I would have a severe attack of diarrhoea, and all these ecstasies would pass out through my bowels.â

GIRISH (smiling): âI am examining your horoscope.â

MASTER (smiling): âI was born on the second day of the bright fortnight of the moon. My horoscope shows the positions of the sun, the moon, and Mercury at the time of my birth. There are not many more details.â

GIRISH: âYou were born under Kumbha. RÄma and Krishna were born under Karkat and Brisha, and Chaitanya under Simha.â11

MASTER: âI had two desires: first, that I should be the king of the devotees, and second, that I should not be a dry sÄdhu.â

GIRISH (smiling): âWhy did you have to practise spiritual discipline?â

MASTER (smiling): âEven the Divine Mother had to practise austere sÄdhanÄ to obtain Åiva as Her husband. She practised the panchatapÄ. She would also immerse Her body in water in wintertime, and look fixedly at the sun. Krishna Himself had to practise much sÄdhanÄ. I had many mystic experiences, but I cannot reveal their contents. Under the bel-tree I had many flaming visions. There I practised the various sÄdhanÄs prescribed in the Tantra. I needed many articlesâhuman skulls, and so forth and so on. The BrÄhmani used to collect these things for me. I practised a number of mystic postures.

âI had another strange experience: if I felt egotistic on a particular day, I would be sick the following day.â

M. sat motionless as a picture on canvas, hearing about these unique visions of the Master. The other devotees also were spellbound. There was a dead silence in the room.

TULASI (pointing to M.): âHe never laughs.â

MASTER: âBut he laughs inside. The surface of the river Phalgu is covered with sand; but if you dig into the sand, water comes up.

(To M.) âDonât you scrape your tongue? Scrape it every day.â

BALARAM: âWell, Purna has heard much about you from M.â

MASTER: âPerhaps the account of my early spiritual experiences.â

BALARAM: âIf Purna is perfect by nature, then what is M.âs function?â

MASTER: âA mere instrument.â

It was nine oâclock. Sri Ramakrishna was about to leave for Dakshineswar. Arrangements were being made for his departure. A boat had been hired at BÄghbÄzÄr. The devotees saluted the Master.

Sri Ramakrishna went to the boat with one or two devotees. GopÄl MÄ accompanied them. She intended to spend the morning at Dakshineswar and go to KÄmÄrhÄti in the afternoon. The camp cot generally used by Rakhal at Dakshineswar had been sent to Calcutta for repair. It was put in the boat, and the boat left for Dakshineswar.

According to the Hindu almanac the day was not auspicious. So Sri Ramakrishna decided to return to Balaramâs house the next Saturday and start again for Dakshineswar on an auspicious day.

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# VISIT TO NANDA BOSEâS HOUSE

Tuesday, July 28, 1885

IT WAS ABOUT THREE OâCLOCK in the afternoon. Sri Ramakrishna was sitting in Balaramâs drawing-room with the devotees. Among others, Binode, Rakhal, the younger Naren, and M. were present. The Master had come to Balaramâs house in the morning and had taken his midday meal there. At Balaramâs house the Deity was worshipped as JagannÄth, and the members of the family partook of the food offered to the Deity. Sri Ramakrishna used to say that the food at Balaramâs house was very pure.

Narayan and certain other devotees had remarked to the Master that Nanda Bose, an aristocrat of BÄghbÄzÄr, had many pictures of gods and goddesses in his house. Hence Sri Ramakrishna intended to pay a visit to Nandaâs house in the afternoon. A brÄhmin woman devoted to the Master lived near by. She often came to see him at Dakshineswar. She was extremely sorrowful over the death of her only daughter, and the Master had agreed to go to her house. She had invited him with great earnestness. From her house the Master was to go to the house of Ganuâs mother, another devotee.

The younger Naren had said to Sri Ramakrishna that he would not be able to visit him often on account of his having to prepare for his examinations.

MASTER (to the younger Naren): âI didnât send for you today.â

THE YOUNGER NAREN (smiling): âWhat can be done about it now?â

MASTER: âWell, my child, I donât want to interfere with your studies. You may visit me when you have leisure.â

The Master said these words as if he were piqued.

He was ready to go to Nanda Boseâs house. A palanquin was brought for him, and he got into it repeating the name of God. He had put on a pair of black varnished slippers and a red-bordered cloth. As Sri Ramakrishna sat down in the palanquin, M. put the slippers by his side. He accompanied the palanquin on foot. Paresh joined them.

They entered the gate of Nandaâs house, crossed the spacious square, and stopped in front of the building. The members of the family greeted the Master. He asked M. to hand him the slippers and then got out of the palanquin and entered the large hall. It was a very spacious room. Pictures of gods and goddesses were hanging on all sides.

Nanda Bose and his brother Pasupati saluted Sri Ramakrishna. The devotees of the Master also arrived. Girishâs brother Atul came, and Prasannaâs father, who was a frequent visitor at Nandaâs house, was there. Prasanna was a devotee of the Master.

The Master looked at the pictures. M. and a few other devotees stood around him. Pasupati was explaining the pictures to them.

The first picture was of Vishnu with four arms. At the very sight of it Sri Ramakrishna was overwhelmed with ecstasy; he sat down on the floor and remained a few minutes in that spiritual mood.

In the second picture RÄma was blessing HanumÄn, with His hand on the devoteeâs head. HanumÄnâs gaze was fixed on RÄmaâs Lotus Feet. The Master looked at the picture a long time and exclaimed with great fervour, âAh me! Ah me!â

The third picture was of Krishna standing with flute to His lips under the kadamba tree.

The fourth was of VÄmana, the Dwarf, who was an Incarnation of Vishnu. The Master looked intently at this picture.

Next the Master looked at a picture of Nrisimha,1 and then at one of Krishna with a herd of cows. Krishna was tending the cows with His cowherd friends on the bank of the JamunÄ at VrindÄvan. M. said, âA lovely picture!â

Sri Ramakrishna then saw pictures of DhumÄvati, ShoraÅi, BhuvaneÅvari, TÄrÄ, and KÄli. He said: âAll these portray the terrible aspects of the Divine Mother. If one keeps these pictures, one should worship them. But you must be lucky, to be able to hang them like that on the wall.â

At the sight of AnnapurnÄâs picture, Sri Ramakrishna exclaimed with great fervour, âGrand! Grand!â

The next picture was one of RÄdhikÄ as monarch. She was seated on a throne in the nikunja grove, surrounded by her woman attendants. Sri Krishna guarded the entrance of the grove as her officer.

Next was Sri Krishnaâs picture. Then came a picture of Sarasvati, the goddess of learning and music. It was in a glass case. She was in an ecstatic mood, playing melodies on the vÄ«nÄ.

After seeing the pictures, Sri Ramakrishna went to the master of the house and said: âI am very happy today. It is grand! You are a real Hindu. You have these pictures instead of English ones. I am surprised!â

Nanda Bose was seated. He said to the Master: âPlease take a seat. Why are you standing?â

Sri Ramakrishna sat down. He said: âThese are very large pictures. You are a real Hindu.â

NANDA: âI have European pictures also.â

MASTER (smiling): âThey are not like these. I am sure you donât pay much attention to them.â

A picture of Keshabâs NavavidhÄn hung on the wall. Suresh Mitra, a beloved householder disciple of the Master, had had it painted. In this picture Sri Ramakrishna was pointing out to Keshab that people of different religions proceed to the same goal by different paths.

MASTER: âThat was painted for Surendra.â

PRASANNAâS FATHER (smiling): âYou too are in that picture.â

MASTER (smiling): âYes, it contains everything. This is the ideal of modern times.â

As he spoke Sri Ramakrishna manifested great spiritual fervour. He was in an ecstatic mood, talking to the Divine Mother. A few minutes later he said, like a drunkard, âI am not unconscious.â Looking at the house, he said: âIt is a huge mansion. But what does it consist of? Bricks, timber, and clay.â

A little later he said, âI am very happy to see these pictures of gods and goddesses.â He added: âIt is not good to keep pictures of the terrible aspects of the Divine Mother. If one does, one should worship them.â

PASUPATI (smiling): âWell, things will go on as long as She keeps them going.â

MASTER: âThat is true. But one should think of God. It is not good to forget Him.â

NANDA: âBut how little we think of God!â

MASTER: âOne thinks of God through His grace.â

NANDA: âBut how can we obtain Godâs grace? Has He really the power to bestow grace?â

MASTER (smiling): âI see. You think as the intellectuals do: one reaps the results of oneâs actions. Give up these ideas. The effect of karma wears away if one takes refuge in God. I prayed to the Divine Mother with flowers in my hand: âHere, Mother, take Thy sin; here, take Thy virtue. I donât want either of these; give me only real bhakti. Here, Mother, take Thy good; here, take Thy bad. I donât want any of Thy good or bad; give me only real bhakti. Here, Mother, take Thy dharma; here, take Thy adharma. I donât want any of Thy dharma or adharma; give me only real bhakti. Here, Mother, take Thy knowledge; here, take Thy ignorance. I donât want any of Thy knowledge or ignorance; give me only real bhakti. Here, Mother, take Thy purity; here, take Thy impurity. Give me only real bhakti.â â

NANDA: âCan God violate law?â

MASTER: âWhat do you mean? He is the Lord of all. He can do everything. He who has made the law can also change it.

âBut you may very well talk that way. Perhaps you want to enjoy the world, and that is why you talk that way. There is a view that a manâs inner spirit is not awakened unless he is through with enjoyment. But what is there to enjoy? The pleasures of âwoman and goldâ? This moment they exist and the next moment they disappear. It is all momentary. And what is there in âwoman and goldâ? It is like the hog plumâall stone and skin. If one eats it, one suffers from colic. Or like a sweetmeat. Once you swallow it, it is gone.â

Nanda remained silent a few minutes. Then he said: âOh, yes. People no doubt talk that way. But is God partial? If things happen through Godâs grace, then I must say God is partial.â

MASTER: âBut God Himself has become everythingâthe universe and its living beings. You will realize it when you have Perfect Knowledge. God Himself has become the twenty-four cosmic principles: the mind, intellect, body, and so forth. Is there anyone but Himself to whom He can show partiality?â

NANDA: âWhy has He assumed all these different forms? Why are some wise and some ignorant?â

MASTER: âIt is His sweet will.â

ATUL: âKedar Babu puts it nicely. Once a man asked him, âWhy has God created the world?â He replied, âI was not present at the conference where God made the plans of His creation.â â

MASTER: âOh! It is His sweet will.â

So saying, the Master sang:

O Mother, all is done after Thine own sweet will;

Thou art in truth self-willed, Redeemer of mankind!

Thou workest Thine own work; men only call it theirs.

Thou it is that holdest the elephant in the mire;

Thou, that helpest the lame man scale the loftiest hill.

On some Thou dost bestow the bliss of Brahmanhood;

Yet others Thou dost hurl into this world below.

Thou art the Moving Force, and I the mere machine;

The house am I, and Thou the Spirit dwelling there;

I am the chariot, and Thou the Charioteer:

I move alone as Thou, O Mother, movest me.

He continued: âThe Divine Mother is full of bliss. Creation, preservation, and destruction are the waves of Her sportive pleasure. Innumerable are the living beings. Only one or two among them obtain liberation. And that makes Her happy.

Out of a hundred thousand kites, at best but one or two break free;

And Thou dost laugh and clap Thy hands, O Mother, watching them!

Some are being entangled in the world and some are being liberated from it.

How many are the boats, O mind,

That float on the ocean of this world!

How many are those that sink!â

NANDA: âIt may be Her sweet will; but it is death to us.â

MASTER: âBut who are you? It is the Divine Mother who has become all this. It is only as long as you do not know Her that you say, âIâ, âIâ.

âAll will surely realize God. All will be liberated. It may be that some get their meal in the morning, some at noon, and some in the evening; but none will go without food. All, without any exception, will certainly know their real Self.â

PASUPATI: âTrue, sir. It seems that it is God alone who has become everything.â

MASTER: âTry to find out what this âIâ is. Is this âIâ the bones or flesh or blood or intestines? Seeking the âIâ, you discover âThouâ. In other words, nothing exists inside you but the power of God. There is no âIâ, but only âHeâ. (To Pasupati) You have so much wealth, but you have no egotism. It is not possible to rid oneself altogether of the ego; so, as long as it is there, let the rascal remain as the servant of God. (All laugh.) The ego that makes a man feel he is a devotee of God or a son of God or a servant of God is good. But the ego that makes a man attached to âwoman and goldâ is the âunripe egoâ. That ego is to be renounced.â

The head of the household and the others were very much pleased to hear this interpretation of the ego.

MASTER (to Pasupati): âThere are two signs of knowledge: first, absence of pride, and second, a peaceful nature. You have both. Therefore you must have received the grace of God.

âToo much wealth makes one forget God. That is the very nature of wealth. Jadu Mallick has become very rich. Nowadays he doesnât talk of God. Formerly he used to enjoy spiritual talk a great deal.

â âWoman and goldâ is a kind of wine. If a man drinks too much wine, he does not show his father and uncle the respect that is due to them. Very often he abuses them. A drunkard cannot distinguish between his superior and his inferior.â

NANDA: âThat is true, sir.â

PASUPATI: âSir, what do you think of Theosophy and Spiritualism? Are these true? What do you think of the solar plane, the lunar plane, the stellar plane?â

MASTER: âMy dear sir, I donât know about these things. Why bother about them so much? You have come to the orchard to eat mangoes. Enjoy them. What is the use of your calculating how many mango-trees there are, how many millions of branches, how many billions of leaves? I have come to the orchard to eat mangoes. Let me enjoy them.

âOnce a manâs inner spirit is awakened, once he succeeds in knowing God, he doesnât feel the desire even to know about all this rubbish. How incoherently a delirious patient talks: âI shall eat five seers of rice! I shall drink a whole tank of water!â âWill you?â says the physician. âAll right! You will have them.â Saying this, the physician goes on with his smoke. But he pays attention to what the patient says when the patient is no longer delirious.â

PASUPATI: âWill our delirium last for ever?â

MASTER: âWhy should you think so? Fix your mind on God, and spiritual consciousness will be awakened in you.â

PASUPATI (smiling): âOur union with God is only momentary. It doesnât last any longer than a pipeful of tobacco.â (All laugh.)

MASTER: âWhat if that is so? Union with God even for one moment surely gives a man liberation.

âAhalyÄ said to RÄma, âO RÄma, it doesnât matter if I am born as a pig or any other being; only bless me that my mind may dwell on Thy Lotus Feet and be filled with real devotion to Thee.â

âNÄrada said to RÄma: âO RÄma, I want from Thee no other favour. Please give me real love for Thee; and please bless me, that I may not come under the spell of Thy world-bewitching mÄyÄ.â

âWhen a man sincerely prays to God, he is able to fix his mind on God and develop real love for His Lotus Feet.

âGive up all such notions as: âShall we be cured of our delirium?â, âWhat will happen to us?â, âWe are sinners!â (To Nanda) One must have this kind of faith: âWhat? Once I have uttered the name of RÄma, can I be a sinner any more?â â

NANDA: âIs there no after-life? What about punishment for our sins?â

MASTER: âWhy not enjoy your mangoes? What need have you to calculate about the after-life and what happens then, and things like that? Eat your mangoes. You need mangoes. You need devotion to Godââ

NANDA: âBut where is the mango-tree? Where do I get mangoes?â

MASTER: âTree? God is the eternal and infinite Brahman. He does exist; there is no doubt about it. He is eternal. But you must remember this, that He is the Kalpataru.

Come, let us go for a walk, O mind, to KÄli, the Wish-fulfilling Tree,

And there beneath It gather the four fruits of life.

âYou must go to the Kalpataru and pray. Only then will you obtain the fruits. Only then will the fruits fall from the tree. Only then will you be able to gather them. There are four fruits: dharma, artha, kÄma, and moksha. The jnÄnis seek the fruit of liberation; and the bhaktas, love of God, love without any motive behind it. âYou ask about the after-life. According to the GÄ«tÄ you will become in the next life what you think of in the hour of death. King Bharata was very much grieved over his pet deer; he died repeating the word âdeerâ; therefore he was reborn as a deer. That is why day and night a man should practise worship, japa, meditation, and other spiritual exercises. Only then, by virtue of practice, will he be able to think of God in the hour of death. If one dies thus, thinking of God, one will acquire Godâs nature.

âKeshab Sen, too, asked me about the after-life. I said to him also, âWhat need have you of all these calculations?â Then I said: âAs long as a man does not realize God, he will return to the world. The potter puts his clay jars and lids out in the sun to bake. If cattle trample them underfoot, he throws away the baked ones. But he collects the soft ones, mixes them with more clay, puts them on the wheel, and makes new vessels from them.â â

The master of the house had not yet shown any sign of serving Sri Ramakrishna with refreshments. Sri Ramakrishna himself said to Nanda: âYou see, you should offer me something to eat. That is why the other day I said to Jaduâs mother: âLook here. Give me something to eat.â Otherwise it brings harm to the householder.â

Nanda Bose ordered some sweets. Sri Ramakrishna began to eat them. Nanda and the others were watching the Master and his actions. After eating the sweets, Sri Ramakrishna wanted to wash his hands. The plate on which the sweets were served had been placed on the sheet covering the carpet; so the Master could not wash his hands in the plate. A servant brought a brass bowl for him to use. But Sri Ramakrishna would not use it, since only rÄjasic people used such things. He asked the servant to take it away. The master of the house said to him, âPlease wash your hands.â Absent-mindedly Sri Ramakrishna said: âWhat? Shall I wash my hands?â

The Master walked to the south verandah. He asked M. to pour water into his hands. M. poured water from a jug. The Master dried his hands with his cloth and returned to the room. Then he was offered betel-leaf on a tray. But the other guests had already taken some from the same tray; the Master did not accept any.

NANDA (to the Master): âMay I say something?â

MASTER (smiling): âWhat?â

NANDA: âWhy didnât you eat any betel-leaf? Everything else you did was proper; this alone seems to be otherwise.â

NANDA: âBut the betel-leaf would have gone to God all the same.â

Sri Ramakrishna was warning Nanda of flatterers.

MASTER: âBeware of flatterers. They are after their own selfish purpose. (To Prasannaâs father) Do you live in this house?â

PRASANNAâS FATHER: âNo, sir, I am a neighbour. Wonât you have a smoke?â

MASTER (very humbly): âNo, please enjoy yourself. I donât feel like smoking now.â

Nandaâs house was like a palace. Sri Ramakrishna said to him: âJadu hasnât such a big house. I told him so the other day.â

NANDA: âHe has built a new house at JorÄshÄnko.â

Sri Ramakrishna was encouraging Nanda.

MASTER (to Nanda): âThough you are a householder, still you have kept your mind on God. Is that a small thing? The man who has renounced the world will pray to Him as a matter of course. Is there any credit in that? But blessed indeed is he who, while leading a householderâs life, prays to God. He is like a man who finds an object after removing a stone weighing twenty maunds.

âOne should pray to God, establishing with Him an appropriate relationship. HanumÄnâs love for God was mixed with knowledge; but NÄradaâs love for God was pure and unadulterated.

âRÄma asked HanumÄn, âHanumÄn, what attitude do you cherish toward Me when you worship Me?â HanumÄn answered: âSometimes I see that You are the whole and I am a part; sometimes I see that You are the Master and I am Your servant. âRÄma said to NÄrada, âAsk a favour of Me.â NÄrada said, âO RÄma, grant me the boon that I may have genuine love for Thy Lotus Feet and that I may not come under the spell of Thy world-bewitching mÄyÄ!â â

Sri Ramakrishna was about to take his leave.

MASTER (to Nanda): âAccording to the GÄ«tÄ a man who is honoured and respected by many people possesses a special power of God. You have divine power.â

NANDA: âAll men have the same power.â

MASTER (sharply): âYou all say the same thing. Can all men ever possess power to the same degree? God no doubt dwells in all beings as the all-pervading Spirit, but the manifestations of His Power are different in different beings.

âVidyÄsÄgar, too, said the same thing. He said, âHas God given some more power and some less?â Thereupon I said to him: âIf there are not different manifestations of His Power, then why have we come to see you? Have you grown two horns on your head?â â

Sri Ramakrishna rose. The devotees followed him. Pasupati accompanied them to the door.

The Master arrived at the house of the brÄhmin lady who was grief-stricken on account of her daughterâs death. It was an old brick house. Entering the house, the Master passed the cow-shed on his left. He and the devotees went to the roof, where they took seats. People were standing there in rows. Others were seated. They were all eager to get a glimpse of Sri Ramakrishna.

The brÄhmani had a sister; both of them were widows. Their brothers also lived in the house with their families. The brÄhmani had been busy all day making arrangements to receive Sri Ramakrishna. While the Master was at Nanda Boseâs house she had been extremely restless, going out of the house every few minutes to see if he was coming. He had promised to come to her place from Nandaâs. Because of his delay she had thought perhaps he would not come at all.

Sri Ramakrishna was seated on a carpet. M., Narayan, Jogin, Devendra, and others were seated on a mat. A few minutes later the younger Naren and some other devotees arrived. The brÄhmaniâs sister came to the Master and saluted him. She said, âSister has just gone to Nanda Boseâs house to inquire the reason for your delay in coming here. She will return presently.â

A sound was heard downstairs and she exclaimed, âThere she comes!â She went down. But it was not the brÄhmani.

Sri Ramakrishna sat there smiling, surrounded by devotees.

M. (to Devendra): âWhat a grand sight! All these peopleâyoung and old, men and womenâstanding in lines, eager to have a glimpse of him and hear his words.â

Sri Ramakrishna laughed.

The brÄhmaniâs sister exclaimed, âHere comes sister!â

The brÄhmani came and saluted the Master. She was beside herself with joy. She did not know what to say. In a half-choked voice she said: âThis joy is too much for me. Perhaps I shall die of it. Tell me, friends, how shall I be able to live? If he visited a place, I should go there, look at him from a distance, and then come away.

âLet me go and tell everybody how happy I am. Let me go and tell Yogin of my good luck.â

Still overwhelmed with joy she said: âA labourer won a hundred thousand rupees in a lottery. The moment he heard the news he died of joy. Yes, he really and truly died. I am afraid the same thing is going to happen to me. Please bless me, friends, or else I shall certainly die.â

M. was amazed to see the brÄhmaniâs sincere joy and her ecstatic mood. He was about to take the dust of her feet. âWhat are you doing?â she exclaimed and saluted M.

The brÄhmani was extremely happy at the sight of the devotees. She said: âI am so happy to see you all here. I have brought the younger Naren; without him, who would there be to make us laugh?â

She was talking like this when her sister came up and said: âCome down, sister! How can I manage things if you stay here? Can I do it all by myself?â

But the brÄhmani was overwhelmed with joy. She could not take her eyes from the Master and the devotees.

After a while she very respectfully took Sri Ramakrishna to another room and offered him sweets and other refreshments. The devotees were entertained on the roof.

It was about eight oâclock in the evening. Sri Ramakrishna was ready to leave. When he came to the door, the brÄhmani asked her sister-in-law to salute the Master. Next, one of her brothers took the dust of the Masterâs feet. Referring to him, she said: âHe is one of my brothers. He is a fool.â âNo, no!â said the Master. âThey are all good.â

A man showed the way with a light. At places it was dark. Sri Ramakrishna stood in front of the cow-shed. The devotees gathered around him. M. saluted the Master, who was about to go to the house of Ganuâs mother.

Sri Ramakrishna was seated in the drawing-room of Ganuâs motherâs house. It was on the street floor. The room was used by a concert party. Several young men played on their instruments now and then for the pleasure of the Master.

It was eight-thirty in the evening. Moonlight flooded the streets, the houses, and the sky. It was the first day after the full moon.

The brÄhmani, who had also come, was visiting the drawing-room and the inner apartments alternately. Every few minutes she would come to the door of the drawing-room and look at the Master. Some youngsters from the neighbourhood also looked at him through the windows. The people of the locality, young and old, came thronging to see the saint.

The younger Naren saw the boys in the street climbing the windows. He said to them: âWhy are you here? Get away! Go home!â The Master said tenderly, âLet them stay.â Every now and then he chanted: âHari Om! Hari Om!â

The floor of the drawing-room was covered with a carpet. The young musicians sat on it and sang:

O KeÅava, bestow Thy grace

To roam VrindÄvanâs glades and groves! â¦

MASTER: âAh, how sweet the music is! How melodious the violin is! How good the accompaniments are! (Pointing to a boy) He and the flutist seem to be a nice pair.â

The orchestra went on playing. After it was over, Sri Ramakrishna said joyfully, âIt is very fine indeed.â Pointing to a young man, he said, âHe seems to know how to play every instrument.â He said to M., âThey are all good people.â

After the concert the young musician said to the devotees, âWe should like to hear some of you sing.â The brÄhmani stood near the door. She said: âNone of them knows how to sing. Perhaps Mohin Babu can sing. But he will not sing before the Master.â

All laughed. A few minutes later the brÄhmani said to Sri Ramakrishna, âPlease come inside.â

MASTER: âWhy?â

Sri Ramakrishna went inside accompanied by the brÄhmani and the young men of the family. The devotees were strolling outside in the moonlight. M. and Binode were pacing the street south of the house and recalling the various incidents in the life of their beloved Master.

MASTER (referring to the brÄhmani and her relatives): âAh! How happy they were!â

The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna

# THE MASTER ON HIMSELF AND HIS EXPERIENCES

August 9, 1885

SRI RAMAKRISHNA was sitting in his room at Dakshineswar. Rakhal, M., Dwija and his father, and other devotees were present. It was about four oâclock in the afternoon.

After returning from VrindÄvan Rakhal had spent a few days at home. Now he was staying with the Master. Latu, Harish, and Ramlal were also staying at the temple garden.

Sri Ramakrishna was not well. It was the beginning of the illness subsequently diagnosed as the fatal cancer. But this did not disturb the serenity of his mind. Day and night he had only one thought, and that was the spiritual welfare of his disciples. He was guiding them toward the attainment of God. He encouraged them constantly to cultivate knowledge and devotion and warned them of the snares of âwoman and goldâ. He was completely indifferent to his own illness and devoted himself whole-heartedly to the fulfilment of his earthly mission.

Dwija was about sixteen years old. After the death of his mother, his father had married a second time. Dwija often accompanied M. to Dakshineswar; but his father did not approve of it.

Dwijaâs father had for a long time been speaking of visiting Sri Ramakrishna. Today he had come to Dakshineswar. He was the manager of a business firm in Calcutta and had passed his examination in law.

MASTER (to Dwijaâs father): âPlease donât mind your childrenâs coming here.

âI ask people to live in the world after the awakening of their spiritual consciousness. After extracting gold through hard labour, a man may keep it under earth or in a box or under water. The gold is not affected.

âI ask people to live in the world in a spirit of detachment. If you break the jack-fruit after rubbing oil on your hands, its sticky juice will not smear them.

âIf the âunripeâ mind dwells in the world, the mind gets soiled. One should first attain knowledge and then live in the world.

DWIJAâS FATHER: âThat is true, sir.â

MASTER (smiling): âI know why you scold your children. You only threaten them. The brahmachÄri said to the snake: âYou are a fool indeed! I forbade you to bite but not to hiss. Your enemies would not have beaten you, if only you had hissed at them.â Your scolding of the children is really a hissing. (Dwijaâs father smiles.)

âA good son is an indication of his fatherâs spiritual nature. If good water comes out when a reservoir is dug, it only indicates the virtue of the owner.

âA son is called Ätmaja, âthe self rebornâ. There is no difference between you and your son. In one way you yourself are reborn as your son. In one sense you are a worldly person, working in a business office and enjoying worldly life; in another sense you are a devotee of God, in the form of your son. I heard that you were a very worldly person; but now I find it isnât so. (Smiling) You know all this. I understand that you are very circumspect. Perhaps that is why you are nodding your assent to what I am saying. (Dwijaâs father smiles.)

âIf your children visit this place, they will be able to know what you really are. How precious oneâs father is! If a person deceives his father and mother in order to seek religion, he gets only worthless trash.

âA man is born with several debts: debts to his father, the devas, and the rishis. Besides, there is his debt to his mother. He also has a debt to his wife. She must be supported. If the wife is chaste, the husband must provide for her after his death.

âI could not live at VrindÄvan on account of my mother. When I remembered that my mother was living in the temple garden here at Dakshineswar, I could not feel peaceful at VrindÄvan.

âI ask people to live in the world and at the same time fix their minds on God. I donât ask them to give up the world. I say, âFulfil your worldly duties and also think of God.â â

DWIJAâS FATHER: âI tell my children that they should attend to their studies. I donât forbid them to come to you, but I donât want them to waste time in frivolities with the youngsters.â

MASTER (referring to Dwija): âThis boy must have been born with some good tendencies. Why are the two other brothers different from him? Why is he alone spiritually minded? Will you be able to compel him not to visit this place? Sooner or later everyone unfolds his inborn tendencies.â

DWIJAâS FATHER: âYes, that is true.â

Sri Ramakrishna came down from the couch and sat on the floor beside Dwijaâs father. While talking with him he touched him now and then.

It was nearly evening. Sri Ramakrishna asked M. and the others to show Dwijaâs father the temples. He said to them, âI should have accompanied him myself if I were well.â He asked someone to give sweets to the young men and said to Dwijaâs father: âLet the children have a little refreshment. It is customary.â Dwijaâs father visited the temples and the images and took a stroll in the garden.

Sri Ramakrishna engaged happily in conversation with Bhupen, Dwija, M., and others on the southeast porch of his room. He playfully slapped Bhupen and M. on the back. He said to Dwija with a laugh, âHow I talked to your father!â

Dwijaâs father returned to Sri Ramakrishnaâs room after dusk. He intended to leave shortly. He was feeling hot. Sri Ramakrishna fanned him himself. In a few minutes the father took leave of the Master. Sri Ramakrishna stood up to bid him farewell.

It was eight oâclock. Sri Ramakrishna was talking to Mahimacharan. Rakhal, M., and one or two companions of Mahimacharan were in the room. Mahimacharan was going to spend the night at the temple garden.

MASTER (to Mahima): âWell, how do you find Kedar? Has he only seen milk, or has he drunk it too?â

MASTER: âNityagopal?â

MAHIMA: âHe too has developed nicely. But he belongs to another class.â
